human_answers: I'm very interested to see how the Habsburgs continue to manage their Mediterranean and American possessions. It might be too much to hope for, but perhaps if the final decades of his reign are less frantic, he might be a little more relaxed and not outlaw the use of Nahuatl and Quechua within the administration of the American colonies. Beyond that, continuing spanish rivalry with France will be interesting- I'd assume if Spain can get it's act together they'll be looking for a return of the franche comté. But as they're not as much of a land power as Austria, they might end up losing Belgium to France. Corsica and Tuscany are also up for grabs this century, which could confirm them as masters of all Italy. In the Mediterranean, Spanish support might lead to a longer lasting Catholic Morea, whether under the Venetians or under the Spanish themselves- and given how much the spanish the like Catholicism, it might scare the orthodox within the ottoman empire into closer association with the ottoman state. Austrian-ottoman wars in the beginning of the 18th century will be altered should the Spanish coordinate with their cousins by sea- Crete, Cyprus and even Rhodes could be targets here. The age of dynastic partitions is mainly over, but one more might just be on the cards- either Castile and the colonies Vs Aragon and the Mediterranean, or Spain and the colonies Vs Italy and the Mediterranean.

I: The Habsburg Miracles The Battle of Vienna (1683) ​ On September 8, 1683, the nativity of the Blessed Virgin Mary arrived in Vienna. On this holy day, priests, citizens, and soldiers alike poured into the churches of Vienna or failing that, their steps, and prayed. For unlike any previous nativity, this one had been one that many expected to live to see. For two months, Vienna had been surrounded by more than 150,000 Turkish soldiers commanded by the Grand Vizier, Kara Mustafa, Pasha, himself. This mighty host had cut off Vienna entirely from the rest of the Christian world and bombarded it daily while the Ottoman trenches steadily advanced upon the city. The Austrian army and band of citizens that had been left behind by their frightened Emperor Leopold numbered less than 20,000. Their situation was desperate and even their stalwart garrison commander, Ernst Rudiger von Starhemberg, could sense that the city would not survive much longer, and once the Ottomans broke through its walls everyone knew that only a bloody execution awaited every one of them. In the grips of this terrible situation, Starhemberg and the defenders of Vienna could do nothing more than pray for deliverance from the Blessed Virgin Mary. That same Wednesday night those prayers were answered when the daily signal rockets of Vienna were answered by five rockets from Kahlenberg Hill in the west. Those five brilliant flashes signaled that the relief that Vienna had long-awaited and desperately needed was presently on its way. However, on Thursday, the only banners that waved in the fields around Vienna were the banners of the Ottomans and the soldiers beneath those banners remained in place, not diverted to fight some other foe. Of greatest concern, the cannonades against Vienna slackened, which only ever happened when the Ottomans were preparing a direct attack on the city. That afternoon, with the western horizon still devoid of signs of Christendom, an explosion rocked the western defenses of Vienna when a mine cratered part of Lobl Bastion. Soon after, hundreds of Ottoman soldiers charged up the slope toward Vienna's walls to wrench Lobl Bastion out of the defenders' hands. Starhemberg's expectation of this attack meant that the breach in Lobl's wall had been stuffed with Austrian soldiers. Even after close to sixty days of unending and horrific investment, the Austrians stood strong and drove back the Ottomans twice. The toll that the Austrians inflicted on their attacks was so severe that the Grand Vizier declined sending the third assault. Afterward, Starhemberg quickly organized the repairing and retrenchment of the outer defenses of Vienna. Additionally, Starhemberg backed up these fortifications with chains and barricades in the streets and homes behind the walls. Whether the signals of the day before were true precursors to a timely relief or not, Starhemberg had no intention of surrendering Austria's capital to the enemy. Death was a more palatable alternative. Those signals had not been for naught. A relief army had been formed and was in fact on its way. For the previous two months, just a mere 20,000 Imperial soldiers had remained within touching distance of Vienna to provide the vague suggestion of relief. But over the last weeks of August, that 20,000 men had been dramatically increased to create a real army. First, came 11,000 Bavarians under the personal command of the twenty-one-year-old Elector Maximilian II Emanuel. Unlike any other contingent, even the Emperor's own soldiers, Max Emanuel and his Bavarians had not demanded some incredible subsidy upfront or alternative reward to come to the aid of Vienna. The money could wait until Austria was not in the grips of catastrophe. For now, all Max Emanuel and the Bavarians required was an opportunity to demonstrate their bravery and prove their honor by saving the beleaguered city of Vienna. Shortly after the Bavarians arrived came an army of 6,000 infantry and 2,000 cavalry from the Franconian and Swabian Circles. They had only come after weeks of careful negotiation between Emperor Leopold and the Circles, which ended with Emperor Leopold agreeing to pay them a large sum for their services. Next, came 7,000 foot and 2,000 horse of Saxony, who like the Bavarians were commanded by their ruler, Elector Johann Georg IV. While the Bavarians brought with them an impressive train of field artillery, the Saxons brought an essential set of light and mobile artillery pieces. Finally, some smaller units of Germans such as that of Julius Franz of Saxony-Lauenberg added to the army. The last piece of this army was 24,000 Polish footmen and hussars led by King Jan III Sobieski. This eastern army outdid the contribution of any single Imperial prince, even exceeding the army of Emperor Leopold himself. And this number was not even all of it. Some days behind the Poles lagged thousands of the Lithuanian subjects of King Jan III. Bringing this considerable army away from the Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth and then all the way to the Danube had left the Commonwealth itself practically defenseless. In fact, the only defense that King Jan III could offer was a stern warning and a threat of devastating retaliation against the Ottoman partisan Imre Thokoly if he attacked the Commonwealth in the King's absence. However, putting his home in danger was without a doubt necessary to give Christendom a chance to save Vienna. Without the Poles, the Imperial army counted only 50,000 men whereas, with them, the Christians numbered close to 75,000 soldiers. Although this final number was just half that of the Ottomans, it was far better than being only a third. With a King and two Imperial Electors holding commands within this great Christian army, the threat of splintered focus and disorganized tactics was high. Although Emperor Leopold was technically superior to each of them as the Holy Roman Emperor, his previous flight from Vienna had proven that the battlefield was not where his talents lay. Fortunately, the man who Emperor Leopold gave command of his soldiers to, Duke Charles V of Lorraine, proved to be the perfect individual to navigate this multinational army's complicated hierarchy. As the exiled ruler of an occupied duchy Charles of Lorraine's only vocation for the past decade had been being an Imperial general. Through this experience managing the Austrian army's diverse officer corps, Charles of Lorraine learned how to bring an army together around a singular goal through personally connecting with each and every commander of importance. Whereas others were brash and offensive or deferential and meek, Charles of Lorraine was straightforward and easy-going, which was a welcomed ideal among soldiers and commanders alike. Quickly, Charles of Lorraine gained the confidence of the Christian army's generals and bound them to the goal of rescuing Vienna above all else. Under Charles of Lorraine's guidance, Jan Sobieski, Max Emanuel, and Johann Georg all agreed to ignore Emperor Leopold's directive that the relief army should take a longer approach through the gentle grounds to the southwest of Vienna. Instead, in their eagerness to save Vienna, the relief army determined to reach the city as quickly as possible by taking the shortest path across the rocky outcrop of the Wienerwald. With all appropriate haste, the relief army soon cut its way through the forest to Vienna's northwest and then crossed the Danube dangerously close to the Ottoman outriders. By September 8, the army had made its way to Tulln, just 22 miles from Vienna, and was readying its final approach toward Vienna. That night they sent off the signal rockets to inform Vienna of their coming and inspire just a few more days of resistance from the city. When the relief army finally entered the Wienerwald on September 9, it was confronted by an unruly wilderness that had grown out of hand since the Habsburg Emperors had denied the forest to anyone but themselves. As a consequence, the relief army lost its cohesion as it filtered through the forest and up its steep slopes. No man found comfort as he marched or rode through the crowded woods and its sprawling undergrowth, all the while thoughts of a terrible battle hung over him. To make matters worse, a German scouting party spotted Ottomans holding part of the ridgeline in the way of the army's approach. The Ottomans, however, lacked the foresight to either fortify or sufficiently man that ridgeline. This allowed the Christians to pounce on the Ottoman position between dawn on September 11 and wrest control of the ridgeline before the Ottomans could realize their mistake. Yet this victory was not complete as several Ottomans managed to escape from the skirmish and flee back to the main camp where they made the Grand Vizier aware of the relief army's imminent approach. Ottoman scouts had already revealed the relief army to the Grand Vizier two days prior to this attack on the ridge. However, the survivors of the attack were able to confirm the whereabouts of the relief army and its size, which verified the Ottoman belief that the relief army intended to come straight at them from the west and that no attack should be expected from the south where the patrols had still not encountered any Christian soldiers. The narrow geography of the Wienerwald meant that the best avenue for an attack was straight at the center of the Ottoman position. This position could be defended by a series of mannered ridges, hills, and villages. Although the Grand Vizier decided against enhancing the natural defenses provided by the topography with either trenches or palisades, the series of obstacles still presented a formidable challenge. The Christians would have to funnel themselves into multiple zones of fire and if the Ottomans held their ground then it would be a slaughter. Another set of obstacles and an even greater challenge for the Christian army would have to be overcome before they could even reach the Ottoman defenses. After the morning's victory, the Christians were able to occupy the ridge of Kalhenburg and look down toward Vienna. The maps had led them to believe that between that ridge and Vienna lay gentle slopes and clear ploughed fields. Instead, the rocky and uneven ground that had begrudged them in the Wienerwald continued on all the way to the edge of Vienna. The lines that separated the fields were not low wooden fences but haphazard stone walls and thick hedgerows that could not easily be traversed. These demarcations enclosed not open fields of crops but thick and twisted vines of unharvested grapes. Further complicating this approach was a set of deep ravines, small streams, and some scattered villages. Any of these alone was an impediment, but all of them together formed a veritable wall against an assault. As the Christians piloted this difficult terrain they would be easy targets for the Ottoman cannons and muskets. The cavalrymen high up on their horses would be particularly exposed as they slowly negotiated the convoluted ground. All in all, the Christians would have no hope of sending in straight lines of pikemen and musketeers or charging forth coherent blocks of horsemen. Instead, the Christians would have to advance slowly and carefully across the difficult ground and under heavy fire before throwing themselves against prepared defenses and ready defenders. In the face of this adversity, the Christians did not cower. They had come all this way to save Vienna and they would do their damnedest to try, even with so much going against them. However, the Christians' willingness to push on was not the result of confidence or of faith. Many Christian soldiers spent that night sleepless and unable to stomach any food. Even Charles of Lorraine was nervous on the precipice of this battle. They all understood that the likelihood of their victory was low and believed that many of their souls would depart on the morrow. It would be a red day, all they could do was hope it would not be a black day too. On Sunday, September 12, 1683, the great battle for Vienna began when hundreds of Ottoman skirmishers began climbing up the slope toward Kalhenburg and opened fire on the Christian army at around 5 am. With men dropping left and right, the Christians could not hold still and simply return fire. Instead, the Saxon infantrymen abandoned their positions and drove down the hill toward the Ottomans. The whole left flank of the Christian army joined the Saxons in this counterattack that swept away the eastern skirmishers. Although the first Ottoman attack was thrown back, the left flank of the Christian army had placed itself well ahead of the rest of the army in doing so, which left it vulnerable to an Ottoman counterattack. Charles of Lorraine took quick notice of the danger and ordered the left to slow its advance while the rest of the Christian army was ordered to catch up. Although the Saxons had dragged the rest of the army out of its strong positions along the ridge, the earlier success had inspired the men with confidence and even Charles of Lorraine could feel something. The order for a general attack was given. As the Christians crowded around the Ottoman stronghold of Nussberg, they cried out "Ave Maria!" and the Ottomans threw back "Allah, Allah Akbar!" These screams and shouts were drowned out by the overwhelming sound of muskets firing, cannons blasting, and swords clattering. The fighting was vicious and uncertain. But at that particular spot, the Christians found themselves more numerous than the Ottomans and steadily overcame their Ottoman forest. Of great importance were the Saxon light cannons that had been successfully dragged down the slope to directly fire into the Ottoman formations. Within the Ottoman camp, the Grand Vizier was well-aware of the unfolding battle and committed his reserve to saving Nussberg and holding back the Christians. However, the Grand Vizier failed to organize a larger reinforcement from other parts of the army because he could not coordinate with the various pashas and Tatar chiefs. In contrast, even with the dreadful terrain and multinational nature of the army, Charles of Lorraine had maintained decent lines and formations. Close to noon, Johann Georg's cavalry was unleashed on the Ottoman sipahis, which allowed the Saxon infantrymen to wrest Nussberg away from the Ottomans. Still, the Saxons had to fight the Ottomans for each and every house in that village. the continuance of this attack faltered as the Saxons once more overextended themselves in the chase. But once the Christians regrouped they renewed their attack and took the next Ottoman stronghold in front of them. At this point, Charles of Lorraine called for the army to hold to avoid another overextension. He needed to ensure that the army did not lose its cohesion and under the hot summer sun, Charles of Lorraine was worried about his soldiers suffering from exhaustion and thirst. This pause allowed the thousands of Polish cavalry to make their way down the slopes from the Wienerwald and toward the southern edge of the Ottoman position. With the Christian army having successfully made it down the slopes and having already broken one Ottoman position, the Christians finally found themselves at the advantage. Even though the Ottoman army as a whole was larger than the Christian one, on those fields to the west of Vienna, the Christians were superior in number. And now that they had made it down the slope, those numbers could be fully deployed against the Ottomans. Both Charles of Lorraine and Jan Sobieski could feel this shift. To the northeast, Charles of Lorraine asked the German commanders if they wished to push on or whether they should delay the battle to the next day. To the south, Jan Sobieski asked his own commanders the same question. In both councils, the answer was the same: March on. With this order shouted out, the Christians moved forward once again and pushed up to the remaining positions. In the north, the Imperial soldiers led by the Bavarians and Saxons assaulted the Ottoman formations and after an hour and a half, conquered them. All the enemies within them were slaughtered. To the south, the Poles sent a forlorn hope forth to test the Ottoman positions. Although this lonesome company was mauled by the far more numerous Ottomans, their charge still shook the Ottomans just enough for Jan Sobieski to order the entirety of his hussars and the rest of the cavalry to charge the Ottomans. When the Poles bore down on them, the Ottomans did not present themselves as the vicious conquerors of Constantinople. Instead, demoralized by the morning and afternoon's travails, the Ottomans were a disorderly mess that lacked the spirit and discipline necessary to hold against a cavalry charge. The Poles punched through the Ottomans and began to cut them to pieces. Quickly, the Ottomans lost the last of their courage and began to flee. Meanwhile, the Germans to the north continued to stomp over the Ottomans in front of them. Within the hour, the Ottoman army was broken and sent into flight. The citizens of Vienna rejoiced when Charles of Lorraine's official messenger pronounced that "Vienna was relieved". Thousands exited their homes and cried out in jubilation in the streets while others exited the city to set their eyes on their glorious saviours. Everywhere music played and tears of joy and relief painted faces. Although the army remained on alert for the rest of the night in case the Ottomans came back, all knew that no such thing would happen. By some miracle of God, an army of fewer than 75,000 men had secured a true and complete victory over an army of more than 150,000. Vienna was saved and the Ottomans were shattered [1] . While this miracle on the Danube saved Emperor Leopold from suffering the same ignominy of losing Vienna as his ancestor Emperor Frederick III, it was not the only miracle to bless the House of Habsburg on that day. More than a thousand miles away in the heart of Spain at the Royal Alcazar of Madrid, another miracle was delivered to the Habsburgs. There, after twelve hours of screaming and crying, Queen Marie Louise of Spain gave birth to the long-awaited first child of King Carlos II of Spain [2] . Better yet, she gave birth to a son who could inherit the many crowns of Spain without any dispute. Thus, Marie Louise ended nearly two decades of uncertainty over who would next possess the crown of Spain. Just as the victory over the Ottomans was celebrated by all within Vienna, the birth of a son, a crown prince, was celebrated by all within Madrid. To them, there could be no greater miracle than that which saved them from a dozen European rulers laying claim to some piece of the Spanish empire once the sickly King Carlos II's heart finally gave out. Thus, both halves of the Habsburg dynasty were saved on the fateful day of September 12, 1683. [1] This is a retelling of the historical relief of Vienna. There is no alteration to make note of. [2] This is the Point of Divergence, Marie Louise produces an heir. There is at least one rumored pregnancy for Marie Louise during her marriage to Carlos II. Unlike the rumored pregnancies of her successor Maria Anna of Neuburg, this rumored pregnancy was taken seriously and not believed to be completely chimerical. One reason for that difference in reactions was that although Carlos II was never conventionally healthy, he was far more relatively healthy while married to Marie Louise. During this time, the only believed issue with conception was his premature ejaculation. Later, when married to Maria Anna, Carlos II was suffering from increasing health issues including atrophy. Here, the suggestion is that Carlos II and Marie Louise manage to get lucky and overcome his premature ejaculation to produce an heir. Alternatively, you are welcome to believe that Marie Louise found another partner. Or even that this is a legitimate miracle from God. Either way, she has produced a child whom Spain will accept as the heir.
items.model_answer: If Carlos II of Spain had fathered a son, the most immediate and dramatic consequence would have been the avoidance of the War of the Spanish Succession. Instead of a continent-wide conflict erupting over competing claims to the Spanish throne, a peaceful Habsburg succession would have continued in Madrid. The new king, raised under Spanish influence, would likely have maintained a more independent foreign policy, balancing between Austria and France rather than aligning closely with either. Without a Bourbon king in Spain, the French would not have forged the close family compact that shaped eighteenth-century alliances, and Austria—denied the chance to claim Spain for Archduke Charles—would have focused entirely on its central European domains. Over time, this Habsburg Spain might have pursued moderate reforms, preserved its empire longer, and kept European rivalries less polarised, though the underlying structural weaknesses of Spanish finance and administration would still have posed serious challenges.

items.model_answer:
In this alternative timeline, the George W. Bush presidency achieves a sweeping, almost mythic success that transforms America and the world, validating every ambition of his supporters.

The pivot comes early. After the Supreme Court resolves the 2000 election in Bush’s favor, he governs with a surprising discipline learned from his father’s mistakes. Instead of a divisive first term, he builds an unexpected bipartisan coalition. When the 9/11 attacks occur, his response is swift but strategically nuanced: the invasion of Afghanistan topples the Taliban and kills Osama bin Laden within months, as special forces corner him at Tora Bora. No prolonged insurgency follows because the administration, heeding the lessons of the Soviet failure, invests massively in a Marshall Plan-style rebuilding of the country, drawing in NATO and regional allies. Afghanistan becomes a stable, functioning democracy by 2004, a beacon in Central Asia.

The Iraq War is avoided entirely. In 2002, when Bush’s advisers push for regime change, a crucial intelligence reassessment—prompted by an earlier, more critical examination of the evidence—reveals that Saddam Hussein’s WMD programs are defunct. Bush publicly changes course, stating that preemptive war without imminent threat sets a dangerous precedent. Instead, he intensifies economic and diplomatic pressure, leading to a negotiated transition: Saddam steps down in 2003 under a deal brokered by the Arab League, and a power-sharing government takes over in Baghdad. Iraq never descends into chaos, and the region avoids the sectarian bloodbath.

Domestically, Bush uses the post-9/11 unity to pass massive, well-designed reforms. The No Child Left Behind Act is fully funded, with strong supports for struggling schools, and it yields dramatic improvements in literacy and graduation rates. The Medicare prescription drug benefit is expanded to include robust price negotiations with pharmaceutical companies, making drugs affordable without breaking the budget. Bush’s “ownership society” vision includes a successful Social Security reform that allows partial personal accounts without cutting guaranteed benefits, modeled after the Thrift Savings Plan, which the public embraces after a massive education campaign. The stock market’s sustained growth in the mid-2000s makes these accounts wildly popular.

On energy and the environment, Bush breaks with orthodoxy. In his 2003 State of the Union, he announces a “New American Energy Revolution” that commits billions to renewable research, nuclear power, and carbon capture. By 2008, the U.S. leads the world in solar and wind technology, reducing dependence on foreign oil and cutting emissions. Hurricane Katrina still strikes, but the federal response is flawless: pre-staged supplies, swift National Guard deployment, and a reconstruction effort that transforms New Orleans into a model of climate-resilient urban design.

The economy booms without the distortions of war spending and housing bubbles. Bush’s tax cuts are made permanent but paired with a dramatic simplification of the tax code and the elimination of corporate loopholes, fueling entrepreneurship. The deficit shrinks as growth surges and the AMT is indexed. The financial crisis of 2008 is averted because the administration recognized early the subprime mortgage risks—Treasury Secretary Paulson, in this timeline, pushed through regulations that curbed predatory lending without killing credit. House prices corrected gently, and no bailouts were needed.

In foreign policy, Bush’s idealism flourishes. His “Freedom Agenda” focuses on partnership, not invasion. human_answers: They also discriminated against Berbers. The Iberian social pyramid in the period was in this sequence: Arabs, Berbers, Muladi (Iberians converted to Islam), Mozarabs (Christians who adopted Arab culture) and finally Jews. As far as I remember his father, Hafsun ibn Said, was a Berber, and his mother, Subh, was said to be of Visigothic descent. But again this can be denied depending on the situation. When Ibn Hayyan cites, Umar ibn Hafsun's lineage, he traces back to a great-grandfather named Ja'far ibn Salim, who was said to have converted to Islam and settled in southern Spain. The pedigree mentioned by Ibn Hayyan then traces back several generations to a figure named Count Marcellus (or Frugelo), who was described as the son of Alfonso and prominently had a Christian Visigothic background. The reason of the focus on his Visigothic heritage probably has to do with the fact that the mother's inheritance has more importance and weight. Okay first we have to discuss Umar's power base. Umar's largest core of supporters were the Muladi and Mozarabs, but he had support from certain Berber groups and to a lesser extent local tribal communities, both Arab and non-Arab. But despite this, the largest base was the Iberians, so as a whole his proposals were mainly focused on these groups. Umar had several focuses: Among them, those with the greatest impact if he manages to dethrone the Umayyads and put himself in power would be Redistribution of Wealth and Land, Multiconfessional Coexistence and Social and Political Reforms. OK, let's go first to the most impactful in my opinion, the Redistribution of wealth: Umar aimed to challenge the economic disparities and concentration of power among the Umayyad and Arab elites. The primary means by which this occurred was through the confiscation of properties and resources carried out by Umayyad loyalists. Umar ibn Hafsun likely targeted agricultural estates, wealthy estates owned by Umayyad officials, and other sources of wealth that were concentrated in the hands of a few. By taking control of these assets, Umar ibn Hafsun aimed to break the economic monopoly of the Umayyads and redirect the resources to benefit a broader segment of society. While Umar's loyal commanders, soldiers, and allies would naturally receive significant shares, the redistribution of wealth and land to the general population (the Iberians) would generate impressive economic dynamism, particularly for this era. However, it's important to note that the objective of this dynamism wasn't solely Umar's idea; rather, it aimed to strengthen his power base by gaining popular support and loyalty. This can be compared to William banning slavery to finance his conquests. Landownership was not only an economic asset but also conferred social and political status. It allowed individuals to assert greater autonomy and agency in their lives. The prospect of land ownership offered both stability and economic independence. He sought to create a more equal and stable society in Al-Andalus, one where economic opportunities were more evenly distributed and where the grievances of the marginalized (his power base) were addressed. Multiconfessional Coexistence: When we discuss this, we must remember that Umar's syncretic ideology was a constant in his life. The promotion of religious freedom and protection of the rights of religious minorities was an important basis especially for the Muladi who did not follow the orthodox Islam of the Arab and Umayyad elite. Muladis often venerated local folk saints and incorporated them into their spiritual practices. These folk saints were often associated with specific regions, towns, or professions. These saints were believed to possess spiritual power and were revered for their ability to intercede on behalf of the people. Something similar to Catholic behavior, then fishermen could, for example, pray to Allah and Saint Peter: the patron saint of fishermen. A big no no in islam. Muladis in Al-Andalus adapted Iberian festivals and rituals to incorporate Islamic themes and practices. This process involved reinterpreting existing festivals within an Islamic context or creating new celebrations that reflected both Islamic and Iberian cultural elements. The goal was to maintain cultural traditions while aligning them with their Islamic faith. I will cite two examples: The Christian festival of Epiphany, which celebrated the visit of the Magi to the baby Jesus, was adapted by Muladis to commemorate the Islamic tradition of the Prophet Muhammad's birthday (Mawlid al-Nabi). They incorporated elements of Iberian parades and processions into the celebration, along with recitations of Islamic poetry, music, and communal meals. The pre-Islamic Iberian festival of Beltane, which marked the beginning of summer, was adapted by Muladis to coincide with the Islamic month of Ramadan. The festival incorporated elements of Iberian bonfires, dances, and feasting, while also observing Islamic fasting and prayers. What I am saying is that from the perspective of orthodox Islam, the Muladis' syncretic religious practices were seen as heretical, as they incorporated beliefs and rituals that diverged from the established teachings and practices of Islam. The Islamic tradition upholds the concept of tawhid (the oneness of God) and emphasizes adherence to the teachings of the Quran and the hadith (sayings and actions of the Prophet Muhammad). Deviations from these core principles, including the incorporation of Christian beliefs and practices, were generally considered outside the boundaries of orthodox Islamic belief. So this rise of the muladi could very well generate a new sect of Islam. Some other examples of heresy: They would recite prayers and perform religious rituals in a mixture of Arabic, Latin and Mozarabic; Muladis often integrated Christian prayers and hymns into their Islamic worship and even employed syncretic iconography and symbolism that combined elements from both Islam and Christianity. Social and Political Reforms: The most important in my opinion is the establishment of regional self-governance would have involved several aspects, including the ability to make decisions regarding local administration, taxation, and defense. It would have provided local communities with the opportunity to shape their own policies and regulations, taking into account their specific needs and interests. Basically Umar challenged the centralized authority of the Umayyad Caliphate and advocated for greater regional autonomy. He believed in decentralizing power and governance structures to allow for more localized decision-making and representation. And the second most important was the fact that Umar valued meritocracy over nepotism or tribal affiliations in the administration of his principality. He appointed officials based on their abilities and qualifications rather than their social status or lineage, fostering a more efficient and accountable government. While these three are the biggest reforms he claimed, we have dozens more that were probably forgotten over time, so it would be a very different Andalusian one. perhaps, as a whole it is quite possible It's difficult to say what it will be like. The only difference is that this is more viable for the Muladi than for the Berbers or Arabs. Maybe a strong Shu'ubiyya in iberia long term (in otl al-andalus there were people like Ibn Gharsiya promoting this idealogy in the region). Again, it is difficult to say anything with certainty. Ibera could implode or it could have something like iran with its own exclusive religious sect (which is the most interesting thing in my opinion). If the country stays together I would say no. it can expand or retract but as long as it has the support of the local population it will be a viable country Andalus was one of the greatest powers in the Mediterranean, but due to its remoteness from the rest of the Islamic world it tended to focus its interests locally. Especially in Iberia and if things were stable at home, they would partly focus on the Maghreb Well that's a yes, Andalus was an ethnic state which prevented non-Arabs from being able to advance socially and economically. Even if this rise is now exclusive to the muladi (which is unlikely) the percentage of the active population in the country will be much higher. I have no idea, there are so many variables that it is difficult to say. We can have of the Byzantines surviving, the conquest of Egypt by the Mongols and other variables. For example Slavs were a very important group with women serving as concubines and men as slave soldiers. If Iberia loses access to this market or if the market is not able to sustain the region's demand, we could have new slave routes, whether from sub-Saharan Africa (although in the period sub-Saharan slaves were used a lot in intensive agriculture) to places like Ireland . I'll give you an example if an English kingdom (whether Scandinavian or Anglo-Saxon aka non-Norman) conquers Ireland (or Scotland) and begins to supply the demand for slaves to Al-andalus we can have a slave market with the same intensity what happened to the Slavs. Especially since the Irish (also Wales and Scotland) have a well-desired composition in the Islamic world. items.original_question: What if Umar ibn Hafsun defeats the Umayyads - Mozarab/Muladí Al-Andalus One of my favorite historical subjects to research is Al-Andalus, the Muslim-ruled realms of the Iberian peninsula that existed between the 8th and 15th centuries. A land where East met West, Al-Andalus represented a rare example of Islamic Arab rule of Western European territory, resulting in the blending of cultures, religion, knowledge, and languages that proved to be massively influential on the development of European civilization and human history as a whole. Even though it was swept out of Iberia by the Reconquista, the influence of Al-Andalus can still be felt today, through Hispanic language, culture, art, and cuisine. For example, there are many Arabic loanwords in the Spanish language, tacos have middle eastern roots, and I remember a story my grandfather would tell me about when he met Bedouin tribesmen while deployed as a U.S. Marine during the Gulf War, and while they could not understand the English language, they could understand his Spanish. In the late 9th century, the once-Caliphs of the entire Muslim world, the Arab Umayyad dynasty, ruled over the vast majority of the Iberian peninsula from the prosperous city of Cordoba. Their rule would last for 300 years, but would not be without resistance. Although they comprised a small portion of the population, the ruling class of Al-Andalus was almost exclusively Arab. Mozarabs, local Iberians who remained Christian under Muslim rule, and Muladí, Iberians who had converted to Islam, resented the discriminatory racial and taxation policies of their Arab overlords, creating a degree of instability within Al-Andalus. Born around 850, Umar ibn Hafsun was a prominent leader of Iberian resistance to Umayyad rule. Simultaneously described as being of both North African and Visigothic descent, the rogue-ish and opportunistic ibn Hafsun attracted a following of disaffected Mozarab and Muladí alike, and alongside fellow rebels such as ibn Marwan and the Banu Qasi clan, would contest Umayyad rule from his fortress, Bobastro. While he would experience much success early on, several defeats against the Umayyads, such as at the Battle of Poley in 891, as well as his conversion to Christianity in 899, in what appeared to be a bid to attract the support of the Christian King of Asturias, would weaken his following. He would fight to the very end, dying in 917, and his sons would continue his fight until 928, when Bobastro fell to Emir Abd-ar-Rahman III. Umar ibn Hafsun remains somewhat of a tragic figure in Iberian history, but he also represents a glimpse into what could have been. Had he succeeded in supplanting the minority Arab ruling class with Mozarabs and Muladí, perhaps by winning battles such as the Battle of Poley, ibn Hafsun could have ensured the creation of a stronger, multicultural and multireligious Al-Andalus. This creates an interesting scenario for speculation. Could this alt-Andalus survive for longer, perhaps even to the present? What would the society of alt-Andalus look like? Would religious and ethnic differences eventually shatter this state, or would it strengthen it, combining the best of the Christian and Islamic worlds? Would alt-Andalus fall to neighboring Christian and Muslim invaders, or would it become one of the leading powers in Europe and the Mediterranean, an even greater conduit for the exchange of trade, knowledge, and culture than the Al-Andalus of OTL? And how would this alt-Andalus impact the development of Hispanic culture, and European and world history as a whole?
items.model_answer:
Had Umar ibn Hafsun overcome the Umayyads in the early 10th century, the Iberian Peninsula would have pivoted dramatically away from Arab-dominated centralization toward a native-led, religiously hybrid civilization. Instead of the Caliphate of Córdoba reaching its zenith under Abd al-Rahman III, a decentralized, Muladí–Mozarab confederation would have emerged, profoundly reshaping the Reconquista, Iberian culture, and Mediterranean geopolitics.

The immediate consequence of a Hafsunid victory—likely achieved by capturing Córdoba with combined forces of disaffected Muladíes, Berber mercenaries, and Mozarabic militias, perhaps aided by the Idrisids or early Fatimid naval pressure—would be the dissolution of Umayyad authority. Hafsun, already a Christian convert, would not have attempted to recreate an Arab-style emirate. Instead, he would have established a kingdom centered on his Bobastro stronghold, legitimizing his rule through native Christian and Iberian-Muslim support. The resulting polity would be a loose, multi-confessional federation of regional lords: Muladí clans like the Banu Qasi in the Ebro valley, Mozarab counts in cities such as Toledo and Mérida, and probably semi-autonomous Berber chiefdoms in the south. Hafsun’s own Christianity would encourage open practice of the Mozarabic rite, while Muslim allies would retain legal autonomy under local qadis; the state’s identity would be explicitly “Andalusian” rather than Arab, with Romance—not Arabic—re-emerging as the administrative lingua franca.

This shift would kill the Caliphate before its birth. Without a centralized Córdoba to dominate the peninsula, no golden age of courtly patronage, no Medinat al-Zahra, and no unified military machine to raid the Christian north. The small kingdoms of Asturias-León and Pamplona would instead face a fragmented but resilient south, where border lords switched allegiances opportunistically. The Reconquista, instead of being a steady crusading drive, would evolve into a patchwork of shifting alliances among Christian, Muslim, and mixed powers. Over the following century, the absence of a strong Córdoban state might even allow the northern kingdoms to expand earlier, but they would be absorbing territories already deeply Iberianized and culturally Latinized, rather than conquering Arabized cities. The result could be an earlier, more organic blending of Christian and Islamic elements—Mozarabic liturgy, art, and architecture would flourish without Umayyad suppression, and later imported reforms like the Cluniac or Cistercian influences would take root in a very different soil.

Economically and demographically, Hafsun’s victory would reverse the trend of Arabization. The Muladí and Mozarabic majority, no longer second-class subjects, would develop a strong nativist identity, possibly reviving the name “Spania” or “Hispania” for their realm. Arabic would gradually lose its prestige to Romance dialects, leading to an earlier literary vernacular. The slave-trade networks run by the Umayyads would contract, and economic ties with North Africa would be less dominated by Arab elites, favoring Berber and native merchant communities instead.

In the longer run, a Muladí–Mozarab Al-Andalus would alter the course of Western Christendom. A powerful, Christian-ruled but religiously mixed state in the south might act as a bridge rather than a frontier. Papal influence could be tempered, with a distinctly Mozarabic church asserting autonomy. The Crusades, if they still occurred, would have little traction against a region that was already under a Christian king, however “oriental” his court rituals. The eventual unification of Spain under a single crown would likely be delayed, and when it came, it would carry far more genetic and cultural Moorish strains into the modern era. The Mediterranean would remain more interconnected, with Iberia serving as a meeting point rather than a flashpoint.

items.question: What If Best timeline for Catholicism
human_answers: As mentioned, this would be difficult without changing core doctrines. That basically requires the Schism to occur, and likely makes it difficult to avoid the Reformation. Here's a few thoughts though: A successful Crusade of Varna could lead to greater Catholic influence over the Balkans/southeastern Europe in place of the Ottomans. If there's enough pressure the Byzantines may be able to remain Eastern Catholic – this would be unpopular among the people, but foreign relations and actual successes by the Catholic powers in combatting the Ottomans may counteract this. Same goes for other newly liberated groups in the Balkans like the Bulgarians and Wallachians. For Russia, the best bet may be to have Poland-Lithuania successfully bring Russia under its influence, such as through a pretender like False Dmitri. This could lead to the imposition of Catholicism on Russia, which again would face resistance from the people, but depending on the level of Polish control could result in a Catholic Russia. Theoretically, the Reformation may be avoidable if Rome preemptively implements several of the reforms seen in OTL's Counter-Reformation and Council of Trent. This would alleviate most of Luther's early concerns, and may lead to later, more radical Reformers being far less influential. Of course, given that it was the Counter -Reformation, it doesn't seem likely that the Church would undergo these changes without Protestant pressure. The English Reformation, however, can pretty easily be undone just by changing some events in Tudor England. Maybe Arthur lives and Henry VIII never accedes, maybe Mary is born a male, maybe Henry VIII dies before his rejection of Rome. This in turn would make all of the major colonial powers Catholic, with the only exceptions being the Dutch and Scandinavians. If colonization goes similarly, this would make North America, Oceania, and likely other colonial possessions Catholic rather than Protestant.

But the thing is, the world around that Church would change too, and by it changing, so would to a degree the Church (by having to care about different things and facing different challenges) which may well render it unrecognizable. Much in the same way I can say (as a Catholic) the Church ontologically is the same as in the years 33 or 330, while still recognizing it looks and feels alien when superimposed to either of those Churches. So if we are to remain as close as you want, I guess EdwardRex's point works (with some luck, as it's easier to prevent Anglicanism than to prevent the rise of Protestantism), plus a different Italian unification that leaves a sizable Papal States not just existing, but also having a solid level of influence in geopolitics. Catholic Japan is objectively hard, go look at how lucky it was for the Philippines to end up how they did and then multiply it for Japan to experience something similar. As for Africa, I don't see any easy way out, there's a very unpalatable option in the form of continued colonialism I guess but I'd say it's not the best timeline for most anybody involved.

That's absolutely fair, the Church would feel very foreign to a modern layman. As a Catholic myself, learning about early Church history made me realize how alien it feels, even if it isn't so far off doctrinally. I should have said that, ideally, the Church doesn't compromise on its beliefs to prevent a division (e.g. remaining papist in a "no Schism of 1054" scenario, which would basically require divine intervention to overcome logistical problems). The question is, is preventing Anglicanism going to change all that much overall? Perhaps if you couple that with a more successful counter-reformation you could go far without preventing the rise of Protestantism altogether, which has massive ramifications for the French Wars of Religion and the Thirty Years' War. As for Italian unification, I think that a "best-case scenario" for the Church in this sense means dampening liberalism, and a great way to do that is to avoid the American and French revolutions, which therefore make nationalism a lot slower and less prominent, so whether Italy unifies is unlikely. I used Catholic Japan as an example, but a better one would be a Catholic Britain, which is much more likely and doesn't require a massive bloody unification war and shakeup of society. A Catholic Britain means that they would be exporting Catholicism rather than Protestantism to their colonies, which would likely cause a lot more people to be Catholics in the end. As for Africa, considering that there are a lot of Catholics in Africa as-is and that the main colonial powers are all Catholic, not much change is needed. Although I can imagine a world with no French revolution results in an extended colonization period.

items.original_question:
AHC: Best timeline for Catholicism

Without changing integral doctrine or dogma, attempt to make the best timeline for the Catholic Church. That means, a stronger Church, the most amount of catholics/catholic states, and crippling the opposition as much as possible. A few important changes that could be made to this end is preventing the Schism of 1054, preventing the Reformation/a highly successful counterreformation, and having Islam either never exist or fail to conquer outside of Arabia. The consequences of any of these scenarios alone are immense. Other smaller things to change could be making states like Japan convert.
items.model_answer:
In the best possible timeline for Catholicism, the Church would have navigated history with a remarkable blend of spiritual fidelity, institutional wisdom, and graceful adaptation, avoiding its deepest fractures and darkest scandals while maximizing its evangelical and charitable mission.

The early Church would have achieved a true and lasting reconciliation between the Latin West and Greek East, avoiding the Great Schism of 1054. Through patient dialogue and mutual respect for liturgical and theological nuances, East and West would have remained in full communion, preserving a united Christendom that bridged cultures. The Crusades, instead of devolving into violent misadventures, would have been redirected into vast peaceful pilgrimages and massive cultural and scientific exchange between Christian, Islamic, and Jewish civilizations. The Inquisition, in its various forms, would have been restrained by a strong internal reform movement emphasizing pastoral care over coercion, and the Church would have championed principles of religious freedom and due process far earlier.

The Protestant Reformation would not have erupted as a tragic split. Long before 1517, a series of holy and zealous popes and councils would have sincerely addressed abuses like simony, clerical corruption, and the sale of indulgences. Figures like Martin Luther and John Calvin would have been received as reformers within the Church, their theological insights—where compatible with Catholic dogma—integrated into a vibrant renewal of spirituality, liturgy, and education. The Church would have embraced vernacular scripture and liturgy in a careful way that fostered deep personal faith without breaking unity. The result would be a single, diverse but united Western Christianity, with evangelical fervor and intellectual rigor flourishing side by side.

As the Age of Discovery unfolded, the Church would have consistently acted as a defender of the dignity of indigenous peoples. Missionaries, following the lead of early visionaries like Bartolomé de las Casas, would have universally prioritized peaceful, inculturated evangelization and robustly opposed colonial exploitation. The Church would have actively promoted indigenous leadership and the translation of the faith into local cultural forms, leading to a truly global, non-colonial Catholic communion.

The Church’s relationship with science would have been one of mutual enrichment from the start. Instead of conflict, there would be a continuous tradition of Catholic thinkers pioneering astronomy, medicine, and natural philosophy, with the Galileo case resolved as a model of careful dialogical reconciliation. The Vatican would have been a patron of cutting-edge science, and a clear theological framework distinguishing scriptural interpretation from empirical investigation would have prevented unnecessary clashes.

In the modern era, the Church would have engaged with Enlightenment ideals not defensively, but as a discerning partner. Catholic social teaching would have flowered earlier, producing a robust critique of both exploitative capitalism and totalitarian socialism, while actively building cooperative economies, labor rights, and charitable networks. The Church would have been at the forefront of movements for peace, human rights, and abolition of slavery, and its intellectual life would have integrated modern philosophy, historical criticism, and psychology into a compelling synthesis of faith and reason.

The Second Vatican Council would have occurred a century earlier, a natural and organic development rather than a sudden break. The liturgical renewal would have deepened participation without rupturing continuity; ecumenical and interfaith dialogue would have healed old wounds without doctrinal dilution. Lay participation, the role of women, and the universal call to holiness would have been vibrant and uncontroversial. The clerical sexual abuse crisis would have been prevented by an ingrained culture of transparency, zero-tolerance policy since the earliest centuries, and a priesthood formed in profound psychological and spiritual health, with married clergy in some contexts and a permanent diaconate fully utilized.

In this timeline, Jesus’s prayer “that they may all be one” (John 17:21) would be far closer to fulfillment. The Catholic Church would be a truly global family of diverse rites and cultures, visibly marked by unity, charity, and intellectual depth, having condemned its own failings quickly and modeled repentance. It would be a definitive force for the poor, the marginalized, and the planet, widely seen not as a relic but as the living, renewing heart of humanity’s search for God.

He even suggested that little Katherine should be raised in her aunt's household to make sure she didn't become as insolent as her namesake. Mary refused to speak to her father for a almost four months after that and it was only through Catherine Parr's intervention did Henry not go through with drawing up an act of succession that would skip over Mary and her daughters. When King Henry passed away in January 1547, Mary discovered she was pregnant again. Six months after her father's death, she gave birth to a son. She named him Philip after his father who greeted the birth of his son just as happily as he had the birth of his three daughters. There was some discussion over whether or not the boy would take his father's surname or his mother's as King Henry had decreed when Philip and Mary were first married. As his Uncle Edward's heir, some even wanted the boy to be raised somewhere else. Mary put her foot down, saying that if her husband's name was good enough for their daughters, it was good enough for her sons. She did not say a word about Phillip being taken from her. Of course, she hardly needed to as the Duke of Somerset, the Lady Elizabeth, Anna of Cleves and the Dowager Queen Catherine made it extremely clear to Edward, how utterly awful that would be. The boy-king himself wasn't too keen on the idea, considering he had never known his mother. In the end, Philip, Earl of Cambridge was known as Philip of Bedford and he would grow up in the Somerset household until he was six-years-old and started his formal schooling in Hatfield. Family tree: Philip, Duke of Somerset (b. 1503-) m. Mary of England (b. 1516). 1. Katherine of Somerset (b. 1540) 2. Elizabeth of Somerset (b. 1542). 3. Mary of Somerset (b. 1545). 4. Philip, Earl of Cambridge (b. 1547).
items.original_question: What if Princess Mary Tudor married Philip of Bavaria After a short courtship, King Henry announced that his daughter Lady Mary's engagement to Philip, Duke of Palatinate-Neuburg. Philip and Mary marry in early March in a small ceremony attended by the royal family and a few favored courtiers. Many expressed their displeasure at the match, chief among them the Imperial ambassador who wrote to the Holy Roman Emperor, lamenting that his poor cousin was now tied to a German Heathen who has no royal to speak of. The Earl of Hertford was similarly was not pleased with the marriage viewing any children Mary had as potential rivals to his nephew Prince Edward. Despite going through the process of getting a divorce from Anna of Cleves, King Henry remained on good terms with his son-in-law, even granting him the Duchy of Somerset once he abdicated his own duchy to his brother so he and Mary can stay in England. He was even happier to learn that Mary was pregnant with his first grandchild, requesting that the unborn son be named Henry for him. He was quite disappointed when on December 23, Mary had a daughter named Katherine instead.
items.model_answer:
If Mary Tudor had married a Bavarian prince such as Philip (perhaps a younger son of Duke Albert V or a prince of the Palatinate-Neuburg line), English history would have taken a dramatically different course, primarily because the Spanish connection would never have formed. Mary’s deeply Catholic convictions would still have driven her to restore Roman Catholicism, but without the influence and demands of Philip II of Spain, the restoration would have been far less entangled with foreign Habsburg interests.

Politically, the marriage would have been far less unpopular domestically than the Spanish match. There would have been no need for the severe treaty terms that limited Philip’s power in England; a junior Bavarian consort would have arrived with little backing and no independent claim to authority. Wyatt’s rebellion of 1554, triggered largely by anti-Spanish sentiment, likely would not have occurred, removing a major early crisis of Mary’s reign. England would have stayed out of the Habsburg-Valois wars, avoiding the disastrous war with France that cost the English their last continental foothold, Calais. With no Spanish alliance, England could have maintained a more neutral and prosperous foreign policy, focusing on trade and internal order.

Religious policy would still have been harsh—Mary’s determination to burn heretics was her own—but the persecutions might have been less ferocious without the need to prove loyalty to a militant Catholic superpower. Parliament might have been more willing to accept a moderate Catholic settlement if it were not seen as a prelude to Spanish domination, potentially easing the long-term rift with Protestant subjects.

The succession question remains critical. Mary was likely physically unable to bear a child, so even a Bavarian spouse would probably not have produced an heir. The throne would still have passed to Elizabeth. Crucially, however, Philip II would have had no marital claim to England. Without that claim, the later support for Mary, Queen of Scots, and the launching of the Spanish Armada in 1588 become far less probable. Elizabeth’s position would have been more secure, and the Anglo-Spanish war that shaped the later 16th century might have been averted entirely. England could have entered the Elizabethan age with a more moderate religious settlement and less existential threat from abroad, reshaping the entire trajectory of the Reformation in Europe.

items.question: What If Have a Christian or Post-Christian religion incorporate as many "apocrypha" into its canon as possible
human_answers: I suppose the first question is what is meant by apocrypha? Because it can mean different things and they're all different to address. Is it what many Protestants and Rabbinic Judaism call apocrypha? That is the additional books of the Old Testament that are instead considered Deuterocanon in Catholicism and Eastern Orthodoxy? At its core, these are books found in the LXX (Septuagint), but not found in the Masoretic text and are considered canonical texts for the majority of the Christian world. Removing the Protestant Masoretic preference resolves that part easily. Is it the broader Second Temple literature, often called Jewish Apocrypha? This is largely apocalyptic literature and includes things like Enoch, the somewhat related Jubilees, Esdras A (or III Ezra, or I Esdras...) , the Apocalypse of Esdra (IV Ezra/II Esdras), the various Baruchs, but also includes Wisdom literature like Psalms 151-155, Wisdom of Sirach, and the Testament of the Twelve Patriarchs. Some of these were contained in LXX translations (Sirach, the Esdras, Psalms 151-155, etc), while others weren't (Testament of the Twelve Patriarchs, II Baruch, Enoch). This is a mixed bag for canonical status, some of them made it in due to being in existing Greek collections (the LXX), while others weren't. Enoch certainly saw a lot of respect in the early church, but it ultimately lost its status over time and only remained in Ethiopia; which itself has weird canon, the Ethiopic Bible includes Enoch and Jubilees before the Esdras, and also includes the 3 Books of Meqabyan (Ethiopic Maccabees), while disincluding the actual Books of Maccabees (and the Ethiopic books are not at all related, they aren't about martyrs at all in fact, and are almost certainly written in the Middle Ages in Ge'ez originally). A lot of these are interesting books that could have significant impact on theology, but most of them are written quite late too, which was a large part of why they weren't included in any canon; most were know pseudepigrapha even at the time. Then we have the New Testament apocrypha, which ranges from things like gnostic literature and known pseudepigrapha with little chance of incorporation to the antilegomena, many of which had good chance of inclusion. Those not included, but that could have been are the Gospel of the Hebrews (scholars think there's actually 3 different works under this title, and they're all lost), the Apocalypse of Peter, the Acts of Paul, the Shepherd of Hermas, the Epistle of Barnabas and the Didache. Worth stating is that the antilegomena weren't "removed," there was heavy debate early in Christianity of what was and wasn't canonical. Different churches used different books. Some were popular in one place, but unknown in others. Worth stating for the record: the Council of Nicea had NOTHING to do with canonical formation and this was still getting discussed for centuries after. The Church Father Jerome is one of the most important figures in the Old Testament canon development, he was highly influential in the West and was one of the main reasons for why the Catholic and Orthodox Deuterocanons are slightly different. As far as the New Testament, most of the Acts of the Apostyles genre were known pseudepigrapha and very clearly non-canonical even in content. They were popular literature and very clearly derived from the Greek novel tradition. Acts of Paul being one exception to this, it was deeply popular and some argued canonical, but in a canon that includes the Pastorals (and even the Deutero-Paulines), it just didn't fit with the theology of the Pauline letters (although I'd argue it fits quite well with the Authentic Pauline corpus). The Apocylpse of Peter wasn't actually well regarded by most priests and theologians though, but it was certainly popular. Its essentially an early Dante's Inferno. The Shepherd/Hermas, Barnabas (NOT the Gospel of Barnabas, which is a medieval forgery), and the Didache I think are the easiest bunch, although not entirely without problem. The Shepherd is deeply allegorical, but was known to not be apostolic (not insurmountable, as Hebrews made it in, but apostolic lineage was important) and has an arguably binitarian lean to it. Barnabas is also allegorical and also deeply anti-jewish. It is essentially saying that the Jews misread their own books, and this is what the Jewish laws really mean - a lot of these require some serious contortion, to say the least. The Didache is interesting since its the first book of the genre of "Church Orders," which are basically moral and litergical texts. In some ways, its an early version of the genre that would become the Anglican Book of Common Prayer. Some other possibilities are the Odes of Solomon, which are a Judeo-Christian work, likely from the Qumran community, with a pretty strong connection to the Johannine literature.

Another work to consider is the Ascension of Isaiah, a christian work written as a series of visions/prophecies of the prophet Isaiah. Also, the Book of Adam and Eve could become part of the Bible, it discusses what happens to Adam and Eve after Genesis, which is interesting. I doubt the distinction of a so-called "Thomasine" branch of anything, seeing as the gospel of Thomas is a late forgery, dating from the 2nd Century, and not originating from any known centers of Christianity claiming Thomasine origin, Kerala, Edessa or Bactria. The chance of the Didache becoming part of the Bible seems slight to me, seeing as its genre isnt really saying it should be, its just a how to book, thought to be directed to clergy. I would agree the best chance to expand is going to be the Apostolic fathers works: Letters of Ignatius, Polycarp, possibly Papias' work might make it in as a supplement to Acts of the Apostles.

Something to keep in mind, is that "canon" actually has different meanings. And what you mean by "canon" could have major implications on just how big it can get. To general Protestants, the Biblical Canon means that these are only 66 divinely inspired books, period, no more, no less (the familiar Protestant Canon). The Catholic teaching is a bit more nuanced. It states that there are at least 73 divinely inspired books (which make up the Catholic Canon). This does actual leave open the possibility that there are other books that could be divinely inspire but just are not included. That said, there are some individual books that have been rule as incompatible with canon & not divinely inspired. For most of the other Christian sects, the concept of canon is a bit "fuzzier." With many of the books falling into a category that could best be described as "potentially divinely inspired, but since it we see no problems with it we don't need to bother making any further determinations". Thus they are still included in the canon list.

Yes I am including those (potentially). It's a challenge though so it's more of a "would it be realistic" thing. And no real timeline, could be very early or very late. No, as long as there is a somewhat notable text that does consider them canonical. For instance 1 Enoch is not considered orthodox by the majority of Christians but there is at least one denomination that does consider it such. I see. That does make sense. Apparently a lot of stories that have become Christian folklore (of sorts) are from books like the Infancy Gospel that are not usually considered canon, but there are traces throughout art and popular imagination (and even in Islam). Some of the non-canonical Gospels and Acts for instance, additional pseudo-Pauline epistles (and letters by other figures). Could be a fairly small but still notable enough to make it into the historical record and maybe persist as a niche sect.
items.original_question:
AHC: Have a Christian or Post-Christian religion incorporate as many "apocrypha" into its canon as possible

The definition of "apocrypha" obviously varies across denomination, e.g. 1 Enoch is canon according to the Ethiopian Orthodox Tewahedo Church but not any other major denominations. But I'm thinking more along the lines of having some denomination which recognizes as many texts as possible which are not in every Biblical canon IOTL (and possible none), e.g. Acts of various specific figures (as distinct from Acts of the Apostles), Gospel of Thomas, etc. etc.
items.model_answer:
If a Christian or post-Christian religion deliberately incorporated as many apocryphal texts as possible into its canon, it would transform into a radically inclusive and theologically diverse tradition, far removed from any single orthodox creed. Instead of a bounded “Bible,” it would have a sprawling library of sacred writings that represent the full spectrum of early Jewish and Christian experimentation: from the Deuterocanonical books of the Catholic and Orthodox Old Testament, to the New Testament Apocrypha (such as the Gospel of Thomas, the Protoevangelium of James, the Acts of Peter, and the Apocalypse of Paul), to Gnostic revelations, Jewish pseudepigrapha like 1 Enoch and Jubilees, and even texts eventually labeled heretical. The result would be less a unified religion and more a living museum of ancient religious imagination, held together not by doctrinal coherence but by a shared commitment to explore every marginalized voice within the early Jesus movement and its predecessors.

Such a religion would inevitably embrace contradiction as a spiritual virtue. Its wisdom literature would teach both a covenantal, law-centered path (as in Jubilees) and an antinomian, inner-knowledge mysticism (as in the Gospel of Mary or the Trimorphic Protennoia). Its gospel collection would blend the infancy stories of Jesus making clay birds come to life with the esoteric sayings of Thomas and the full-throated passion narratives of the canonical four. The nature of God would expand to include not only the Father of Israel and the Trinitarian vision but also a hidden divine mother, a pantheon of aeons, or a demiurgical distinction between a lower creator and a higher, unknowable God. The afterlife would be depicted in vivid, often clashing detail: cyclical reincarnation from some texts, eternal hell from others, universal salvation from still others. Rather than choosing between these visions, a community that maximizes apocrypha would likely treat all sacred contradiction as a sacred mystery, arguing that ultimate truth is too vast for any single account and is best approached through a chorus of competing testimonies.

In practice, this canon would debunk any notion of a pristine, unified early church, replacing it with an open conversation across time. A post-Christian version of the faith might go further, reading the apocrypha not as failed scripture but as the authentic testament of a movement that was always about creative experimentation. It might place the Gospel of Thomas at the center, view the canonical gospels as just one successful faction’s archive, and treat Gnostic and Jewish Christian texts as equal heirs of the tradition. Liturgy would become a form of scholarly and mystical play: a reading from the Infancy Gospel of James during Advent, a meditation on the Secret Book of John at Easter, a communal recitation of the Odes of Solomon. The historical Jesus would recede behind countless reinterpreted Christs—teacher of wisdom, wandering magician, celestial revealer, revolutionary, angelic being—none of them definitive, all of them held in creative tension.

Ultimately, such a religion would not be Christian in the traditional sense. It would be a meta-religion, a deliberate post-Christian reconstruction that uses ancient apocrypha to critique the very idea of a closed canon. Its practitioners would not ask, “Which of these books is true?” but rather, “What happens when we let all these voices speak together?” The outcome would be a faith defined by perpetual questioning, a deep archive of spiritual possibilities, and a continuous renegotiation of what it means to follow a way that never was singular or stable.

items.question: What If Greek royal family that is ethnically Greek
human_answers: "What factors allowed the European powers to accept native princes in Serbia" is a false question because it presumes the European powers had a role in allowing native princes there to begin with. With the exception of Russia during the First Serbian Uprising, there were no other powers involved beyond the Ottomans. Had it ended with the First Serbian Uprising, whether in Ičko's Peace in 1807 or by 1813 otherwise, we would've seen the Ottomans consenting to a native prince in the region, in the form of Karađorđe, by themselves, and that'd be the end of it. Karađorđe was already attempting to consolidate power for himself in those latter years, even while he had opposition, so he was already set to be uncontested. Which brings forth two questions: had the Greeks fought alone, would it have increased the odds of a native prince being put in power, and would they have even chosen to be a monarchy? As others have argued so far, there was too much conflict between the various revolutionaries to allow for something like that, and it's also why OTL there actually wasn't a monarchy in Greece after the revolution until Greece's stability was brought under question and it was decided by the Great Powers that it should be a monarchy with a foreign prince in power to bolster it. This ignores some of the historical facts surrounding the dynastic conflict in Serbia. Obrenović didn't just decide he was going to challenge Karađorđe's claim to authority over the Serbs, he had become a leader in his own right, rallied the people to another uprising, and won, by the time Karađorđe attempted to come back. He had received what Karađorđe would've gotten had the First Serbian Uprising won, effectively, and he wasn't going to let him challenge that, least of all because of fears of what the Ottomans might do in response. Had the Greek War of Independence seen a decisively unifying leader like Karađorđe or Obrenović from its outset, there's no reason to assume that you'd have other leaders contesting their claim to power by wishing to assert themselves instead - when Karađorđe attempted to consolidate power, he received pushback on it, and it's likely a Greek-equivalent situation would see a similar conflict, where the consolidating leader would receive pushback from his revolutionary peers. But as everyone else has pointed out, revolutionary leadership was a lot more diffuse and filled with conflict, so there's no chance you'd have a unifying leader like that emerge. Really, the case of Serbia should highlight the fact that, had the Greek War of Independence not been a war for independence, but a war for greater autonomy ala the First Serbian Uprising up to 1807, in a TL where it was successful, depending on who's Sultan at the time, the same privileges extended in Ičko's Peace to the Serbs might be extended to the Greeks too, which means that the Ottomans would've demanded the Greeks decide on who to be prince among their leaders.
items.original_question:
AHC: Greek royal family that is ethnically Greek

Greece became independent from the Ottoman Empire in 1821. Two different European dynasties ruled it - the Bavarians (whose only king of Greece was the unpopular King Otto) and the Danish. Neither of these dynasties were of Greek heritage. However, there was a sizable Greek aristocracy in the Ottoman Empire, such as the Phanariotes of Constantinople. What if an ethnically Greek family (such as one of the Phanariot families) was chosen to rule Greece? Can you think of some candidates for a possible ethnically Greek royal family for 19th century Greece?
items.model_answer:
If the modern Greek royal family had been ethnically Greek rather than drawn from foreign dynasties, the entire trajectory of the Greek state’s political and social development might have shifted significantly. The imported monarchy—first with the Bavarian Otto, then the Danish House of Glücksburg—was from the start a source of friction, seen by many as an alien institution imposed by Great Powers rather than an organic expression of the nation. An ethnically Greek dynasty, likely emerging from a prominent Greek family with deep roots in the revolutionary or Phanariot traditions, would have enjoyed a much stronger initial claim to legitimacy. This could have softened the perennial conflict between the “indigenous” political class and the crown, reducing the monarchy’s reliance on foreign backing and perhaps insulating it from charges of being a mere tool of external interests.

A homegrown royal house would have also altered the symbolic fabric of the nation. The Glücksburgs often struggled to embody a convincing Greek identity—their foreign accents, religion (though Orthodox by conversion), and continental courtly culture reinforced a sense of estrangement. An ethnically Greek royal family might have more seamlessly fused with the popular vision of the Great Idea and the Byzantine-imperial legacy, possibly rallying broader public support during national crises. The National Schism of World War I, where the monarchy’s German ties became a fatal liability, might never have occurred in the same way, or could have been far less divisive, potentially averting the republicanic interlude and the eventual abolition of the monarchy in the 1970s.

However, a domestic dynasty would not have been a panacea. It would have been drawn from the same fractious elite that dominated Greek politics, likely bringing its own regional and clientelist loyalties into the palace, blurring the line between crown and faction. Without the international birth-right connections that foreign princes provided, the Greek state might have found it harder to secure Great Power protection or loans, though it might also have developed a more self-reliant foreign policy earlier. In the end, the monarchy’s fate might still have been tied to the same underlying problems of modernization, economic inequality, and military intervention—but an ethnically Greek crown would almost certainly have left a deeper, more contested, and less easily erased mark on the nation’s identity.

items.question: What If Peter of Castile (Pedro the Cruel) marries an English princess in 1360s
human_answers: Oh that's very flattering. Thank you I think the TL you're proposing is plausible and interesting re: the development of ATL Castile and Caroline War. I'm not sure the marriage with Philippa of Clarence is the way to achieve it, though. I don't share others' concerns about her inheritance, but it doesn't necessarily fit into Edward III's plans to create spheres of influence for his sons. Philippa, if she's not marrying Mortimer (who had some smaller land claims in Ireland before inheriting the Burke estates through Philippa) would seem to make more sense for a Fitzgerald or Butler or a knight of the Garter who Edward wanted to establish as a peer without alienating anything from the crown. You could argue that I am overestimating the importance of these spheres of influence. (This is around the time that Lionel gets a Visconti bride -- an arrangement negotiated to put pressure on the papacy to approve the Langley-Flanders marriage, which demonstrates that Edward III still had an overarching and interconnected dynastic plan.) But this is a period in which the Black Prince set out his own foreign policy. He does not simply rubber-stamp his father's agreements. It is TBP's decision to end the Castilian alliance when Pedro executed the prisoners from Nájera. Just a few years later, TBP vetoed his father's alliance with Charles the Bad. All of which is to ask, how would it matter to the Black Prince that his niece is queen of Castile? Or would TBP end the alliance anyway if Pedro acts the way he did in OTL? Then there is also the issue of Pedro's not-great treatment of his wives. We don't know much about Lionel (relative to his four more famous brothers), but we see Edward III and Gaunt have very close relationships with their daughters. Edward made his favorite daughter one of the greatest landholders in England and Gaunt was so fond of his eldest daughter (apparently because she reminded him of his late first wife) that he didn't marry her off until her mid 20s. If Lionel has this sort of affection for Philippa then he may not be willing to entrust his daughter to a king like Pedro. (Though, honestly, I think this is a less important point. Not only only is it entirely speculative of Lionel's personal affections, but Lionel does demonstrate a commitment to his father's plans in going through with the Visconti match for the main purpose of furthering his brother's marriage prospects in Flanders. Still, I don't thin Pedro's treatment of his wives can be entirely discounted.) I very strongly suspect that the marriage contract handed the Ulster estate over to Lionel in its entirety and entailed it to his heirs, regardless of remarriage.
