Heiresses in weak negotiating positions often lost everything to their husbands and, considering both that a) Elizabeth de Burgh only became an heiress because her father was assassinated by his cousin -- i.e., the man who would inherit if Elizabeth did not -- and b) that Elizabeth's guardian was her mother, Maud of Lancaster, who was a member of the English royal family herself, it just seems very likely that the marriage contract gave Lionel everything. Maud was predisposed to favor the royal family as a relative herself and would be very strongly predisposed to screw over the Burghs who murdered her husband by disinheriting them in favor of Lionel.

To be fair, when the negotiations presumably happen (1366 or 1367 the latest) Philippa's father Lionel is alive, healthy and about to be married for the second time. I don’t think the perspective of Philippa inheriting his estates looks all that close at this point. Moreover, I don’t think that the perspective of Pedro potentially inheriting domains in England and Ireland should scare Edward all that much. If anything, they could potentially serve as a hook to ensure the favorable Castilian policy towards England or otherwise they can be easily confiscated (it’s not like Castile can really try retain those estates against the wishes of Plantagenets). If after Lionel dies Edward really wants to revert these estates back to the crown (although as mentioned before there are arguments for Edward not to do it), I think there is a really neat way to do it. Presumably Philippa’s dowry however large can it be (BTW how large can it be? Up to £10,000 perhaps?) would not be enough to pay for Black Prince’s army (even if ITTL Edward, helping the future husband of his niece, can be a bit more moderate in his pricing). While Pedro can raise some money on his own (he was ready to pay de Guesclin 200000 gold coins – presumably florins - in 1369, so he had some money, although of course it wouldn’t be enough to settle his OTL bill with Edward), he would probably still need to pledge some his territories in lieu of the rest of the payment. So, after Philippa inherits her father’s estates, the mortgage can be rearranged with English and Irish estates now serving as a collateral instead of Castilian territories. Or even perhaps these estates can be given to the Black Prince staight away in lieu of the rest of the debt. @material_boy , what do you think about the proposed PoD and some of its consequences? I have been toying with the victorious Pedro for several years now, but the perspective of modeling the alternative HYW always seemed to daunting. It was your amazing TL that inspired me to approach it. So your opinion would be especially appreciated (although of course I would be happy to hear feedback from everyone).
items.original_question: What if Peter of Castile (Pedro the Cruel) marries an English princess in 1360s UPD: I have updated both the PoD and who is the most likely bride for Pedro. See up-to-date details here and further ( link ). However all the potential consequences of Pedro surviving described in the second part of this message are still very much valid. UPD 2: Please find the TL draft for 1362-1364 in this message ( link ) I've always had a soft spot for Pedro the Cruel (aka Pedro the Just) of Castile. His victory over Henry of Trastamara would have monumental consequences both for Iberian Kingdoms and for Europe in general (I will list some of them further down). While there are a few threads on the forum discussing the possibility of his victory over Henry they are all rather short and usually either discuss earlier PoDs (e. g. Joan of England surviving and marrying Pedro) or more decisive battle of Najera (with Henry being killed or captured in battle). The former is definitely plausible, but would alter 1350s and 1360s quite a bit, while the later doesn’t strike me as all that consequential (after all in 1367 Henry has a son as well as two brothers who could potentially lead the Trastamara party to victory even without Henry). IMHO the main reason for Pedro losing the Castilian Civil War were not particular mistakes on his part or successful moves on Henry’s, but rather the military dominance of du Guesclin’s routier army over Castilian one. So, if we want Pedro to retain his throne, we need to either occupy or counterbalance routiers until the Caroline Phase of the Hundred Years’ War starts. The latter was successfully done IOTL with the help of Edward the Black Prince in 1367, but the relations between Pedro and Edward quickly deteriorated mainly because Edward didn’t receive his pay as per treaty of Libourne and thus Pedro was left to his own devices in 1368-1369 and was defeated and killed. Presumably Pedro didn’t pay Edward simply because he was unable to raise such an enormous sum. The PoD I present is Pedro marrying Philippa of Clarence as part of negotiations with English. Philippa is the eldest granddaughter of Edward III and has just reached marriageable age in 1367. IOTL, she married Edmund Mortimer but of course king of Castile is a way more prestigious match (there are conflicting records about when exactly Philippa was betrothed to Edmund IOTL, but for the purpose of this PoD let us pick the latest option 1368). Pedro on the other hand is in his thirties, has not legitimate issue and both his wife and his beloved mistress are dead since 1361. The purpose of the marriage is twofold: firstly, to bring Castile closer to England and secondly to be a neat way to subsidize Edward’s expedition. I am not sure how large Philippa’s dowry was IOTL, but presumably if she has a royal marriage, it definitely should be quite large. So Edward’s army can at least partly be subsidized with his niece’s dowry. I am not sure if such an arrangement is plausible, but if it does happen consequences are massive. Presumably if the relationship between the Black Prince and Pedro is unstrained (or at least is significantly better than IOTL), the second invasion of Henry and de Guesclin would seem futile and probably doesn’t happen. In 1369 the Caroline Phase begins (even if IOTL Charles V summoned Edward because he already realized that Castille would fall to Henry, which is debatable, ITTL Charles presumably understands that Edward would help Pedro no matter what and thus he might as well go on with his plan). Thus, Henry would have very little military support and will stand no chance against Pedro and his allies. Possible consequences of the PoD: 1. Castille itself has a radically different social structure. a. IOTL Henry and his heirs had to give out large parts of royal domain for their supporters from lesser nobility that formed new aristocratic elites (since pedristas were active until mid-1380s Trastamaras needed their continous support for an extended period of time and thus royal domain suffered greatly). Quoting from Teofilo F. Ruiz-Spain's Centuries of Crisis 1300 - 1474: The new dynasty came to power having given lavish grants and titles to supporting nobles, and territorial concessions to their royal allies in France and the Crown of Aragon. Henry II’s initial hold on the crown was a tentative one. New men came to the fore demanding a share of the victory, and the king also granted them substantial privileges and lands. Historians have long argued that the first decades of Trastámara rule witnessed the disappearance of the old nobility, a nobility dating to the late eleventh and twelfth centuries, and its replacement by a new nobility. In reality, the transformation was signaled by the rise to prominence of lesser branches of the great old noble houses, with a few new lesser nobles rising to very high status. This promotion in rank was tied to the granting of large estates and to extensive royal privileges. Such erosion of the royal domain and authority had, in turn, disastrous consequences for Castile over the next hundred years. Not unlike France or England in the late fourteenth and fifteenth centuries, the rise of the nobility led to waves of violence and instability. Securely grounded in their new economic power and high standing, the Castilian nobility challenged royal authority and even coveted, as was the case in the reigns of John II and Henry IV, the control of the Crown. Pedro unlike Henry is a legitimate king and thus doesn’t need such drastic measures to obtain necessary support. b. In the first half of XIV century one of the main pillars of royal power was municipal nobility (or more precisely non-noble municipal knights). At first kings bought their support against magnates by granting municipal knights’ extensive privileges, but since the latter felt constant pressure by disenfranchised bourgeoisie, they continuously welcomed royal entrenchment in cities and thus by 1340s urban centers were under firm royal control. Once again, quote from Teofilo F. Ruiz-Spain's Centuries of Crisis 1300 - 1474: In less than 50 years the non-noble knights monopolized municipal offices in most Castilian cities, bought most of the land around the cities, and gained control, as they did in Burgos and Avila, of the most important ecclesiastical benefices. In return the king hoped for, and often received, their military support against the magnates and access to the cities’ fiscal resources. Moreover, as the non-noble knights gained control of their respective cities, they came into conflict with those below them. Pressured from below by the disfranchised petite bourgeoisie, the non-noble knights welcomed royal interference in the affairs of the cities and, by the 1340s, the takeover of municipal administration by royal officials (the regimiento) became a political reality. For a brief period, royal control of the urban centers became one of the most significant gains of the Castilian monarchy, but then the disorders of the late fourteenth century weakened royal control anew. IOTL many cities supported Pedro against Henry and thus were severely punished by victorious Trastamaras which greatly weakened both cities themselves and royal control over them. Thus, if Pedro retains his throne Castile is a lot more centralized with a strong royal power based on resources from a reasonably large royal domain as well as prosperous cities under firm royal control which is a stark contrast to magnate-dominated early Trastamara Spain. 2. Pedro IOTL had a firm alliance with Portugal. His uncle Pedro of Portugal helped him in his wars against both Peter of Aragon and Henry of Trastamara. When Pedro of Castile was slain, it was Portugal that was the main base for anti-Trastamara action in Iberia. Ferdinand of Portugal, Pedro of Castile’s cousin waged several wars against Trastamaras (first claiming the crown of Castile in his own right, later supporting John of Gaunt’s claim). Pedro of course is a very strong clamant to Portuguese throne in his own right, but he can further cement his claim by marrying Beatrice of Portugal to his son (who presumably should be born in early to mid 1370s roughly similarly to OTL Roger Mortimer birth date and thus ideally match Beatrice). Moreover, before Trastamara coup Portugal and Castile had the same allies and aligned economic interests (both benefited greatly from maritime trade between Northern Europe and Mediterranean, both had Genoa as a most important trade partner and England as a main ally outside of Iberia). IOTL when Portuguese interregnum happened the nobility was split with a significant portion of it supporting Trastamara claim. It were municipal elites of 4 main Portuguese cities (Lisbon, Porto, Coimba and Evora) that bankrolled anti-Trastamara faction. The main reason for these was economic (i. e. retention of profitable maritime trade with Genoa, England etc.) as well as desire to cancel Ferdinand’s pro-noble reforms (which were conducted in order to fund extremely expensive campaigns against Castille). If IOTL Pedro continues to rule Castille, Portuguese municipal elites have no reason to dislike the union with neighboring kingdom (because Ferdinan’s reforms would be unnecessary and Castile and Portugal economic and political interest would continue to be closely aligned) and thus we can encounter Castilian-Portugese union in 1380s. 3. Pedro had an advantage in the War of Two Peters against Peter of Aragon. Presumably if Henry of Trastamara is no longer a threat, he can continue pressing Aragon for economic, political (most important one being the termination of Trastamara support) and perhaps even territorial concessions (getting back Alicante, Elche and Orihuela as part of kingdom of Murcia) 4. If Pedro marries Philippa, presumably John Gaunt and Edmund Langley would have alternative brides. IOTL the marriages happened to establish a claim over kingdom of Castile. ITTL Pedro would have legitimate heirs related to English royal family without such a match and thus daughters of Peter with at best debatable legitimacy are not ideal brides for English prices. Does anybody have suggestions who John and Edmund would marry in such a scenario? 5. Perhaps the most consequential consequence of the PoD is alternative Caroline Phase of HYW. The battle of La Rochelle that crippled English fleet IOTL was won by Castilian navy. If Castile continues to be an English ally, Castilian navy either doesn’t participate or participates on English side. Thus, English are able to get significant reinforcements to Poitou and Saintonge as well as £12,000 that were supposed to be used to pay for service of local troops (IOTL this booty fell to the hands of Castilians). This potentially a least allows English to retain control over Poitou, Saintonge and Angoumois and perhaps even reverse some French gains made in previous years. Moreover with English fleet still dominating the waters around France, the main reason for the disastrous Great Chevauchee of 1373 is gone. ITTL, it makes a lot more sense to bring reinforcements by see, as was done in previous years. Thus, the Caroline Phase of HYW can be radically altered in 1372-1373, perhaps to the extent of it being a draw rather than decisive French victory. All these consequences seem rather juicy, but I am not sure if the marriage of Pedro and Philippa is all that plausible. What do you guys think? (of course if you have comments on consequences of PoD rather than the PoD itself, I would be happy to hear those too).
items.model_answer:
If Peter of Castile had married an English princess in the 1360s, the most likely candidate would have been a daughter of Edward III who survived to marriageable age—such as Margaret (1346–1361), had she lived. A dynastic union of this kind would have transformed the Anglo-Castilian alliance from a transactional military pact into a deeply personal and permanent bond. The immediate effect would have been the birth of a legitimate male heir, something Peter desperately lacked. With a son carrying Plantagenet blood, the claim of his half-brother Henry of Trastámara would be fatally weakened, and Castile’s fractious nobility—already hostile to Peter’s rule—would face a far stronger dynastic reality, backed directly by English arms and treasure.

England’s commitment to Peter would no longer turn on unpaid debts. An English queen and an Anglo-Castilian prince would make the Black Prince’s intervention a matter of family honour, not just a mercenary venture. The English might have garrisoned key Castilian strongholds, secured the succession against Trastámara’s French-backed bid, and likely prevented Peter’s murder in 1369. A loyal Castile, under a half-English monarch, would permanently tilt the Iberian balance away from France. The Castilian galley fleet—which historically ravaged the English Channel and enabled decisive French naval victories like La Rochelle in 1372—would instead remain at England’s disposal, protecting Aquitaine and disrupting French trade. This alone could have prolonged the Plantagenet presence in southwestern France, possibly averting the Black Prince’s humiliating withdrawal and the subsequent collapse of English power on the continent.

The marriage would also redraw English dynastic ambitions. John of Gaunt’s later claim to the Castilian throne, through his marriage to Peter’s daughter Constance, would never arise. Freed from the costly and distracting “Spanish venture,” Gaunt and the English crown could concentrate their resources on the French theatre, perhaps altering the outcomes of the Caroline phase of the Hundred Years’ War. Meanwhile, a robust pro-English Castile might discourage Aragon from leaning as heavily on France, rearranging the web of Pyrenean alliances and insulating Iberia from the grand Franco-Castilian axis that so menaced late-fourteenth-century England. Over time, a Pedro-English dynasty would embed Castile firmly within an Atlantic-Plantagenet sphere, setting the stage for a very different pattern of marriage alliances, trade, and conflict well into the fifteenth century.

items.question: What If Europe colonized the Americas four centuries earlier? 1092 Instead of 1492
human_answers: Lots of feedback and responses! Thank you all! I'll get to responding to other replies later on. The Crusades! That's a good point for the year 1092 and the 11th century. Also lots of good points here. Very good points. Crusader-style polities and principalities in the New World, given the attitudes of the 11th century. 1. Why wouldn't a less-weakened Muslim power establish their own colonies? As long as they're in Iberia or Morocco, they got a good chance of colonization with that geography, I think? 2. Also why not? What if the Apache or some other First Nations group taking over the North American interior, like a counterpart to the Mongols. Hopefully less bad and deadly and painful though, though that's probably too much to ask for when it comes to warfare in general. "What if the Americas were colonized by Europe beginning in 1292?" Could be worth it's own thread! Here in this one we're talking about what if 1092 instead of 1292, or OTL 1492.

That's a fun scenario to consider. One way to get Medieval America... Not sure about the naval tech of the time though. Or the ressources given the voyage between Europe and the Americas are going to be months long. These are the two crucial things that need to be fixed to get the possibility. The North Route via Greenland and Vinland probably is the best shot to make this work. Think the issue is the fact the Atlantic Ocean is pretty devoid of islands that can make effective island-hoping stops. There are the islands of Macaronesia (Azores, Canarias, Madeira, Cape Verde) close to Europe but otherwise it's a long trip until you reach the Carribeans or one of the American coasts. This isn't the same situation as the Pacific where you have tons of small islets... unless you go into ASB territory and raise the Azore plateau but that basically is making Atlantis a real thing... Naturally this situation limits the abilities of Muslim powers to colonize. Europeans at least have the Viking routes, even if that requires a successful Vinland. Though one has to remember the legend of Abu Bakr II of Mali, the most likely fictionnal predecessor of Mansa Musa. It's a stretch and we're more dealing with an African power than a European or Arabo-Muslim one, but the distance between West Africa and Brazil is a lot shorter... But then again, it's basing ourselves on a myth.

As for how would see a medieval colonization of the Americas, I would expect it happened across the Northern Atlantic and would likely focus first on the region around St Lawrence Bay, which offer several good settlements, than we would see it spread up the St, Lawrence River and later down the East Coast. Early settlements would simply be normal Norse settlements, and outside Norse settlers the main early source of “settlers” would be slaves. The need for labor would drive this slave trade and the victims of this slave trade would likely mainly come from the British islands, the Baltics, Central Europe and the post Frankish kingdoms in order of importance and it would likely disappear by the 13th century. The early settlements would likely mostly be peasants republics, as the Norse seems to mostly have established those on the frontiers. Over time we will likely see consolidation of power under large land owners both secular and ecclesia and the rise of city states. Also as the Norse runs into more powerful native societies, we may also see more centralized frontier states lead by Norse war leaders, these may also turn on the less centralized Norse states and begin to establish true kingdoms. As the population we also see the arrival of Low German merchants, who establish merchant quarters in the cities, we will likely see German artisans also moving. We could also see something like the Ashkenazi migration to Poland, but it’s more likely that Low Germans simply will fill that niche as they did in the Baltic and Nordic countries. This may result in the rise Low German city states. At the same time the Catholic Church will likely introduce more warm weather crops as the Norse moves south. As the economy of Norse America grows and expand, others will likely look into establish alternative trade route to it. Here we may see the Portuguese doing their own Columbus expedition in the early 15 century. At that point I would expect a European presence already in the Caribbean, even if it’s not fully developed. So the Portuguese establish trade routes to the Caribbean and introduce Mediterranean and Middle Eastern cash crops. We likely also see the rise off the African slave trade, but with greater European and Mestizo presence in the region already, it likely doesn’t reach OTL levels and the more traditional European structure likely means a more serfdom like structure for the African slaves. I suspect the Norse will run into the Mesoamericans in the 14th century and we will see it falling to Norse invaders or crusaders, with it being relative far away from Norse American strongholds (which will likely be the Mississippi and St. Lawrence basins and the East Coast), I expect the model of conquest will be more like the Baltic crusades. Conquest mostly by knightly monastic orders and Mexico under a knightly Grandmaster. We could easily see a repeat in the Andeans, but we could also just instead see Christian missionaries converting them.

I am not familiar with the shipbuilding industry, but I believe this is possible. There was no fundamental difference like scale or materials between shipbuilding in the 15th and 11th century. They likely needed only to devise a few new designs, or simply undertake bold try using the vessels they already have. As for the difference? An 11th-century conquest of the Americas would have been far more likely to result merely in the emergence of independent states, rather than colonies subservient to Old World powers. At best, the Italian city-states might have established a few small commercial colonies (perhaps in the Caribbean region?), but inland colonies dominating an entire continent would have been highly unlikely. This aligns more closely with the norms of that era, and the comparatively weaker commercial and artisanal capabilities of Europe would not have generated the centripetal force required to establish such a relationship; Europe could not produce so many goods that American colonists were unable to manufacture for themselves. Two rather interesting questions: 1. Could a less weakened Iberian/North African Muslim power have established its own colonies in the Americas? 2. Could a nomadic polity have been established in the North American interior?

The major issue is that open ocean travel isn't really possible before the 15th century so you'd be island hopping like the Norse did. That's certainly possible but your probably looking at a more Polynesian or Greek heroic age style model (or for that matter the Norse in Iceland and Greenland) where people are leaving to found a separate colony rather than one controlled from the Metro-pole as its to far away. Also most of the early arrivals will be in the North (Canada, then moving into New England and points south as the Little Ice age bites) and while trade webs will probably see the European diseases spread there is a good chance the native powers will have time to recover before actual Europeans reach them. That could allow the Mexican civilizations and the Inca a good chance to survive especially if they've obtained European tech in trade before the newcomers have the forces to go after them (the Aztec are probably doomed whatever as the events of OTL strongly suggest they were hated by all and someone was taking them out eventually). Also its likely they understand pretty quickly this is a new land and not a route to China (or at least not an easy one, especially once they finally sight the great desert of the Plains prairie and realize just how big America really is) so there will probably be a much stronger focus on going south to round Africa to reach the Spice islands. With actual transoceanic travel developed much earlier (and the need to improve links with the New World driving sailing tech along at a fair clip) that's likely to see Portugal starting its investigations long before Spain is finished with the Reconquista and probably with England and France nipping at her heels this time. An early rediscovery (or more dissemination of the original Norse discovery) probably doesn't completely prevent the Crusades (there is still the issue of Jerusalem) but with a bigger target for expansion and as an outlet for violence the majority of settlers will probably go there rather than the rather precarious Outremer and even if the First Crusade succeeds it may not establish an enduring polity (they had enough trouble getting immigrants as it was. Usually Europeans only went East when the states were in deep trouble). Although with a Europe that has an outlet for its expansionist desires in the Far West and doesn't feel so under siege for the first time in centuries might be able to patch things up with Islam a bit more easily. Hard to say about Religion although by 1092 the Great Schism has already happened so the Catholics will be very much the first ones there and its hard to say if there will even be a Reformation after four centuries of altered history. However if the Crusades are averted, or at least blunted there is a good chance Byzantium survives in its original form and without the damage from the Latin occupation it might be able to hold out and reform enough that they can avoid falling to the Ottoman's. Also Venice and the Italian city states may not rise as quickly if the focus on trade switches to the Atlantic (especially if the wealth of America is discovered).
items.original_question: What if Europe colonized the Americas four centuries earlier? 1092 instead of 1492 What if widespread European colonization of the Americas started 400 years earlier in 1092, the end of the 11th century? The idea I got in my head so far involves rapid advances in naval/seafaring technology to allow for trans-oceanic voyages, and the sponsor of the first voyage and colony I'm thinking would be the Duchy of Normandy, but this can change if that's not plausible enough. What I want out of the timeline spawned by the question of thread title, is a medieval retro-future colonial-frontier sort of scenario, also going by another idea-spawning question. What if the 11th century had the technology of the 15th century? What sort of tech advances, and other sorts of points of divergence, would be needed to make the beginning of European colonization of the Americans begin its proliferation in 1092 instead of 1492? And what other ideas and questions and things should I also take into consideration? My apologies for not being able to go in-depth at explaining scenarios. I'm unfortunately a very simple person with a limited education and understanding of history and other topics needed for writing alternate history. I hope to get a discussion going that will help broaden my horizons of learning more history to write better alternate history.
items.model_answer:
If Europe had attempted to colonize the Americas in 1092, four centuries before Columbus, the entire project would have been limited, fragile, and likely short-lived. The Europe of 1092 was a fragmented feudal patchwork with no centralized states capable of sponsoring large transatlantic expeditions. The most plausible colonists were the Norse, who had already reached Newfoundland around 1000 CE but abandoned their settlement. A renewed Norse push in 1092 could have established small, subsistence-based coastal outposts in northeastern North America—similar to their Greenland colonies—relying on livestock, hunting, and intermittent trade. These settlements would have lacked the numbers, advanced weaponry, and economic motive that drove the Spanish conquests. Without firearms, horses, or the lure of known rich empires, expansion would have been a slow, grinding affair, confined to the Atlantic fringe.

Interaction with indigenous peoples would have been radically different. The great empires of the Aztec and Inca did not yet exist; the Mississippian culture was at its height, with complex chiefdoms and Cahokia’s massive influence. Norse iron, wool, and shipbuilding might have intrigued local groups, but colonizers lacked the overwhelming technological and demographic punch to topple large societies. Diseases like smallpox and measles could still have leaped from the tiny settlements and spread along trade networks, causing catastrophic epidemics over centuries rather than decades. This slower depopulation might have allowed some Native societies to rebound and adapt, perhaps acquiring metalworking or ship technology through exchange, leading to a more competitive dynamic. In many areas, indigenous polities might have absorbed or expelled the Europeans entirely.

Back in Europe, the Crusades and internal strife would have consumed attention and resources, preventing any sustained imperial follow-up. Without the later Renaissance navigational breakthroughs, the transatlantic link would have remained tenuous. The net result might have been a handful of ethnically mixed, semi-autonomous coastal enclaves—a blend of Norse, indigenous, and perhaps even Basque or Irish fisherfolk—never amounting to full-blown colonization. The Columbian Exchange would have begun in a trickle, with crops, animals, and germs moving slowly in both directions. The transformative global cascade of 1492—the rise of Atlantic empires, the mass extraction of silver, and the remaking of entire ecosystems—would not have ignited. Instead, the Americas might have developed along a more insulated but still profoundly disturbed path, until a later, more technologically equipped wave of European contact inevitably arrived.

items.question: What If an earlier, more thorough modernization of Russia
human_answers: I would highly recommend you watch NojRant's NOT the Origins of Russian Authoritarianism . If you'd like a forum post, read my posts in another thread from here onward to here : they briefly go over parts of what you're interested in, and some of it is repeated below. If you want good detail, I'd recommend Robert K. Massie's book Peter the Great . tl;dr - clothes were only a small part of the reforms, there was major modernization of the economy, education and the legal system, and you seem to have a very, very stereotyped and caricaturish understanding of the topic to speak with such confidence. The problem with the reforms was not in their superficiality, but that most of them required follow-through by Peter's successors that, for reasons I'll get into, did not happen until Catherine II some 40 years later. A highly ideological statement if ever I've heard one. Define what it means to be 'European' in clear terms. Absolutism is actually a major benefit in this situation, mainly because it is not a parliament. Parliament is essentially a tool for the ruling class to give themselves endless privileges and benefits: a ruling class composed of rural nobility would see urbanization as a threat to their power over their tenants (and ultimately their wealth) and pursue policies that deurbanize the country, whereas one dominated by bourgeois interests would be enriched by urbanization. Urbanization ultimately leads to a richer, stronger, more industrialized nation overall, while deurbanization does not. As long as Russia has a strong nobility and a comparatively weak bourgeoisie, parliament is a nonstarter for your purposes because the default net effect of parliamentary actions will be to increase nobles' control over their tenants, hence limiting urbanization, hence limiting development of private capital for industrialization. A country with no strong king to keep the nobility in check will increasingly resemble basketcases like high medieval Hungary or early modern Poland, where the nobility could ignore the king as they pleased and even fight each other as warlords ( picrel ). Even in a lesser form, this can have severe consequences: for example, under the Dual Monarchy, the Hungarian half of the empire was granted wide-ranging autonomy, which the Magyar nobility used to systematically and shortsightedly block the development of industry. The result was that Hungary remained agrarian and economically backward, even failing to compete in agriculture - the thing the Magyar nobles had sought to protect - to the extent that Russian grain imported via the Adriatic was undercutting Hungarian grain on the Austrian market. In a strong monarchy, even if the king still has to appease the nobility somewhat, he has control over the spigot of privileges and benefits and only gives them out when he has to, and expects loyal service in return - and can even retract privileges if his position is strong enough, like Ivan the Terrible did in Russia or Charles XI did in Sweden (ref. the Great Reduction ). This is constitutionally impossible with a strong parliament, though the king can always try his luck with a coup or a civil war. Even strong monarchs who retained parliaments as vestigial organs of the state, like Louis XIV, actively avoided involving them in political decisions because they knew that weak parliaments were made strong by getting involved in decisions that could've been made by the king's bureaucrats instead. However, monarchies can be weakened by unexpected deaths, child kings / regencies, changes in dynasty, coups, successful riots by the urban population against taxes, and successful rebellions by uppity nobles. These events force the king to repeal unpopular laws and grant new privileges to the nobles in exchange for their support, because his normal ability to make himself obeyed by his subjects is drastically reduced and he needs to sweeten the pot for them to obey him again. This must be avoided to preserve the king's power and prevent the nobility from pressuring him to grant more privileges. 17th century Russian tsars were weakened by the Time of Troubles, which allowed the nobility to demand a host of new concessions in exchange for their support of Mikhail Romanov as the next tsar. The most notable concession was that their pomestie fiefdoms, which were previously non-hereditary and granted to them in exchange for service to the state, were made hereditary. Russian tsars spent the next century trying to repeal these various privileges with limited success, and were occasionally hampered by new setbacks, such as the 1648 salt riot , which led to tighter restrictions on serfs being introduced to satisfy the nobility. 18th century Russian tsars were weakened by chronic succession problems, which resulted in the new tsar/tsarina having to bribe the nobility as a class with extra privileges to get them to accept their rule. The reason was that Peter had revised the succession law from male primogeniture to "Whoever the tsar chooses," meaning that the tsar's will could be forged or denied by any member of the imperial family who could bribe the palace guards to support them in a coup. Catherine I, Elizabeth, Catherine II and Alexander I all rose to the throne this way. Doable - NojRants covers this succinctly in the Serfdom section of his video. If you can't avoid the Time of Troubles, then you need to avoid all further destabilizing events which allowed the nobility to wring additional concessions out of the tsar. If you want participation in European scientific exchange, look to the Russian Academy of Sciences. Its alumni included such giants as Lomonosov: they corresponded regularly with their peers in the rest of Europe, and many foreign luminaries visited to teach at the academy, such as Euler. Many advances in cartography, botany and geology came from the work of scientists who had been educated in the Academy or invited from abroad to work there. But given the list of names you chose, I suppose your chief interest in the Enlightenment is politics. Of which I frankly don't see the point. If you want to be welcomed at the salons of Paris and London, dressing in European fashion is a bonus, otherwise you might taken as a neat little foreign curiosity. What led you to this conclusion?

I would like to see that properly thought out! ... but: You'd probably need to address the "modernisation challenge" that any Eastern European polity would face and that stems from the divergent socio-economic foundations on which society rested in Western and Eastern Europe respectively. This hearkens back to the Middle Ages and the long-term demographic consequences of the Mongol devastations and the division of labour that only became more and more entrenched over the centuries: The High Middle Ages saw a trend towards slow re-urbanisation, communalism, development of crafts, revitalisation of trade, a new surge in scholarship and education, and while the epicentres of this were in Italy, France, along the Rhine and across the channel in England, this was, in the 11th and 12th centuries, a trend that spread everywhere, towards the North and towards the East. Kiev was a huge bustling urban centre of trade, learning... I know that the "Mongol explanation" is criticised for being overused in the history of Eastern Europe. But the Mongols did wipe out particularly the urban populations and, where their influence lingered, continued to be an important indirect factor working against urban communal independence, hemming the kind of social milieu from which early modern advances stemmed. And so, even before the conquest of the Americas by Western European powers, Eastern Europe became tendentially focused on exporting unprocessed raw materials while Western Europe developed proto-capitalist structures and more and more complex structures of value addition - and while the latter fomented the growth of a bourgeoisie, the latter could do with mostly just landowners and peasants. This is the situation you're still facing in a 17th century Russia, and every new world crop that was invented and massively increased agricultural productivity in Russia would, under these circumstances, only deepen the continental division of labour. The basic difference between Dutch society and Russian society was not clothes, you are right, but it also wasn't some political or religious agenda of its individual rulers. It was, I would argue, that the Netherlands had a sizable and growing bourgeois class where ideas which we consider "modern" grew and were pushed, while Russia had much less of that. Thus, in my eyes, the real challenge you're faced with is how to close or bridge this gap of bourgeois development.

This is more thinking aloud on possible developments that you'd need than dismissing this as impossible, but "the modernization didn't go deep enough" raises the question on what would be enough. Russia is rather removed from being comparable in some significant ways to England and France even in Ivan's (as in Ivan the Terrible) time for a multitude of reasons, and that's with quite a bit longer than a POD in Fyodor III's time. You'd probably need something where there's more capital (and that going into trade and industry) for Russia to meaningfully resemble the West in the sense you're aiming for, which is not something any tsar can simply make from sheer determination and energy or Peter would have managed it OTL. Saying this was OTL too much focused on clothing and beards is being rather unfair when he genuinely wanted a stronger and richer Russia and was trying to make one, not just imititate Western European fashions. I'm not saying someone else couldn't have done better than him (I'm very sure someone more familiar with economics than I can describe his failings much better than this post), but anyone in this position has a lot of work ahead of them.

Actually, modernization did start almost immediately after the ToT. However, it is rather difficult to expect some kind of a miracle from a poor country with very limited natural resources surrounded by the aggressive enemies. So obviously the progress was slow and not because of the Dutch clothing. The beards considerably shortened during Alexey’s reign and by time of FIII death the Hungarian dress became popular. FIII conducted a fundamental administrative reform when he abolished appointments by the pedigree. Formally, it was: the imperial status was recognized throughout Europe and after the GNW it became a dominating regional piwer. Serfdom in a form everybody is talking about only started during the reign of PI and reached its apogee during the “enlightened” reign of CII. BTW, a “popular perception” among the noble classes, merchants and manufacturers by the time of CII was that serfdom is beneficent for economy. How and why would it change? AFAIK, since mid-XVII the “enlightened absolutism” was a trade mark in what you are calling “Europe” (geographically, Russia was the biggest European country). Now, this is a truly interesting part. Can you please elaborate on how exactly it will get richer within social and economic framework reasonably well related to OTL? This is a genuine question and a meaningful answer will be greatly appreciated. How Enlightenment improved life of the French lower classes in the XVIII century? Well, some of these “giants” had been simply bought (reasonably cheap) by CII, which guaranteed acceptance of the Russian aristocrats in the salons Paris as welcomed equals regardless of their intellectual capacities. I’m sure that in London’s and Paris’ equivalents of the saloons they were even more welcomed. BTW, by mid-late 1700 Russia had a reasonably well developed literature. Unfortunately, Russian drama of that time was, as in the rest of Europe, under the French influence (eek) but this did not apply to the comedies. This is quite possible by the virtue of him not being Peter and a chance to avoid the GNW. However, the problem of the natural resources will not go away and neither would one of the fools and roads.
items.original_question:
AHC: an earlier, more thorough modernization of Russia

PoD: the 1600s. I mean a Russian modernization with less emphasis on shaving beards and adopting Dutch clothing but more on modernizing the economy, education and the legal system. The end state - Russia becomes an European country by the 1700s. Serfdom isn't abolished yet (albeit it's weakened), neither is absolutism, but Russia is genuinely richer and it participates fully in the Enlightenment - by the mid-late 1700s Russian thinkers stand alongside Montesquieu, Rousseau and Diderot (or their ATL equivalents) as the intellectual giants of the era, they aren't just curiosities, they're welcomed at the saloons in Paris and London as equals. I think a healthy Fyodor III might be a good starting, IOTL he died in 1682 aged just 20, if he lives until 1720s, things might be significantly different.
items.model_answer:
If an earlier, more thorough modernization had taken root in Russia—beginning perhaps in the early 19th century rather than stuttering through incomplete reforms—the entire trajectory of Russian and global history could have been fundamentally different. Economically, an earlier industrial revolution would likely have created a more balanced, diversified economy, reducing the extreme dependence on agriculture and raw material exports that plagued the late tsarist era. A larger urban middle class and a more prosperous peasantry (freed from serfdom earlier and given access to land and education) might have fostered a stable civil society, chipping away at the autocratic monolith and making the rigid, brittle social hierarchy more fluid and resilient.

Politically, a deeper modernization would have almost certainly required constitutional limits on the tsar’s power and the growth of genuinely representative institutions—not the grudging, half-hearted Dumas of 1905. With a legal, evolutionary path for political expression, revolutionary extremism might have been marginalized. The Bolsheviks would have remained a fringe group, and the disastrous cycle of repression and radicalization that defined the late empire could have been broken. Russia might have evolved into a constitutional monarchy or a republic with strong democratic norms, avoiding the convulsion of 1917 and the subsequent civil war.

Internationally, a modernized, politically stable, and economically self-confident Russia would have been an even more formidable great power, but perhaps a less paranoid and expansionist one. The Crimean War might have been avoided or won decisively, altering the balance of power in the Ottoman Empire and the Balkans. A stronger Russia could have deterred the catastrophic gamble of World War I, or if it did break out, a more efficient logistical and industrial base might have prevented the military disasters of 1915–1916 that fatally undermined the tsar. Without the collapse of Russia into revolution, the war might have ended earlier, and the subsequent Versailles order would have been shaped by a Russia that was a victor, not a void. No Soviet Union means no Lenin, no Stalin, no Cold War, no Iron Curtain dividing Europe. The 20th century’s nightmares of totalitarian ideology, purges, and the global rivalries that fueled proxy wars might have been dramatically lessened, and the fate of democracy and empire in the modern world would have looked very different.

items.question: What If Britain and France made peace in 1811?
human_answers: I definitely agree that the conflict in Spain would continue, and that some form of renewed conflict in Europe down the line is inevitable, but I don’t think Napoleon wouldn’t try to conclude a peace with Britain, so long as it was on terms favourable to him. Now, whether that is possible is a rather different question. The Whigs at least had no interest in continuing to fund the peninsular war regardless, but in negotiations, they are likely to push for a restoration of Portugal and Hannover, and for France to at least withdraw from direct control of the rest of the Hanseatic cities and the Netherlands. It’s quite a lot for Napoleon to be willing to give up, though could possibly be paired with his longstanding designs on Sicily and a British withdrawal from Malta, as well as the return of occupied Dutch and French colonies. Regardless, I don’t think the British could get everything they want.

No mention has been made of the Continental System. I presume it is abolished as part of the peace treaty. And Britain's blockade is lifted. Anything less makes peace a non starter. Predictions from here: Overall peace is going to be short lived. Every one will be watching France waiting for a propitious moment to reduce the almost total hegemony France has. Nap will maintain a large military to enforce his hegemony. I don't know that this is sustainable. Spain will remain a bleeding ulcer. The Spanish people will continue to resist. Nap's best chance at lasting peace is to pull out and return a Bourbon to power. Remaining in a constant state of this kind of war drains resources, but brings no benefits. The best he can hope for (remaining in the conflict) is an uneasy truce where Joseph is somewhat accepted/propped up, while a low level of guerilla warfare continues. The entire Spanish colonial sphere is lost even faster than OTL. Cuba/puerto rico might remain attached, but I doubt it. I don't know whether Britain has destroyed Spain's infrastructure yet, but if not, Spain could actually emerge from the conflict in better shape without Britain's help than with it. Portugal might be able to hold out behind the line of T, as their soldiers have been trained up to a better level than before 1807, but as the British had supplied the top chain of command, they'll be left rudderless. I think their fate lies in how much stomach Nap has for continuing his Iberian adventure. It would be interesting to see what results if Nap simply walks away. OTL, the British acted as a regency while the Braganza court remained in Brazil. Joao did not want to return. Pedro was too young. Portugal is likely to be chaos. Should France manage to take control, Portugal itself may end up in better shape, but the entirety of the colonial sphere attaches to Brazil. I don't think the return of French colonies does much for France. Haiti is finished as a rich colony. Martinique and Guadeloupe, where Britain ironically enforced the status quo maintaining the slave system after capturing the islands, might still hold value. When the Nap Wars resume, Britain faces a hard choice - join in and try to reset the balance of power, or stay on the sidelines and have the European dynamic dictated to them. If they join in, they're quickly going to regret dropping out in the first place. They had France on the ropes in Portugal/Spain, and now they'll have to start all over again. Who knows what has become of Wellington.

The default of the Revolution certainly left its mark, but Napoleon was also ideologically opposed to debt, in part because of fiscal conservatism (there was a hyperinflation crisis during the Revolution), but also because it would have meant making himself dependent on the financial market, and he feared that the banker would try to exert political pressure on him. But I don't think he necessarily tried to raise a large amount of debt from the public market, he preferred to use a sinking fund controlled by one of his appointees for that. For the reparation, he had ways to force the issue, like sending his army in and making the host pay for its quartering. This was the way he was making his puppets, like the Kingdom of Italy, contribute, and alongside their allied contingent, it saved him as much money as the reparations brought him. For Prussia specifically, they were raising a large debt to pay the reparation, with Napoleon himself being one of their creditors, so they probably intended to pay. But you also have to take into account that Napoleon did not hesitate too much to raise taxes (he essentially brought back every indirect tax of the Ancien Régime) or defer payment, after the Restoration, the Bourbons had to pay the equivalent of one year of fiscal revenues in unpaid expenses.
items.original_question: What if Britain and France made peace in 1811? In 1810 King George III suffered a mental breakdown, and in early 1811, his son the Prince of Wales, later to reign as King George IV, was installed as regent by Parliament. The Prince Regent was widely expected to dismiss Spencer Percival’s government, and appoint Lord Grenville as Prime Minister, but was dissuaded from this course by his mother. Unlike the Tories, Grenville and the Whigs were sceptical of the conflict with France, particularly the expense of maintaining Wellington’s army in the Peninsula War, and had they taken power in 1811, whilst Wellesley’s army was holed up behind the lines of Torres Vedras, attempts at negotiating a peace with France are not an unrealistic prospect. Negotiations in 1807 touted an exchange of Sicily for Hannover, and Britain would retain the Cape Colony and Malta, whilst returning other Dutch and French colonial possessions, though these ultimately broke down over Sicily. Talks in 1808 even saw Napoleon offer to concede both Hannover and Portugal, though there is some question of how serious both sides were in this later negotiation. Both of these were also viewed by the Tory governments as a chance for a respite alike to Amiens, rather than to conclude the conflict. The Whigs, less intractable towards the idea of a French dominated Europe would be willing to pursue a long term peace. In addition to questions over Portugal, Hannover and the colonies though, France had by this point annexed the Netherlands and the Hanseatic cities, both of which are likely to be sticking points for British negotiators (although these annexations were in part to enforce the continental system). What terms could realistically be feasibly agreed by both sides at this time? With the end of the war with Britain in 1811, Napoleon’s invasion of Russia appears unlikely to my mind, though relations between the two emperors would undoubtedly continue to deteriorate. The peace would also presumably be unpopular domestically in Britain, where support for the war remained high. Austria, Prussia and Sweden all additionally had cause to want revenge against France and Napoleon, and so it seems unlikely that this peace would be entirely conclusive, and some form of renewed conflict seems eventually likely, even if it only comes with Bonaparte’s death. The aftermath of Amiens however suggests that this might well come sooner. There is however also the question of whether France could afford to maintain their precarious financial situation, and in particular continue to field their army without the subsides of allies, the reparations of former enemies and loot. It seems unlikely France can afford to demobilise in the face of their European rivals, so would this possibly prompt further campaigns? Perhaps against Russia regardless or the Ottomans?
items.model_answer:
If Britain and France had made peace in 1811, the Napoleonic Wars would have ended abruptly at their height, with Napoleon as master of continental Europe from Spain to the Russian border. The immediate trigger might have been mutual exhaustion: Britain’s economy was strained by the Continental System and a credit crisis, while France was bogged down in the grueling Peninsular War and facing growing unrest in annexed territories. A settlement would likely have recognized Napoleon’s dominance over western and central Europe, with Britain withdrawing from Portugal and ceding occupied colonies in exchange for French abandonment of the blockade against British trade.

The most transformative effect would have been the survival of Napoleon’s empire. Without the Russian catastrophe of 1812 and the subsequent War of the Sixth Coalition, the Corsican’s regime could have consolidated for decades. The Confederation of the Rhine, the Duchy of Warsaw, and the satellite kingdoms in Spain, Italy, and Naples would have endured, permanently reshaping the European map. Prussia and Austria, crammed and disarmed, would have remained sullen but powerless, while Russia, without the shock of invasion, might have drifted into a cold peace punctuated by occasional frontier skirmishes.

With peace, the British economy would have revived swiftly as continental markets reopened, but Britain’s strategic position would have been transformed. The Royal Navy would still rule the waves, but without a landward threat to contain France, Britain might have pivoted more aggressively toward imperial expansion overseas—accelerating the takeover of India and competing with Russia in the “Great Game” earlier. The War of 1812 with the United States might never have occurred, since the core grievances of impressment and trade restrictions would have faded; an earlier Anglo-American rapprochement could have followed, altering the balance of power in North America.

France under a secure Napoleon would likely have seen the completion of the Napoleonic Code’s reforms, the consolidation of a rationalized administration, and continued secularization across Europe, all while suppressing nationalist stirrings by severe repression. The Industrial Revolution might have spread more slowly on the continent without the dismantling of guilds and internal barriers forced by the wars, but France’s own industrialization could have accelerated with British technology flowing freely in peacetime.

In the long run, a lasting Napoleonic order would have muffled the rise of German and Italian nationalism, forcing those movements to mutate or wait. Liberal and constitutional ideas, championed by Britain, would have been locked in a decades-long ideological struggle with French autocracy, possibly bursting out in a later, even more violent wave of revolutions in the 1830s or 1840s. A peace in 1811 thus would not have simply ended a war; it would have created a bipolar European order, with Britain as the oceanic hegemon and France as the continental colossus, profoundly shaping the course of modern history.

items.question: What If the Mongol Empire had gone to Western Europe instead of the Levant?
human_answers: You are thinking of the Mongol's as a unified force which by this time is not exactly correct. Hulegu and the Ilkhanate were based in Iran (mostly) so the OTL force would not be interested in expanding in Eastern Europe. Batu / Berke and the Golden Horde started their drift towards Islam in this period but their control over the European fringe via their vassals in Kiev and Muscovy wasn't absolute and relied on the tolerance of their Orthodox faith. Any attack on Europe may well become religious in nature (which by itself is an interesting counterfactual) and I suspect any support from the Russian principalities would be lukewarm perhaps even moving towards outright rebellion. It would also be short lived given that the Mongol Civil War is coming. Biggest outcome if the Russian principalities do revolt could be a more Islamised Russia which would be a huge change for world history.

Is there any reason to assume that the forests of western europe were somehow “denser” than those of the eastern? Specifically, those of the Central Russia? BTW, it is not like the Mongols uniformly came from the open steppe: IIRC, Subotai came from Uryankay area which, AFAIK, mostly forests and mountains and he was doing quite well in the Russian forests and pretty much everywhere else. Of course, the Southern direction was much richer than the western one but #1 was the eastern one - China. AFAIK, the South ended up being problematic due to a limited feeding base for the horses but all theories about Mongolian conquest of the west are seemingly ignoring allocation of the resources. The western campaign (including Russia) presumably started with a big force but its second stage, Hungary and Poland, was on a much lesser scale. The map on the OP has “Ulus Jochi” and “Ulus Batu” as separate entities but this was not the case: Batu was a titular head of the Ulus of Jochi. Was there an interest in Mongolia in expanding Ulus Jochi even further at the expense of other endeavors (and other family members)? IMO, this is unlikely because China remained the main theater (BTW, Subotai was sent there after the european campaigns). Were there unlimited human resources? Hardly: part of Hulagu’s force were troops “lended” by Batu. So, with what would Batu conduct his european conquest and why would the Great Khan be interested in its continuation? Formally, the task as formulated by Genghis was fulfilled: the Kipchaks punished and subdued and “the last sea” (Adriatics would do) reached. Was Batu too interested? It does not look like this was a case because he had to create a brand new state from the scratch with the very limited resources (something like 5,000 Mongols).
items.original_question: What if the Mongol Empire had gone to Western Europe instead of the Levant? https://www.reddit.com/r/imaginarymaps/comments/pkb97x/what_if_the_mongols_invaded_europe_the_old_world A sudden interesting thought came to mind. What if, unlike in OTL, the Mongol Empire had not expanded into the Levant and had instead resumed its campaign into Europe? In this TL, during the reign of Möngke Khan, the Mongol Empire invaded Europe again instead of attacking the Abbasid Caliphate. Assume that, starting with the Kingdom of Hungary, they continue pushing westward into the Holy Roman Empire, France, and beyond Western Europe for as long as they keep winning. What I’m curious about is this: 1. What kind of POD would be needed for this to be possible? 2. To what extent would this actually be feasible? - Could the Mongol Empire conquer Western Europe as well, just as it did in Eastern Europe? - Or, unlike in Eastern Europe, would it struggle in Western Europe? 3. If this did happen, what changes would follow? - The Mongol Empire’s advance into Western Europe. - The survival of the Abbasid Caliphate.
items.model_answer:
If the Mongol Empire had directed its full military might toward Western Europe instead of the Levant, the continent would have been reshaped in a cataclysm of fire, terror, and radical transformation. In the mid-13th century, the Mongols were at the apex of their power, having perfected a war machine of unmatched speed, coordination, and psychological ferocity. The fragmented political landscape of Europe—a patchwork of feudal kingdoms, quarreling principalities, and independent city-states—would have presented a rich target, far less coherent than the Mamluk Sultanate that halted them at Ain Jalut in 1260. A concerted push west, likely building on the earlier incursions into Hungary and Poland, would have begun with the systematic obliteration of Eastern Europe’s remaining military forces, followed by a thrust into the heart of the Holy Roman Empire.

The initial Mongol advance would have been devastating. European armies, built around heavily armored knights and rigid feudal levies, were ill-suited to counter the nomadic composite bow, feigned retreats, and the encirclement tactics that had already crushed Russians, Poles, and Hungarians in the 1240s. The great pitched battles—whether at the gates of Vienna, on the plains of France, or in the passes of the Alps—would almost certainly have ended in catastrophic defeats for the defenders. Popes might have called for Crusades, but the slow muster of religiously inspired armies would have arrived piecemeal, only to be annihilated in detail. Cities that resisted, like Paris, Cologne, or Rome itself, would have suffered the same fate as Baghdad: sack, mass slaughter, and deliberate psychological terror designed to compel others to surrender without a fight. The Mongols, experienced in siege warfare from their Chinese counterparts, would have adapted to European fortifications, deploying trebuchets, gunpowder (if balloons of the period), and sappers against stone castles, though the dense forests and countless fortified points would have slowed their momentum.

Yet permanent conquest would have been far more challenging than terrorizing the countryside. Western Europe’s terrain—heavy woodlands, river networks, and mountains—limited the vast grasslands necessary to sustain Mongol herds. Logistics and the difficulty of controlling a population of hostile Christians, much larger and more entrenched than the steppe nomads, would have forced the invaders to adapt in ways they had not in Persia or China. The most plausible outcome is that the Mongols would have established a European khanate, perhaps a western offshoot of the Golden Horde, that dominated the continent through a combination of direct rule over the plains of Hungary and the Pannonian Basin, and tributary arrangements with subjugated kingdoms further west. Local rulers who submitted might have been allowed to remain as vassals, while others were replaced by Mongol-appointed governors. The Khagan’s distant capital at Karakorum would have struggled to maintain control; a European khanate would likely have drifted toward autonomy, much as the Ilkhanate did in Persia, and might even have adopted Latin Christianity over time, following the pattern of Mongol elites blending with local cultures.

The long-term civilizational consequences would have been profound. The sudden destruction of the feudal nobility in battle, followed by Mongol-imposed peace and taxation, could have shattered the manorial system and accelerated the rise of centralized states, perhaps triggering an earlier Renaissance—fuelled by Mongol patronage of trade and knowledge exchange along a safer Silk Road that now stretched from China to London. The Black Death, if it still arrived later in the century, might have found a radically different demographic and political landscape, possibly even originating from altered trade routes. Culturally, the Mongol destruction of monasteries and universities could have meant the irrecoverable loss of classical learning, or conversely, the infusion of Asian technologies like printing, gunpowder, and advanced astronomy might have sparked an earlier scientific revolution. Meanwhile, with the Mongol focus redirected, the Levant would have remained a contested zone between the surviving Crusader states and a Mamluk or Ayyubid power unchallenged by Hulagu’s invasion. Baghdad might have survived as an Islamic intellectual center, and Islam would have faced no equal to the psychological blow of its sack, possibly leading to a more resilient and earlier Ottoman-like ascendancy in the Eastern Mediterranean, free from Mongol rivalries.

In essence, a Mongol conquest of Western Europe would not have been a simple extension of their Asian empires, but a messy, violent collision that recast the West as a frontier of greater Eurasia. The immediate result would be unimaginable destruction; the legacy would be a Europe transformed—earlier unified in some form, yet permanently woven into a global tapestry of trade, disease, and ideas centuries before its historical Age of Exploration. The world we know, built on a Europe that was able to develop in relative isolation after the Mongols turned away, would never have come to be.

items.question: What If Americans capture Quebec in 1775. How does Quebec's culture & society develop?
human_answers: I can easily see Quebec not wanting to be part of either France, or USA. So they'll opt for independence. France never really wanted it back, so they won't get into their own American Revolution. Even if they did, it is the cost that will impact the French Revolution. The cost will add to French woes. This notion that France will rise up in revolution because Quebec wants independence is erroneous. France wanted regime/gov't change, which is not at all what Quebec wants (independence). France will add Quebec to the list of grievances. That does NOT make Quebec the birthplace of this alt FR. There were various causes of the ARW. One of them was putting Ohio under Canadian jurisdiction. Plus the French and Indian War was fought over the Ohio Valley, and led to a lot of the grievances leading to ARW. No one considers Ohio the birthplace of the AR. Semantics? maybe, but I don't think so.

It is difficult to ascertain how the French in Canada felt, as they lived in a quasi-medieval subsistence economy. Although not under full-blown feudalism, their society was paternalistic, hierarchical, and agrarian. The Church and the seigneurs (many of the seigneuries were owned by religious orders) were the pillars of authority. This is crucial in explaining the lack of widespread revolutionary fervour. However, in the late eighteenth century, there remained a cultural and sentimental connection to France, particularly to the Ancien Régime and the monarchy. After the executions of Louis XVI and Marie Antoinette, masses were said for them, and the French press in Quebec noted this. They were mourning the grandson of their last French sovereign, not celebrating the secular republic that executed him. In December 1778, from Boston, French Admiral d’Estaing called on the Canadiens to rise and rejoin their motherland, but this was difficult as Canada was where most British forces were stationed. It is unclear whether they wished to return to France, but the Continental Congress felt uneasy about the French returning to North America. Because the Canadiens were largely illiterate (literacy was still below 40% in 1850), it is difficult to say whether they were politically sophisticated, as the colony had been largely marginal and lacked a large merchant class under French rule. Education was not widespread and was largely controlled by seminaries or convents. It was even less politically sophisticated than the Spanish colonies in the Americas. My guess is that independence would have been the least likely of options, unless the Bishop of Quebec assumed the role of head of government.

Then the place will find a way to get out of American control ASAP. Mismatched expectations and all that because of a fundamental misreading by the Continental Army/Congress of the situation, particularly WRT the Quebec Act. The French never wanted to retain Canada après la Conquête because the sugar colonies in the Caribbean were far more valuable, plus lots of bad blood between the Canadiens and Versailles about which direction their part of New France should go. You'd basically be accelerating the French Revolution's TL but with a Canadien cause - and this time the British would come off as the good guys by allying with the habitants, whether or not it takes it back under its wing or accepts it as an independent country but under the British sphere of influence. And it finds a way to get out of the US ASAP, particularly if the initial military occupation goes as OTL and they basically alienated everyone. More probable than getting annexed by the US. Considering Quebec in this case would be a direct cause for the French Revolution ITTL, that's easy to remark on. While still predominantly Francophone (albeit with Canadian French given the same recognition as, say, Brazilian Portuguese), society and culture would take a more, say, Argentine or Uruguayan-like direction but w/ its own quirks (including probably far more indigenous influence) and probably different relationships among groups that would be relatively more egalitarian and opposed to reinstating the colonial relationship. Considering the British would still be next door viz. Newfoundland and Nova Scotia, as well as the HBC doing its thing, British influence would remain strong and that would include the cultural sphere, too.

It depends on how the Americans treat the Canadiens, and how they handle the Iroquois. If the Americans can't keep the Iroquois mostly neutral, and if they prevent them from trading with the Canadiens, then Quebec will want want to leave in a hurry. If the Americans could be deft in the administration of Quebec, better in battle, luckier with allied victories, and more skillful in peace negotiation I think there is a good chance that the Canadiens would want to be in a confederacy, or a customs union with a mutual defense pact. The centralizing reforms of the Constitution would likely have been opposed by the Canadiens as antifederalism, which brings me to the next point, though it is possible they could remain in the union if it transitions from Articles of Confederation to Constitution. While the Canadiens would most likely have forbade slavery, that doesn't mean they would have been abolitionists in the vein of the northeastern Calvinists and Quakers. While they could have been like the 1840s and 1850s Free Soilers, their antifederalism and relative lack of industrialization might have moved them into common cause with Southern states. The Canadiens also could have been aligned with the "Westerners" in looking for federally funded internal developments to help with their access to Atlantic ports, and their access to settling Upper Canada and Indiana/Illinois Territory. Being so close to Nova Scotia and Newfoundland the Canadiens could also be interested in a strong navy. So perhaps an American Quebec could be allied with someone like Calhoun. As for the issue of Loyalist Migration, their emigration would likely have been reduced if they didn't have British Upper Canada as a destination. Many of the Loyalists would have resigned themselves to life in the new government. There still would have been Loyalist emigration from both America and Lower Canada, and there would still be a movement of Loyalists to Upper Canada and other territories despite them being no longer British Empire owned. So those populations would have thrown a new political impulse into the country later especially after the Constitution is ratified.

I'd assume a French route with independence after the French revolution. Maybe some nobility or rich flee to Quebec during the revolution. I'd think US keeps what it would get otl plus Nova Scotia, New Brunswick and Prince Edward island. Ontario might go to the U.S. While Newfoundland and Labrador goes to Quebec. The American loyalists could be moved into western Canada to try to colonize Western Canada. England might be more harsh in dealing with the Oregon territory. You could see a war over it with Quebec siding with a side. Should U.S. Win they might get British Columbia in the treaty. Quebec might get islands in Nunavut. Russia in this timeline would probably favor selling Alaska to England. With more northern territory. I can see the South looking for more Mexican territory. There's a possibility the slave and free state addition could continue on longer. This causes a delay of the civil war potentially.
items.original_question: What if Americans capture Quebec in 1775. How does Quebec's culture & society develop? So having just watched a new video from Blue, it gave me an idea of dusting off an old topic I used to talk about In 1775, the Continental Army under Generals, Richard Montgomery, Daniel Morgan, James Livingston, and Benedict Arnold (Yes, that Benedict Arnold) marched north into Canada in an attempt to capture Quebec from the British and persuade the French Canadians in joining the revolution. It went well for part of the expedition at first, with Montgomery nearly capturing British Govenor Guy Carleton in Montreal. Meanwhile Arnold's part journeyed through the wilderness to get to Quebec City, which was very difficult. However, by the time the Americans gotten to Quebec, a snowstorm occurred and the battle turned into an utter disaster. Montgomery got killed, Arnold was wounded, smallpox plagued the Americans, the British suffered few causalities, and the Americans managed to alienate the Canadians. Meanwhile, Carleton received reinforcements and made a counter offensive that drove the Americans back to Fort Ticonderoga. For context, what if the Americans captured Quebec? Say Montgomery captured Govenor Guy Carleton and the Americans managed to catch Quebec City by surprise. In my previous thread about the fate of Quebec (Roughly around Lower Canada; Upper Canada is a whole other can of worms), there were four possibilities I gave, but we're going to talk about three: A) French route- The Americans offer Quebec back to France for support in their war, meaning France regains Quebec by the end of the war B) American route- The Americans annex Quebec, making Quebec part of the USA. C) Independent route- The Americans make Quebec into a sister republic, making Quebec independent by the end of the war. (There's no British route since that OTL) Now, I want to focus on one particular aspect of the fate of Quebec: Culture. If Quebec wasn't under the British/TTL Canada, what would culture be like for the French Canadians. Depending on the route we take, how would culture, society, art, cuisine, fashion, etc, develop for the French Canadians? In the French route, how would Quebec be affected by the French Revolution? In the American route, how would Quebec develop under the USA? In the Independent route, how would Quebec develop stuck between the British and Americans while having access to the St Lawrence?
items.model_answer:
If the American invasion of Quebec had succeeded in 1775 and the province had become part of the fledgling United States—likely as the 14th state—its cultural and societal trajectory would have diverged sharply from the path it took under British rule and eventual Canadian Confederation. Rather than evolving as an isolated, French-Catholic bastion within an Anglo-Protestant empire, Quebec would have been thrust into a revolutionary republic deeply suspicious of Catholicism and monarchical institutions. The likely outcome is a more rapid and profound Anglicization, but one tempered by political necessity and the resilience of the local population, producing a distinct, bilingual, and politically complex society.

In the immediate aftermath of conquest (or, from the American perspective, liberation), the Continental Congress and local occupation authorities would have faced the same dilemma that the British confronted with the Quebec Act of 1774: how to govern a vast, agrarian, French-speaking, Catholic population with deeply different legal and social traditions. The American leadership, despite its anti-Catholic rhetoric, would have been forced into pragmatism. Figures like Washington and Franklin understood that alienating the *Canadiens* would risk losing the territory. Thus, early American governance likely would have guaranteed religious freedom, retained French civil law in local matters, and left the seigneurial land tenure system temporarily intact, much as the British had done. The Catholic Church, which historically became the institutional backbone of French-Canadian identity, might have been allowed to function—perhaps with some restrictions initially—to secure the clergy’s loyalty. However, unlike under the British, the Church would face a state with no established religion and a powerful republican ideology that emphasized individual liberty over hierarchical intermediaries. Over time, the Church’s social and political influence would have eroded faster, challenged by American secularism, the franchise, and the diffusion of Protestant voluntary associations.

The critical engine of change would have been migration and political integration. With peace, American land speculators, merchants, and settlers from New England and New York would have flowed into the St. Lawrence lowlands, drawn by farmland and the fur trade’s reorganization advantage. Montreal might have grown into a major entrepôt for the Great Lakes trade, its merchant class increasingly Anglo-American. English would have gradually replaced French as the language of commerce and upward mobility—much earlier and more pervasively than it did under the British, where French was sustained by a rural majority and clerical nationalism. In an American Quebec, French-speakers would have had political rights from the start, but the demographic balance would shift against them sooner. However, the sheer size and rootedness of the *Canadien* population—some 70,000 in 1775—would have ensured that they remained a potent voting bloc, likely commanding substantial influence in state politics. A unique political culture might have emerged: a strong, Catholic-flavored Democratic-Republican faction defending agrarian interests, customary law, and linguistic rights against Yankee Federalist merchants and Protestant reformers. This tension could have made Quebec an electoral battleground and a corridor of cultural compromise.
