EPISODE THREE​ German Pact ​ ​ A sudden storm breaking out across Europe had created a massive shockwave. Austria, still struggling to recover from the economic and military wounds of the War of the Second Coalition, was deeply displeased by France’s abrupt rekindling of hostilities. Emperor Francis II had been expecting a long period of peace, one he intended to devote to revitalizing Germany. Unfortunately, history had once again disappointed him. His federalist ambitions had not yet completely faded, but this meant confronting French republicanism earlier than anticipated. Moreover, following the referendum held on 18 February 1803 and the subsequent election, the country transitioned into what was called a presidential system. As a result, Fourier—who came to power and was a prominent representative of socialist thought—began spreading his ideas more widely across Europe. This signified a gradual shift of the German peoples toward republicanism. Although the Kingdom of Prussia and the Habsburg Monarchy did not hold each other in high regard, they shared a common enemy: France and republicanism. Approximately one week had passed since the outbreak of the Franco-Spanish War. French armies advanced rapidly, exploiting the dire condition of the Spanish forces to seize Catalonia and push toward Eastern Aragon. The Basque region had also fallen. Emperor Francis convened his cabinet, and they debated at length what course of action should be taken. Johann Amadeus Franz, the Minister of Finance of the era, was firmly opposed to breaking the peace with France, as any potential war would further devastate Austria’s already fragile economy. József Alvinczi, the Chief of the General Staff, argued that this war represented an opportunity to eliminate both France and the spread of republican ideas on the European continent. He maintained that, as demonstrated in the previous conflict, the Austrian army was not in as poor a condition as believed and demanded that an open ultimatum be issued to France. However, the Emperor had a different plan in mind. Although there was no certainty it would succeed, he deemed it worth attempting. For this reason, he decided to send a delegate to the Kingdom of Prussia, carrying a note requesting a private meeting with the King. The delegation set out on 15 March 1803. Meanwhile, across Europe, no clear decision had yet emerged from the British Isles. Prime Minister Henry Addington had no desire to see Spain under French control, but he also believed that the British Army was not yet prepared. After lengthy discussions with other statesmen, he sent an envoy to the Kingdom of Portugal to further expand the Anglo-Portuguese Alliance and present several proposals. In the meantime, the delegation sent by Austria to Prussia returned two weeks later. The Emperor’s proposal to the King of Prussia was to intervene in the Franco-Spanish War by forming a German coalition. The Prussian King, eager to enhance his prestige among the German states, responded favorably and announced his acceptance. Thus, the German Pact was formed. Both sides began final preparations for their already mobilized armies, and within approximately two weeks, everything was ready. A note bearing the personal signatures of both the Emperor and the King was delivered to the French delegates by a joint Austro-Prussian mission. The note demanded that France sever its alliance with the United States, withdraw from Spain, and agree to certain trade arrangements. French President Charles Fourier tore the original document to pieces in parliament. This act provided the Habsburg Monarchy and the Kingdom of Prussia with sufficient legitimacy to launch a military intervention against France. Emperor Francis II was deeply uneasy about Russia’s ambiguous stance. He neither wanted Russia to emerge excessively strong nor excessively weak. Poland could be the first step, and the Russian flag might one day fly over Hungary or the borders of the Holy Roman Empire. Taking such a risk seemed irrational. Therefore, depending on the course of the war, he considered enticing Russia into joining their side by offering the Balkan territories of the already weakened Ottoman Empire—despite his preference for preserving the balance of power in the Balkans and Eastern Europe. The French threat, however, took precedence. Although the United States did not yet pose a direct threat to Europe, it continued to threaten the colonial powers in the Americas. While it had not yet entered the conflict, such an involvement was not impossible. On the other hand, the Emperor foresaw that the French government’s aggressive and overly idealistic actions would ultimately lead to its downfall. By initiating this war, France had effectively shot itself in the foot, and these events would pave the way for a rise in anti-French sentiment throughout Europe.

Without Napoleon’s return in 1799, the coup against the Directory would still likely have occurred, but it would have taken a very different shape. Sieyès, the political mastermind seeking a strong executive, had already lost his first choice—General Joubert—at Novi. Without Napoleon as his “sword,” Sieyès would have turned to a less charismatic general like Moreau, Jourdan, or perhaps Bernadotte. These men lacked Napoleon’s personal ambition and ruthless political instinct, so the resulting regime—probably still a Consulate—would have been more collegial and less authoritarian, with Sieyès as the dominant civilian figure.

Militarily, the absence of Napoleon’s genius would have been felt immediately. The War of the Second Coalition was not going well for France before Marengo; without that stunning victory, the Republic might have been forced into an earlier and less favorable peace, ceding Italy and the Rhine frontier. Internally, royalist forces would have been emboldened, and the fragile republic could have collapsed, leading either to a restored Bourbon monarchy by 1804–1805 or to prolonged instability and civil strife. Reforms such as the Civil Code, the Bank of France, and centralized administration were not solely Napoleon’s ideas—many were in the air—but their systematic implementation required his singular drive. Without him, France would have modernized more slowly and unevenly.

Europe would have been spared the Napoleonic Wars, but also the sweeping reform of legal systems, the dissolution of the Holy Roman Empire, and the spread of nationalism. The Concert of Europe might never have formed in the same way, and the revolutions of the 19th century would have unfolded against a more conservative, fragmented map. In short, removing Napoleon from 1799 changes not just French history but the entire trajectory of the modern world, likely delaying constitutionalism, national unification, and the rise of the modern state.

Considering their interest is not even religious (GB: Protestant, France: Catholic, Russia: Orthodox) and that really none of these Great Powers saw the Greek War of Independence with positive eyes (to them it was no different than the revolutions in Spain, Portugal and Naples; which, btw, they sent huge armies to crush). If the Greek War of Independence had triggered the sudden, complete collapse of the Ottoman Empire in the 1820s—and an expansive “Great Plan” had immediately restored a Hellenic-dominated state stretching from the Peloponnese to Constantinople and western Anatolia—the European order would have been convulsed decades before the Crimean War and the Balkan crises that actually unfolded. No power was prepared for a rapid Ottoman vacuum, and the result would have been a chaotic, multilateral free-for-all rather than a clean Greek revival.

First, the very survival of a Greater Greece would have depended on the forbearance of the powers that had just crushed Napoleon. Russia, which saw itself as the Orthodox heir to Byzantium, would likely have invaded the Balkans under the pretext of protecting Christians but in reality to seize Constantinople and the Straits. A Russian occupation of the city would have triggered an immediate British and French naval intervention, risking a general European war far earlier than 1853. The Concert of Europe, still fragile in the 1820s, could have shattered, and the “Eastern Question” would have been answered not by decades of managed decline but by a partition crisis in which Austria, Britain, France, and Russia carved up Ottoman territories into spheres of influence.

Greece itself would have been too weak to hold its maximalist claims. The fledgling state had no navy capable of matching the Great Powers, no administrative machinery to govern a multi-ethnic empire, and a society riven by factional conflicts. Even if a Greek king (perhaps Leopold of Saxe-Coburg, who briefly accepted and then refused the Greek throne) had been installed in Constantinople, he would have faced immediate revolts from Muslims, Bulgarians, and other groups who had no desire to trade Ottoman rule for Greek domination. A “Byzantine” restoration would have been stillborn, quickly reduced to a rump state by foreign pressure or internal collapse.

Elsewhere, the early disintegration of the empire would have accelerated national movements not only in Serbia, Wallachia, and Moldavia but also in Bosnia, Albania, and among the Armenians and Kurds. Without the Ottoman framework, these groups would have fought each other and the encroaching empires, producing a patchwork of conflict early in the 19th century. The Middle East would have fractured: Egypt under Muhammad Ali had already demonstrated its autonomy; with the sultan gone, he would have openly seized Syria and the Hejaz, challenging the Greek claim to Jerusalem and setting off an Arab–Greek–Russian contest for the Holy Places. North Africa would have fallen under some combination of French, British, and local rule, with Algeria’s conquest perhaps accelerated.

In short, an early Ottoman collapse after a sweeping Greek success would not have meant a peaceful realization of the Megali Idea but an earlier and more violent version of the Eastern Question, with the Great Powers imposing a settlement that redrew borders far more radically than in 1832 or 1878. Greece would have been left with a modest coastal enclave at most, while the bulk of the lost Ottoman domains would have been divided into protectorates or absorbed by Russia, Austria, and Britain. The nationalist energies that the Greek cause inspired would have been channeled into rival movements, and the 19th-century Balkan powder keg would have begun exploding even before the term “Balkanization” existed.

If the French had become one of the largest communities in the United States, the nation’s cultural, linguistic, and political landscape would likely be profoundly different, weaving a strong Francophone thread into the fabric of American identity. Such a scenario could have emerged from a more successful French colonial strategy, a massive wave of immigration from France or other Francophone regions (like Canada, Haiti, or West Africa) at a critical juncture, or even a different outcome of the Louisiana Purchase that preserved a vast French-speaking territory.

The most immediate and visible change would be linguistic. Instead of a largely monolingual English-speaking nation with a significant Spanish-speaking minority, the U.S. might function as a de facto bilingual country, with French enjoying widespread use in government, education, and daily life. Entire regions—beyond modern Louisiana and New England—could be Francophone strongholds, perhaps the Great Lakes, the Mississippi Valley, or the Pacific Northwest, where French place names already hint at another history. Public signage, official documents, and national media would routinely accommodate both languages, and the vitality of French might spark earlier and more robust bilingual education movements, softening the historic nativist resistance to multilingualism.

Culturally, a large French community would reshape America’s self-conception. The dominant Anglo-Protestant narrative would be balanced by a powerful Catholic and secular republican tradition rooted in the French Enlightenment. The tension between a puritanical work ethic and a more Mediterranean joie de vivre could lead to a different rhythm of life, with stronger protections for leisure, culinary culture, and the arts. Gastronomy, wine consumption, and café society would likely be more deeply entrenched across the country. In literature, philosophy, and political thought, French intellectual currents—from existentialism to postmodernism—might find a more direct and earlier purchase in American universities and public debate, potentially shifting the national penchant for pragmatism toward a greater embrace of abstract theory.

Politically, the presence of a large French community would introduce a distinct electoral bloc with its own historical preoccupations. Unlike the English colonial legacy of limited government and common law, the French tradition carries a strong centralizing, étatist impulse and a civil law system in its heartland. This could manifest in greater support for state-led social programs, universalism, and a more assertive foreign policy that at times aligns with—and at other times tugs against—Anglo-American hegemony. The community might serve as a bridge between the U.S. and the Francophone world, deepening ties with Canada (perhaps averting Quebec’s isolation), the Caribbean, Africa, and Europe, and making the U.S. a more active member of international bodies like La Francophonie. Religious dynamics would also shift: a large French population would swell the ranks of American Catholicism and possibly secularism, challenging the historical dominance of Protestant denominations and reframing debates on church-state separation, education, and morality.

Even the psychology of American exceptionalism might evolve. With a strong internal voice that remembers an alternative colonial experiment—one that produced a different revolution and a different notion of liberty—the American historical narrative would become more pluralistic. The foundational myth of the Pilgrims and the frontier would share space with the legacies of Champlain, Lafayette, and the Code Noir. This richer, more complicated past could foster a more self-critical and globally aware national identity, less tempted to view its path as uniquely ordained.

In essence, a French community of such magnitude would not merely add a new accent to the American chorus; it would fundamentally re-key the composition, infusing the United States with a deeper duality between Anglo-Saxon pragmatism and French humanist idealism, and blurring the lines between what the world considers “American” and “Francophone.”

Sea journeys at the time were extremely dangerous (I don’t remember if Catalina got lucky, but both Joanna and Margaret got close to die in their respective wedding journeys) reason for which Philip used his friendship with the French King for securing a land passage into France for going to receive the investitures. Eleanor and Charles at the time were too little for making safely the long journey, for not talking about baby Isabella, and Philip would never agree to bring them in Castile in any case. And if she had been so inclined Catalina, being the youngest of her sisters, could very well be allowed to take the veil. The year 1502 starts very rough for Catalina of Aragon. This began a struggle over Catalina. Queen Isabella was adamant that her youngest child be returned to her, since there was not a hope of an English grandchild to seal the alliance with Spain and England. King Henry VII, however, did not want to lose her or her dowry. He offered to marry her to his younger son and she could still be Queen of England one day. items.original_question: Independent Naples: What if Catherine of Aragon marries Ferdinand, Duke of Calabria in 1505? Hey all! This question has been on my mind a little too. What if instead of the long seven years in England in virtual poverty, Catherine of Aragon returns to her parents in the summer of 1502 and they arrange a marriage for the young King of Naples, which is still an independent Kingdom in this timeline? In this timeline, Henry VIII will instead marry Eleanor of Austria instead.
items.model_answer:
If Catherine of Aragon had married Ferdinand, Duke of Calabria in 1505, Naples would almost certainly have emerged as a fully independent kingdom ruled by a restored Trastámara line, permanently reshaping Italian and Mediterranean power dynamics.

The match was highly plausible in its own terms. After Queen Isabella’s death in 1504, Ferdinand II of Aragon needed to shore up his contested hold over Naples, which he had seized from France only a year earlier. Ferdinand of Calabria, the son of the last independent Neapolitan king, was his prisoner in Spain and a focal point for local discontent. Marrying his widowed daughter Catherine—stranded in England after Prince Arthur’s death and with her betrothal to the future Henry VIII mired in dowry disputes—to the legitimate heir would have been a masterstroke. By uniting the rival Trastámara claims, Ferdinand could present the new regime as a restoration rather than a conquest, while binding his daughter’s fate directly to Spanish dynastic interests.

The key difference from actual history is that this marriage would not have been intended as a viceroyalty. The couple would have been installed as sovereign rulers of an independent Naples, and Ferdinand of Aragon would have relinquished direct control in exchange for a permanent alliance, the return of his daughter to a throne, and the marginalization of French pretensions. In our world, Ferdinand of Calabria was kept in honorable captivity for decades and later married Germaine de Foix only after Ferdinand II’s death, receiving the viceroyalty of Valencia—a provincial consolation. But in this counterfactual scenario, Naples becomes a separate Trastámara kingdom from the moment of union.

The immediate consequences for Italy are dramatic. An independent but Spanish-allied Naples alters the balance of power: it removes the centerpiece of Spanish direct rule in Italy a century early, likely preventing the long, costly Spanish involvement in Italian wars that drained the treasury. The kingdom, now with a resident monarch and not a distant viceroy, would develop its own court, bureaucracy, and foreign policy. The local nobility, which repeatedly revolted against Spanish administrators, would instead be co-opted into a functioning Neapolitan government. Over time, Naples might have evolved into a significant regional power, acting as a buffer between Habsburg and Valois ambitions.

For the broader “what if” of Catherine’s life, she escapes the humiliating limbo in England and the eventual tragedy of her marriage to Henry VIII. As Queen of Naples, she would have wielded real influence, perhaps even becoming regent or co-ruler in the model of her mother Isabella. Her well-documented piety and education would have shaped the Neapolitan court, and her children would have inherited a stable crown—eliminating one of the deepest sources of instability that in our timeline led to the War of the Spanish Succession.

The English dimension is equally momentous. Without Catherine as his queen, Henry VIII likely marries a French princess or a domestic noblewoman far earlier, producing an heir with less marital strain. The entire chain of events that triggered the English Reformation—the search for a male heir, the annulment, the break with Rome—is averted or at least deeply delayed. Mary I is never born; the Tudor succession follows a wholly different path. In a single stroke, the marriage unburdens England of its most infamous marital tangle and gives Naples a royal house capable of surviving the storms of early modern Europe.

Thus, the marriage of Catherine and Ferdinand of Calabria in 1505 would have created a durable, independent Kingdom of Naples, prevented the long Spanish hegemony in southern Italy, and fundamentally altered the religious and political trajectory of England. It is one of those rare counterfactuals where a single changed match produces three centuries of divergent history.

items.question: What If Curb Global Warming after 1980
human_answers: India has only recently emerged as one of the world’s chief polluters; some two decades ago, Russia and Japan had a bigger mark, and in 1980 Canada was the bigger polluter. Depending on how decarbonized the economies of the First World are by 2000, India’s subsequent economic growth could be magnitudes cleaner than it was OTL. China you have a better point about, though first, their massive economic rise in the three decades after Mao’s death or so is pretty contingent, and second, they still only caught up to the already carbon stagnant EU in 2002. Imagine if the US was still comparable, as they were OTL until the mid 1980’s; now imagine, as China is getting ready to join the WTO in the late 90’s and early 2000’s, the west is also pushing a world climate treaty that (among other things) pushed these three major blocs (the US, Europe, and China) to curb their emissions going into the future. Even if India still sees their emissions rise, wouldn’t the fact that by far the largest producers are simultaneously cutting emissions lead to net reduction?

Well, is the point of your question, can we limit temperature rise by today , or in perpetuity? If the former, then greater adoption of nuclear energy in the West is probably a good enough answer; by the time Chinese and Indian energy use spikes, the resultant temperature spike won't come until after today. Maybe. But that seems like the wrong question, I interpret it as how to prevent such a spike from EVER occurring, rather than just occurring 10 years late. And for that, there's a big challenge. How do developing countries get off the ground? Hydrocarbons are great for that. If the big emitters of the 60s all switched to nuclear, that's fantastic--but China and India can't afford to START with nuclear, nobody can, which means a huge amount of hydrocarbons being burned when they start heavily industrializing. As a solution, perhaps their rise as industrial powers can be delayed a few decades? If they started industrializing in 2025 instead, they might use shale gas or solar, which are now the cheapest sources of power. But the production of those isn't domestic to China, which is a huge part of their use of coal--they don't have to import it. Tentatively, maybe the Soviet Union needs to have greater economic development and a softer landing when it falls? If they can be an industrial exporter while powered off domestic nuclear and natural gas, and remain so in the 1990s, then Chinese growth will be very different, and overall emissions will be lower. Cars and planes are obvious problems. I would also posit beef as a problem--methane is significantly more powerful than carbon in greenhouse effect, and is estimated as responsible for 20 to 30 percent of human-origin warming. Sixty percent of methane emissions are estimated as human-caused, with a big one being agriculture, and beef is responsible for a LOT of agriculture. So a poorer world, that eats less meat, would have lower methane emissions. So too would a world with fewer wetlands, so perhaps a little more paving of swamps would be good from the perspective of this question. Just thoughts. I'll be back for more, probably.

No, because they're already too anti-nuclear. The R&D and thus cost curves on silicon-based solar cell production, and on improved battery capacity, are both pushed pretty hard historically by electronics industry spinoffs. It's hard to see any sort of policy pushes for renewables accelerating those more than marginally, and dramatic acceleration is what you need to make them cost-viable decades ahead of schedule. On the other hand, nuclear was deliberately hobbled by US policy in the 1970s. People like to blame 1979's Three Mile Island, but (for a couple examples) the AEC to NRC switchover was passed by Congress and signed by Ford in 1974, while Carter's anti-reprocessing moratorium was in 1977. If you instead have the US adopt its own version of France's Messmer Plan in 1974 (which is tricky, because Messmer was able to simply ignore anti-nuclear sentiments due to government and economy structure in ways the US government couldn't), you get nuclear power economies of scale driven by the joint US-French demand that make it a more-attractive alternative throughout the rest of the industrialized world. Imagine Thatcher's government nuclearizing Britain in part to undercut the coal unions, for example. Then, if US electricity is something like 75% nuclear in 1990 (like France in 1990, instead of the historical 20%), with the UK fast-following? Now you have the necessary condition (it not hobbling the US) for international trade treaties and the like based on carbon emissions, after a decade of greenhouse effect publicity (since the 1979 NAS report), with the first IPCC report coming out. (Yes, sure, butterflies will scramble the details, but "coal is bad" science, if anything, will be better-funded if the US is transitioning from coal.) If Japan has (as is likely) lagged the US/France/UK in adoption of nuclear, this will be a particularly easy sell, since everybody in the West in 1990 is looking for an excuse to be protectionist against "Japan, Inc." And with that set up, you have the trick for going forward. If China (etc.) has to avoid coal power to export to Western markets, China either will figure out how to avoid coal, or it won't develop because it won't have markets to sell into.

I can give you two, PODs, One being no 3 Mile Island and the other being no John Sununu. So the real easy way to cut down on CO2 emissions is to cut down on coal use, and both PODs give easy ways to do just that. After the banning of CFCs in the late 80s, momentum existed for much harder caps on carbon than were discussed later. In particular, serious curtailment of coal as an energy source in the developed world was mooted. However, this momentum was handicapped with a lack of US Presidential support, with Bush Sr being advised against supporting these efforts by his Chief of Staff, John Sununu. Remove Sununu, and US support for carbon caps become more likely earlier. In addition with no 3MI incident, nuclear technology in the west could become less taboo, giving a viable alternative to coal fired power earlier. I could see a scenario where industry, much like CFCs, sees the financial opportunities in replacing coal with a nuclear/gas mix, and does not get in the way of any cuts to carbon emissions. A good book on the subject in your timeframe is Loosing Earth, by Nathanial Rich, which goes into detail about the drive to curtail emissions in the late 80s. would highly recommend giving it a read.
items.original_question:
AHC: Curb Global Warming after 1980

So you know how Global Surface Temperatures have increased 1.3°C over pre-industrial levels at present, and how a big part of the current Climate Movement is trying to limit further change as much as possible, 1.5°C being the best known* goal? Well, as recently as circa 1980, GST above PIL was only about 0.3°C, and had been hovering just below those levels for decades since the aftermath of WWII; in other words, a full degrees celsius of global warming only happened in the past 45 years alone. This is actually pretty astonishing when you realize how much of a turning point circa 1980 was to global carbon emissions -- both the biggest producers world-wide at the time, the US and Europe, initially saw their emissions peak, with Europe remaining controlled even as the US reversed course after a few years; Japan and Canada have a similar "false peaks" around the same time as the US; the USSR, of course, collapse circa 1990 and saw their emissions collapse thereafter, never to recover; and China was about to undergo a massive economic expansion that would see them become the world's largest emitters. So what I want to determine here is -- what is the latest PoD for avoiding this massive escalation of climate change, or of making it as small as possible? Could a PoD in the late 1970's (eg a continuation of Carter's energy policies in the US) have done the trick? If avoiding a full degrees celsius of warming wasn't seriously avertable by, say, 1975, how early do we need to go? 1960? The aftermath of WWII? In the event we can come to a consensus on the latest possible PoD and what would do the trick, we might also discuss how those changes to said countries' energy polices and to the global economy as a whole would have changed things overall. Thanks. *I'm really trying to avoid getting sidetracked in this discussion for the thread, so for anyone wanting to weigh in on whether its still feasible or how big of a deal missing that goal is, please take that to one of the Chat discussions -- much thanks!
items.model_answer:
If the world had taken decisive, coordinated action to curb global warming starting in 1980, the planet would be in a far less precarious climate state today. Global average temperatures would likely have risen by only about half of the observed 1.2°C above pre-industrial levels, avoiding much of the intensification of extreme weather that has already occurred. Arctic sea ice would be more stable, summer ice loss far less severe, and permafrost thaw would have been significantly slower, preserving more frozen carbon stores. Sea level rise would still be underway due to emissions already committed, but the rate would be noticeably lower, buying precious time for coastal communities to adapt. Coral reefs, though not unscathed, would show less frequent and severe bleaching, and ecosystems worldwide would be under less immediate stress from rapid climate shifts.

Economically, an early transition would have been disruptive but ultimately cheaper than the cost of inaction. The fossil fuel industry would have declined gradually rather than facing abrupt asset stranding, and clean energy technologies—solar, wind, nuclear, and storage—would have matured sooner, driving down costs through decades of sustained investment and learning. Energy independence would be more advanced, and geopolitical conflicts over oil and gas would be less acute. Air quality improvements from phasing out coal and oil would have saved millions of lives prematurely lost to pollution, reducing healthcare burdens and boosting productivity.

Socially, the generational burden would be lighter. Today’s youth would not face the same level of climate anxiety, and vulnerable nations—many in the Global South—would have experienced fewer climate-driven disasters, preserving livelihoods and reducing migration pressure. The political polarization around climate science and policy, while not eliminated, would be less entrenched, as early action would have built broad, bipartisan consensus before the issue became a culture war flashpoint. Instead of scrambling to meet distant net-zero targets against a ticking clock, the world would be in a managed, steadily decarbonizing state, with a fighting chance to stabilize the climate near 1.5°C and avoid the most catastrophic tipping points. The transformation would stand as one of the great cooperative achievements of the 20th century, a pivot from a collision course with nature to a sustainable path, proving that foresight and collective will can reshape the future.

items.original_question: What if No Seven Bishops' Death in 1558? Everyone knows about the death of Cardinal Pole, Archbishop of Canterbury shortly after Queen Mary in 1558. But less known- as in, not even listed when you google them- is that there were six other bishops who died around the same time (including Maurice Griffith, Bishop of Rochester). This led to the opening of several vacancies in the English Catholic Church at the start of Elizabeth I's reign. To the seven bishops who died, can be added Bishop Oglethorpe of Carlisle (who, while he crowned Elizabeth, was no fan of hers after she stormed out of his celebration of Christmas Mass in 1558 because he defied her) and Nicolas Heath, the archbishop of York, who, as the highest ranked cleric in England should've crowned Elizabeth, but declined the "honour". He lost his see in 1559. What would've happened to the Elizabethan Settlement if those seven (or nine) sees had not fallen vacant at exactly the same time (many remaining vacant until 1561). How much opposition would there be to Elizabeth TTL? And how would Elizabeth have dealt with the situation TTL? @BlueFlowwer @isabella @RedKing @HortenseMancini
items.model_answer:
There is no historical event in 1558 involving the death of seven bishops. You may be thinking of two separate moments in English history. One possibility is the Marian Persecutions (1553–1558), during which several Protestant bishops were burned at the stake—most famously Thomas Cranmer, Hugh Latimer, Nicholas Ridley, John Hooper, and Robert Ferrar. Mary I’s death in November 1558 ended the burnings. The other is the trial of the Seven Bishops in 1688, a landmark event that led to the Glorious Revolution, but those bishops were acquitted and did not die.

Assuming you mean **“What if the key bishops executed under Mary I had not died?”**, the counterfactual alters the English Reformation profoundly. If Cranmer, Latimer, Ridley, and others survived into Elizabeth I’s reign, the Elizabethan Religious Settlement (1559) might have faced a stronger, more unified Protestant leadership with direct links to earlier reform. Cranmer’s martyrdom had made him a powerful symbol; his survival could have sharpened theological disputes rather than allowing Elizabeth to steer a moderate via media. The memory of the martyrs also fueled John Foxe’s _Acts and Monuments_, which cemented anti-Catholicism in English identity. Without their deaths, popular Protestant mythology would be weaker, possibly softening the long-term antagonism between England and Catholic Europe.

If instead you mean **“What if the Seven Bishops had been executed in 1688 instead of acquitted?”**, the consequences would be even more dramatic. James II’s attempt to re-Catholicize England would have backfired sooner and more violently. The execution of seven respected Anglican prelates would have triggered widespread outrage, likely sparking an earlier, bloodier revolution. The invitation to William of Orange might have been replaced by open rebellion, possibly resulting in a more radical political settlement—perhaps a republic or a stricter constitutional monarchy. The public memory of such a judicial murder would have poisoned Catholic-Protestant relations for generations and made later toleration far more difficult.

In either case, the survival or death of such prominent churchmen was not a minor detail: it shaped the myths, politics, and religious direction of the nation for centuries.

items.question: The Heir to Sulla: What If Sulla Fought Mithridates VI And Marius Marched On Rome Instead?
human_answers: Alright, so here are some changes: I wash my hands of the issue with the Marian reforms. Let's move on from that. Marius helps coordinate the Dimidiatio Senatus by spreading rumors and disrupting trade and grain shipments. After the creation of the Roman Tribunal Republic, he stays in Italia, raises an army of soldiers, professionally trains them, and leads the early Tribunal Republic. Sulla comes to Rome, and while the battle is intense, Marius and Rome win a pyrrhic victory, with Marius dying later that year. During the Battle of Rome, which even enters the city itself and causes immense destruction, young Gaius Julius Caesar dies. The Tribunal Republic fights remnants of people sympathetic to Sulla, and just continues on as normal. The proscriptions never happen. The closest equivalent is that many wealthy families were killed by poorer people and their wealth confiscated during the Sullarian War. But there's not really a reign of terror, just a violent popular revolt. The way the Roman Tribunal Republic gets set up still gradually happens, and the Tribunal Senate eventually creates a regular militia force within Rome itself, so that way no general can march on Rome like Sulla did. Christianity already exists, but doesn't spread far, remaining a religion in Levant and Egypt. It's never institutionalized. Because of this, and other butterfly effects with regular peoples, Mohammed is never born, so Islam never comes to be. The Tribunal Republic is still militarized, but focuses on strategically allying Celtic and Germanic kings against their allies, trading with them using Rome's vast reach and access to trade routes, and slowly integrating them. Rome stays mostly to the coastline to enforce this and use the sea as easy travel, so the navy becomes larger. Once trade settlements eventually reach southern Morocco and find the sub-Saharan trade route and its goods, the effects from trade deals are amplified. Attila still happens, and while it shakes up Rome, they fight them off thanks to alliances and mercenaries. Cassius still exists, and he helps kickstart Roman mercantile economics after the Hunnic Invasion, beginning the gradual plutocratic trend in Roman politics with merchants. Also, slavery still exists. With wars not bringing in as many war-slaves, laws increasingly punished severe crimes with debt slavery, and also enslaved the children of slaves if both parents were enslaved at the time of birth. Chattel slavery and debt/penal slavery still firmly exists, and slaves are traded across the Mediterranean. Sources of war slaves are largely from rivals of allied Celtic, Germanic, African, or Arabic tribes, plus some hostile invading tribes, such as the Norse, the Avars, the Khazars, and various Turkic tribes, keeping Anatolia as "Anatolia" and Greek/Roman/Persian. By 1000, Rome has slowly expanded militarily, commercially, and culturally. There are Roman trade ports along the coast of the whole Mediterranean, the Red Sea, and Western Europe, including Britannia and Hibernia. There are military presences, but the trade of goods from far away was used as a carrot to keep Celts, Germans, Africans, and Arabs in line (alongside the stick of Roman military garrisons). It's less depopulation and colonialism and more commerce and trading settlement (think Islamic merchants). Zoroastrian Persia, having not collapsed from Islam in this timeline, is still around. However, the House of Karen took over after a civil war in the late 800s, so now they're the Karenian Empire, not the Sasanian Empire anymore. Instead of an emergency military command being called "Caesar," it's instead called a "Consul." However, Consuls explicitly only lead armies, while the Tribunal Senate and the Orator did their thing, with the highly-professional, well-paid Roman city garrison (named the "Custodes Romae") preventing any Consuls or generals from marching on Rome, as well as acting as the final line of defense against barbarian Invasions. The title of "Res Publica Inter Marium" (RPIT) is put on legion banners, and is otherwise just a term that proud Romans use to praise the Roman Tribunal Republic, or the "Res Publica Tribunorum Romanorum" (RPTR). Roman poets and generals say things like "Ave res publica inter marium!" Did I miss anything?

To a certain point, it may have been possible, given what happened in parts of Medieval Europe, but that was only possible because of Christianity, and even then, forced labour continued being an important part of the economy, but in the form of serfdom instead of chattel slavery. Also, some other things I'd like to point out: I can guess the inspiration for this, but in all likelihood it wouldn't work like that - remember that given the way Roman politics works all of those people have their own clients to call on, and who would likely be around the forum in Senate meetings - visa how quickly Scipio Nasica gathered enough support to take on the supporters of Tiberius Gracchus in 133. The senators wouldn't be sitting ducks, and what you'd probably see is a street battle between each side's mobs of supporters, more like the riots of 52 BC or 100 BC than anything else. Also, remember that the Senate wasn't continuously in session - each session had to be convened by a magistrate and each session only lasted one day, for religious reasons. May I remind you that (assuming this happens in 88 BC) Caesar is 12 years old around that time? Even Pompey was twice that age when he first gained military proeminence, and he only did so by raising and equipping a legion out of his own pocket, because he was too young to be officially appointed to any command.

Okay, let me try to tackle this. Keep in mind this is just my opinion, with the primary goal always being plausibility: As mentioned by others, Marian reforms is a historiographic myth. You'll have to find a reason for the optimates to support land reform. If your main PoD is Marius failing to outmaneuver Sulla, then that's a good starting point. A sunken grain ship won't be enough to inspire the people to want to topple the government. A year or two of very little grain coming in could do that. Remember Marius is very old and probably mentally sick by now. I doubt he lives far beyond early 87 BC. Other populares can take up that mantle, but again, they have to deal with all the rest of the First Class in the years following. Remember also in OTL how the Sullans won literally every single military engagement. In another thread I called it a curbstomp, and it really was a curbstomp. There is extreme support for the optimates in this time period in the Senate, and among soldiers too. There would be no reason to go to Anatolia to fight Sulla, since the populares control Rome. They would force Sulla to come to them as in OTL. Citizen militia can't do anything against legions. Rome has no garrison. Caesar is a teenage kid who's never led armies, he would never be given command. Unless you mean Caesar's father, who is kind of a nonentity. There are dozens of grown men who would command before he's even considered. No such thing as patrician armies. You might mean optimas/optimate armies. The vast majority of forces and leaders on both sides are plebeians. Patrician versus plebeian is by this time almost entirely a religious and social distinction, not a political one. I'll end it here, since the rest of it rests on ever deepening misunderstandings. It's not bad for a story that doesn't mind plausibility and wants to go by "Rule of Cool", so if you want to do it, go ahead. The way I'd try to do something similar, realistically: 1. Marius never breaks with Saturninus and Glaucia 2. Saturninus passes increasingly radical laws, with Marius supporting him due to thinking he can control him 3. The Senate comes into open conflict with Saturninus, passing a Senatus Consultum Ultimum against him and Glaucia 4. With the support of Marius's wealth and veterans, Saturninus and Glaucia are able to subdue the Senate; some senators are killed, others exiled 5. The Republic retains her name, or perhaps is renamed Populus Senatusque Romanus, thus putting the people first; tribunician powers are greatly expanded, to the point where consuls have little legislative power 6. Marius and allies legislate for Italian citizenship to increase their support 7. The crowd begins to realize Marius and allies can't provide the easier life and reforms they promised 8. Decreased provincial incomes due to recalcitrant governors and uncertain political situations create an economic slump Then there are several ways this could go, depending on what the author wants. Romans resistant to Italian citizenship start a much smaller Social War; hard economic times cause worse slave rebellions; a few governors gang up to march on Rome and topple this regime? There are multiple interesting paths. Things that would not happen: 1. Romans peacefully integrating barbarians into Roman government. Most you can expect is Friends and Allies, or barbarians living free but under Roman law in Roman provinces. Rome succeeded for a reason, and part of that reason was being chauvinistic. It's not a moral judgment, just something that made them very good at obtaining and maintaining control completely loyal to decisions emanating from the city of Rome. Famously Cato the Censor, a man from Tusculum (not even 15 miles from Rome), whose ancestors were all Roman and whose father and grandfather had had several horses killed under them in combat, was considered as being a barely Roman peasant by the senators of Rome. Even in OTL the first non-Julio-Claudian emperors were of old senatorial families. Then men whose ancestors had been Roman for generations 2. Anything touching the institution of slavery. Unfree labor is, to this very day, the basis of civilization. Not even in their wildest crack-smoking, mushroom-eating, smoke-puffing dreams would anybody in antiquity think of seriously ending unfree labor 3. A divorce of military from politics. That's an extremely modern concept, and even today not true of the vast majority of states. Prior to the 18th century it would be almost laughable to think the two aren't intertwined. Whoever has the force of arms makes the decisions; where there are more groups with force, they bargain to make decisions, or go to war. That's politics. It's also why barbarian emperors happened, because that's who started having military power. While ever Romans held military power, they made the decisions, they were the emperors. When they left that to barbarians, the situation quickly turned in the barbarians' favor 4. A centuries-long run of kumbaya where wars decrease in intensity and rivalries are mostly commercial. Commercial wars turn into military wars really quickly when one side can't establish complete dominance very quickly. Starting out commercial, the money comes in handy paying mercenaries to fight. Things only escalate from there. Commerce, the control of cash and goods and people, is actually one of the only reasons wars were fought historically. The only bigger one I can think of is agriculture (land) itself, that produces those goods and people Anyway, interesting idea. I would say read some more history, and understand how these processes actually evolve and shape the world. Also how the government in Rome worked. History works in grand, broad strokes and movements, so don't expect cultures and governments to turn on a dime. Even the transformation of Rome from a Republic to the Principate was gradual. People forget the civil wars actually took over five decades to get through. It was very much a process, and in the end rested very much on preserving some image and veneer of the old. For example Augustus holding imperium maius everywhere, becoming eventually pontifex maximus, retaining tribunician powers (despite being patrician by adoption), etc. were all very old, traditional things just twisted acceptably by time and political necessity (and with the force of legions backing it, of course). Changing how Rome works? Fine! Changing how Rome is called? Hmmmm, not so good! It took over three centuries, from Augustus to Diocletian, before it became acceptable to verbally acknowledge the emperor as Dominus (Master), and to prostrate before him. That's how long it took from Rome's government to transform from an Italian city-state to a Hellenistic autocracy. Anyway I've written too long anyway. Learn more and never stop thinking, you'll do fine with any timeline you write
items.original_question: The Heir to Sulla: What If Sulla Fought Mithridates VI And Marius Marched On Rome Instead? This is a scenario I've imagined for a Rome that never becomes an empire. And also because I wanted to create a Roman Republic I could call "Intermarium" because I wanted to. This is how I see it happening as an origin lore for the story following this: In the 100s BCE, the Marian reforms happen. However, Optimates senators ensure that land reform is decided by the Senate. Eventually, when the Mithridatic War happens, Marius fails to outmanuever Sulla, and Sulla goes to fight King Mithridates VI. Resentful, Marius uses his populist rhetoric, connections with Roman tribunes, and a sunken grain ship to incite a riot in Rome. This riot, later called the "Dimidiatio Senatus," resulted in the Roman Senate being attacked and half of the senators killed, with the majority of the remainder (all Populares senators) joining the rioters, and the surviving Optimates senators fleeing Rome to the countryside. Following the Dimidiatio Senatus, Marius declares the creation of the "Tribuni Romanae Res Publicae" (TRRP), or "Roman Tribunal Republic," denouncing the old Senate as a now-dead continuation of the old hated kingdom and their sycophants. Marius establishes a Tribunal Senate of people aligned with him (later called Marians) to govern Rome, then marches to Anatolia to fight Sulla. In a battle in Greece, Sulla defeats Marius and executes him. Sulla marches his legion into Italia. At Rome, Sulla finds a large citizen militia and the Roman city garrison opposing him, and a bloody battle begins. With the help of a certain Gaius Julius Caesar, Rome defeats Sulla, albeit it's a pyrrhic victory due to larger casualties on Rome's side. Sulla is beaten to death by a furious mob. Following the Battle of Rome, Caesar asks the Marian Tribunal Senate to entrust him with command of the Roman Army in the fight against remaining Patrician armies outside of Rome that seek to crush what Marius created. The Tribunal Senate trusts Caesar, and orders him to quash the opposition (later called Sullarians). In what is later known as the Sullarian War, Caesar crushes Patrician armies and confiscates the families' wealth and grants it to a Tribunal Senatorial Treasury, which is used as the central place of wealth of Rome, and funds from it are used to pay standard wages to soldiers. Caesar is a revered war hero, praised as Marius' heir. Caesar then relieves himself of command of the Sullarian Campaign, and suggests expanding Rome into Gaul. However, before his request his accepted, he suffers a stroke and dies. In the aftermath of the Sullarian War, around the 1st Century AD, the Tribunal Senate tries to stabilize the Tribunal Republic. The previous classifications of plebeian or patrician are abolished; Romans are just "Civii," or "Citizens" (Civis for singular). Additionally, some laws are established or confirmed, such as the ban on mobilized troops within Italia, the prohibition of army officials in public offices, and a system where Roman Provinces each elect two senators to the Tribunal Senate, plus two senators elected by the city of Rome itself to the Tribunal Senate. Following the Sullarian War, there is a huge cultural shift away from militarized politics and aristocracy. Two new factions emerge: the Marians, who are reformists loyal to Marius' rhetoric and believe in helping the common people and pragmatically responding to crises, and the Caesarians, radicals who idolize Caesar that believe that all aristocracy should be destroyed and the republic only serve the common people. In the decades that followed, Rome would gradually expand, but mainly by courting Celtic and Germanic tribes and negotiating integration into the Roman Tribunal Republic. New provinces emerge, and Celtic/Germanic warriors are used as mercenaries alongside Roman armies. Trade and commerce began to prosper, and so the Roman Navy was prioritized for funding and seen as less corruptible. Also, Christianity happens. However, it does not expand as fast because of a lack of a Constantine figure, and eventually becomes a recognized, non-persecuted religion within Rome, like the Roman Pantheon, Celtic paganism, Germanic paganism, and the slowly-dying Cult of Mithras. Basically, Rome slowly turns into a mercantile, seafaring republic with integration treaties with as many Celtic and Germanic tribes they could negotiate with. Kind of like a republican Carthage, ironically. Additionally, as wars reduce in scale and more non-Romans join provincial and senatorial administration, slavery is gradually banned. Persia remains a strategic rival over competition for Arabia and Mesopotamia, yet wars reduce in intensity and the rivalry turns mostly commercial. Rome expands through trade and treaties, sticking to the coast, where ships can easily transport goods and protect cities (again, Carthage-like and kinda Venice-like). It also trades with Aksum, Nubian Kingdoms south of Sudan, and sub-Saharan nations like Mali and Ghana (since North African coastal settlements reach Morocco and the Canary Islands eventually). Eventually, the Hunnic Invasions happen. Rome managed to better deal with the invasion thanks to greater stability, Germanic cooperation/mercenary armies, and more stable politics. The Tribunal Senate appoints a general to the position of "Caesar," which becomes the title of a military commander charged with winning a campaign vital to Rome's survival. The Huns are repelled, but Rome's maritime and mercantile economy is disrupted. In the aftermath, a young merchant named Cassius Atticus Felix emerges. A shrewd merchant and tactical investor, he focuses on creating merchant fleets and creating more merchant outposts along the Mediterranean and Mare Hibericum (the Atlantic Ocean). It is because of him that coastal cities in Morocco expanded as far west as they did, and he advocated for reduced taxes and regulations on Roman merchants, calling for "Mercator Autonomia," or "Merchant Autonomy," to revitalize Rome's economy and create prosperity. Cassius was heading to personally found a trading town on the Canary Islands when a hurricane hit the area and killed him. However, Cassius becomes immortalized as a rebuilder of post-Hun Rome's economy. The merchant class, and those sympathetic to them, form a new faction based on his ideals, called the Cassians. A while after this, conservative Romans who disliked the existence of "uncivilized barbarians" in Rome and merchant "luxury and decadence" form a traditionalist faction named the Catonians, named after Cato the Elder. They believe in the superiority of Roman culture, worship the old Roman/Greek Pantheon, oppose luxury, and don't oppose the idea of re-establishing slavery. Gradually, merchant oligarchy seeps into the Roman Tribunal Republic as merchants start buying out senators and provincial representatives. The Caesarians firmly oppose it, and so grow closer with the Catonians. Inside the Caesarian faction, a schism slowly begins to brew as those who oppose Catonian traditionalism and Romano-centrism clash with those who do support it. After some more tribal integration, province establishment, commerce expansion, and minor warfare, Mohammad creates Islam, and unites the Arab tribes (slowly being integrated by the Romans and the Persians) in opposition to them. Rome and Persia temporarily create a defensive pact against the Islamic Invasions, otherwise known as the "Crisis of the 7th Century." While Rome and Persia lost some cities along the coast of the Indian Ocean and the Persian Gulf, the Sasanian Empire retains Mesopotamia, and Rome defends the cities on the western coast of the Arabian peninsula, bordering the Red Sea and Judea. The Arabian Empire is then created as a religiously fanatical, militarized, yet mercantile and diplomatic empire. Islam still spreads through Islamic traders, though not as strongly in North Africa or the Mediterranean as a whole thanks to the Roman Tribunal Republic's stability and already existing religions. [By the first millennium CE, Rome's political system works like this:] [Provinces are ruled by Provincial Tribunes, elected by the people of the province from those who have not been in the military for at least four years. Additionally, some large cities, particularly coastal entrepot cities, become provinces in their own right. Each province can pass their own laws and manage their own administration, paying taxes to the Tribunal Treasury in Rome and following senatorial law]. [Each province (plus the city of Rome) elects two senators to represent them in the Tribunal Senate. No senator may have been in the military within the previous four years. The Tribunal Senate has no Consuls, instead having an "Orator," which is basically their Speaker. The longest-serving senator automatically becomes Orator. If the Senate passes a law, it can be vetoed by Provincial Tribunes if at least half of them vote on to veto the Senate law within one year of its passing. Provincial Tribunes may vote to send a law to the Senate for consideration, and if it is sent to the Senate and the Senate approves it, it cannot be vetoed no matter how many tribunes veto it]. [Caesars are appointed by the Senate in a time of dire war with a term of two years, after which point (if the war is still ongoing) the Senate can either replace them or affirm their trust in them. This repeats until the dire war is over]. In 1000 CE, to celebrate one thousand years of popular rule following the Dimidiatio Senatus, celebrations are held across Rome, and the Roman Tribunal Republic changes its formal name to the "Res Publica Inter Marium" (RPIM), or "Republic between seas," for the grand republic lies between multiple seas: Mare Ponticum (the Black Sea), Mare Mediterraneus (the Mediterranean Sea), Mare Hibericum (Atlantic Ocean west of Iberia and the Canary Islands), Mare Britannicum (the North Sea and Atlantic Ocean around Britain and Ireland), and Mare Rubrum (the Red Sea and Indian Ocean). Thoughts?
items.model_answer:
If Sulla had sailed east to fight Mithridates while Marius marched on Rome, the late Republic’s spiral into autocracy would likely have been more chaotic in the short term but might have converged on a similar endgame—just with a different cast of strongmen and a more brittle constitutional legacy.

In our timeline, the crucial break came when Sulla, as consul in 88 BC, defied all precedent by turning his army on the city to wrest the lucrative Mithridatic command from Marius. That act made legionary loyalty to a commander more important than loyalty to the state. Sulla then left for the East, and Marius returned with Cinna to seize Rome in a bloodbath before dying naturally within weeks of his seventh consulship. Sulla eventually came back, won the civil war, and imposed his proscriptions and constitutional reforms as dictator—a model that later inspired Caesar to cross the Rubicon.

Reverse the roles: Marius, the aging “third founder of Rome,” uses his popular support among veterans and the urban *plebs* to forcibly take the Mithridatic command for himself, but instead of heading east, he uses the legions recruited on his promise of booty to march on Rome. Sulla, meanwhile, is already in Greece with the Senate’s legitimate mandate, waging war against Pontus. Marius’s move would have been even more brazenly factional than Sulla’s: not a consul defending his dignity against a tribune’s sacrosanctity, but an embittered *novus homo* overriding a senatorial appointment by sheer military threat. The Senate, largely sympathetic to Sulla, would have branded Marius and his allies hostes (public enemies) immediately. Marius, in his late sixties and in poor mental and physical shape, would have had to hold Rome against inevitable Sullan counterattack while also managing the fickle support of Cinna and the popular party.

The likeliest immediate outcome is a brief, violent Marian domination. Marius seizes the consulship for 87 BC and unleashes a purge of leading optimates, far bloodier than the original. But his health fails quickly—he died a little under two years after his historical march on Rome, and the stress of civil conflict would hardly prolong his life. The true power would pass to Cinna or, if Marius anoints his inexperienced son (Marius the Younger), to a fractious military clique. Sulla, meanwhile, would have defeated Mithridates much as he did historically, perhaps even more decisively, because he wouldn’t be racing back to fight a civil war; he could finish the siege of Athens and negotiate a peace from a position of unbroken strength. With the East settled and a treasury full of plundered gold, Sulla would land in Italy in 85 or 84 BC, leading seasoned legions loyal only to him.

That sets up a civil war between Sulla’s hardened veterans and the Marian forces—still formidable but led by lesser men, since both Marius major and probably Cinna (who historically lost control of his troops and died in a mutiny in 84 BC while preparing to meet Sulla) would be gone. Sulla wins that war almost certainly, and perhaps faster. But the crucial difference is the political aftermath. In history, Sulla’s march on Rome was a one-time shock that he tried to institutionalize away: as dictator *legibus scribundis et rei publicae constituendae*, he stacked the Senate, emasculated the tribunes, and restricted the military commands of governors. His whole model was a reaction to what he saw as the Marian destabilization of the state—making the Republic safe for senatorial oligarchy again, but doing so through naked force.

If Marius had struck first, Sulla would have returned not as the original plague but as the righteous avenger, the savior of the legitimate Senate. His counter-purge would thus have even greater veneer of legality. He’d likely still become dictator and impose similar reforms, but with even broader support from the traumatized senatorial class. The title “Heir to Sulla” in this timeline takes on a different meaning. In our history, Pompey and Caesar both learned from Sulla’s playbook: raise a private army, court popular favor, defy the Senate, and march on Rome when cornered. But in an alternate world where Marius was the primal transgressor, the lesson for ambitious nobles would be twofold: first, that a popular general can seize power even without a formal command, and second, that the Senate’s only salvation is a loyal strongman with a private army. The precedent for both popular mobilisation and military counter-revolution would be set even more starkly.

The real “heir to Sulla” would still probably be Pompey. He raised his own troops to support Sulla historically, and in this version, he’d still attach himself to the returning victor. After Sulla’s inevitable death (from natural causes or not), the system would hold no longer than it did originally; by 70 BC, Pompey and Crassus would dismantle the Sullan constitution to gain popular favor. But because the Marian trauma would be seen as the archetypical attack on the *res publica*, the Senate might cling more desperately to conservative leaders like Cato and Bibulus, provoking an even sharper conflict with a rising popular general—perhaps still Caesar, who would inherit the Marian legacy from his uncle’s more aggressive, failed attempt. The crossing of the Rubicon would happen on the same principle, just under a different lineage of wrongdoing. The Republic’s fatal illness was not who struck first, but the irrevocable fusion of consular power with personal legionary loyalty. Swap the protagonists, and the tragedy still plays out, only with a longer first act and an even more petrified senatorial establishment before the final collapse.

items.question: What If al-Andalus survives
human_answers: There are a number of good surviving Al Andalus timelines like moonlight in a jar on here. Obviously it can go however the author wants it- my suspicion though is that an Al Andalus which remains relatively centralised is more vulnerable than the taifas were otl to crusades- if the events over the next century don’t butterfly the Turkic incursions into Anatolia and the papal call to crusade, a crusade would certainly be directed towards Spain as well. A centralised state is often easier to conquer than decentralised ones, all you need is one battle that allows the conquerors access to the capital and central bureaucracy and you’ve done it. I think it’d be interesting to see such a fundamentally different pattern of reconquista, where instead of small northern principalities gradually extending southwards, one decisive battle/sack of Cordoba puts crusaders in charge of cordoba like happened in 1204 Constantinople, you end up with a Christian kingdom with Cordoba as its capital and likely a French king. This kingdom of Cordoba could be instantly much more powerful than the northern Christian kingdoms. Its administrative languages would be Latin and Arabic, and the language of the nobility (unlike otl) wouldn’t be an Iberian Romance language, more likely a northern French dialect, ruling over a population of Arabic and Mozarabic speakers. Unlike otl there would be no real reason for northern romance dialects to spread southwards, as even though northern Christians would settle the south, without state backing they’re more likely to assimilate to local Mozarabic or Arabic speaking Christian populations.

It wasn't unexpected, so to speak; he was ill throughout the year 1008, contracting the disease in February and dying in October. He had an angina attack. Whether this was caused by the illness, the stress of managing the country, or poisoning is difficult to say. Adding to that, instead of recovering in Cordoba, he spent a good part of the year campaigning, which probably didn't help. The reason Al-Muzaffar couldn't remain idle was the large number of problems he faced during his six-year reign. Early in his reign, there was a sharp decline in gold and silver coinage, which may indicate economic difficulties in al-Andalus or problems with the supply of gold and silver from Africa. A few months after succeeding his father, al-Muzaffar faced a conspiracy to assassinate him and his vizier, Ibn al-Qatta. The conspirators, with the commander of Saqaliba and the court secretary as the most prominent figures, intended to replace the hajib with his underage son, Muhammad, who would be a puppet (So, Puppet Squared), just as Caliph Hisham II had been. Al-Muzaffar, unlike his father, was a king-soldier, not a philosopher king (who had legal and literary training). Muzaffar had no interest in administration, politics, arts, or sciences. Leaving this to his vizier. Later, his vizier and friend, Ibn al-Qatta, who was married to his sister, organized a failed coup against Muzaffar. Al-Muzaffar, in a simple way, could not catch a break; it was one coup attempt followed by another assassination attempt, followed by another coup attempt. He had to kill people who were important to the functioning of the government during his father's era. During one of his campaigns in 1006, he attacked the territory of King Sancho Garces III of Pamplona and ended up being defeated in this campaign, which, along with his poor governance (partly due to numerous coups and open intrigue at court), brought him a bad reputation. To be honest, it was difficult to match his father's greatness. The government would remain in crisis because al-Muzaffar's biggest problem was that he was not a Umayyad, and anyone with ambition could find legitimacy in trying to dethrone him to establish the Umayyads (on paper). This, coupled with the fact that he was not as competent as his father (who was far superior), generated this crisis. Perhaps that's quite debatable. It could have been much worse or better; it depends on many factors. I don't know if he would last the rest of the century. Seriously, the kingdom is having serious internal problems. I don't know if it would last until 1020. The kingdom would collapse; the kingdom died informally when al-Mansur exterminated the Arab elite who had maintained the emirate/caliphate for the past centuries, replacing them with enslaved soldiers and Berbers. Al-Mansur possessed exceptional skill in managing the political, military, and ethnic intrigue of the kingdom. However, his son inherited the problems without possessing the necessary competence. He had to contend with enslaved soldiers and Berbers vying to become the new Al-Mansur, the remaining Arab elite wanting to return to power, pressure from the north, and governmental instability.

items.original_question: What if al-Andalus survives The 11th century was a pivotal moment in Hispanic history. At the beginning of the century, the Caliphate of Córdoba was the dominant power on the peninsula. The city of Córdoba rivaled Constantinople as the largest city in Europe. Ostensibly ruled by the Umayyads under Caliph Hisham II, in reality he was merely a puppet of his ambitious hajib (chamberlain) Abu Amir Muhammad ‘ al-Mansur ’ more famously known as Almanzor. A highly ambitious man, Almanzor would import thousands of Berber tribesmen into al-Andalus to serve in Córdoba’s army. He would utilize this army to not only keep the disgruntled Arab elites in line but also to bring the Christian north to heel through large-scale annual raids. While this arrangement put strain on the treasury and created ethnic strife, it was effective, and upon his death in 1002 AD Almanzor would be seamlessly succeeded by his son al-Muzaffar. Al-Muzaffar would continue his father’s regime, continuing to import Berbers, continuing to raid the north, and keeping the state stable. It was looking like a dual-power dynamic was emerging in Córdoba just as it had back east in Baghdad. However, while on campaign against Castile, al-Muzaffar would die unexpectedly in 1008 AD. His younger brother Sanchuelo would succeed him as hajib , but he would lack the brilliance of his father or the prudence of his brother. Sanchuelo would offend the Arab nobility by having Hisham II name him as his heir as Caliph. This act would trigger the Fitna of al-Andalus, reducing the grand city of Córdoba to ruins and shattering the country into 30+ squabbling petty kingdoms or taifas. Suddenly, the power dynamic was reversed. Now the Muslim south was paying tribute to the Christian north. The north would consolidate under the Jiménez dynasty, and then push south, culminating in the capture of Toledo in 1085 AD, followed by the occupation of the rest of al-Andalus by the Berber Almoravid dynasty from Morocco. The rest of the Reconquista would unfold in the following centuries. The Fitna proved to be a lucky break for Christian Iberia, as without the might of Córdoba crushing them, the Reconquista started to truly gain steam. However, what if the Fitna was averted or delayed by having al-Muzaffar not die prematurely in 1008? Had he not died young, Sanchuelo likely never comes to power. This alone averts the triggering of the Fitna . Of course, the underlying financial issues and ethnic strife still exist, so the Fitna may still occur under different circumstances. However it’s likely to be nowhere as devestating for al-Andalus as IOTL. How would a continuing Caliphate of Córdoba navigate the rest of the 11th century? Would al-Andalus remain powerful and prosperous as we transition into the High Middle Ages? Could the Andalusi withstand pressure from both Christians and Berbers alike? Will the Reconquista ever happen without al-Andalus collapsing?
items.model_answer:
If al-Andalus had survived as a flourishing Islamic polity in Iberia beyond the 15th century, the trajectory of European and global history would likely be profoundly altered. Instead of the finality of 1492 with the fall of Granada and the edict of expulsion, we might imagine a resilient, pluralistic state—or a constellation of Muslim-ruled taifas—that continues to act as a bridge between the Islamic world and Christendom. Its persistence would have dampened the militant, homogenizing impulse of the Spanish Reconquista, perhaps preventing the unification of Spain under a strictly Catholic identity. The Spanish Inquisition might never have gained its later ferocity, and the mass expulsions of Jews and Muslims that drained the peninsula of economic and intellectual vitality could have been averted.

Culturally, a surviving al-Andalus would remain a conduit for the transmission of classical Greek philosophy, Arabic science, and advanced mathematics into Europe. The Renaissance might have unfolded differently, with less dependence on Italian city-states for the rediscovery of ancient texts and more direct, continuous dialogue in Cordoba, Seville, or Granada. The intellectual climate of early modern Europe could have been less steeped in the adversarial relationship between faith and reason that later marked the Enlightenment—instead, the Andalusian model of convivencia, however imperfect and mythologized, might have offered a persistent example of coexistence that softened religious conflicts elsewhere.

Politically, the survival of a Muslim kingdom in southwestern Europe would have recalibrated the balance of power. The Hapsburgs and later Bourbons could not have poured American silver into endless European wars with a thriving Islamic rival at home on the peninsula. The Ottoman Empire, already a Mediterranean superpower, would have found a natural ally or at least a cultural kin in al-Andalus, potentially creating a pincer effect on Charles V’s domains. This might have blunted Spanish colonial ambitions or redirected them more firmly toward the Atlantic, while a Muslim state on the Strait of Gibraltar could have contested control of the gateway between the Mediterranean and the Atlantic, altering the dynamics of exploration and trade. Columbus’s voyage, if sponsored at all by a fractured Castile, might have been delayed or competed with by Andalusian navigators who had their own long tradition of Atlantic sailing and contact with West Africa.

The religious map of Europe would be transformed. A living al-Andalus would stand as a counterweight to rising Protestantism and Catholic reform, showing that Islam could be a European religion, not merely an external “other.” This might have diffused the binary of Christendom versus Islam that fueled the Crusader mentality and later colonial expansion into Muslim lands. Instead of a clash of civilizations, southern Europe could have hosted a multi-confessional society that, for all its frictions, normalized Islamic presence. The Sephardic Jewish community, which found its last Iberian refuge in Muslim Granada, might have continued to flourish, producing a Jewish renaissance alongside an Islamic one, further enriching European thought.

Economically, al-Andalus had been a centre of agricultural innovation, urban craftsmanship, and trade that linked sub-Saharan Africa, the Mediterranean, and the Levant. Its survival would have preserved these networks, and the influx of New World crops like maize and potatoes might have been eagerly adopted and diffused northward by Andalusian farmers. Capitalism might have developed with a more hybrid character, blending Islamic commercial law with European merchant practices, potentially moderating the predatory extractivism that marked early colonialism.

In the long run, a surviving al-Andalus would challenge the very idea of “the West” as a purely Judeo-Christian inheritance. The Enlightenment might have drawn consciously on Ibn Rushd (Averroes) and Ibn Arabi as direct ancestors. Nationalism in the 19th century could have taken very different forms: perhaps an Andalusian identity defined by language (a Romance tongue with heavy Arabic lexical influence) and culture rather than by religion, offering an alternative to the mono-confessional nation-state. Colonial scrambles for Africa and the Middle East might have been complicated by a European state that was itself Muslim, sympathetic to anti-colonial movements, and able to serve as a third-party broker. Today, we might see a Spain or al-Andalus that is a federation of religions, a tourist heartland of architectural wonders still living rather than museumified, and a constant diplomatic bridge between continents. The psychological and cultural wall that many Europeans build between “Europe” and “Islam” would be far harder to maintain when Islam had been part of Europe’s soil for over a millennium without interruption.
