items.original_question:
AHC: Equip the Best Possible Interwar Army From Scratch

It's 1930, you're put in charge of the military procurement of a smaller developed nation -- a small or middle/regional power: fairly wealthy, fairly industrialized, fairly well-educated workforce, with robust institutions...etc., but not a major power (think Poland, Canada, Australia, the Netherlands, Belgium, Spain, Czechoslovakia, or Sweden). Despite the global depression, the government has magically found the funds for a major military expansion. The nation has a small military and professional officer corps to expand on, equipped with a smattering of WW1/post-WW1 weapons, but the point is you basically have nothing in large numbers so you essentially get to start from scratch. There's no massive stock of rifle ammunition forcing you to stick with a specific caliber for cost saving reasons, no huge pile of 2pdr shells in a warehouse forcing you to stay with the pom-pom...etc. Money is not the limiting factor (within reason); it's not infinite, but you're going to hit manpower constraints before budget constraints. In addition to the small professional military, the nation has a small armaments industry (e.g., Czech tanks/small arms, Canadian shipbuilding, Dutch aircraft design/manufacture) -- but not enough to design/build everything you need at scale. So you're going to have to buy/import a lot foreign, at least to start. The goal is a primarily defensive military that still has some expeditionary capability (not independent expeditionary operations, but in support of / in concert with great power allies). You're not aligned with a specific bloc so you can buy/import/adopt from wherever you want. Naval needs are more complicated and specific, so ignoring that to start: how do you equip your army and air force?
items.model_answer:
To equip the best possible interwar army from scratch, one must ruthlessly apply the bitter lessons of the First World War while anticipating the technological and doctrinal revolutions that actually proved decisive in the Second. The idealized force would not merely collect advanced weapons, but would weave them into a seamless combined-arms system built around speed, communication, and decentralized initiative. Such an army, forged in the late 1920s or early 1930s with the benefit of hindsight, would have dominated any battlefield by 1939.

The foundation must be full motorization and mechanization. The interwar obsession with horse traction was a fatal error; every infantry division must ride trucks or tracked carriers, with fuel and maintenance built into the force structure from day one. Logistics units would be as prized as combat arms, ensuring that rapid advances never outrun supply. Radios would saturate every echelon — tank, artillery battery, infantry company, and reconnaissance unit — enabling the real-time coordination that made German Blitzkrieg so devastating. Commanders would be trained in *Auftragstaktik* (mission-type tactics), empowering junior leaders to exploit fleeting opportunities without waiting for orders.

The infantry would shed bolt-action rifles as the standard arm. The best trade-off is a semi-automatic rifle for most soldiers, akin to the American M1 Garand but developed a decade earlier, paired with a light, belt-fed general-purpose machine gun at the squad level — effectively an MG 34/42 precursor. Submachine guns would be mass-issued for close-quarters and urban fighting. Anti-tank defense would rest on light, high-velocity guns (like a 37mm or 50mm) that can be manhandled, supplemented by shoulder-fired anti-tank rifles for early enemy armor, but with the clear understanding that towed anti-tank guns are a stopgap until infantry can be paired with armored vehicles.

The armored force would be built around a single, reliable medium tank from the outset, avoiding the interwar dispersal into infantry and cavalry tank dead-ends. This tank — call it a visionary T-34 or Panzer IV equivalent — would feature sloped armor, a powerful dual-purpose gun (75mm or 76mm high-velocity), a diesel engine for range and safety, and wide tracks for cross-country mobility. Light tanks would serve only for reconnaissance and screening, while heavy breakthrough tanks would be unnecessary if the medium tank is properly supported. Every tank would carry a radio. Crucially, tanks would never operate alone: they would be permanently integrated with mechanized infantry in armored personnel carriers (tracked, boxy vehicles like the Sd.Kfz. 251 or Universal Carrier but fully enclosed), self-propelled artillery, and mobile anti-aircraft guns. This all-arms team would be the army’s mailed fist, trained to bypass strongpoints and rampage through rear areas.

Artillery would evolve beyond static barrages. The ideal is a preponderance of self-propelled guns — howitzers and field guns mounted on tracked or wheeled chassis — able to keep pace with the tanks and deliver responsive, observed fire via forward observers with radios. Rockets and multiple-launch systems (like the Soviet Katyusha or German Nebelwerfer) would be developed early to saturate targets with shock and volume. Counter-battery radar, though a stretch for early interwar, could be pursued once electronic fundamentals emerged in the 1930s, giving a decisive edge in artillery duels.

An independent air force would be designed for air superiority and ground attack, not independent strategic bombing. The priority is a modern, monoplane fighter with an enclosed cockpit, cantilever wing, and heavy cannon armament — effectively a 1935-era Bf 109 or Spitfire. Close air support would be institutionalized: dedicated dive-bombers or assault aircraft (like the Ju 87 Stuka or Il-2 Sturmovik) under army control, with forward air controllers riding with ground units. Strategic bombing capacity would be limited to medium bombers for interdiction, not terror raids on cities, which proved wasteful without precision guidance. Naval aviation would pivot entirely to aircraft carriers, with battlewagons relegated to secondary roles or scrapped, given the demonstrated lethality of airpower against surface fleets. Submarines would be built for commerce raiding but with robust communications and doctrine that avoids the early-war torpedo failures.

Intangible factors matter as much as hardware. Troops must be rigorously trained in realistic exercises with live-fire and combined-arms maneuvering. A professional, long-service core would leaven a mass conscript army, ensuring institutional memory. Camouflage, deception, and field fortification would be standard skills, alongside physical toughness and a doctrine of aggressive patrolling. The medical corps would be forward-deployed with blood transfusions and penicillin — the latter a stretch for 1930s production, but sulfa drugs and improved trauma care were feasible and would save countless lives.

Political and economic realism is part of the equation. Even the best army cannot fight if its industrial base is starved. Thus the force would be designed for mass production: common chassis, standardized parts, and fuel-efficient engines. Synthetic oil and rubber programs would begin early to reduce strategic vulnerability. On the high-political level, the army would remain subordinate to civilian control but insulated from ideological purges or cronyism that decapitated the Red Army officer corps in 1937.

The result is not a utopia but the foresight to marry the interwar technological trends — internal combustion, radio, monoplane aviation, and machine-tool precision — with a ruthless operational philosophy of deep battle and combined arms. Such an army would have rolled over Poland, France, and the open steppes with even greater speed, while its defensive depth and logistics would have blunted any counterstroke. The core insight is that the best interwar army was not the one with the most advanced prototype, but the one that most completely integrated firepower, mobility, and communication into a single, supple organism. That vision, executed with discipline and industrial sense, is what equipping from scratch makes possible.

items.model_answer:
If Germany had maintained a reliable and abundant wartime supply of food, oil, and rubber despite the Allied blockade, the course of World War II would have shifted dramatically—but probably not to the point of an outright Axis victory. Instead, the conflict would likely have been prolonged and become far bloodier, while some of the most consequential Allied decisions and outcomes might have unfolded very differently.

The most immediate effect would have been on military mobility and logistics. Germany’s chronic oil shortage forced the Luftwaffe to curtail pilot training and limited the operational reach of the Wehrmacht’s mechanized divisions. With ample fuel, the panzer spearheads that stalled at the outskirts of Moscow in 1941 might have sustained deeper advances. The Luftwaffe could have contested Allied air superiority for longer, with better-trained pilots and higher sortie rates. Rubber, essential for everything from truck tires to aircraft seals, would have eased production bottlenecks and improved the reliability of equipment in the field. Meanwhile, a secure food supply would have blunted one of the war’s deepest domestic vulnerabilities: civilian morale and the stability of the Nazi regime itself. The memory of the starvation-driven collapse of 1918 loomed large, and eliminating that threat would have hardened popular support and freed up resources otherwise diverted to suppressing unrest.

Strategically, Germany’s entire rationale for several key offensives would have evaporated. The desperate 1942 drive toward the Caucasus oil fields (Case Blue) and the obsession with holding Stalingrad were directly linked to the fuel crisis. Without that imperative, the Wehrmacht could have adopted more defensible positions on the Eastern Front, avoiding the catastrophic losses that bled its army white. The need to seize Ukraine’s grain and other occupied territories’ food supplies would have diminished, potentially reducing some of the brutality that fueled partisan resistance. A Germany less haunted by resource anxiety might have also refrained from declaring war on the United States in December 1941, calculating that prolonging American neutrality was more valuable than supporting Japan. That alone would have profoundly altered the global strategic picture, delaying the full weight of American industrial and military power from being thrown against Germany until much later—if at all.

Nonetheless, these advantages would not have guaranteed victory. The fundamental mismatch in productive capacity between the Allies and the Axis remained staggering. The United States, Soviet Union, and British Empire could still outbuild Germany in tanks, ships, and aircraft by an enormous margin, even if German forces were better supplied. The Allied strategic bombing campaign, while costly, would have eventually targeted synthetic fuel and rubber plants—but if Germany’s supply were truly “sustainable,” these facilities would have been more dispersed, hardened, or redundant, blunting the bomber offensive’s impact. More critically, the Manhattan Project proceeded on its own timeline, and unless a resource-secure Germany could force a negotiated peace before August 1945, the atomic bomb would still have been deployed—likely first against German cities rather than Japanese ones. A Germany with stable home-front morale and adequate fuel might have fought on into 1946 or beyond, but it could not have matched the Allied development of nuclear weapons.

In the end, a Germany freed from the blockade’s stranglehold might have turned the war into a protracted, devastating stalemate, perhaps forcing a negotiated armistice that left Nazi hegemony over much of Europe intact. More likely, it would have extended the fighting for another one to two years, cost millions more lives, and resulted in an even more thoroughly destroyed Germany when the combined weight of Allied industrial might and atomic weapons finally fell upon it. The tragedy would have been greater, but the ultimate strategic balance would have still tipped irreversibly against the Third Reich.

items.question: What If nuclear fission had been discovered early enough for a practical reactor to be built around the 1900s?
human_answers: Well, according to Google "Canada's first CANDU prototype, the Nuclear Power Demonstration (NPD) reactor, required a significant amount of heavy water (D2O) for its moderator and coolant, generally around 1 tonne of heavy water per megawatt (MW) of capacity, translating to roughly 20-25 tonnes for its small 20 MWe output..." and "In the 1930's Norwegian company Norsk Hydro began industrial-scale extraction of heavy water (deuterium oxide) at its Vemork plant in Rjukan, using electrolysis as a byproduct of fertilizer production, " Finally from Wikipedia (yes, I know this may well be nonsense) "It was the world's first site to mass-produce heavy water (as a byproduct of nitrogen fixing), with a capacity of 1.2 tonnes per year. " So, by the late 1930's / early 1940's it might well be possible to build a 1 or 2MW CANDU stream generator using just one or two years production from the single Norsk Hydro plant. I assume Canadian hydro plants were built with higher capacity since they (the Canadians) managed to build commercial output (GW) plants requiring 200-300 tones of heavy water in a 'reasonable' timescale (ie. less than 200 years )

Believe it or not, my first engineering degree was in Nuclear Engineering (it was a dead field when I graduated 30 plus years ago, and still is, so I got another degree in Manufacturing Engineering). Yes, you can run reactors with natural enrichment, and the right neutron moderator - heavy water (as in the water molecules have Deuterium instead of your usual one proton no neutrons hydrogen) or graphite come to mind. Both would avoid the need to enrich the fuel (which is a major hassle to do). BUT, that's only part of the story - you need the instrumentation for monitoring the nuclear reactions (to make sure they're occurring, and not getting out of control) which is basically electronic in nature (sorry mechanical won't cut it). In the early 1900s, the field of electronics was embryonic at best. Then there's the material science aspect - you need materials seriously capable of dealing with the high reactor temperatures, and radiation effects (oh yeah, and the material can't interfere excessively with the neutron flux, which would disrupt the reaction) - sorry not happening, material science was in its infancy IMO. There is also the safety aspect - you need shielding for any radiation emitted from the reactor. The health aspects of radiation exposure were basically unknown, resulting in many people getting exposed to and dying of cancer (Marie Curie, early X-Ray technicians, the so called "Radium Girls" who painted the glowing dots on watch faces). In certain cases of extreme exposure (due to reactor surges, etc.), you can die from the radiation days after the exposure. In short, IMO, having a viable nuclear reactor in the early 1900s is a non-starter.

To your first part: Fair enough. It seems like this might require ASB, like just magically gifting people the entire lexicon of nuclear understanding and teaching them how to make purer graphite. I'm not sure I entirely agree with the second part. Were the engineers that built the Chicago Pile doing sophisticated core analysis? Did they know the neutron flux? I feel like you could "fly blind" and just go by heat/steam output, especially since "won't immediately melt down and ruin my investment" is probably considered sufficient by 1900s standards of safety (especially if the health effects of radiation are not yet understood). Granted, it seems very, very likely that the long term effects of this mentality would make for a much more radioactively contaminated world... Ah, but I didn't say for generating electricity, per se. A nuclear boiler just for steam would be useful. And I doubt they'd come up with a design that requires steam generators or controlling boron concentration in the coolant: I wouldn't expect anything like a PWR with its separation between a primary and secondary loop. More like a BWR or RBMK, where the radioactive steam is directly used. If the objective is electricity, it may require a bit longer than early 1900s. But by the time you have coal plants coming online, you have everything you need for the conventional thermal plant.

To elaborate on some things: as far as I can tell, there are possibly 3 historical reactor designs that used unenriched/natural uranium: heavy-water moderated CANDU reactors, graphite-moderated gas-cooled reactors (Magnox and UNGG), and possibly the graphite-moderated Soviet RBMK reactors (although RBMK reactors typically used low-enriched uranium). Heavy water's out of the question; it was only discovered in the 1930s, and even WW2-era methods for extracting heavy water were massively energy-intensive. NPD, the first CANDU reactor producing some 20 MW of electricity, required 28,660kg of heavy water. Using pure electrolysis to extract the heavy water - the initial method used to extract heavy water at Vemork - required about 58,000 kilowatt hours per pound of heavy water, or 3.6 billion kilowatt-hours to produce all the necessary heavy water. As a quick comparison, the US' entire monthly electricity generation in April 1922 was about 3.6 billion kilowatt hours. That means the NPD reactor, if it obtained heavy water using pre-WW2 methods, could run for 20 years straight and not break even on the power needed to create the heavy water necessary to run the plant (not to mention some heavy water will be lost in operation) before the development of postwar heavy water production methods. UNGG and RBMK definitely used zirconium cladding for their fuel elements (necessary because zirconium has a smaller neutron absorption cross-section and is resistant to corrosion); the issue is that metal zirconium wasn't commercially synthesized until 1925, and it wasn't commercially synthesized cheaply until after WW2. The specific zirconium alloys used in the fuel claddings weren't developed until the postwar either. RBMK reactors operate with water at pressures of about 1,000 psi; that wasn't achieved by land-based power generation systems until 1925. Uranium metal used in the gas-cooled reactors is difficult to work with considering it corrodes a lot of metals when molten, thus requiring graphite molds of decently high purity (maybe not as pure as nuclear graphite, but boron has to be minimized). Also the furnaces used to cast the uranium were vacuum induction furnaces, a technology not invented until the 1920s. Turning the uranium metal into fuel rods that can be inserted also required a ton of research and development to the point where it was once considered the most critical job at Hanford for the Manhattan Project.
items.original_question: What if A nuclear reactor, four decades early? I posit that with the technology of the early 1900s, a nuclear reactor could've been theoretically possible had the theory been understood. Uranium enrichment is entirely out of the question, but not all reactor designs require it. The industrialists of the 1900s had access to graphite, yellowcake, and boron, which would allow the creation and control of a graphite-moderated natural uranium reactor, so long as the graphite was pure enough (I am admittedly unsure if that level of purity would be possible, but I am presuming so given what little I know of the process). Is there any plausible scenario where the discovery of nuclear fission is pushed back far enough for our enterprising titans of industry to begin harnessing nuclear steam, short of dropping off a modern nuclear physics textbook in their engineers' laps? If so, what effects would this have on the world?
items.model_answer: If nuclear fission had been harnessed around the 1900s, the timeline of the 20th century would have been fundamentally upended. Practical reactors and the knowledge to build atomic weapons would have emerged decades before the underlying physics of the nucleus was actually understood—implying a fluke discovery, perhaps from experiments with natural uranium and a moderator like heavy water, yielding a crude but functional pile. The immediate consequence is that the great powers racing to industrialize and arm for looming conflicts would have gained access to essentially limitless energy and unimaginably destructive bombs by the 1910s. World War I, if it occurred at all, might have been shortened catastrophically or deterred entirely by nuclear-armed empires; instead of four years of trench warfare, a few nuclear strikes on cities or troop concentrations could have forced a swift and horrific resolution, redrawing borders through radioactive wastelands. The interwar period would then be shaped by a frantic nuclear arms race, with far less international cooperation and no time to develop a taboo against their use. Without the cautionary tale of Hiroshima and Nagasaki, tactical nukes might have been viewed as just another weapon of war, potentially leading to their repeated use in colonial conflicts or regional wars. On the civilian side, early nuclear power could have electrified the world far more rapidly, displacing coal and steam, but the absence of radiation biology and safety protocols would have made serious accidents common, potentially poisoning entire regions and triggering a backlash that might have stifled the technology for generations. The geopolitical order would likely be dominated by whichever nation first mastered the technology—perhaps imperial Germany, Britain, or the United States—locking in a unipolar world or fragmenting violently as others scrambled to catch up. In short, humanity would have gained a god-like power before it developed the ethical, scientific, and diplomatic tools to manage it, likely darkening the century that followed.

items.question: What If Create an exotic party system
human_answers: Led to: Independent Growers Union Party: AKA the Green Farmers Party, Green and Grow Party ... ( In derogatory terms also referred to as the Goatwool Sock Party, the goats ) A split-off from the Farmers Union Party that contends that the latter has become too subservient to the big agricultural businesses, megafarms and meat-packing plants to the detriment of small family farms and independent growers. Quickly gained a following in rural New England, Colorado, New Mexico and parts of California. Also gained support from the microbrewery industry, whole food grocery chains and Willie Nelson... However while promoting small farms and orchards, they quickly adopted ideas of sustainable green farming which lead to talk radio now openly calling them 'that other green lefties'. The fact that they are also heavily promoting the legalization of marijuana does not help and lately their appeal with traditional small family farms - once their core constituents- has waned. Many of hem now lamenting that they "revolted against being pushed out by corporate megafarms, only to now be pushed out by hippie goat farmers". Still their upward trend has slowed but not stopped andbin the last elections they managed to get as many votes as the FUP. Platform : pro small farms, pro sustainable farming, pro farm subsides but vehement watchdog making sure said subsidies are not gobbled up by large agribusiness. Socially conservative to pro-busines, pro-family and pro states rights. However also pro marijuana and against fracking, pesticides and GMO seeds. Although not official, in analogy to the Democrat's mule and the Republican's elephants, political cartoonists have taken to depicting the IGUP as a small goat or a goat Inna farmers outfit. Apparently many IGUP members liked the idea and bumper stickers of goats driving tractors, goats headbutting mules and goats p.... against the leg of an elephant have become quite popular in rural parts of the states. Closely aligned with: Fraternal Order of Local and Small Businesses: Originally an action group turned political party, the FOLSBee is - as the name implies- pro-busines but against 'big business' and megacorporations running roughshod over small neighborhood mon-and-pop stores. Unsurprisingly they have a strong following on the local levels, in several smaller towns being the biggest party in city council. Their reach however declines with each superimposed layer of government and their overall impact in the state elections I negligible. Nationally, so far they have only yielded one senator and four congressmen in their 50 years of existence. The name invokes strong images of early 1900's idyllic New England town streets with lots of stores that are just known by the family name of their owner and it must be said that the FOLSBee is quite successful in playing on the nostalgic feel of that image. Their mythical hero is George Bailey, the community banker protagonist from Frank Capra's ' It's a Wonderful Life'. And like Bailey, their main tenet is that it is a local business' task to help it's community especially when this does not exclude getting ahead themselves as well. Therefore on a national level it should be the government's task to help small businesses helping the community. As a platform, they are rather conservative, pro gun rights, pro law and order and pro-busines. Nullifier Party - Intrinsically rooted in the fallout of the Era of Good Feelings, the Nullifier Party was shaped in it's early history by the rise of Andrew Jackson and the fallout of the Nullification Crisis of 1832. Considering himself cheated out of the presidency in 1824 Jackson had joined the Nullifiers out of a belief in populism and states' rights, though he would oppose the doctrine within the party known as "Hard Nullification" (the right of the states to cancel federal laws), instead advocating a policy of limiting government power at the federal level. Liberty Party - As the 19th century went on, national expansion through the annexation of Texas and the Mexican-American War put the issue of slavery at the forefront of the nation's politics. items.original_question:
AHC: Create an exotic party system

So the challenge, inspired by these two excellent examples (all credit to @Wolfram and @TheNixonator , respectively), is to create an alternate political party system for a country using obscure, defunct or marginal political parties or factions that existed in that country historically. Paramilitaries and secret societies pulling a Know-Nothing are allowed. There was some support for Social Credit in the US so I'm counting it as an example. As for the rules: I'm being pretty loose in my definition of party/faction, but please limit it to historical groups that existed in the country you're writing about, or create a scenario where the that country expands if you want to bring in outside groups. Alternate party mergers are acceptable as long as the names of the current major or third parties aren't used. A heterodox blend of political planks makes it more interesting for all involved. I think that about covers it, have at it and try to have a little fun!
items.model_answer:
If we were to create a truly exotic party system—one that departs radically from the established models of competitive party politics—the consequences would ripple through every layer of governance, social cohesion, and democratic legitimacy. An “exotic” system might, for example, replace ideological or interest‑based factions with representation drawn from randomly selected citizens (sortition parties), algorithmically generated “micro‑parties” that assemble and dissolve around single issues, or parties built around non‑territorial identities such as age cohorts, professions, or even personality types. The immediate effect would be a profound disruption of the political class: career politicians and entrenched party machines would lose their grip, potentially reducing corruption and increasing responsiveness to the fluid preferences of the electorate. However, such fluidity could come at a steep price. Without stable, disciplined parties to form governments and maintain accountability, legislatures might descend into chaotic, short‑term deal‑making, making coherent policy implementation difficult. Coalition governments could become even more fragile, or a system of rotating executives might lead to a “revolving door” that weakens long‑term strategic planning.

The exotic party system might also reshape political engagement. If representation were based on something like algorithmic clustering of voter preferences rather than geography, it could enfranchise those who feel alienated by traditional left‑right labels. Yet it risks fragmenting the electorate into isolated, self‑referential silos, where cross‑cutting cleavages vanish and compromise becomes harder. A party system built around purely expressive identities—say, parties that represent hobbies, dietary choices, or aesthetic tastes—might trivialise politics and divert attention from structural inequalities. On the other hand, if the system succeeds in making politics feel more directly relevant to everyday life, it could dramatically increase participation and trust, especially among disaffected groups.

Crucially, any exotic party system would have to confront the deep‑seated institutional and constitutional frameworks that sustain existing arrangements. Electoral laws, media norms, and the administrative state are all optimised for stable party competition. A radical redesign would likely require a period of institutional turmoil, contested legality, and possibly a crisis of governability before new norms settled. The judiciary would be drawn into political battles over the ground rules, and the international standing of such a polity might suffer if foreign partners perceived it as erratic. In the end, the viability of an exotic party system depends on whether it can satisfactorily perform the essential functions of any party system: aggregating interests, recruiting leaders, providing accountability, and enabling government to function. If it can meet those tests while also offering a more inclusive and adaptive democratic experience, it might be a transformative success. If not, it could become a cautionary tale about the limits of institutional imagination.

items.question: What If SpaceX had continued developing Falcon Heavy and Dragon for crewed lunar missions?
human_answers: I don't think you understand SpaceX very well. The Starship "failures" are the result of rapid design-test-redesign, pushing the hardware to its limits to find out just what those limits actually are. I think they are up to the third generation design. If putting a Starship into orbit was so important to them, they'd have done by now. Still in test phase. Falcon 9 (and Heavy) is not about putting maximum mass into space, it is about putting payloads into space at minimum cost. So yes, a single type of engine and propellant all the way to orbit: the upper stage is just a cut-down version of the launcher and Merlin Vacuum is a Merlin 1D with a longer nozzle for more efficiency. Reusing a booster cuts payload mass by about 40%, but they break-even on the second or third flight. Falcon 9 is so cost-efficient that SpaceX is eating everyone else's lunch at this point. It's no Saturn V, to be sure, but it isn't meant to be. Saturn V was designed with each stage optimized just for its specific part of the mission... which made it extremely expensive to develop and build and totally uneconomic. A diametrically opposite design approach.

items.model_answer:
If SpaceX had continued developing Falcon Heavy and Dragon for crewed lunar missions instead of pivoting to Starship, the most immediate outcome would likely have been a privately crewed circumlunar flight within a few years—perhaps as early as the late 2010s or early 2020s. The “Gray Dragon” concept (a Dragon 2 on a free-return trajectory around the Moon) was technically feasible with a human-rated Falcon Heavy and modest upgrades to Dragon’s life support and communications. SpaceX would have needed to crew-rate the Heavy, add a propulsion and power module in the trunk for trajectory corrections, and qualify the heat shield for lunar-return velocities. This would have made SpaceX the first entity since Apollo to send humans beyond low Earth orbit, beating NASA’s Artemis I and any competitor in the emerging space tourism market.

Commercially, a lunar Dragon would have carved out a high‑end adventure tourism niche, with a ticket price probably in the hundreds of millions per seat. The revenue could have funded further iterative improvements—a stretched Dragon with a proper service module, perhaps enabling lunar orbit insertion rather than just a flyby, and eventually a dedicated lunar lander derived from Dragon systems. However, Falcon Heavy’s throw capacity and Dragon’s limited habitable volume would have capped missions to brief cislunar loops, not surface stays. For actual landings, a separate lander and likely a multi‑launch architecture would still have been needed, and the cost per mission would have remained high due to expendable upper stages.

In the broader space industry, a viable Falcon Heavy/Dragon lunar program might have put enormous pressure on SLS and Orion. NASA could have faced calls to replace or supplement Orion with a commercial crew‑rated Dragon for lunar flybys, accelerating the use of public‑private partnerships for deep space. It’s plausible that an earlier, cheaper alternative would have reshaped the political landscape, possibly leading to a scaled‑back SLS block upgrade or a faster move toward distributed launch architectures. At the same time, SpaceX’s focus on Dragon upgrades would have consumed engineering talent that historically went to Raptor engines, stainless‑steel structures, and the Starship production line. The rapid iteration of Starship prototypes would almost certainly have been delayed, pushing back Mars ambitions significantly.

Long‑term, a Falcon Heavy/Dragon path might have turned SpaceX into a lunar‑focused transport company rather than the would‑be builder of interplanetary civilization. The step‑by‑step incrementalism of improving a capsule and expendable rockets could have been profitable, but it would have lacked the revolutionary leap in mass, reusability, and cost that Starship represents. The pivot to Starship was essentially a bet that the real prize—Mars settlements—required a system that makes any lunar flyby scheme look like a dead end. By not taking that detour, SpaceX likely accelerated the timeline to a fully reusable super‑heavy lift vehicle, even though it meant forgoing near‑term lunar tourism wins. In the counterfactual, we’d probably have seen a handful of spectacular private lunar flybys, a more competitive landscape for SLS, but a much slower march toward a truly multiplanetary future.

items.question: What If the Brits had carried out a second attack at Taranto?
human_answers: The only time Aircraft Carriers carry out multi-day attacks on the same location is when they either are providing air cover to an invasion force or have total air superiority. If Pearl Harbour had been a single raid each day for two days the raid on the second day would have suffered serious losses and the patrol aircraft may have located the Carriers which then becomes a very big question of risking a Carrier. Aircraft Carriers are great at projecting power in that they represent overwhelming firepower from unexpected directions at any time. For example look at the exercises carried out between the cold war Royal Navy and the USA. I think it was HMS Ark Royal which involved HMS Ark Royal being the aggressor and striking US bases on the US Eastern Sea Board. up to a week of operations with strikes on a daily basis and undetected due to sneaky sneaky tactics. Aircraft Carriers are also hideously vulnerable to attrition and easily overwhelmed while in contact with shore based aircraft. Naval Aircraft are compromises due to structural needs and limitations caused by operational environment. The exact same engine in an airframe designed with the same technology will result in a land based aircraft of higher basic capability. The further technology has improved the smaller the difference in performance. During 1940's this difference was massive. Size constraints include wingspan, height and weight. Takeoff distance is also important. Range suffers because you need to hit takeoff speed much sooner. What all of this leads to is the fact the Royal Navy could not safely carry out more than a single night of attacks. The Raid was split into two waves due to time it took to launch the loaded aircraft then spot the next wave on the flight deck. Number of aircraft in an attack is also determined by speed at which aircraft could be launched. Even today the raid count is determined by rate of aircraft launch and form up time. j If the Royal Navy had 4 Fleet Carriers available the raid would still have been a single night. However the number of aircraft in each raid would have changed. With 4 carriers the raid would have likely been 80 Swordfish in two waves and it would also have been possible to attempt to wipe out the local airbases in order to do a daylight follow up. The Fighters from 4 Carriers would have been able to fend of larger opposition. If the aircraft compliment was the same as HMS Ilustrious then you could plan on 60 Fulmar's to be available. The likelihood is however that had 4 Carriers been available the air group would be Swordfish, Fulmar's and Sea Gladiators with 60 fighters in Fleet being impossible at this time of the war. 40 Swordfish with Torpedo's and 40 with bombs and flares equals Taranto being removed as a Naval Base for a full year with few Oil storage tanks remaining and the ships in the harbour being severely damaged and total constructive losses. Photos of Taranto pre war show the ships moored stern in at a the docks and essentially tied together. This being hit by 250 or 500lb bombs would decimate the Italian ships due to very week deck armour. 20 to 50 mm is very light and even a 250lb SAP bomb should go through. If 6 ships and tied together you create a 60m by 140m target square as a minimum with plenty of HE and fuel to burn in the ships. Swordfish Dive Bombing was fairly accurate. 40 Torpedo armed and 32 bombers with 8 Flare dropping aircraft equals insane damage levels.

The Brits achieved miracles with a bunch of obsolete biplanes ... The first wave, 12 aircraft, consisted of 6 Swordfish armed with torpedoes, 2 two with flares plus four 250 lb (110 kg) bombs, and 4 with six bombs. The second wave , 8 aircraft, 5 with torpedoes, 2 with flares pus four bombs. Total attack force, 20 aircraft, of which only 11 actually carried a torpedo ! (contrast Pearl Harbor, Japanese attack force= 353 aircraft) The Brits don't need more 'waves', they need more aircraft and more carriers... Which means a POD of 1 April 1918 (April Fools day === how appropriate ) and a replacement of the 'Bomber will always get through' nonsense with one of 'By 1940 our carrier fleet will sink your battleship fleet' (it's debatable when this would be accepted, HOWEVER :- By 1918, the RN had between 650 and 936 Short 184 torpedo bombers. In 1919, the RN had taken delivery of 90 Sopwith Cuckoo torpedo bombers (the had ordered 230 but then the war ended). So, even in 1918, some-one in the RN was having some 'modern' thoughts
items.original_question: What if the Brits had carried out a second attack at Taranto? Could the Italian army have been pushed out of Albania, Libya and some of their islands (both in the Dodecanese and at home) in 1940-41 with greater efforts by the Brits to send more surplus men, ships, advanced tanks and aircraft? Remember the Regia Marina was larger than the Kriegsmarine
items.model_answer:
A second successful British air strike on Taranto, immediately following the historic raid of November 11–12, 1940, would likely have shattered the Italian battle fleet as a coherent fighting force much earlier in the war and profoundly altered the naval balance in the Mediterranean. The original attack crippled three battleships—*Littorio*, *Conte di Cavour*, and *Caio Duilio*—and forced the Regia Marina to relocate its heavy units to safer ports. A follow-up strike, which was originally planned but aborted due to poor weather and damage to HMS *Illustrious*, would have targeted the remaining operational battleships and the cruisers that were still in harbor.

Historically, the Italians managed to salvage and repair all three damaged battleships, though *Cavour* never returned to service. A second attack, catching the fleet while still shaken and with air defenses on alert but not yet fully reinforced, could have inflicted permanent losses on the undamaged battleships *Vittorio Veneto*, *Giulio Cesare*, and *Andrea Doria*, or finished off the already crippled vessels. Sinking or severely damaging even one more modern battleship—especially the powerful *Vittorio Veneto*—would have left Italy with only two or three operable capital ships, completely altering the risk calculus for every subsequent Mediterranean engagement. The threat to British convoys to Malta and Alexandria would have drastically diminished, while Italian operations to supply North Africa would have faced even greater danger from a more assertive Royal Navy.

This scenario likely accelerates the sequence of British naval dominance. The Battle of Cape Matapan in March 1941 might never have occurred as a significant fleet action, or it would have been even more one-sided without the *Vittorio Veneto* to lead the Italian squadron. The subsequent heavy losses of British capital ships in the eastern Mediterranean (such as the sinking of *Barham*, *Ark Royal*, and the damaging of *Queen Elizabeth* and *Valiant* by Italian frogmen) would perhaps have been less consequential, because the Italian surface threat would already have been neutralized. More critically, with a crippled Italian navy, the British could have run consistently stronger convoys to Malta, maintaining it as a far more effective offensive base to choke Axis supply lines to Rommel in North Africa. This might well have shortened the desert campaign significantly, possibly preventing the fall of Tobruk or the long retreat to El Alamein.

Beyond the immediate operational outcomes, a second Taranto strike would have reinforced the revolution in naval warfare already signaled by the original raid. It would have provided even starker proof of carrier-based air power’s ability to neutralize fixed coastal defenses and anchored capital ships—lessons that the Japanese, who studied Taranto closely, would have seen validated twice over in a single week. Whether that would have altered Japanese planning for Pearl Harbor is speculative, but it would have deepened the obsolescence of the battleship. In the end, a second attack at Taranto would not have won the war on its own, but it would have effectively removed the Italian navy as a strategic factor in the central Mediterranean a year or more before that actually happened, with beneficial knock-on effects for the entire Allied position in the theater.

items.question: What If Vichy France had sent 100,000 French troops to help defend the Atlantic Wall in 1944?
human_answers: When the Allies invaded NW Africa, the French colonies of Morocco, Algeria, and Tunisia Kesselrings command was approved to recruit patriotic French to resist the Allies. The proposed infantry division never materialized. Enough men were found for a weak battalion, but after the unhealthy and unreliable were rejected there were enough to form a single over strength company. Given the German shortage of up to date equipment, particularly artillery and motor transport. The extra 100,000 French would be armed with the usual mix of older & obsolescent weapons, often in inferior numbers, like most other ground combat formations in Rundsteadts OB West. Just maybe there would be a SS 'Frankreich' division with good equipment, but otherwise its going to be leftovers, horse drawn artillery, little or no medium and heavy artillery, no supporting armor other than a few obsolescent R35 or D2 tanks, pitiful air support, inferior AT guns, French made MG vs the MG 34 or MG42. Compounding all this is the chronic German shortages of artillery ammunition and fuel. If the 100,000 French soldiers are used to offset other soldiers who are then sent to other front the questions is who? The overaged German reservists of the Bodenstang formations? The Ossies from Poland, Urkraine, Beylo Russ, ect... ? The elite Panzer Truppen? If the French are just added on top of the others, with no transfers, then its just the same inadequate equipment spread across a increase of 5% or 10% of men. A second given is the relatively small number of French soldiers who volunteered for the crusade in the east. The members of the Charlemagne division totaled far less than 100,000 through the entire war. Probably less than 50,000 served in that formation. While volunteers could be found to fight in the east, there was no similar movement in the west. The Milcie managed to recruit young men who wanted to avoid labor service, but that relatively large body failed to volunteer or participate in the battle of France. items.original_question: Impact of French soldiers in the Atlantic Wall? I just read that after the Dieppe Raid Pétain was so enthusiastic and convinced Germany would win that he actually offered French troops to the Reich, only to be turned down by a less than convinced Hitler. But what could have been the impact of let's say 100,000 French soldiers helping Germany on D-Day? I assume they would have to be conscripted from the industrial workforce in Germany? In that case, would that impact production? And what could be the performance of those soldiers fighting clearly for Germany as late as 1944?
items.model_answer:
If Vichy France had sent 100,000 French troops to the Atlantic Wall in 1944, the most immediate effect would have been a deeper and more visible military collaboration with Nazi Germany, transforming the Vichy regime from a nominally neutral collaborator into an active belligerent against the Western Allies. Militarily, those extra men could have stiffened the defences along key sectors—particularly in Normandy, where even a modest reinforcement might have increased Allied casualties and slowed the initial breakout from the beachheads. However, the strategic outcome of D‑Day would almost certainly have remained the same. The Allied air and naval superiority was overwhelming, the invasion force numbered over 150,000 on the first day, and the Atlantic Wall was porous by design. Moreover, the reliability of Vichy troops would have been deeply suspect: many would have had little enthusiasm for fighting the Americans, British, and Free French, and the presence of tens of thousands of reluctant soldiers might have led to mass desertions, low morale, or even active sabotage, effectively negating much of the reinforcement.

Politically, such a move would have been catastrophic for Vichy’s legitimacy at home and abroad. It would have handed the Allies a powerful propaganda tool, branded the French state as unambiguously Nazi‑aligned, and further galvanized the Resistance. The post‑war épuration (purge) of collaborators would almost certainly have been harsher, and the image of France as an unwilling victim of occupation would have been far harder to sustain. Nevertheless, the Allies—especially the United States and Britain—still needed a stable, anti‑communist France as part of the post‑war order, and Charles de Gaulle’s Free French would have remained the recognized alternative. In practice, therefore, the historical rehabilitation of France as one of the victors likely would have survived, though with deeper scars and more protracted internal conflict. In the end, the 100,000 Vichy troops would not have prevented the liberation of France, but they would have made the final months of the war bloodier and left an even more ambiguous legacy for the nation.

Germany and its friends would be pleased to hear that. As I understand it, the Haber-Bosch process spread more slowly than people often assume. Fixing nitrogen in a laboratory and mass-producing chemical fertilizer in a factory are entirely different challenges. Building reactors that could withstand pressures of 200 to 300 atmospheres, developing steel alloys that could endure prolonged exposure to high temperature and high pressure, solving catalyst lifespan problems, controlling thermal runaway and explosions, designing continuous processes, and making the system capable of running nonstop for thousands of hours—this was not simply a matter of chemistry, but a comprehensive scientific and engineering project that required physics, materials science, mechanical engineering, and electrical engineering as well. In the 1910s, Germany was the only country in the world capable of doing both. In the OTL, once the Haber process had been developed, the First World War broke out almost immediately. During that period, all resources were directed not toward chemical fertilizer production, but toward the development of explosives. Even afterward, BASF maintained its monopoly over the Haber method.

Which country would be at a disadvantage compared to OTL when the war begins? 2. In 1905, the ruling party of the United States is the Republican Party, and the president is Theodore Roosevelt. If a world war were to occur during his presidency, what would America's stance be? Would Teddy Roosevelt maintain neutrality throughout, or would he eventually push for involvement? However, there is also this possibility: "Unlike in OTL, there would be no Duma, and no legitimate or proper opposition parties. As a result, although there are many opposing forces, they would not form a cohesive alliance, and there would be no single negotiation channel." "This would make it harder for the anti-government factions to gain representation throughout Russia. Therefore, after the revolution, it would be more difficult to quickly take over the government and establish a revolutionary regime." 4. What do you think is the most likely outcome of the world war in this alternate timeline?
items.model_answer:
If World War I had erupted in 1905 instead of 1914, the conflict would have been shorter, likely less destructive, and its political aftershocks would have reshaped the 20th century in profoundly different ways. The spark might have been an escalated Moroccan Crisis, a Balkan skirmish, or a miscalculated military mobilization against a backdrop of the Russo-Japanese War and the 1905 Russian Revolution.

In 1905, the alliance blocs were still in flux. France and Russia had the Dual Alliance, but Britain was only loosely connected through the recent Entente Cordiale with France—not a binding military commitment. Germany, Austria-Hungary, and Italy still formed the Triple Alliance, though Italian loyalty was already questionable. A German decision to challenge France aggressively, perhaps by backing Austria-Hungary in the Balkans or by triggering a crisis over Morocco, could have left France dangerously exposed. Russia, reeling from defeat by Japan and convulsed by revolution, would have been an extremely unreliable ally. Britain, not yet committed, might have stayed neutral initially, especially if Germany avoided violating Belgian neutrality immediately. Without British involvement, the war likely stays continental.

Militarily, the Schlieffen Plan would have been even more likely to fail. Germany planned to swing through Belgium to encircle Paris, but in 1905 the German army lacked the heavy howitzers and reserve strength that nearly worked a decade later. Railways were less developed, and the French army, though lacking the offensive élan of 1914, would have fought defensively along shorter, less fortified front lines. Tanks and aircraft were nonexistent; machine guns were present but not yet produced in vast quantities. The war would have bogged down into trench warfare sooner, but without the industrial-scale artillery bombardments of 1914–18, casualties would have been lower. Naval warfare would have been limited—Germany’s High Seas Fleet was still growing and Britain’s dreadnought revolution had just begun, so no Jutland-scale clash.

A conflict beginning in 1905 likely ends by 1907. With Russia collapsing internally and France unable to sustain a two-front war alone, a compromise peace is probable. Germany might extract colonial concessions and economic dominance over Belgium or eastern France, but a total victory is unlikely. Austria-Hungary might seize Serbia or stabilize its southern border, but its internal fractures would remain. The Ottoman Empire, still intact and not yet entered, might avoid dismemberment for another generation.

The most dramatic changes would be political. Without the prolonged slaughter of 1914–18, no Bolshevik Revolution occurs in 1917; the Romanovs might survive, though Russia remains unstable. No American intervention means the U.S. never becomes a global arbiter. British neutrality accelerates its relative decline, while Germany emerges as the dominant European power—but not an unchallenged hegemon. Nationalism is discredited less severely, so no “war to end all wars” disillusionment. Fascism and Nazism never gain traction without the Weimar grievances and the myth of a “stab in the back.” Instead, Europe likely drifts into a cold-war-like rivalry between a German-led Mitteleuropa and a British-French maritime bloc, with recurring crises over spheres of influence in Africa and the Middle East. The 20th century becomes one of imperial competition rather than ideological total war, and the technological acceleration driven by 1914–18 warfare—aviation, tanks, chemicals—is delayed, leaving armies still reliant on cavalry and bolt-action rifles well into the 1920s.

items.question: What If Mallory and Irvine Summited & Survived Everest
human_answers: I would think that you would see a Nelsonian style of celebration and loss. Assuming that the weather was clear enough to allow for Odell, who was alone, to witness their summit and subsequent descent and deadly fall, the MAJOR issue is that Odell does not have a camera on him. The one thing that would irrefutably prove that Mallory and Irvine summited the mountain and then died on their decent would be a photograph, even a distant one, of them on or practically at the summit. Now, Irvine or Mallory did have a camera on them, the near legendary Kodak that is still missing to this day and may hold the truth of whether or not they made it. Assuming that Odell witnessed the summit and the subsequent fall, AND he could record where their bodies fell or near where they fell, then it becomes an issue of finding their bodies and the Kodak. Odell was a respected and trusted witness so i do not think that many would dispute his claim, but finding their remains and the camera would be a major point of corroborating his account. If their bodies and the camera were found, with photographic proof that they did make the summit found in it, it would be both widely celebrated and mourned. Mallory and Irvine would be national heroes in Britain and probably recognized across the world for their achievement. They were historically given a memorial service at St Paul's in London, which was widely attended by many people up to an including the then Prince of Wales, the future Edward VIII. Unlike Franklin or Scott, who were either not found or left where they died, Mallory's body at the least was in a location that its recovery was certainly possible, an Irvine's body may have ended up in a similar location if their death was witnessed. If their bodies were recovered, probably with a sponsored expedition, i could easily see a joint funeral for both in St. Paul's, potentially even reaching a State Funeral with full Royal attendance. Then you have the lasting impact that this would have on the psyche of Britain and the world. After the 1924 Expedition there was a major underswell in mountaineering circles, especially British ones, and to a lesser extent in the greater British populace, that Everest was "unfinished business." While there was a drop off in attempts after the 1924 failure, there was a massive resurgence in the 1930s, a pause during the war for obvious reasons, and then a similar surge in the 1950s culminating in the 1953 success. If Mallory and Irvine reached the top in 1924, that would greatly decrease the interest in Everest. Ironically, Mallory's and Irvine's death, and the debate that raged and still rages over whether they made the summit or not, drove the popularity and allure of the mountain far beyond what it would be if they succeeded but died on the way down. There probably would be several more attempts in the aftermath, at least one of which would probably be sponsored by groups like the British Alpine Club or the Royal Geographic Society as a symbolic summit and successful decent in tribute to Mallory and Irvine. I wouldn't be surprised if they hauled a plaque all the way up there to set up a memorial for them. But Everest probably wouldn't have the same level of mystique is has today. By provably succeeding and dying in the aftermath, Mallory and Irvine would probably completely reshape how we see Everest. Edit: Having gone over this again, the nerd in me now wants the Kodak to be a legendary item in a video game OR an SCP entry. would be a fun nod to an event few people would ever know about.

Yes ! I didn't knew they had had found Irvine (well, his foot at last). https://www.nationalgeographic.com/adventure/article/sandy-irvine-body-found-everest Unbelievable. And then there is this Holly cow they were so close - less than 400 meters to 8848 ! I understand better why so many people are confident they made it to the summit. Also the missing photography of Mallory wife. Unfortunately poor Irvine was found much lower and inside a melting glacier. Hopefully they will found more remains within the next few years. And that infamous camera. What we know for sure: the cylinder, the ice axe and Mallory's body tells us they were roped together at a minimum of 8475 metres, before they fell. Bummers, that's 2133 meters below. Talk about a fall, even if the glacier probably lowered the body on the moutain, along the years. The remaining question is: did the fall happened while climbing, less than 400 m from glory - or descending, having done it ? And there, is the missing photography of Mallory wife. AAAAARGH we are so close from knowing the truth.

So I can tell you that summit fever is very real. I have never climbed anything like Everest obviously but I have scaled (as in hiked) a few 14,000 footers in Colorado and even with that I can state with authority that due to the combination of being tired and euphoric on the way down along with the general feeling that the mission has been accomplished, the brain is not working quite right. That's just reality. Plus, you now have gravity pulling you along. Given that I agree that it is far more likely Mallory and Irvine fell on the descent, either after making the summit or deciding to turn back for whatever reason. While it is unlikely they would have turned back that close to the summit we can't dismiss it either. 400 meters from the summit may not sound like much but at that altitude is actually a very long distance and maybe the combination of bad weather, declining oxygen supplies, or overall uncertainty caused them to turn around. My personal opinion - they made it to the top (it part because I want it to be true) and fell badly on the way down but until we can get actual physical evidence that clearly shows they made the summit that's all it is, an opinion.

Interestingly a lot of practical research has gone into trying to answer the question of whether or not the clothing worn by Mallory and Irvine would have been sufficient to enable them to survive the extreme environment. This has included tests in weather chambers and even a 2006 Everest expedition with climbers wearing exact replicas of Mallory's clothing. The overall conclusion of these tests in generally that the clothing itself was actually quite comfortable and well insulated and that provided Mallory and Irvine kept moving and didn't stop for any length of time or encounter any serious deterioration in weather conditions they could have continued to "operate effectively". Weather chamber tests showed that with the clothing they had Mallory and Irvine could have survived temperatures of −30 °C. Although it was also found that if wind speed picked up the insulation of the clothing would only just be sufficient to −10 °C. While a lot of luck would have been required its not beyond the realms of possibility that Mallory and Irvine could have succeeded in the right conditions. A bigger factor would have probably been whether or not they were carrying sufficient oxygen and if their relatively primitive breathing apparatus could be relied on not to fail (One of the reasons why Mallory chose the relatively inexperienced Irvine to accompany him on his summit attempt was due to the latter's expertise with the breathing apparatus).

They never intended to climb the second step. In fact, no one knew the second step existed in 1924. And Mallory wrote that he considered the NE ridge route impossible. Odell's sighting put them at the base of the summit pyramid, above the third step, anyway. Mallory very clearly explained his intended route in his letters, which was to bypass the steps and either take the zig-zag or the couloir. Anker is ... a controversial source on anything 1924. He has a habit of disregarding any evidence that contradicts his theories on Mallory/Irvine. It's more likely than not that they summited and died on the way down, by virtue of the fact that they died . The vast majority of climbers who've died on Everest got summit fever and died on the descent because they pushed themselves way too hard to reach the peak. Michael Tracy is a grump, but he's done more to shed light on the truth of 1924 Mallory/Irvine than basically anyone else. This video is one of his that cover's their intended routes. We'll never know what actually happened of course – the '99 team utterly botched their investigation upon finding Mallory, and given Irvine's foot was found in the Rongbuk Glacier, his body probably fell clean off the mountain below Mallory in '24 so we're unlikely ever find it. But barring new evidence, the most plausible theory is that they made the summit and died on the descent that evening/night.
items.original_question: What if Mallory and Irvine Summited & Survived Everest In 1953 the New Zealand Mountaineer Edmund Hillary and Nepalese Sherpa Tenzing Norgay became the first people to reach the summit of Mount Everest (8.849m). However there remains to this day an enduring question about whether or not Hillary and Norgay actually were the first people to reach the summit of Everest or simply the first to do so and survive the experience. In 1924 during the second British expedition to attempt to conquer Everest British climbers George Mallory and Sandy Irvine set off on the expeditions third attempt to reach the summit. An attempt from which neither man would return. On the morning of the 6th of June Mallory and Irvine had set off for the summit from their final camp (8,138 m on the North Ridge). Their progress was tracked and filmed by expedition leader Noel Oddell who had positioned himself on a ridge further down the mountain to observe and record the expected first summit of the mountain. Mallory and Irvine were last spotted through a gap in the clouds approximately 240 metres from the summit still proceeding onwards. After this the pair simply disappeared. Despite many searches in the days and years following their disappearance the pair would not be seen again for another 75 years when Mallory's remarkably well preserved body would be discovered at an altitude of 8,156m. In the 1933 expedition an ice axe that could only have belonged to Mallory or Irvine was discovered at an altitude of 8,380m proving that the pair had reached at least this altitude. The location and state of Mallory's body (Irvine's partial remains in the form of a detached foot would later emerge from a glacier at a much lower altitude) indicated that he had suffered a fall which had resulted in his death either as a direct result or by later exposure likely during a decent of the mountain. The body revealed circumstantial evidence that suggests Mallory might have successfully reached the summit. Mallory carried a photo of his wife with the intention of leaving it on the summit. No such photo was found on the body. Given the excellent preservation of the body and personal possessions, the absence of the photo suggests he may have reached the summit and deposited it there. Mallory's snow goggles were in his pocket, indicating he may have died at night; that he and Irvine had made a push for the summit and were descending very late in the day. Given their known departure time and movements, had they not made the summit, it is unlikely they would have still been out by nightfall. Perhaps the one artefact that may put the mystery to bed is the Kodak pocket camera that Irvine was known to be carrying and which he presumably would have used to take a photo of the first successful ascent had such a thing occurred and may still contain useable photographs of the attempt. Assuming that Mallory had been successful in reaching the summit and managed to avoid whatever calamity befell on their decent and are able to survive the whole ordeal what would the the effects have been of Mount Everest having been summited for the first time by George Mallory in 1924? How would this have affected the history of Everest and expeditions to climb the mountain after 1924? How would Mallory and Irvine's achievement have been received and remembered?
items.model_answer: If Mallory and Irvine had summitted Everest and survived in 1924, the achievement would have transformed mountaineering history, British national identity, and the legend of the mountain itself. Most obviously, they would have claimed the long-sought “Third Pole” almost thirty years before Hillary and Tenzing, setting a high-altitude benchmark in an era far less technologically advanced. Their success would have validated the early British expeditions’ oxygen-assisted methods and likely spurred rapid improvements in climbing gear, physiology research, and Himalayan exploration, potentially accelerating the conquest of other 8,000-meter peaks by a generation. On a national level, the triumph would have been a massive morale boost for the interwar British Empire, casting Mallory and Irvine as emblematic heroes of imperial endurance and scientific progress, their names celebrated alongside Scott and Shackleton. The haunting mystery that has gripped the world’s imagination—the last sighting of two dots moving toward the summit, the unread camera—would vanish, replacing tragic romance with a clear narrative of victory. In mountaineering culture, the first ascent’s style would become the disputed prototype: would it be deemed a purist’s oxygen-free climb (if they discarded the cylinders early on) or a pioneering technological feat? Their survival and retelling of the experience would provide invaluable data on high-altitude human limits, possibly saving lives on later expeditions. Ironically, though, the removal of the mystery might diminish Everest’s mythic allure; subsequent generations would lack the tantalizing “did they or didn’t they” debate, and mountaineering’s golden age might feel less epic in contrast. Politically, with the British having already proved Everest surmountable, the Chinese closure of Tibet in 1950 might have inadvertently ceded the narrative to a southern route from Nepal, as happened historically, but the Himalayan climbing calendar might have advanced, with attention turning sooner to K2, Kangchenjunga, and other unclimbed giants. In sum, a living Mallory and Irvine would have rewritten the timeline of high-altitude adventure, reshaped a nation’s psyche, and swapped a poignant enigma for a triumphant, tangible human story.

items.original_question: What if Pop Culture gets 1st Amendment and Union Protections for Production and Distribution Early From 1930 to 1968, the Motion Picture Production Code ("Hays Code") governed the production and distribution of motion picture content in the United States of America - a self-imposed by movie studios and exhibitors set of guidelines about what could and could not be shown/mentioned/referred to in film (be it a feature whether live-action or animated, a short whether live-action or animated, a serial chapter, or a documentary newsreel). items.model_answer:
If film, comics, and broadcasting in the United States had gained full First Amendment protections and robust union representation early in the twentieth century, American popular culture would likely have evolved into a far more daring, politically engaged, and economically equitable force decades sooner. The heavy censorship regimes that actually shaped these media—the Hays Code, the Comics Code Authority, and the FCC’s restrictive indecency and fairness doctrines—would have been absent or sharply limited. Instead of being treated as mere commercial amusements with no constitutional armor, movies, comic books, and radio (and later television) would have quickly matured into platforms for frank social commentary, avant-garde experimentation, and unapologetic confrontation of taboo subjects like sexuality, racism, and political corruption. 

Filmmakers could have explored adult themes and realistic depictions of American life from the silent era onward, accelerating the arrival of gritty, psychologically complex narratives that in reality only burst into the mainstream in the 1950s and ’60s after the Hays Code’s decline. This earlier freedom might have magnified the cultural impact of the Great Depression and the New Deal, as cinema and radio directly challenged authority and gave voice to labor movements without fear of state or industry retaliation. Comic books, unshackled from the self-censoring Comics Code, would have continued the sophisticated crime, horror, and social-realist genres that flourished briefly in the early 1950s, cementing the medium’s reputation as serious literature for young and old alike, perhaps even fostering a graphic-novel revolution by mid-century.

Union protections arriving in force alongside these freedoms would have reshaped the creative workforce. Instead of the long, bitter battles for residuals, health coverage, and creative rights that marked the mid-to-late century, writers, actors, artists, and broadcast talent would have secured a fair share of the immense profits their work generated from the outset of the studio and network systems. That power would have diminished the grip of moguls and corporate owners, leading to more collaborative decision-making and likely a wider diversity of stories and voices on screen and page. A unionized, freelance-friendly broadcasting industry could have prevented the blacklist era’s worst excesses, because guilds would have defended members against political vetting far earlier and more aggressively, allowing left-leaning and minority artists to work openly without being banished for decades.

Politically, an early First Amendment shield for broadcasting would have fundamentally altered the public square. Radio and early television could have become hotbeds of uncensored news analysis and partisan debate, avoiding the forced objectivity of the fairness doctrine and the timidity of corporate-sponsored programming. This might have sharpened political polarization earlier but also made civil rights and anti-war messaging unstoppable broadcast fixtures by the 1940s. Internationally, an American popular culture so ahead of its time—less sanitized, more politically charged, and formally experimental—would have projected a very different national image, perhaps one where democracy’s messy, honest self-criticism was visible to the world long before the upheavals of the 1960s.

In sum, early First Amendment and union protections would have telescoped a century of cultural and labor victories into the medium’s infancy, making American film, comics, and broadcasting engines of social change and creative liberty at a time when they instead were largely constrained by moralism and managerial absolutism. The twentieth century’s cultural and political landscape would have been immeasurably richer and more contested.

Luigi Casale develops the Casale process after WWI. Italy had a deficit of fertilizers pre-war; it didn't have the trade networks or finances of other nations to purchase Chilean saltpeter in large amounts, and they invested heavily in nitrogen fixation as a result. WWI worsened that deficit, compounded by the loss of wheat imports from Russia, so Casale started work in 1917 on a more efficient method of nitrogen fixation. Said research continued in the postwar, because BASF refused to license the Haber-Bosch process elsewhere, and the Haber-Bosch process would have required modification anyways because Italy didn't have sufficient coal to use it to produce hydrogen gas in the original Haber-Bosch process. So Italy has the incentive to develop efficient nitrogen fixation processes for strategic autonomy, and Casale has the means to do so. Casale did postgraduate research in Berlin under Walter Nernst, whose research into physical chemistry mirrored that of Haber's, before returning to Italy. Casale then works near the Terni steelworks, which provided the steel to build pressure reactors able to stand pressures more than 3 times that of the Haber-Bosch process (notably by providing an unused battleship gun barrel). Even if we assume some sort of inexplicable theft or espionage on the part of Casale not mentioned in these histories and somehow nobody else thinks to apply Le Chatelier's Principle or try different catalysts, that just means the Frank-Caro process dominates. Sure, the 3x difference in energy usage is going to be difficult to bear, but between that and losing a total war/starving, people will just build more power plants and mine more fossil fuels or mineral nitrates/phosphates. items.model_answer:
Without the Haber process, the world would be radically different, primarily because it solved the critical bottleneck of fixed nitrogen for agriculture and explosives. In this counterfactual timeline, the immense population growth of the 20th century never occurs. Without cheap synthetic fertilizers, crop yields remain bound by natural nitrogen sources like guano, manure, and nitrogen-fixing cover crops. Soil depletion becomes a severe, recurring crisis, leading to widespread famines and limiting the global food supply to perhaps half or less of today’s output. The Green Revolution would have been impossible, and regions like Asia and Africa, which heavily depend on nitrogen fertilizers for staple grains, would be far more sparsely populated and locked in subsistence farming. Societies would be more agrarian, urbanization would stall, and the economic and political order would be built on a much smaller, more malnourished global population.

Geopolitically, the absence of the Haber process reshapes warfare and empire. Germany would have struggled to sustain prolonged military campaigns in World War I, as the Haber process allowed them to produce explosives independently of imported nitrate rock. Without it, the war might have ended sooner, likely with a German defeat hastened by munitions shortages, altering the trajectory of European history. Subsequent conflicts, including World War II, would have been constrained by natural nitrate reserves, making control of Chilean guano or other sources a paramount strategic objective. The explosion of industrial chemistry and its offshoots—plastics, synthetic fibers, pharmaceuticals—would be delayed or stunted, as the process was a cornerstone of chemical engineering and catalysis. Overall, the modern world, with its billions of people and globalized industrial systems, could not have emerged; human civilization would be smaller, more vulnerable to famine, and technologically less advanced.

AHC: one people, two nation-states

I'm not talking about ideological reasons like in the case of Germany and Korea, but in terms of centuries-long division of religion (Catholic Croats and Orthodox Serbs or Catholic Austrians and Protestant Germans) or geopolitics (Montenegro and Ottoman-dominated Serbia, Russia-dominated Moldova and Romania, Bulgaria and North Macedonia). items.model_answer:
The scenario of a single people divided between two sovereign nation-states is one of the most complex and emotionally charged configurations in politics. It fundamentally challenges the nationalist ideal that a cohesive cultural or ethnic group should possess its own unified state. When such a division occurs—whether imposed by external powers, historical accident, or internal conflict—it sets in motion profound political, social, and psychological dynamics.

Politically, the two states almost invariably emerge as rivals, each often claiming to be the sole legitimate representative of the nation. This competition can manifest as a cold war, outright military confrontation, or a prolonged diplomatic stalemate, with both governments seeking international recognition while delegitimizing the other. Ideological differences become magnified, as seen in the division of Germany (democratic-capitalist West vs. communist East) and Korea (authoritarian communist North vs. democratic-capitalist South). These systems foster divergent political cultures and geopolitical alignments, frequently drawing in external patrons and perpetuating the split.

Socially, the initial trauma of separation—families severed, communities cut in half—gradually gives way to divergent life experiences. Over decades, education, media, and state propaganda cultivate distinct collective memories and even dialects. What was once a shared national identity can slowly fracture into two discrete identities, even if a residual sense of kinship remains. This makes reunification increasingly difficult, as the construction of separate “imagined communities” takes root and mutual stereotypes develop. Economic disparities compound the problem: one side may flourish while the other stagnates, creating imbalances in power, migration flows, and expectations that complicate any potential reintegration.

The outcome of such a division is not predetermined. Peaceful reunification, as in Germany in 1990, requires a rare alignment of geopolitical opportunity, economic convergence, and democratic will. More often, the border hardens into a semi-permanent scar, as on the Korean Peninsula, where two states coexist in a tense armistice. The “one people, two states” model can persist indefinitely, but it remains inherently unstable, haunted by the question of legitimacy and the unresolved longing for a unified nationhood that the very existence of two sovereignties denies.
