If Cuba and the Philippines had swapped their 20th-century trajectories—with Cuba remaining a long-term U.S. territory and eventually a close capitalist ally, while the Philippines underwent a communist revolution and aligned with the Soviet bloc—the geopolitical, economic, and cultural landscape of both regions would be dramatically different.

Cuba, as a stable U.S.-aligned state in the Caribbean, would likely have developed into a major tourist and trade hub akin to Puerto Rico or Hawaii, with heavy American investment, a robust service economy, and a strategic military presence. The island would have avoided the U.S. embargo, becoming a showcase of U.S.-style capitalism in Latin America rather than a symbol of anti-imperialist revolution. Without Fidel Castro’s regime, there would have been no Cuban Missile Crisis, significantly altering the Cold War’s early trajectory; the absence of that nuclear brinkmanship might have reduced the urgency of later arms-control agreements and changed U.S.-Soviet dynamics. Domestically, Cuba’s political system would likely be a multiparty democracy with strong ties to Washington, though not without internal tensions over inequality and U.S. influence.

The Philippines, on the other hand, would have become Asia’s premier communist state—a large, strategically vital archipelago on the doorstep of China and the Pacific sea lanes. A successful Hukbalahap or Maoist revolution in the 1940s or 1950s would have transformed it into a Soviet or Chinese ally, hosting foreign bases and projecting communist influence across Southeast Asia. This would likely have intensified the Vietnam War and prompted a much heavier U.S. military footprint in the region, possibly leading to direct interventions to prevent a domino effect. The Philippine economy, rather than adopting a mixed capitalist model, would have collectivized agriculture and industry, potentially stagnating like other communist states and creating a large diaspora of anticommunist Filipinos. The country might have become a flashpoint for regional tensions, with the South China Sea disputes taking on a deeper ideological dimension. Domestically, its cultural and religious identity (with a strong Catholic majority) would have faced radical secularization and state control, possibly sparking enduring resistance movements.

In essence, reversing these two nations’ fates would have shifted the Cold War’s center of gravity, moving a key Soviet-aligned outpost from the Caribbean to the Pacific and replacing a Pacific American stronghold with a communist bastion. The ripple effects on U.S. foreign policy, regional stability, and the lives of millions in both countries would be profound and lasting.

items.model_answer: If West Germany and Italy had withdrawn from the PANAVIA Tornado program at the outset, the trilateral venture would have collapsed immediately. The United Kingdom, left as the sole partner, would have faced the stark choice of funding the entire Multi-Role Combat Aircraft (MRCA) project alone or abandoning it. Given the immense development costs and the RAF’s pressing need for a long-range interdiction and strike aircraft, the most likely outcome would have been a direct purchase of an American off-the-shelf design—almost certainly the General Dynamics F-111K, which the UK had already evaluated and ordered before cancelling in favor of the MRCA. This would have left Britain fully reliant on US technology for its deep-strike capability, with no high-performance European collaborative fighter to follow. The British aerospace industry would have been severely set back, missing out on two decades of shared design and production work, leading to earlier consolidation and a loss of advanced combat aircraft design expertise. For West Germany and Italy, separate national paths would have emerged: the Luftwaffe might have pursued a simpler, lighter replacement for its F-104s through a different European grouping or gone for the F-4 Phantom, while Italy would likely have turned to the F-104S or a US attack aircraft. The ambitious model of tri-national defense industrial integration pioneered by Tornado would have been stillborn, delaying or entirely reshaping the later Eurofighter Typhoon program and leaving Europe strategically dependent on American airpower for a generation.

items.question: What If No nuclear weapons?
human_answers: As has been noted it is pretty much impossible to avoid having nuclear weapons ever being created. The science is pretty obvious. What CAN be altered, to a degree, is the "when". The U.S. threw a dramatic amount of funding at the effort, along with huge amounts of resources (Manhattan literally built the entire city of Oak Ridge TN to house the workers on the project. It was farmland, with about 3,000 people living in the area then in less than 2 years, it was a city with a population of 75,000. Government just walked in and "acquired" 59,000 acres, evicted everyone in the local farms and villages, and started building a fence (BIG ASS fence). The same thing happened in Washington with Hanford, except it was 500,000 acres and 39,000 people, Just a little less funding, or a project manager less driven than General Groves and the Bomb isn't ready.

Based on the described scenario, the USSR becomes the first country to test a nuclear weapon in the early 1950s, whereupon the US and UK governments demand an explanation for who filed the relevant reports in the wrong section back in 1940. In the case of the US, it's probably Lyman Briggs, who in OTL actually did lock away a key report in his safe without showing it to anyone else, which may have delayed the start of the Manhattan Project by several months. But even then, uranium fission was discovered in France in December 1938. The Einsten-Szilard letter warned the US government of the possibilities in August 1939. The Frisch-Peierls memorandum, the first description of a nuclear weapon, was written in March 1940 for the British government. By Frisch's own description, the work he and Peierls did was straightforward for any competent nuclear physicist. There might be a PoD wherein Frisch and Peierls are interned as enemy aliens and not allowed to work as physicists. Oliphant is focussed on the higher priority radar work, so Thomson's conclusion that it was not worth pursuing a chain reaction in uranium is accepted by the British government. There is therefore no MAUD committee, no report for Briggs to ignore, and no reason for Oliphant to kick things into gear. Instead, what is likely to happen is that eventually someone in the US does ask the questions that Frisch and Peierls asked, and they reach similar answers. Given OTL's trajectory, it's hard to see why that would happen any earlier than August 1941, given that US research was initially largely concerned with power plants rather than weapons. If we say it does, it might take the best part of a year for a US equivalent of the MAUD report to be carried out and an atomic weapons programme started. That puts a US weapons programme without the MAUD input as starting in mid-1942 - so about a six month delay. An arbitrarily longer delay is entirely plausible, but eventually - and probably sooner rather than later - someone is going to ask the right questions, and then things will start moving very quickly.

items.model_answer:
The world without nuclear weapons would be profoundly different, shaped by the absence of both their terrifying destructive power and their paradoxical role as guardians of great-power peace. The most immediate, concrete divergence occurs at the end of World War II. Without the atomic bomb, the United States would have had to launch a massive invasion of the Japanese home islands in late 1945, an operation that military planners estimated would result in hundreds of thousands, if not millions, of additional casualties on both sides, along with the continued firebombing of Japanese cities. The Soviet Union, having declared war on Japan just before the atomic bombings, would have likely swept into Manchuria and Korea, and potentially occupied significant portions of Japan itself, leading to a divided Japan akin to post-war Germany. The Pacific war would have dragged on longer, ending only through a brutal ground campaign.

The Cold War’s central dynamic of mutually assured destruction would simply not exist. Without the nuclear sword hanging over humanity, a direct, massive conventional war between the United States and the Soviet Union becomes far more likely. The ideological and geopolitical tensions that fueled the Cold War would have found release on the battlefield rather than through proxy wars and espionage. Europe, still recovering from the devastation of two world wars, might have become the primary theater for a World War III, with armored divisions and conventional air power deciding the fate of the continent. The large-scale conventional arms race would have been even more intense, consuming a far greater share of national resources, as each side sought a decisive edge in tanks, aircraft, and troop numbers. The relative stability of the nuclear era’s “long peace” might have been replaced by cyclic great-power conflicts, potentially even more destructive in cumulative toll than the singular threat of nuclear annihilation.

Geopolitical hierarchies would look very different. The status of great power would be determined by industrial capacity, population, and conventional military strength alone. Powers like the United States, Soviet Union, a united or resurgent Germany, Japan, and perhaps China would contest dominance in a multipolar world less stabilized by nuclear bipolarity. Decolonization and regional conflicts would still occur, but without nuclear-armed superpowers forcing restraint, they could escalate more easily. On the other hand, the asymmetrical pressure that pushed smaller states to seek nuclear weapons would vanish, eliminating proliferation crises and the black-market networks that feed them. The debate over nuclear energy would be decoupled from weapons, though public fear of reactor accidents would remain.

Culturally and psychologically, humanity would have been spared the deep, pervasive dread of instant apocalypse that defined the late 20th century. No duck-and-cover drills, no doomsday clocks, no constant background terror that shaped art, philosophy, and daily life. The environmental legacy of nuclear testing—radioactive contamination at sites from New Mexico to the Pacific islands—would not exist. But the price for this reprieve would be steeper: a world more prone to total war, where the memory of Hiroshima and Nagasaki as a stark moral barrier is replaced by the gruesome realities of protracted conventional slaughter. In this world, war remains thinkable in a way our nuclear age has not dared to allow.

items.question: What If the USSR was leaked information about OB just before it happened and were thus better prepared and more competent in 1941? (No strike though)
human_answers: A couple days or weeks isn’t really enough if you’re going with the “Stalin finally makes a good decision” scenario. You need at least a couple months to have the Soviets dug in and prepared at more defensible spots further east than iotl, and considering the German initial manpower advantage (to say nothing of the purges creating widespread incompetence in the red army and said incompetence making their logistics horrible), they still probably lose pretty hard, although not quite as much as iotl. I think at least 6 or so (probably a bit more) months is needed to help close the manpower gap and create a Minsk-Kiev line that the Germans can’t penetrate if you don’t want Soviet losses to be seen as proportionally a lot bigger (though there’s a strong chance they still are in this scenario, just not enough to give the impression that all you need to do is kick in the rotten door enough and it’ll fall).

The Soviet Union possessed highly precise intelligence indicating that the German military's logistics were insufficient to sustain a protracted war and that its armaments factories had not yet shifted to a wartime footing. (This intelligence was derived from the infiltration of German industry by communist sympathizers.) Hitler also couldn't been so foolish as to believe that the mighty Soviet Union could be conquered within three months—at least, no analyst would have dared to venture such an insulting conjecture. Consequently, the less reliable intelligence from military and western country must have been false, and war is in next year. This chain of logic is remarkably robust; You cannot convince the Soviets that Germany is about to attack without introducing collateral changes—and different changes would inevitably lead to different outcomes in the war. Would they perceive their own military as weaker? Would they place their trust in Anglo-American intelligence while disregarding the Comintern’s own network? Or would they have managed to plant exceptionally reliable spies deep within the German military itself? Each of these scenarios would necessitate a distinct defensive strategy, thereby altering the very trajectory of the conflict. One thing, however, remains certain: if the Soviet Union were to lose the war while the United States remained an active belligerent, the Americans would undoubtedly drop the nuclear bomb.

Again, as usual these scenarios entirely depend on one or both sides failing to react to changing circumstances. Firstly, USSR had information about possibility of German attack and was reacting. 'Stalin refused to believe the intelligence' is basically a myth. Soviet problem was not lack of the information or anyone's willingness or unwillingness 'to believe'. Soviet problem was lack of definitive information because everything that they had on Barbarossa was either utterly wrong, contaminated with enough false intelligence to make discerning what is true and what is not quite impossible or simply arrived too late for any sort of meaningful reaction. Secondly, USSR primary issue was that Germans at any point of preparation to Barbarossa were in position to speed these preparations up if they see an obvious Soviet reaction . And Germans were positioned to attack better than Soviets were positioned to defend. Let's say USSR starts mobilizing mid-April. And yes, it could screw Mussolini by preventing Germany from bailing him out, but it was simple question of Germany already having mobilized army and having a better logistical infrastructure on their side of the border, so whatever obvious thing Soviets would do, Germans will have an opportunity to react. items.model_answer:
If the Soviet Union had been fully briefed on Operation Barbarossa just before the German invasion and had acted decisively on that intelligence—without launching a preemptive strike—the Eastern Front in 1941 would have looked dramatically different. Stalin’s historical refusal to believe warnings from his own spies and Churchill was a key reason the Red Army suffered catastrophic surprise. With detailed knowledge of the German attack plan, force concentrations, and timing, the Soviets could have shifted from a forward, offensive posture to a deep, layered defense.

In this scenario, frontline units would have been placed on full alert, dispersed, and camouflaged. Pre-planned artillery fires would have targeted likely German crossing points and assembly areas. Extensive minefields, anti‑tank ditches, and field fortifications would have been constructed along the new border, with echeloned defensive belts extending back to the Stalin Line, which had been partially dismantled. The Red Air Force would not have been caught on the ground in neat rows, so its losses would have been far lower, and it could have contested German air superiority more effectively. Strategically, the Soviet command would have pulled mobile reserves back from exposed salients like Białystok and Lvov, avoiding the massive encirclements that historically destroyed the Western and Southwestern Fronts in the first weeks. Industrial evacuation would have begun earlier, and scorched-earth preparations would have been more thorough.

German forces would still have advanced, given their tactical skill and experience, but their progress would have been far slower and bloodier. Instead of racing hundreds of kilometers in days, they would have ground forward against prepared defenses, supply columns already strained, and a Red Army that bent but did not break. The historical pockets at Minsk, Smolensk, Kiev, and Vyazma-Bryansk would likely be replaced by a series of costly frontal battles. Army Group Center’s drive on Moscow would have been delayed not by the diversion to Kiev, but by Soviet defenses that refused to collapse, pushing the timetable deep into autumn mud season. Without the huge Soviet losses of men and matériel—over 4 million casualties by winter—the Soviet counteroffensive in December would have been launched with a much larger, better-fed, and better-equipped force, possibly from positions well west of the Dnieper River.

The Wehrmacht, bled white far earlier and without the illusion of imminent victory, would have faced a strategic crisis by late 1941, with no chance of reaching Moscow, let alone the Volga. The war in the east would likely have been shortened by one to two years, with the Red Army entering Poland and the Balkans by 1943 or early 1944. The geopolitical consequences would be immense: a faster Soviet advance might have led to a very different Cold War map, with perhaps all of Germany occupied by the Red Army and Western Allied influence curtailed. The human and material cost to the USSR would still have been staggering, but the near-fatal initial defeats—and the desperation of 1941–42—would have been averted.

items.question: What If Modern Music without The Beatles and Elvis Presley.
human_answers: No Elvis will have minimal effect. Yes he was a popular Singer but he didn’t write anything. So the songs he is famous for will still exist. Will his lose have effects on music? Obviously. But it is not like music won’t more or less still evolve as it did. The lost of one singer is not going to have that drastic an effect there are simply to many of them. I’m not saying that nothing would change. There absolutely would be changes from neither artist existing. It’s just that fundamentally: You still have popular music derived from Black American musical traditions. You still have a push away from large swing-style bands and towards smaller guitar-based bands - especially since before the digital era the guitar is the most accessible music instrument for young people wanting to make music. You still have the Baby Boom yielding a much larger youth cohort than before - thus yielding a significant generational divide by the early to mid 1960s as they’ve grown up having not known the struggles of their parents or older siblings - and have more room tackling lifestyle changes without worry for economic precarity. You still have big labels and radio stations wanting to play “different music” for “different races” so to speak. And with that you still have white singers becoming popular for their heavily sanitized covers of black R&B songs ( looks at Pat Boone ). You still have the post-WWII dominance and saturation of American pop culture - including music - in Europe and across the globe. And since the UK and the Commonwealth have virtually zero language barrier with the US - music that imitates American musical traditions (twice removed from Black American roots) has the potential to take off. You still have the advancements in recording technology that gave artists room to make more experimental and groundbreaking music than before. Plus the steady rise of FM radio later in the 1960s to provide a market for more ambitious music. You still have the Sexual Revolution to loosen norms around sex. On top of the various other drivers of the counterculture. You still have the payola scandal and the burnout of 1950s rock stars causing the 1959-64 dearth in the quality of pop music. But that’s just structurally speaking. Aesthetically speaking, things could be shifted around - with some new genre inspired by surf rock and garage rock (though realistically not actually either one of them) blowing up out of nowhere by 1964-65 - and Pat Boone is the King of Rock ‘n’ Roll all the artists of the 1960s are inspired by in terms of singing style and aura. While British rock bands are basically seen as a store brand that only gains later appreciation in the social media era decades later a la Japanese city pop. But it would still fundamentally fit the bigger variables that had been brewing years or even decades before the mid 1960s.

While the absence of the Beatles (and particularly Lennon and McCartney) would deprive us of some very good songs, there were vast numbers of competent bands in Britain that could have filled the niche if given the opportunity- whether together or singly. The bigger impact would probably have been on the penetration of British artists into the USA [1], but that's quite likely to happen eventually because there's money to be made from big crowds of relatively wealthy teenagers who happen to hit on a good enough band. The other impact might have been on the pressure to become singer-songwriters, rather than just singers/performers. Again, money is a big driver so it's likely to happen sooner or later. Otherwise, US innovation is likely to remain largely unchanged (Iggy and the Stooges will still form, and the drivers for hippy culture and rock bands is still there). Meanwhile, the Rolling Stones would still be experimenting with blues and quality musicians like Buddy Holly, Carl Perkins will be filling the niche that Elvis is no longer dominating. In short, different but still broadly recognisable. [1] The Monkees are unlikely to be formed, but songs like Day Dream Believer are too good not to end up being a success, even if it takes a few cover versions to become a real hit.

By the time Carl recovered from the car crash it was too late, Elvis had overshadowed him. Jerry Lee Lewis, courtesy of his flamboyant personality might have become the 50s rock 'n roll superstar (how long he would have lasted would have depended upon whether or not he was still foolish enough to marry his underage cousin). The 60s? Hmmm that's not so certain - in the early 60s, rock 'n roll seemed to be on it's way out (or at least heading towards just being a niche genre of music). What rock 'n roll there was on Top 40 radio was mostly bland, and barely even qualified as rock 'n roll (Frankie Avalon anybody?). The Beach Boys were making songs with lame-o lyrics ("Be True to Your School", etc.). Even in Europe it was only doing so-so - I remember reading an interview of Jimmy Page (who along with playing guitar in Led Zeppelin, and the Yardbirds, was an in-demand session guitarist in the early and mid 60s), where he stated that in the early 60s, it was hard to even find rock 'n roll recording sessions to play on. Without the Beatles, rock'n roll might have just kept on being 50s-style teen hearthrob music performed by Cliff Richard, instrumental music played by bands like The Shadows (who also happened to be Cliff Richard's backing band), and possibly music played by 50s American rock 'n roll musicians, who were going nowhere in the USA with their careers (Bo Diddly, Eddie Cochran, etc. performed extensively in Europe in the early 60s when their careers fizzled out in the US). One of the big elements of the Beatles that helped to propel them to stardom IMO, was that for its time (the early 60s), the Beatles' music was considered HARD ROCK. As a result, it had more energy to it than your typical music of the period, and people liked it. The Stones? They were in their infancy, playing what is to me, watered down blues, that sounded nowhere near as intense. That hard rock edge the Beatles had is what kick started rock 'n roll again, and resulted in a million bands wanting to sound like them (even in the US, after they were on the Ed Sullivan Show). No Beatles and IMO, rock 'n roll continues its decline into a niche music genre, with the occasional Top 40 hit by bland groups like Gary Pucket and The Union Gap, Gary Lewis and The Playboys, etc. Not much in the way of edgy, interesting music. In the US, Link Wray never charts as high as he did with "Rumble" (which was actually banned by radio stations because it was "too threatening - it'll incite people to riot"), and Lonnie Mack at most has a few very modest hits like he had with "Wham".

Oh, for the love of Pete, not THIS again.... I just don't understand how some on this board can analyze military events down to the level of minutiae where they can argue that if a particular German general farted at a given moment in 1940, the entirety of World War II would come out differently, and yet at the same time assume that popular culture would remain essentially unaltered without the presence of two of its most important figures. Just as one example: before the Beatles, there was no such thing as a "British rock and roll group" in the eyes of Americans, and particularly American record companies, radio programmers, and concert promoters. Cliff Richard, who was Britain's biggest rock and roll superstar prior to the Beatles, went absolutely nowhere in America. Americans knew that rock and roll had originated in the U.S., and they were very parochial about it - the assumption, and it was not often wrong, before the Beatles was that anything coming from Britain would be a poor copy of records American teenagers already owned. (And it WAS teenagers almost exclusively who listened to rock and roll in 1963; projecting one's own current cultural dynamics into the past is part of the reason one gets lost). No British rock group - not one - had broken in the U.S. before 1964. The Beatles themselves at first were turned down by Capitol, the American division of EMI, who held their recording contract in the UK; Capitol refused to issue their first four singles in the U.S. It took the "Beatlemania" phenomenon to convince Capitol that it was worth giving the Beatles a shot, which enabled Beatlemania to cross the Atlantic. I'm sorry, but it's not as if "Holliemania" or "Dave Clark Fivemania" simply takes the place of that. There's a whole set of intangibles here. You can't just assume that you like the Rolling Stones better, so they automatically take the place of the Beatles. It would never have worked like that. What happens to the Rolling Stones becomes essentially undefinable. And that's just one example. I didn't even address the fact of no Elvis - which probably would have meant no Beatles AND virtually none of the other British Invasion acts either. Removing Elvis from the picture (which automatically would remove the Beatles as we know them) changes the ENTIRE trajectory of popular music from that day to this, in well-nigh unpredictable ways. Period.
items.original_question: What if Modern Music without The Beatles and Elvis Presley. American Singer and Actor Elvis Presley and British Rock Band The Beatles are the most Influential musicians in existence. With the former codifying Rockabilly and is credited for advancing the Feminist movement in America, and the Latter spearheaded the British Invasion, increased public interest in Psychedelic Drugs, Asian Spirituality and heralded the Album Era. Let's say both the musician and the Band never had any interest in music, preventing the codifying of Rockabilly and The British Invasion. How would this influence modern music?
items.model_answer:
Without The Beatles and Elvis Presley, modern music would have evolved along a radically different path, likely lacking the cohesive, explosive moments that defined rock and roll’s ascent and later pop’s global spread. Elvis, as the charismatic catalyst who fused rhythm and blues with country, brought Black musical energy into white mainstream culture and crystallized the teenage rebel identity. Without him, the mid-1950s rock-and-roll explosion might have remained a niche genre, championed by regional acts like Buddy Holly or Carl Perkins, but never achieving the same cross-racial, cross-class breakout. The youth market would have taken longer to awaken, and the "rock star" archetype—the sexually charged, hip-shaking performer—might have never fully formed.

In a world without The Beatles, the 1960s would lack their songwriting revolution, their studio-as-instrument innovations, and the concept album’s artistic legitimacy. The Beatles transformed the single-based pop single into a cohesive album-driven art form, influence that pulsed through all subsequent pop, rock, and even electronic music. Without them, the British Invasion wouldn’t have happened in the same way—there would be no template for bands like The Rolling Stones, The Who, or The Kinks to follow into the American market. The ripple effects mean: no Sgt. Pepper's, no Abbey Road medleys, no "Strawberry Fields Forever" psychedelic textures; producers like George Martin might never have pushed multitracking and tape-loop experimentation into pop. Instead, American pop might have remained more rooted in Brill Building craftsmanship (Carole King, Neil Sedaka), vocal groups (The Beach Boys would be the dominant studio innovators, but Brian Wilson, without the friendly rivalry with The Beatles, might not have pushed Pet Sounds to the same extent), or folk revivalists. Soul and Motown might have taken an even greater hold globally, but the synthesis of rock, pop, and high art would be years behind.

Culturally, the 1960s counterculture would lose its unifying soundtrack. The Beatles’ championing of meditation, psychedelics, and peace activism gave a musical voice to the hippie movement. Without them, the movement’s music would be more fragmented, leaning on Bob Dylan’s poetic folk (which itself might have stayed acoustic longer without The Beatles’ electrified influence on Dylan), or on San Francisco jam bands like the Grateful Dead, but lacking the mainstream pop accessibility that spread those ideas worldwide. The late 20th-century pop landscape would be unrecognizable: no glam, no punk, no new wave, no Britpop, no indie rock in the forms we know—because all these genres trace lineage back to the innovations and attitudes normalized by Presley and The Beatles. Even hip-hop, while rooted in funk and soul, borrowed from The Beatles’ sampling culture and from the idea of the artist as auteur.

In essence, modern music without Elvis and The Beatles would be a quieter, more segregated affair. Rock might have simmered as an underground sound, pop might have stayed closer to its Tin Pan Alley roots, and the global youth culture that united around music might have never coalesced with the same fervor. The missing DNA would leave a more fragmented, less icon-driven soundscape—perhaps richer in folk traditions, R&B, and country, but without the transformational fusions that shaped everything from stadium rock to lo-fi bedroom pop.

human_answers: Far too big Even with folding wings I don't think they would fit on the elevators and would take up too much room in the hanger even of they fit which again I suspect not Its landing on performance of he Beaufighter is about the same as an avenger (60 knots?) but its much heavier than the TBF so I am not sure the arrestor cables of the day could handle such a plane. Its a nice idea but its too much of a plane for the carriers of the day - might work on an Audacious class but not the carriers built in the late 30s. The Whispering Death is already doing sterling work as a land based anti shipping aircraft during the war and it has great range - not quite 'Rikko' (G3m and G4m Japanese bombers) range, but close too it, but still a scourge where ever it operated.

In the last thread on the subject I mentioned, given any wing-break would have to be somewhat outboard the engines*, that you could probably take one up and down on Implacable's forward lift but the hangar height would preclude you rolling it off. You could store one in Illustrious's hangar, if you made it from a kit of parts, as the lift is too narrow. So deck parks only. items.original_question: What if Sea Beaufort and Sea Beaufighters used on Royal Navy aircraft carriers? What if the Royal Navy used a possible Bristol Sea variant of both Beauforts and Beaufighters on their carriers starting in 1940 replacing Fairy Swordfish aircraft in the torpedo attack role for example? Would this be possible design wise? Would they be better than the bomb and torpedo attack aircraft available at the time? Would the aircraft actually be able to be used like this or would they be too large? How effective would they be if used on aircraft carriers? Regards
items.model_answer:
If the Royal Navy had fielded carrier-borne Sea Beauforts and Sea Beaufighters from 1940, the impact on the maritime war would have been substantial, accelerating Allied offensive power and plugging critical capability gaps years earlier. Both aircraft, adapted from robust land-based designs, would have given the Fleet Air Arm a formidable, long-range strike and air-defense combination at a time when its carrier air groups were dangerously obsolete.

A carrier-based Sea Beaufort would have provided a genuinely effective aerial torpedo bomber from the opening stages of the Mediterranean war. Instead of relying on the slow, vulnerable Swordfish and Albacore biplanes, the Royal Navy could have launched fast, monoplane torpedo attacks against the Italian fleet at Taranto with heavier payloads and higher survivability. The same capability, deployed from carriers like HMS *Illustrious* and *Ark Royal*, would have posed a far more lethal threat to Axis convoys supplying North Africa, potentially strangling Rommel’s logistics much earlier. In the Atlantic, Sea Beauforts could have operated from escort carriers, closing the air gap and hunting U-boats on passage with torpedoes and depth charges, or striking German surface raiders before they could break out into the shipping lanes.

The Sea Beaufighter, with its four 20mm cannon, heavy machine guns, and later rocket projectiles, would have transformed carrier air defense and anti-shipping strike. As a long-range fighter, it could have engaged enemy reconnaissance aircraft and bombers well beyond the fleet’s visual horizon, providing a combat air patrol that no single-engine fighter of 1940–41 could match. In the strike role, its cannon and rocket fire would have devastated Axis destroyers, flak ships, and coastal convoys. Paired with the Sea Beaufort, the two types could have conducted coordinated, self-escorting strikes against heavily defended targets, something the Swordfish-only strikes could never achieve. In the Far East, the arrival of carriers equipped with these aircraft in late 1941 might have blunted the Japanese advance, allowing for powerful hit-and-run raids against invasion fleets well before the arrival of American carrier groups.

There were, however, significant practical obstacles. Both were large, twin-engine aircraft, and operating them from the Royal Navy’s small, armored-deck carriers of the period would have required extensive modifications: strengthened undercarriages, folding wings, arrestor hooks, and catapult launch capability. The hangar deck heights and lifts on the *Illustrious*-class were not designed for such large airframes, so deck parks would have been essential, reducing the number of aircraft carried. Twin-engine maintenance and fuel consumption would have strained early war logistics. Nevertheless, these were engineering problems, not fundamental impossibilities—the U.S. Navy operated twin-engine aircraft like the Lockheed Hudson and later the Grumman Tigercat, and the Royal Navy itself introduced the Sea Hornet in 1945. With sufficient urgency, a 1940 introduction was feasible.

On balance, the early deployment of Sea Beauforts and Sea Beaufighters would have given the Royal Navy a punch and reach that it lacked until much later, saving ships, closing the Atlantic gap sooner, and making Axis naval operations in the European theater prohibitively costly years ahead of history. The war at sea might have been shortened, with fewer merchant losses, and the Mediterranean might have become an Allied lake by 1942.

items.question: What If : FDR picks a Segregationist VP in 1944
human_answers: The only Southerner who got any serious support at the DNC in 1944 was Alabama Senator John H. Bankhead II, who came in a distant third with 98 votes (8.33%) on the first ballot. The only other (non Alben W. Barkley) Southerners who got even one vote were: J. Melville Broughton (Governor of North Carolina), Prentice Cooper (Governor of Tennessee), Robert S. Kerr (Senator from Oklahoma), Herbert O'Conor (Governor of Maryland), Claude Pepper (Senator from Florida), Sam Rayburn (Speaker of the House), and Bascom N. Timmons (D.C. based newspaperman who grew up in Texas). Of these, only Bankhead II, Barkley, Broughton, Cooper, Kerr, and O’Conor got double digits. So your best case scenario is Roosevelt and/or the convention see a need to nominate a Southerner, and go with Bankhead II who IOTL died on June 12, 1946 following a stroke on May 24, 1946, which means you end up with three Presidents in little over a year. Based on the 1886 Succession Act, Bankhead II’s successor would be none other than… James F. Byrnes. IOTL, Truman appointed him in July of 1945, and it’s pretty likely Bankhead II does similarly, wanting to support a follow Southerner. (Prior to the Succession Act of 1947, neither the Speaker of the House nor the President pro tempore of the Senate were in the line of succession.) So in a roundabout way, you do end up with Byrnes as President…

Right. Byrnes thought he was Roosevelt's choice. Truman went to the DNC planning to make a nominating speech for Byrnes. If Byrnes does get the nod... FDR wins in 1944 anyway. But things diverge after that. IMO the Republicans sweep in 1946 as OTL. Byrnes was a very capable man and won't make any big missteps, so IMO he will be renominated in 1948. There may be a feeling that the 1948 nomination is a poisoned chalice, what with the 1946 GOP sweep and general public fatigue with 16 years of Democrat Presidents. The "Humphreyite" liberals may still try to push a civil rights plank at the DNC, but against Byrnes' at least tacit opposition will fail. They won't bolt to support Wallace overtly. Instead they may sit back to watch Byrnes crash and burn in November, while they regroup for 1952. Byrnes will lose a fair number of voters to Wallace outside the South. Also, AIUI, Dewey chose to soft-pedal civil rights OTL in the vain hope of winning some Upper South states with the Democrats divided. TTL that ignis fatuus isn't around, so Dewey probably emphasizes civil rights to draw the increasingly important black vote in the North and also some white liberals. This should be enough for Dewey to win. The next question is whether he has enough "coat tails" for Republicans to hold Congress. Another question is how the civil rights issue shapes across the next decade. OTL, leadership on the issue was taken by liberal non-Southern Democrats, with the low-key support of Republicans. The first cracks in the "Solid South" came in the 1950s, as a few white Southerners who could no longer rely on the national Democratic party to protect Jim Crow found they could vote Republican. If under Dewey, Republicans claim the leading role, that's not going to happen. The "Humphreyites" will gain control of the Democrats by 1952; there may be a Dixiecrat ticket that year. Dewey will be re-elected, barring some debacle in Korea or whatever. Warren won't be Chief Justice, but the Court will still be making rulings like Brown .
