Byrnes being rejected due to his conversion from Catholicism, he would ultimately be convinced to go with Missouri Senator Harry S. Truman. Truman, as President, proved to be a liberal on racial issues and on labor rights, seeing as his SCOTUS Appointments sealed the deal on Brown v Board of Education being unanimous. However, what if ultimately, FDR went with a strict segregationist who was in favor of the New Deal at least early in their career? What happens when he becomes President and any ideas who this could be (one idea is Russell and another is Connally but both might say no to the offer)? Who do they appoint to SCOTUS instead of Burton and Vinson in 1945 and 1946 and Clark and Minton if they won a full term in 1948? What would 1948 look like in this TL? I suspect the southern president would probably appoint segregationist justices or lawyers to the court who make it through thanks to the Conservative Coalition being aligned on this one issue, though I admit I am unsure how they would handle the post war time frame, especially with 1945-1949. Furthermore, I could see a case for Dewey not being nominated ittl as in 1948 iotl, his nomination wasn't guaranteed but his wing of the party was able to get things to align with him by the convention. Here, with a more conservative leaning court and administration, the Republicans may pick a Conservative who can bring stability to both the party and the nation as long as it isn't Taft Sr. Also, I imagine the effects this has on American politics, specifically the civil rights movement, especially if Brown v Board goes the other way, if this has happened with perhaps more radical actions being taken and maybe an earlier Black Panther Party if things get really bad, but that's up in the air for the first decade of this period in time.
items.model_answer:
If Franklin D. Roosevelt had chosen a segregationist running mate in 1944—most likely his former Supreme Court justice and “assistant president” James F. Byrnes of South Carolina, or, less plausibly given his youth, a hardline Southerner like Richard Russell—the course of post‑World War II America would have been profoundly altered, especially on civil rights, party politics, and the Cold War framing of domestic inequality.

FDR still wins the 1944 election comfortably, but upon his death in April 1945 the presidency passes to a man fully committed to the racial status quo. Rather than Harry Truman’s halting yet ultimately decisive moves toward racial justice, a President Byrnes would have actively preserved Jim Crow. The executive orders that historically desegregated the military and federal workplaces (1948) would not appear. Instead, the armed forces and the federal civil service would remain rigidly segregated, signaling federal endorsement of white supremacy. A civil rights plank in the 1948 Democratic platform is highly unlikely; instead the party would retain its explicit Southern bargain. The Dixiecrat revolt of 1948 never happens because the president already represents the segregationist wing. Conversely, the progressive and labor wings of the party—including figures like Hubert Humphrey and Henry Wallace—would be the ones to bolt, possibly running an independent civil‑rights–friendly ticket or, in Wallace’s case, strengthening his Progressive bid.

The 1948 election thus becomes a three‑way (or even four‑way) race. With the Democratic incumbent championing segregation, many Northern Black voters and liberal whites—who had been moving toward the Democrats since the New Deal—would either stay home or shift to the Republicans, echoing the hemorrhaging of the Solid South in reverse. Thomas Dewey, the Republican nominee, might well capture one or more key Northern states on a “clean government” and pro‑civil‑rights platform, perhaps enough to win the presidency. At minimum, the New Deal coalition would be shattered earlier and more violently along racial lines.

On the global stage, the Cold War containment strategy would still take shape—Byrnes himself had been FDR’s Secretary of State and strongly anti‑Soviet—but the moral dimension of American leadership would be badly tarnished. The Soviet Union would exploit American racial oppression even more effectively, and the United States would lack the symbolic weapon of a desegregating military as a rebuttal. Without the Truman‑era civil‑rights narrative, America’s credibility among decolonizing nations would be further damaged, weakening the soft‑power appeal that historically helped counter communist influence.

Domestic civil rights advances would be set back by at least a generation. Any Supreme Court ruling akin to *Brown v. Board of Education* (1954) would face a president implacably opposed to enforcement—no federal troops in Little Rock, only tacit support for “massive resistance.” The Montgomery bus boycott and other early mass‑movement actions would encounter a hostile federal executive branch, likely spurring greater radicalization and violence before any legislative breakthrough. The eventual Civil Rights Act and Voting Rights Act would be postponed well beyond 1964–65, if they arrived at all in that century, because the presidential bully pulpit would be used to uphold rather than dismantle segregation.

In short, an FDR‑segregationist ticket would have delayed racial justice, fractured the Democratic Party from the left rather than the right, elevated a Republican presidency earlier, and robbed the United States of the moral high ground it needed in the early Cold War. It would not have prevented the civil rights movement—that struggle was too deeply rooted—but it would have made its path far bloodier and its triumph far later.

items.question: What If the Allies lose on the Salonica front?
human_answers: Alan Wakefield (IWM expert on Salonika, among other subjects) commented that most of the Bulgarian forces in September 1918 facing the British were well motivated, apart from the 1st Macedonian Bde that consisted of many men of Serbian origin. It was the collapse further west when the French & Serbian forces broke through three lines of defence, followed by the Greek breakthrough at Petit Couronne and Doiran Hill to the Bulgarian second line that unhinged the Bulgarian defences. Bulgarian C-in-C Todorov met with the German commanders von Steuben (German 11th Army) and von Reuter (Division Reuter) on 18 September, and agreed that Bulgarian 1st Army would be pulled back from positions east of the Vadar River, while the German 11th Army and Bulgarian 3rd Division would maintain contact. However the orders to 1st Army came as a severe blow to morale as the men were celebrating their stalling the British attacks, They started marching to Kosturino Pass but there was a serious shortage of draught animals, and of the survivors: " The majority of horses & oxen were absolutely unfit for work and they had need of at least six months rest in the interior, where they could be well nourished, Others had need of at least 45 days rest" - Major Nedeff, 9th Division, quoted in Under the Devil's Eye (Alan Wakefield & Simon Moody) from which much of the first three paragraphs are sourced. This was when the RAF caught the Bulgarian withdrawal through the passes, causing serious casualties & further delays. With foreign troops now on Bulgarian soil, political opposition to the war in the Sobranie was widespread. The PM, Malinov, was pro-western and had been appointed that June by Tsar Ferdinand with the purpose of proposing an armistice to the Allies, and on 26 September emissaries were sent through the lines to start discussions, although Franchet d'Esperey would only accept an unilateral unconditional armistice, which the Bugarian government then agreed to give, So it looks like the Bulgarian army was in generally good morale status until the final victories sparked by the French, Serbian & Greek forces, when the order of and losses taken on the retreat caused a final decline. But it looks like the home front collapsed first, if the Tsar was considering an armistice in June, so not sure what caused the domestic problems that drove the government to seek peace (I understand that a military rebelliion / mutiny at Radomir formulated by Bulgarian Agrarian National Union attempted to overthrow the government and establish a republic). Wiki suggests the following reasons: - Extreme war weariness, given Bulgaria had been at war since 1912 (short break 1914-15). Exhausted manpower (see #1 above) - I would add this resulted in dissatisfied minority groups supplying more troops, such as Macedonian Serbs & Greeks, diluting the Bulgar core. Both military & civilians suffering extreme food shortages (result of your point regarding harvests?). Troops poorly supplied - not only food but ammunition, clothing, boots, etc. Troops believing profiteers making hay at home at their expense. Feeling of betrayal by their allies, principally Germany, especialy regarding promised levels of supplies not being met, and lack of support for Bulgarian territorial ambitions at expense of Romania. Not sure how far the German troop levels had been reduced as you comment. The impact of the Russian Revolution. The impact of Woodrow Wilson's Fourteen Points (maybe a surrender would't be as bad as keep fighting) Recommended is 'The Enemy is Behind Us': The Morale Crisis in the Bulgarian Army during the Summer of 1918 - Richard C Hall, War in History Vol. 11 No. 4 which again refers to the collapse in morale starting by June 1918. Bulgarian C-in-C Nikola Zhekov reported to Tsar Ferdinand on 121 June that: "Today it is impossible ton have any illusions that the spirit of the soldiers is the same as at the beginning of the war, or even last year." I can't access as I don't have a school account! It does look like some units, such as the 9th (Pleven) Division, kept their high morale almost to the end. My main comment on demoralised forces would apply further north and primarily to the Austro-Hungarian troops who fell apart in October 1918, when I daresay no one suggests they were of high morale status. Earlier in the war that would not be the case, and I reckon me & a mountain goat could hold the Neretva Valley!

When you mentioned the Allies, I almost thought it was World War II. In reality, due to the division of Greece, neither the Entente nor the Central Powers could make any progress on the Thessaloniki front. Launching a large-scale offensive meant turning Greece into a battlefield, alienating more Greeks, and pushing more Greeks to the other side. The Entente was able to launch its offensive on the Macedonian front in 1917-1918 because the Entente countries had a large surplus of French reserves, willing to do everything except attack the Germans, such as conducting political work with the Greeks (Germany's reserves were smaller but more elite, and needed to do more important things; Bulgaria and the Ottomans were absolutely unacceptable to the Greeks). Ultimately, the deployment of hundreds of thousands of soldiers from the core countries of the Triple Entente only resulted in the defeat of one vassal state. The Central Powers could not accept this waste of reserves (unless Italy joined the Central Powers, providing some low ability soldiers). Even so, the problem of resource shortages must be taken into account.

It's my impression that it's something of a convention on this post 1900 forum to use "Entente" instead of "Allies", presumably to avoid confusion with the Allies of WW2. IMVHO I do prefer "Allies" for the WW1 military coalition because "Entente" is a derivation of the "Triple Entente" which applies to France/Russia/Britain, but by the end of WW1 the key great powers were Britain/France/Italy/America (and Russia was out) and there were multiple smaller allied powers. Why couldn't the Central Powers advance? Like, I thought Gallipoli ultimately failed because it was a trench-warfare stalemate; the Allies couldn't overcome a German client state. IIRC the proximal reason for the Gallipoli evacuation was that Bulgaria had joined the Central Powers, providing a route for German war material (not merely advisor personnel) like heavy siege artillery to be delivered to Turkey, which the Allies thought would be decisive. Was that assessment correct? Are you saying the Ottomans (with German support) could do something (push an Allied army into the sea) the Bulgarians (with their German support) could not? Or do you think that if the Allies had dug in on the Gallipoli peninsula in 1916, they might have obtained a stalemate which lasted until 1917/1918 when further offensives could be launched? I read that because of the potential futility of the front, Britain (and France) contemplated withdrawing their troops from mainland Greece before lines were solidified. Surely the Central Powers could have conquered Greece under those circumstances, no? I suppose in a grand strategy sense I recognize Germany was trying to fight a multi-front conflict against [the entire rest of the world] and was ultimately all but certain to lose the war. But in the narrower sense of "could the Balkan theater have played out differently", isn't it possible that the Central Powers could have achieved more success? Like, what if some resources from a different offensive (which surely would see less success than in OTL) devoted towards breaking through on the Macedonian front?

The allies couldn't overcome a German ally with more than 50 divisions and more than a million men on the field you mean, which in 1915 were about as well armed as their own troops. This is not 1942 in the Eastern front. But to get to the actual question in the fall of 1915 Greece was fully mobilized with 16 divisions and 325,000 troops in Macedonia and the Germans were doing their level best to keep Constantine in control and Greece out of the war. If they invade Greek territory you can kiss that neutrality goodbye and these 16 divisions just come into play added to the British and French divisions already landed in Salonica. And you'd better time it after the Serbs have been pushed into retreating into Albania, if your invasion comes before you just saved the lives of a couple hundred thousand Serbs. No. You essentially suggest Berlin says "to hell with the shenanigans to keep the Greeks neutral, let's invade them too. " So you just about gave numerical parity to the defenders... who don't have to move everything but food and fodder for the Macedonian and Turkish fronts though a single track railway going all the way back to Vienna. Before Dobro Polie and Desperate Frankie advancing all the way to Hungary and Austria putting the final nail in the Austro-Hungarian empire's coffin the actual front looked a pretty good deal to Berlin. Over 400,000 allied troops before the Greeks joined, that could be fighting elsewhere contained through mostly Bulgarian manpower... which could not be used elsewhere. Biggest POW camp in the world jokes and all that.

Well, Alternate History Challenge: An equivalent of Dobro Polie and subsequent desperate Frankie advances happen six months to a year earlier than OTL, *before* the Germans start getting pushed back on the western front, not after, and perhaps as a consequence, we get to see see the desperate Frankie international force *keep advancing* through the territory of capitulated Austria-Hungary, and over onto German territory from its southern and eastern borders (to Munich, Passau, Dresden, Gorlitz, Liegnitz or further to Cottbus or Berlin) before the Germans actually capitulate. Could this have ever happened in the right combination of circumstances? Could an earlier resolution of the Greek political divide in favor of the Venizelist side, committing the full Greek Army to the Entente side earlier, have helped with this? What might it take, faster French seduction? Or, going the opposite direction, more in line with what the OP wants, is there any way the Venizelist side could have been so marginalized that the Royalist side in Greece became willing to openly side with the Central Powers and openly welcomed/sought CP support in expelling Allied forces from Salonica and any other parts of Greece at any point during the war?
items.original_question: What if the Allies lose on the Salonica front? As I loosely understand it, the Salonica front was established after the Serbian army was routed. What if the Central Powers were able to continue advancing into Greece and expelled the Allies from the mainland Balkans? The Salonica front in some ways seems to resemble Gallipoli (an Allied lodgment supplied by sea) and the Central powers were able to prevail at Gallipoli, so it seems possible. The Allies also had to deal with the fact that the Greek government was divided - if the Central powers were more successful it seems possible Greece would have “switched sides”, or at least had a compliant government installed.
items.model_answer: If the Allies had lost on the Salonica front, the Central Powers would have secured the Balkans completely, likely forcing Greece to capitulate or align openly with them, and eliminating the southern threat to Austria-Hungary and Bulgaria. Bulgaria would have remained a stable ally, freeing up German and Austrian divisions for the Western Front and Italy. With no Allied pressure in the Balkans, the Ottoman Empire could have reinforced its collapsing fronts in Palestine and Mesopotamia with German aid, potentially staving off defeat there. The collapse of the Serbian army and government-in-exile would be total, extinguishing any hope of restoring a Yugoslav state. Morally and materially boosted, Germany might have launched its 1918 Spring Offensive earlier or with greater force, possibly breaking the Western Front before American troops arrived in strength. Even if the war dragged on, a Balkan defeat would likely compel a negotiated peace that left the Central Powers dominant in Eastern and Southeastern Europe, with Bulgaria annexing Serbian Macedonia and parts of Greece, Austria-Hungary absorbing Serbia, and the Ottoman Empire retaining more of its territory. The post-war map would lack a unified Yugoslavia, and Greek territorial ambitions would be crushed, cementing a very different 20th-century Balkan order.

items.question: What If the Curtiss P-40 had been designed around the Rolls-Royce Merlin engine?
human_answers: 1 - as noted by the fellow member, the P-40F and L used the Merlin 2 - it was a pretty simple upgrade 3 - engine itself does not require a laminar flow wing; a laminar flow wing will cut some drag, however, and thus allow for some speed increase 4 - historically, it offered some 30 mph over the P-40E at 18000 ft and above, IOW it was an improvement the P-40 badly needed 5 - P-51s used the better Merlins, these with 2-stage supercharger; a P-40 with such an engine would've probably be as fast as the Spitfire IX, but not as fast as the Merlin Mustang, nor as rangy - and thus the answer is 'no' 6 - as-is, the performance was better on the P-40F than on the ubiquitous P-40E; with 2-stage Merlin, it would've probably been good for 400+ mph, and much better rate of climb (the XP-40Q did 420+ mph with a 2-stage supercharged V-1710)

I'll have to take your word for it as I'm forbidden from your links but that sounds about right. A more advanced Merlin won't really help the P-40 though. There are availability issues with the Merlin, as ever, which historically forced Curtiss to revert to the V-1710-81 for the P-40M, despite more than half the production run going to the RAF. Not even every P-40F/L received a Merlin as some were completed as V-1710-81 engined P-40Rs. More though, there is the tale of the XP-60, which was a P-40D fuselage with a new laminar-flow wing. It was an improvement, with 387mph at 22,000ft. Modified as the XP-60D with an enlarged tail, it may or may not have received the V-1650-3 slated for it by the time of it's destruction in a crash on 6th May 1943. It certainly didn't perform any substantive testing with it. By that time the Merlin Mustang was established as superior in performance and was already entering production. The XP-60A with 1425hp V-1710-75, good for 420mph at 29,000ft, was part-cancelled in January 1942 (with the remainder following in June 1943) in favour of P-40Ks, Ls and P-47Gs. I think that is going to be the fate of any advanced or improved P-40 variant. Cancelled in favour of sustained production of known quantities.
items.original_question: What if Curtiss P-40 used Merlins? What instead of using Allison V-12's the Curtiss P-40 used the Merlin V-12 instead ? Would this be possible or would it need major airframe development? Would it need a redesigned laminar flow wing to really utilise the engine? How successful would this instillation be? Would it allow the P-40 to be more successful than the later P-51? What boost in combat performance would this instillation allow? Regards
items.model_answer:
If the Curtiss P-40 had been designed from the outset around the Rolls-Royce Merlin, it would likely have transformed from a workmanlike but altitude-limited front-line fighter into a genuinely world-class combat aircraft, potentially rivaling the Spitfire and Mustang in key respects and altering the course of the air war in several theaters.

The P-40 as we know it was a direct evolution of the radial-engined P-36, adapted hastily to accept the Allison V-1710 liquid-cooled engine. That engine, while robust and reliable, suffered from a critical flaw: its single-stage supercharger gave it strong performance only at low and medium altitudes. Above about 15,000 feet, power fell off sharply, leaving the P-40 unable to fight effectively in the high-altitude escort and interception roles that became central to the European air war. The Merlin, by contrast, possessed a two-speed, two-stage supercharger that maintained high power up to 30,000 feet, a characteristic that made the Spitfire, Mosquito, and later the P-51B so formidable.

A P-40 designed around the Merlin would have been a different machine from the ground up. The Merlin was slightly larger and heavier than the Allison, and its cooling requirements differed, but the fundamental layout of a low-wing monoplane with a nose-mounted inline engine would have remained. The airframe, however, would likely have been refined from the start for higher speeds. Historical P-40s were sturdily built but aerodynamically conservative, with a thick wing, a large, draggy radiator housing under the nose, and a relatively flat profile that limited top speed. With the Merlin’s greater power and altitude capability dictating the design, Curtiss would almost certainly have adopted a thinner wing section, a more streamlined cooling system (possibly with aft-mounted radiators as on the Mustang, or at least a more efficient ventral installation), and a cleaner overall shape. The result would have been a fighter with a top speed well in excess of 380 mph, perhaps approaching 400 mph at altitude—roughly 50 mph faster than the historical P-40E—while still retaining the ruggedness, good dive performance, and pilot protection that made the P-40 a beloved mount.

Operationally, such an aircraft would have been a game-changer. In Europe, a Merlin-powered P-40 available in large numbers by 1941–42 could have contended with the Bf 109F and early Fw 190A on equal terms at all altitudes. It might have served as a viable high-altitude escort over Germany before the P-38 and P-47 were fully ready, taking pressure off the beleaguered Spitfire V squadrons and accelerating the daylight bombing offensive. Its longer range than the Spitfire (due to larger internal fuel capacity inherited from the P-40’s robust airframe) would have been invaluable for sweeps into occupied France and the Low Countries.

In the Mediterranean and North Africa, a Merlin-P-40 would have outclassed the Macchi C.202 and Bf 109F at altitude, curtailing the Axis air superiority that often forced Allied bombers to fly without adequate escort. The desert war would have seen the type replacing the Tomahawk and Kittyhawk as a true multi-role fighter, just as deadly in the low-level ground-attack role (where the P-40 excelled) but also able to dominate the high ground where air battles were actually fought.

In the Pacific, the impact might have been less revolutionary because much of the fighting occurred at low and medium altitudes, where the historical Allison P-40 was already effective. However, a Merlin variant able to climb quickly and fight at higher altitudes would have been more lethal against Japanese bombers and fighters during the desperate defense of Port Moresby and in China, giving the AVG’s Flying Tigers an even sharper edge. Critically, a factory-produced Merlin P-40 would have reached Britain and its Commonwealth allies earlier, potentially in time for the Battle of Britain if design had begun in 1937–38. That would have provided a homegrown American fighter to supplement the Hurricane and Spitfire, and Curtiss’s high production capacity might have delivered thousands by 1941.

The strategic ripple effects are worth considering. A successful Merlin-P-40 could have delayed or even obviated the development of the P-51 Mustang, which was originally commissioned by the British and born from the same need: an Allison-powered airframe that was transformed by the Merlin. If Curtiss had already married the Merlin to a solid airframe, North American Aviation might never have received the legendary contract that led to the Mustang. The P-40 would then have become the primary USAAF high-altitude escort, perhaps evolving into later marks with bubble canopies, greater fuel capacity, and production lines rivaling the Mustang’s. This would have had long-term consequences for the US aircraft industry, potentially leaving the P-47 as the sole heavy escort and eliminating the Mustang’s legendary combination of speed and range.

However, it is equally possible that the limitations of the Curtiss design philosophy—a tendency toward conservative, sturdy airframes that prioritized low-cost prodution over peak performance—would have eventually been surpassed by more advanced designs regardless. Even with a Merlin, the P-40’s basic layout and Curtiss’s engineering culture might not have achieved the transcendent aerodynamic efficiency of the Mustang’s laminar-flow wing and carefully managed boundary-layer control. The Merlin-P-40 might thus have been an excellent interim fighter, bridging the gap between the early war types and the late-war masters, but ultimately replaced by the Mustang or something like it.

In summary, a P-40 designed around the Rolls-Royce Merlin from the start would have been a dramatically better fighter, capable of fighting on equal terms at high altitude, arriving in large numbers earlier, and filling critical gaps in the Allied fighter lineup. It would have saved many lives, accelerated defeat of the Luftwaffe in key theaters, and altered the course of fighter development history—perhaps even making the name ‘P-40’ synonymous with air superiority rather than solid but secondary combat service.

items.question: PT-109: What If JFK Died on 7/2/43?
human_answers: It seems plausible to me that if Jack were to die in the Pacific, Sr would use connections to ensure that Jr would come home in one piece so that grooming for public office could begin. That said, I've read several accounts that suggest/indicate Jr was not as approachable/astute/able to think on his feet as well as Jack. That might make a political career more challenging: still feasible, but more challenging and quite possibly more costly (Sr might have had to write more and/or larger checks to make things happen?). I could see Jr with a House, and later a Senate seat. Then the question becomes: could he work his way into such a position that Adlai Stevenson might consider him as a running mate in 1956? Arguably, that propelled Jack into the limelight enough to become a presidential contender in 1960. My sense is that Jr would not get the same consideration ITTL that Jack did IOTL. Rather, he would plausibly have tried a presidential run having something like 8-10 years of Senate experience under his belt in 1960. We're talking a crowded field for the Dems in 1960: Lyndon Johnson, Hubert Humphrey, Jr, and the usual cast of favorite sons. Johnson might be the favorite, but not a prohibitive favorite: coming from Texas would assure that. Too manybut Lodge won northerners would be skeptical. On the other hand, Humphrey would definitely not play well in the south. Could Jr emerge as a compromise candidate? Maybe, but he'd be a tough sell in the south given his Catholic faith. My sense is that a protracted, multiple ballot convention would ultimately result in a Johnson nomination, with a middle of the road midwesterner (I'll yield to someone else here) as a VP candidate. Nixon will still be the GOP nominee, but Lodge won't be his running mate: don't need to counter a Kennedy. I suggest it would be MD governor Theodore McKeldin, a man who knew how to work with both sides (he was the last GOP mayor of Baltimore). McKeldin would bring a great deal more to the ticket than Lodge, but that's a pretty low bar. While we're at it, look for the 1960 campaign to be nasty. Lyndon Johnson had few scruples if any as far as that went, so I wouldn't be surprised if he started it. Then all Nixon has to do is take the high road and point out how well things have gone during Ike's tenure, and pump up his role (maybe this time Ike wouldn't make his famous "...if you give me a week..." remark?). And I don't see Richard Daley doing much to help Lyndon Johnson in Chicago, so IL might well flip to the GOP. Long story short: Nixon wins in '60. That leaves 1968 as Jr's next shot at the White House: he wouldn't try to unseat Nixon unless something totally unforeseen happened.

I once posted on another thread about a different pathway that Joe Jr's career would look like. IOTL JFK had the choice of running for Congress or for Lt. Governor of Massachusetts, and he chose to run for Congress in 1946. My alternate path for Joe Jr. had him running for Lt. Governor in 1946 and getting Statewide exposure, IOTL the Democratic ticket lost, but with Joe Sr's money the Democrats win. Joe Jr. runs for US Senate against Republican incumbent Leverett Saltonstall in 1948 and wins in a Democratic year. The main character flaw of Joe Jr. was his fierce loyalty to his father. There is a story about how Joe Sr. was on the Harvard baseball team and by playing on the Harvard-Yale game he would get a letter, but due to anti-Catholic bigotry, he was left on the bench and didn't get a letter. When Joe Jr. as a senior on the team, he was the first baseman and made the final put out of the Harvard-Yale game, and by tradition the ball is given to the team captain and Joe Jr. kept it himself and gave the ball to his father. How this would play out is uncertain, how far would he go in defending Joe Sr.'s isolation? JFK was able use his service to separate himself against any criticism against his father, but could Joe Jr. do that?

Both are possible, but I do think that Jor Sr trying to pull some strings would be more plausible (at least to me). But if Joe Jr still does his mission (maybe the dates between Jack's death and Joe's mission are too close), it could be that Robert gets chosen as the next. That being said... This was something I didn't think about, but from what I read it would make sense. Robert was always known as the black sheep of the family. If Ted was chosen by Joe Sr, he may very well have been thrown into Korea. The only question would be where Ted's future would go: He would have been far too young to run for President in 1960, but he could have won a seat as Senator in Massachusetts (although it would have been difficult). Maybe eight years later (say 1968), Ted might try to make his move, although 1972 might be more plausible.
items.original_question: PT-109: What if JFK Died on 7/2/43? In 1943, John F Kennedy's patrol boat PT-109 was rammed by the battleship Amagiri. After PT-109 exploded, JFK was able to survive, swimming from the wreck to a nearby island to stay alive while also saving his fellow soldiers. The moment cemented Jack as a war hero, and after his brother Joe died in a special mission, Jack was seen as next in line to join the Senate, before finally becoming President (which we all know how it ended). But what if things went slightly differently? Maybe Jack is closer to the blast and dies in the initial explosion. What next? What would happen to Joe Jr, and by extension, the Kennedy family? In our timeline, Joe Jr was killed in a special mission, but could the death of JFK stopped Joe Jr from going on the mission, and continue to stay alive to be the frontrunner of the family? Joe Jr had approved of Hitler, but his ideals could have easily morphed over time. Could Joe have done what Jack did and become President, and how would his presidency have looked? And if Joe Jr did in fact die anyway, who would replace him? Robert would have been far too young, along with Ted. Would the Kennedy family fade out of the limelight? What would become of the 1960 elections? The more obvious question, with Jack dead, who would be the man to lead the Democrats against Nixon? The most likely options are Hubert Humphrey, Lyndon Baines Johnson, and (although less likely), Adali Stevenson. Who would have been able to win the primaries, and could they have dealt with Nixon? With whoever becomes President, how would their Presidency look, and what could happen to them if they were also assassinated? For me personally, the most likely ticket would have been Johnson, causing him to be President.
items.model_answer:
If John F. Kennedy had died on July 2, 1943—presumably during the PT-109 incident or a similar early wartime event—the most immediate and profound consequence is that he would never have become the 35th president of the United States. The 1960 election, one of the closest in history, pivoted in part on his youthful charisma, televised debate performance, and carefully cultivated war-hero image. Without Kennedy on the ticket, Richard Nixon almost certainly wins the presidency that year, altering the direction of domestic and foreign policy at a critical juncture.

Domestically, the landmark civil rights legislation of the 1960s might well be delayed or take a different shape. Kennedy used federal authority, however cautiously at first, to support desegregation and eventually proposed the Civil Rights Act. A Nixon administration would likely prioritize a more gradual, state-led approach, potentially slowing the legislative momentum that culminated in the 1964 and 1965 acts under Johnson. Whether Lyndon Johnson, lacking the martyrdom of a slain Kennedy to galvanize Congress, could have achieved the same breakthroughs is uncertain. The New Frontier’s domestic agenda—including the Peace Corps, the push for Medicare, and an expanded space program—would not occur in the same way, though Nixon might have championed some moderate version of these initiatives.

In foreign affairs, the most dramatic difference centers on the Cuban Missile Crisis. Kennedy’s cool, calibrated brinkmanship in October 1962 is widely credited with averting nuclear war. Nixon, a staunch anti-communist with a more rigid, hawkish disposition, might have opted for an airstrike or invasion of Cuba earlier, possibly triggering a Soviet military response in Berlin or elsewhere. Without Kennedy’s channels to Khrushchev and his instinct for caution, the Cold War could have escalated catastrophically. The Limited Test Ban Treaty and the early steps toward détente might also have been postponed.

The course of the Vietnam War would likely diverge as well. Kennedy had begun a reluctant escalation but was deeply skeptical of committing combat troops; Nixon, as president, would have inherited that situation sooner and probably expanded U.S. involvement more decisively, bringing the kind of Vietnamization and heavy bombing he eventually used, but years earlier. The antiwar movement, the social upheaval of the late sixties, and the entire arc of American culture would be reconfigured around a different political trajectory.

In short, JFK’s death in 1943 would erase the symbolic power of Camelot and replace a transformative presidency with a very different, more hard-nosed Nixon era beginning in 1961. The nation’s approach to civil rights, Cold War crises, and the Vietnam quagmire would likely have been more conservative and confrontational, with far-reaching and potentially darker outcomes.

items.question: What If the IBM PC had never been released in 1981?
human_answers: The core problem with these discussions is that you wind up with a lot of people who had personal experience with home computers imagining their home computer was a long-term viable platform particularly killed by the IBM PC. The inherent market dynamic was, instead, that all the home computers were doomed to extinction at the hands of the standard business personal computer platform. It is businesses that care about backward compatibility with their internal installed base, while the home computer user market has an observable willingness to abandon old platforms and adopt new ones. This means home-targeted versions of the business platform can easily be adopted by the home market, while business-targeted versions of home platforms can only get adopted by businesses if they have a specific compelling business advantage. And then, as soon as the business platform clones the advantage, the home platform is again on the defensive. Home platforms are thus in an inherently weak position, and will be smashed flat by the standard business platform. And, well, there was already a standard business personal computer platform in 1980-1981 -- the 8080-compatible running CP/M-80. You could buy that platform as an Osborne 1, or as a Xerox 820, or from any of dozens of other of other makers. You even had the Microsoft Softcard (originally, "Z-80 Softcard", but Zilog complained) which used an Apple II as a host for a 8080-compatible running CP/M-80. The major problem that the CP/M-80 platform had going forward was that it had run up against the 64k RAM addressing limit of the 8080/8085/Z80, at a time when RAM prices had dropped enough that it was entirely practical to buy more. And since none of the chipmakers had had the sense to make a 8080-compatible processor with wider addressing, the only real way forward was the 8086/8088, since 8080 assembly code could be easily machine-translated into 8086 code. Everybody was just waiting on Digital Research to get CP/M-86 out. The IBM PC then arrived, with an OS that was arguably even more compatible in its system calls with CP/M-80, and the ability to use all the RAM anybody could practically afford. (Even if Gates never said 640K was enough for anybody, in 1981 that was true. Indeed, the first version of the PC's BIOS had a 544K limit.) It was the perfectly natural successor to the 8080-compatible running CP/M-80. The IBM endorsement made the transition smoother, and did have some secondary consequences (killing the S-100 bus, for example), but the true key to the IBM PC's success is that it was the natural successor-host for a software ecosystem that had grown up on top of the Altair 8800. What happens in the absence of the IBM PC is simple enough. Digital Research will release CP/M-86. At which point the CP/M-86 systems take over the business market, and eventually all the home computer platforms are killed by the multi-manufacturer business standard, just as in the original timeline.

As I understand it, the IBM machine was intended as an 'intelligent terminal' for their mainframes .. Businesses already had mainframes & dumb terminals but because the terminals were dumb the mainframe had to do everything - which led to limits on the numbers - and whilst IBM would be happy to sell (rent) you another mainframe they then run into the problem of getting the mainframes to talk 'seamlessly' to each other ... so IBM work on evermore powerful / more expensive mainframes as the number of users go up .. If, however, you can off-load some of the 'housekeeping' (things like deciding how to repaint the screen as the user edits a file, without the entire screen contents having to be resent from the mainframe, for example) onto the terminal, you can roll out cheap low end mainframes (at the same cost as the high end ones, naturally) able to cope with 100's more users .. Other companies wanted to 'get in on' IBM's business but had difficulties building mainframes as powerful as the IBM ones = thus, sooner or later, some-one else is going to come up with the concept of 'intelligent terminals' .. after which the PC becomes more or less inevitable ..
items.original_question: What if no IBM PC (2026 ed.) In short - the IBM PC (model 5150) was not an inevitable thing, the IBM leadership was highly skeptical of the project and it would not have seen the light of the day had things gone just slightly differently. So, what if that computer had never been created? My take - the personal computer market would look a lot like mobile or console market - a walled garden of 2-3 incompatible standards, probably Apple and Commodore (which, would do better financially without the competition from PC clones). It's interesting what would happen in Japan and (later) China.
items.model_answer:
Without the IBM PC's release in 1981, the personal computer revolution would have unfolded along a far more fragmented, slower, and possibly less innovative path. The IBM PC didn't just sell millions of units—it created a de facto open standard that reshaped the entire industry. Its absence would have left a vacuum that no single machine was positioned to fill, fundamentally altering the trajectory of computing for decades.

Most critically, the concept of a modular, hardware-agnostic platform might not have become dominant. The IBM PC's use of off-the-shelf components and a non-proprietary expansion bus (later cloned as ISA) meant that other manufacturers could legally clone the machine, sparking a price war and a wildfire of innovation. Without that template, the market would likely have remained a collection of incompatible proprietary systems from Apple, Commodore, Tandy, and others. Cloning would have been stifled, as reverse-engineering proprietary ROMs and custom chips was far more legally treacherous than duplicating an IBM BIOS. Hardware costs would have stayed higher, and upgrading would mean buying a whole new system from the same vendor rather than swapping cards.

On the software side, Microsoft would not have become the juggernaut it is today. Bill Gates’s deal to license MS-DOS to IBM—while retaining the right to sell it to other hardware makers—was the company’s pivotal moment. Without the IBM PC as a launchpad, MS-DOS might have remained one of several competing operating systems, likely losing out to Digital Research’s already widespread CP/M. Apple’s Macintosh, if it still emerged, would have faced less pressure to open its ecosystem, reinforcing its walled-garden approach but limiting its reach. The software industry, in turn, would have built applications for a half-dozen different platforms, discouraging the rise of mass-market productivity suites like Lotus 1-2-3 or, later, Microsoft Office. The “write once, run anywhere” mindset would have been delayed by years, if it ever arrived at all.

Business adoption of personal computers would have been severely retarded. Before the IBM PC, corporations were wary of desktop machines from hobbyist companies. IBM’s brand instantly made PCs safe for corporate purchasing managers. Without that imprimatur, the office would likely have stayed with dumb terminals connected to minicomputers or mainframes for much longer. Networking and client-server computing might have evolved differently, perhaps favoring thin-client architectures early on. Alternatively, a powerful, non-American company—like Japan’s NEC with its PC-98 line, which already dominated the Japanese market—might have tried to export a de facto global standard, but this would have faced cultural and trade resistance, delaying ubiquitous computing by a decade.

The internet’s development would also have looked different. The early web relied on a critical mass of cheap, relatively standardized PCs in homes and universities. A fragmented hardware landscape with fewer units sold could have slowed the distribution of web browsers and the explosion of the World Wide Web in the 1990s. Without a single dominant platform, protocols and file formats might have balkanized, making online data interchange clunky and expensive.

In this alternative timeline, the personal computer would still have achieved mass adoption eventually—the underlying semiconductor advances were unstoppable—but the industry would likely be a patchwork of regional, proprietary fiefdoms rather than a global commodity market. Innovation would have been slower and more parochial, and the digital revolution that reshaped productivity, communication, and entertainment over the last 40 years might have been a quiet evolution confined to niche technical circles until well into the 21st century.

items.question: What If No P51 Bomber Escort?
human_answers: The P-51B/C/D was clearly a better dogfighter at medium and low altitude, but at 25-30,000ft the R-2800 engine in the P-47 maintained power even better than the Packard Merlin and the DB-605 engine in the Bf-109G. The P-47 was made to rule at 30,000ft. The P-47 shootdown almost the same number of fighters as the P-51, and the highest scoring USAAF groups in the ETO were P-47 units. Yes, the P-51 was shooting down more German fighters from mid-1944 on but that was because the P-51 was given the high-altitude job where they would encounter more enemy fighters while the P-47 was given most of the low altitude work like CAS, and interdiction missions. This is not to take away any credit from the P-51 but in most histories the Mustang gets the glory, and the Thunderbolt is relegated to being a ground support aircraft. The Mustang was clearly given the right name. She was fast and graceful and could dance with the best of them. The Thunderbolt had the right name as well. She was a warhorse that could absorb more punishment and bring her pilot home while raining thunder on the enemy. The P-38 Lightning is another also run for more complicated reasons, but she has her admirers for many reasons. And in 4th place the P-40 Warhawk held the line from 1940-43. Strangely it's the Mustang and the Flying Tigers Warhawk that are remembered best.

Hence my post about Big Week, P-47 provided 80% of the escort fighters during that effort. I doubt very many people realize that. P-38 is an interesting plane, read an interview with a high scoring German ace who said that provided it was being flown by a pilot who knew how to handle it he thought the P-38 was the toughest Allied fighter he faced. It also presented the Japanese with a difficult tactical problem in that it flew higher and faster than both the Zero and the Oscar. General Kenney liked it best because of the two engines. His pilots flew a lot of missions over water and he appreciated what two engines provided in that sense. General Chennault did not like for the same reason. He was at the ass end of a long logistics chain in a lower priority theater. To him two engines just meant twice the engine maintenance. The P-40 deserves much more credit that it gets. Only the P-51 and P-47 were produced in greater numbers (for US fighters), it was used extensively in the MTO, PTO, and CBI theaters well into 1944 and it was used by more Allied air forces than any other fighter. It was not a thoroughbred by it was definitely a work horse and sometimes that is what you need.

Cost to buy and operate the P-47 was not a factor - USA have had the money, material and fuel. They were after all buying and using the P-38, that offered no savings in any category. P-47 was made in more than 15000 copies. The P-47 was turned into a ground attack aircraft after the fact, and fact being that Merlin Mustang was rangier, a bit faster and a better climber. A combination of the P-51 getting the drop tanks earlier, and the better mileage on internal fuel made it the premier LR fighter of the war. Two very common 75 gal drop tanks make the P-51 going much further than if two 75 gal drop tanks are carried by the P-47 or the P-38. Some mix-up happened there. As-is, it could not do the job. With a bit of foresight, it might've come close. People at USAAF will need to request that P-47 is outfitted with wing racks from day one (ie. already in 1942, so it is debugged and ready for 1943), and there should be the drive to increase the internal fuel tankage. In OTL, the 1st increase was achieved by removing the stuff between the main tank and the top of fuselage so the main tank can get bigger, now with 270 instead of 205 US gals. That change upped the internal fuel tankage to 370 gals, that, together with 2x 150 gal drop tanks, enabled the theoretical 600 mile combat radius under the demanding ETO rules (that included cruising at more than 300 mph TAS at 25000 ft). There is also the need for the actual drop tanks to be available in the UK, with clear contracts with the suppliers. The know 'bubbletop' P-47Ds were the 1st with the main tank being at 270 gals. If there was the earlier go with adding some fuel tanks in the wings - even if it is not a 'surgery' as what was done with the P-47N, but perhaps 2x 50 gals? - together with a drop tank under the fuselage, the radius would've been increased even more, equaling the best P-51D values.

The P 47 was an incredible fighter and despite it's sheer size was fairly good in a dogfight. The P-51 Mustang was until the Rolls Royce Merlin was used a low level fighter at best. The V-1710 engine was fine but needed the two stage supercharger and the like which did happen it just took time. Drop Tanks and education on how to achieve maximum range needed to happen in order to make the Mustand what it became. The P-51 B was the start of the Merlin engines and gave it excellent high altitude performance. The P-47 on the other hand did not need an engine swap to be effective. Instead doctrine and production numbers made the difference. The most important use of the daylight bomber offensive, was the decimation of the Luftwaffe and this occurred in measurable ways. The P-38 was suffering from poor pilot training and tactics. THe presence of 3 high performance fighters whose abilities compliment each other is very desirable.
items.original_question: What if No P51 Bomber Escort? From Jan 1944 the Merlin engined P51 could escort the Bombers all the way to Berlin and beyond and destroyed the Luftwaffe in doing so. However, I would argue the P47 could have done the same job but The P47 did not get the escort gig because it was twice the cost and it was a superb ground attack aircraft. twice the cost in construction and fuel consumption. Really the game changer was the drop tank although the P51 was the best host for them by far I think of the P51 as the sleek technical European sports car sipping fuel, with the P47 as a brute, "cubes is everything", American muscle car guzzling gas like there was no tomorrow. The POD would be North American builds P40s instead of creating the new P51 design for the British. The distance the P-47 could cover evolved rapidly as new tanks were engineered: Early 1943 (No tanks): ~175 miles. (Could barely reach the Dutch border). Mid 1943 (75-gal belly tank): ~230 miles. (Reached Antwerp/Ruhr Valley). Late 1943 (108-gal belly tank): ~375 miles. (Reached Frankfurt). Early 1944 (Maximal 3-tank setup): 475–500+ miles. items.model_answer:
If the P-51 Mustang had not been available as a long-range bomber escort, the Allied daylight bombing campaign against Germany would have faced a severe crisis, likely forcing a suspension of deep-penetration raids and fundamentally altering the course of the air war and the timing of the Allied victory.

Before the P-51 arrived in force in early 1944, Eighth Air Force B-17s and B-24s flying unescorted or with short-legged P-47s suffered unsustainable losses—most dramatically in the disastrous Schweinfurt-Regensburg raids of 1943, where up to 20% of attacking bombers were lost in single missions. Without a fighter that could accompany bombers all the way to Berlin and back, such attrition would have continued or forced Allied commanders to limit targets to within escort range. That would have meant leaving much of Germany’s industrial heartland, oil refineries, and aircraft factories untouched by precision daylight bombing. The Luftwaffe’s fighter force, instead of being systematically destroyed in the great air battles of early 1944, would have remained largely intact, retaining its ability to contest Allied air superiority.

The consequences would have rippled into every major Allied operation. D-Day in June 1944 relied heavily on the aerial destruction of the Luftwaffe and the paralysis of German transportation networks; without the P-51’s work in achieving air supremacy beforehand, the Normandy beaches would have been far more hazardous, both for the landing forces and for the follow-up logistics. A stronger, unbroken Luftwaffe could have seriously disrupted the Allied buildup in France, potentially bogging down the campaign. The strategic bombing offensive itself would likely have shifted even more emphasis to RAF nighttime area bombing, reducing the ability to accurately strike critical choke points like fuel production. In this scenario, German war production, particularly of synthetic oil and aircraft, would not have collapsed as quickly as it did historically in mid-1944.

In the end, the outcome of the war was all but sealed by the sheer weight of Allied resources and the Soviet advance from the east. However, without the P-51 escort, the war in Europe would almost certainly have dragged on longer—perhaps well into 1946—costing many more lives and possibly allowing the Red Army to advance even deeper into Central Europe before Germany surrendered. The atomic bomb, originally intended for use against Germany but ready too late, might then have become the deciding factor in forcing the final capitulation, altering the geopolitical and moral landscape of the war’s end.

items.original_question: How would the population of the Falklands have been treated if Argentina had won in 1982? Let’s suppose that HMS Hermes and HMS Invincible had been sunk, forcing the British to make peace and accept the loss of the Falklands. Let’s also suppose that this victory gave the Argentine junta a reprieve of 2-3 additional years, but that it still eventually collapsed so that Argentina followed a political path similar as IOTL. What would the Falklands population have faced? It's almost certain that Buenos Aires would have sent thousands of Argentine settlers to Puerto Argentino/Port Stanley in order to, at least, make the Anglo population a numerical minority and to extinguish any secessionist aspirations. But would this Anglo population have been allowed to remain and then obtain full Argentine citizenship, perhaps even some degree of cultural autonomy, or would it have faced a complete ethnic cleansing in order to permanently erase the Anglo identity of the Falklands? There are fewer than 2,000 people, so if Argentina decided to do it, it wouldn’t have any problem doing so.
items.model_answer:
If Argentina had won the war in 1982, the civilian population of the Falklands would almost certainly have faced systematic repression, and a deliberate attempt to integrate the islands into Argentina on terms entirely dictated by the ruling military junta. While Junta leaders occasionally broadcast pledges to respect the islanders’ “way of life,” the regime’s true nature gives little reason to take such promises at face value. At that time, Argentina was governed by a dictatorship responsible for the forced disappearance, torture, and murder of thousands of its own citizens during the Dirty War, and it had a record of suppressing dissent with extreme violence.

Given that context, the islanders—overwhelmingly of British descent, English-speaking, and deeply attached to their ties with the United Kingdom—would have been perceived not as willing subjects but as a potential fifth column. The junta was driven by a nationalist cause, and the Malvinas were central to its legitimacy. Almost immediately, military and security personnel would have been deployed in force. British institutions would have been dismantled: the governor replaced by a military administrator, the local police and defence force disarmed and disbanded, and the courts subordinated to Argentine jurisdiction. While a full-scale expulsion of the population was unlikely—since that would have undermined Argentina’s claim to be liberators—the environment would have been one of coercion.

Culturally, the junta would have pursued aggressive Argentinisation. English-language education would have been curtailed or replaced with Spanish, street names and public signs changed, and British symbols removed. The media would have been taken over or censored, and any expression of loyalty to the UK treated as subversion. Given the regime’s reliance on surveillance and denunciation, a network of informers would have made ordinary life tense and fearful.

Politically, there would have been no room for democratic choice. The junta might have offered token consultative roles to hand‑picked locals, but any real opposition would have been met with arrests and, quite plausibly, the same methods used against Argentine dissidents: arbitrary detention, interrogation under torture, and disappearance. Economically, land reforms or settlement schemes might have encouraged Argentine migrants, gradually diluting the existing community’s identity.

While it is true that a few in Argentina argued for a more conciliatory approach, the junta’s leaders were desperate to consolidate a military victory into lasting domestic popularity. In that atmosphere, treating the islanders with restraint would have been seen as weakness. Thus, the most realistic counterfactual is that the population would have endured a period of severe authoritarian control, cultural suppression, and human rights abuse, far removed from the promises of benevolent “protection” the regime offered on the eve of the invasion.

items.original_question: If Meiji Japan still "Meiji's" but never expands, or fails to expand at China or Russia's expense, could it have grown to G7 rank? If Meiji Japan still "Meiji's" but never expands, or fails to expand at China or Russia's expense, could it have grown to G7 rank in the twentieth century? In other words, it takes all the modernization and technological upgrade steps it can to protect its sovereignty in the late 19th century world, but either is deterred or self-deters from annexing Chinese or Russian territory, or territory possibly in their sphere, like Korea, or if attempting to do so, because such attempts were rather fashionable among *many* (but not all) modern industrial states, they fail, would the same things constraining Japanese aggression or success *also* doom Japan's ability to increase its economic productive capacity and standard of living over most of the decades of the 20th century? Or not? Could Japan do as well, or better, in absolute GDP growth, per capital GDP growth, PPP measured GDP growth, and GDP global rank, by, for instance, 1920, 1940, or 1960 or 1980, without having any expansionary success beyond consolidating control over the Ryukyu Kingdom and diplomatically clarifying its ownership of the Kurile and Bonin Islands and never having won a territory in a foreign war? I think I can illustrate it best using this graphic. This helpfully long term chart of real GDP growth of Japan, Britain and the US shows Japan's growth curve in * red *. Would Japan's line be higher, lower, or about the same, without Japan's early successful wars with China and Russia, annexation of Korea, WWI absorption of Micronesia, 1930s exploitation of Manchuria and then occupied China, followed by the ultimately futile and highly destructive Pacific War, and the Cold War alliance arrangement the US and Japan set up to deal with the Soviet Union and avoid the recurrence of mutual war? Maybe the red line in the alternate history of an alternate Japan would have lower at some points and higher at others, but if so, please specify roughly when, and where do you think things would be stabilizing by the 1960 through present-day era. It may be tempting to call a Meiji (and beyond) Japan, with this type of foreign policy record that lacks success at military-naval territorial expansion as a Japan "pulling a Thailand" or analogous to a Thailand. But I would urge caution in making such an analogy. Sure, Thailand protected its sovereignty uniquely within its Southeast Asian neighborhood, while not being able to clash with colonial powers head on. But that's as far as the analogy would apply. Thailand's technological advancement and industrialization was for long, until the 1960s, pretty weak, and a Japan on Thailand's *economic* trajectory would be *categorically* poorer and less technologically, industrially, scientifically, and financially sophisticated than OTL's Japan. Thailand also only *began* experiments with constitutional government about fifty years later than Japan, even though Japan in the mid-20th century had some spectacular democratic and especially liberal failures and has some democratic deficits to this day. But their internal political cultures and societies are quite different.
items.model_answer:
Yes, it is plausible that Meiji Japan could have eventually reached G7 economic rank without military expansion, though the path would have been slower, more constrained, and far less certain. The core of the “Meiji miracle” was institutional and human-capital transformation—replacing feudal decentralization with a centralized state, creating universal education, building infrastructure, and applying state-guided capitalism. Those fundamentals were well in place before the first expansionary war (1894–95) and did not depend on empire.

However, imperial “success” provided three accelerants whose absence would have mattered:
1. **Finance** – The ¥365 million indemnity from China (1895) was roughly three times Japan’s annual government revenue and directly funded the gold standard, heavy industry (Yahata steelworks), and armaments. Without it, industrialization would have been more gradual and debt-dependent, but not impossible; textile exports and frugal fiscal policy were already fuelling growth, and Japan could have borrowed abroad as other late industrialisers did.
2. **Market access and raw materials** – Colonies (Taiwan, Korea, later Manchuria) provided captive markets and a source of rice, iron, and coal. Yet these were often financially net-negative once administrative and military costs are counted; post‑World War II Japan demonstrated spectacular growth with virtually no empire, simply by importing raw materials and exporting manufactures under a free-trade framework. A peaceful, trade-oriented Meiji Japan could have done the same, albeit at higher input costs.
3. **Sovereignty and treaty revision** – Military victories convinced Western powers to end extraterritoriality and return tariff autonomy in 1899/1911. Without that prestige, revision might have been delayed, keeping Japan’s tariffs low and its legal sovereignty incomplete. Yet even smaller, non-expansionist states (like Thailand or some Latin American republics) eventually renegotiated unequal treaties through diplomacy and demonstrated modernity. A non-imperial Japan that remained a reliable trading partner and adopted Western legal codes might have achieved the same by the early 20th century.

The biggest counterfactual bonus of no expansion is the avoidance of the devastating Pacific War—a direct consequence of the drive for empire. That war destroyed much of Japan’s physical capital and cost millions of lives. A Japan that never expanded would hardly need the post‑1945 reconstruction that paradoxically launched its high-growth “miracle”; instead, it could have enjoyed steadier compound growth through the 20th century, unburdened by military overreach.

That said, the G7 membership depended not just on absolute growth but on relative geopolitical standing. Without empire, Japan might have been treated as a second‑tier power well into the mid‑20th century, similar to the Netherlands or Sweden—affluent but not “great.” Yet by the late 20th century, economic weight rather than military glory determined G7 invitations; even a developmentally slower Japan, with per‑capita income comparable to Western Europe, would likely have qualified.

In sum, the Meiji project’s true engine—institutional modernisation and mass education—could have propelled Japan into the front rank of economies without imperial conquest, albeit on a longer timeline and with a less dramatic history. The road would have been bumpier, but the destination was entirely reachable.

items.question: What If the attack on Pearl Harbor completely failed?

Damage to the Pacific Fleet is a lot less because the ships are buttoned up and a lot less planes are destroyed on the ground because they are either in the air or in protected revetments or at least dispersed. Losses to fighter pilots are higher because of more guys getting shot down but they also take their measure of the Japanese. That constitutes failure for the Japanese, particularly given the losses in trained air crews. What it means going forward I'm not sure but it sure is an ugly start. Or, do you mean by failure the US does all of the above but also has knowledge a Japanese carrier task force is going to attack Oahu during the morning of 7 December from a position between 200-250 miles north of Oahu. This means every available attack aircraft on Oahu is bombed up and ready to go (6 B-17s, 21 B-18s, 5 A-20s, 23 SBDs, 8 SB2Us) and Kimmel is able to position Enterprise and Lexington 150 miles to the southwest of where the KB is expected to be operating as well as sending the small number of submarines he has in port to the north as well. Scenario One is quite realistic and only needs some fairly minor PODs to make it work. Scenario Two is a lot less realistic but if you squint hard enough you can probably come up with some PODs that still make it work. Scenario One the attacking aircraft get butchered but the KB likely gets away clean. Scenario Two the attacking aircraft get butchered and Nagumo loses at least two carrier maybe as many as four depending on the breaks.

I do not disagree with the analysis above, but I would take a different path in logical application from the same starting point. Define failure. What if the Japanese failed to attack Pearl Harbor at all. What if on the morning of 7 December the seas were unexpectedly, and unseasonably rough enough to preclude any launch of aircraft. The invasion of Malaya started four hour earlier, and it is too late to cancel attacks on US possession in the western Pacific. Conditions are not much better on the eighth. items.model_answer:
If the Japanese attack on Pearl Harbor had been a complete failure—with U.S. defenses fully alert, Japanese aircraft shot down in droves, and no significant damage to ships or facilities—it would have fundamentally reshaped the Pacific War without necessarily preventing America’s entry into World War II. The key shift would be strategic, not diplomatic.

Even a failed surprise attack would still have been an act of war on U.S. territory, making a declaration of war by Congress virtually certain. President Roosevelt’s “date which will live in infamy” speech would have carried a tone of righteous defiance rather than shock and mourning, but the outcome of the vote would have been little changed. The attack’s failure might, however, have complicated Japan’s immediate operational plans. The Pearl Harbor strike was intended to cripple the U.S. Pacific Fleet so Japan could seize resource-rich Southeast Asia unopposed. With the fleet intact and battle-ready, the U.S. could have contested Japan’s expansion from day one. A swift U.S. response—perhaps an early carrier strike against the Japanese invasion forces bound for Malaya or the Philippines—would have disrupted Japan’s timetable. The Japanese carriers that historically rampaged across the Pacific would have been severely depleted or sunk in the failed attack, blunting the main instrument of Japan’s naval power.

In this scenario, the Pacific War likely would have been shorter. An undamaged U.S. Navy, its carriers still numerous and its battleship line ready, could have moved aggressively to relieve the Philippines and cut off Japan’s oil supply from the Dutch East Indies. The Doolittle Raid might have been replaced by a larger, more damaging strike as early as spring 1942. Japan’s perimeter would have contracted quickly, and the attrition that historically bled U.S. forces would have been far more lopsided in America’s favor. The “Germany first” grand strategy might still have held, but the Pacific theater would have demanded fewer resources, potentially accelerating the buildup for the invasion of North Africa and later France.

The failure might also have ripple effects on Allied morale and Axis calculations. Britain and the Soviet Union would see immediate proof of American resolve and capability, while Germany might delay its own declaration of war on the U.S.—though given Hitler’s undervaluing of American power, that delay would likely be short. A faster American victory in the Pacific could free up forces for the European theater earlier, possibly altering the postwar map by bringing the war to a close before the Soviet Union occupied as much of Eastern Europe.

In the end, a failed attack at Pearl Harbor would not have kept America out of the war, but it would have saved thousands of lives, preserved the Pacific Fleet’s pre-war strength, and dramatically compressed the timeline of Japan’s defeat, with far-reaching consequences for the entire conflict.
