By t=30 ms, the locomotive is being hit by a half dozen new bullets every millisecond. At t=150 ms, the locomotive has crawled forward about six meters, but it’s absorbing several hundred bullets each millisecond. This has begun to slow its forward momentum (and tear it apart—let’s assume it’s loaded full of some kind of lightweight material that distributes the shock of the bullet evenly). At around t=300ms, the full quarter of a million bullets are in the air. Most people have gotten off a total of six shots between their two guns. Interestingly, the bullets from the front rows of shooters occasionally catch up with—and collide with—slower bullets from the shooters behind them. This doesn’t happen a lot, but it does happen. The locomotive creeps forward to seven meters, seven and a half, seven and three quarters … and then seven and a half again. Success. But the shooters have only fired about a dozen rounds so far. Their magazines are still mostly full. At t=1s, almost a million shots have been fired. The locomotive is sliding backward at about 100 m/s (220 mph). At t=2s, the locomotive’s backward acceleration slows down quite a bit. This is partly because it’s starting to get out of range of the shooters. But it’s also because the locomotive is traveling at nearly the speed of sound, and the bullets are having a harder and harder time catching up. When they do, they have so little relative velocity that they can’t accelerate it much more. By this point, drag from the atmosphere is the dominant force on the locomotive’s motion. The rear end lifts from the tracks, the locomotive starts to tumble, and finally disintegrates into a cloud of shrapnel and spent bullets. Now bring on that asteroid. [Image: image]
items.original_question: 在《世界末日》中，美国宇航局的一名人员评论说，向小行星发射激光的计划就像“向货运列车发射BB枪”。仅使用 b.b. 怎样才能阻止失控的货运列车？枪？
items.model_answer:
If you had to stop a runaway freight train using only a BB gun, you would be attempting a nearly perfect exercise in futility—and the physics explains why with brutal clarity.

A typical freight train might weigh around 10,000 tons (roughly 10⁷ kg) and could be rolling at even a modest speed of 10 m/s (about 22 mph). That gives it a momentum of 10⁸ kg·m/s. A standard BB gun fires a 0.35-gram steel BB at maybe 150 m/s, imparting a momentum of about 0.05 kg·m/s. To completely cancel the train’s momentum, you would need to fire directly against its motion, and every BB would have to transfer its full momentum perfectly elastically backward (which it won’t—most of the BB’s energy would be lost as heat and deformation upon impact). Even if every BB magically reversed direction at the same speed, you’d need roughly two billion BBs. At a rate of one shot per second, that would take over 60 years of continuous fire—and by then the train would be long gone.

In reality, a BB striking a steel freight car does almost nothing. The momentum transferred is minuscule, slowing the train by an imperceptible amount. The train’s kinetic energy (around 500 million joules) dwarfs the BB’s (a few joules). The impact might not even be noticed amid the vibrations and noise. Ultimately, you have zero hope of stopping the train with a BB gun; it’s like trying to empty the ocean with a teaspoon.

items.question: What If It Were Actually a Tie?
human_answers: In most states, a popular vote tie is broken by a coin toss or drawing names from a hat. The odds of a many-state tie are slimmer than the odds of the hat being hit by a bale of cocaine dumped from a drug-smuggling airplane. Nate Silver flippantly posted his 'tie' question on Twitter during the tallying of the extremely close 2012 Republican Iowa Caucus results. In that case, an exact tie was averted—Santorum ended up winning by 34 votes out of 121,503. And since it was a non-binding nominating vote, the Iowa Republican Party could handle a tie any way they wanted. But since it’s Election Day, let’s apply his question to the current contest. What will happen if there's a tie? I don't mean an electoral college tie. There’s probably about a 1 in 500 chance of one of those this year, and the consequences are thoroughly explored (http://blog.constitutioncenter.org/2012/11/an-electoral-college-tie-explained/). Instead, the question concerns both candidates getting the same number of votes in a state. Several researchers—including Silver himself (http://www.stat.columbia.edu/~gelman/research/published/probdecisive2.pdf)—have calculated the odds of a state winner being decided by a single vote, which is effectively the same as the probability of a tie vote. For typical close states, the linked article calculates the probabilities to be in the neighborhood of 1 in 100,000—which makes intuitive sense, since 100,000 is the sort of vote margin by which swing state elections are typically decided. So what if there's a tie in a close state this year? [Image: image] For that matter, what if there’s a tie in every battleground state? [Image: image] Well, for starters, recounts happen. But since recounts happen in close elections in general, these are just as likely to create ties as to break them. They don’t change the underlying probability. So let’s assume that after all recounts, there’s a tie. What then? The short answer is that it’s up to the state’s laws. I went through the general laws of nine competitive states to see how they handle popular vote ties. In most of them, the tie is broken by “drawing lots”—that is, randomly. (If you’re curious, here are links to some tie vote laws in each state: Virginia (http://leg1.state.va.us/cgi-bin/legp504.exe?000+cod+24.2-674), North Carolina (http://law.onecle.com/north-carolina/163-elections-and-election-laws/163-182.8.html), Florida (http://election.dos.state.fl.us/publications/pdf/2012/2012_Election_Laws.pdf), Ohio (http://codes.ohio.gov/orc/3505.33), New Hampshire (http://www.gencourt.state.nh.us/rsa/html/lxiii/667/667-17.htm), Wisconsin (http://docs.legis.wi.gov/statutes/statutes/5/I/01), Colorado (http://www.state.co.us/gov_dir/leg_dir/olls/sl1999/sl_154.htm), Iowa (http://search.legis.state.ia.us/nxt/gateway.dll/ic/1/13/2174/2175/2582/2629?f=templates$fn=document-frameset.htm$q=[field%2050.44]$x=Advanced), Nevada (http://www.leg.state.nv.us/NRS/NRS-293.html#NRS293Sec400)). [Image: image] “Drawing lots” can mean a coin toss, drawing straws, or picking a name from a hat. Most states leave the details up to the Secretary of State or an electoral board, although Iowa Code 50.44 specifies that the names be written on pieces of paper and placed in a “receptacle”. In North Carolina, however, a tie vote (when more than 5,000 votes are cast) results in a new election. (Which could potentially itself result in a tie ...) But let’s imagine that there’s not just one state that’s tied—instead, the nine most competitive states are tied (and the rest go as expected). If North Carolina held a runoff to break the tie, and the other eight states flipped coins (or picked from Iowa’s receptacle), Obama would be reelected in 431 out of 512 cases (http://www.nytimes.com/interactive/2012/11/02/us/politics/paths-to-the-white-house.html)—about 84% of the time. But how likely is a nine-state tie? If we ballpark the odds of a tie vote in each close state at 1 in 100,000, then the odds of a tie vote in all nine states is in the neighborhood of one in a quattuordecillion—1 followed by 45 zeroes. (This ignores vote correlation between states, but it’s good enough for a first-order estimate). Florida is hit by an average of 66 tornadoes per year (http://www1.ncdc.noaa.gov/pub/data/cmb/images/tornado/clim/ann-avg-torn1991-2010.gif). If each tornado is 50 yards wide and has a path 1.5 miles long (which is typical (http://www.crh.noaa.gov/lmk/soo/docu/tornado_faq.php), if not necessarily the mean), we can calculate that a typical location in Florida experiences an average 1.4 picotornados per second: \[66\tfrac{\text{tornadoes}}{\text{year}}\times\frac{1.5\text{ miles}\times50\text{ yards}}{\text{Area of Florida}}\approx1.4\times10^{-12}\tfrac{\text{tornadoes}}{\text{second}}\] Astronomer Alan Harris calculates that a person’s lifetime odds of death from a comet or meteorite impact are about 1 in 700,000. If a typical person in the calculation lives 70 years, this suggests a Florida resident suffers an average of 0.64 femtodeaths per second from meteorite impacts: \[\frac{\tfrac{1}{700,000}\text{deaths}}{70\text{ years}}\approx6.4\times10^{-16}\tfrac{\text{deaths}}{\text{second}}\] In 1994, drug smugglers fleeing the authorities dropped an estimated 20 bales of cocaine from an airplane over Florida—one of which crashed through the roof of a Crime Watch meeting and narrowly missed the Homestead Chief of Police (http://www.deseretnews.com/article/392575/ONLY-IN-FLORIDA-DOES-COCAINE-DROP-FROM-SKY.html?pg=all). If Florida has been hit by 20 bales of cocaine over the last 20 years, then the average person in Florida is struck by an average of 29 zeptobales of cocaine per second: \[\frac{20\text{ bales}}{20\text{ years}}\times\frac{\left (\tfrac{75\text{ kg}}{\text{Density of cocaine}} \right )^\tfrac{2}{3}}{\text{Area of Florida}}\approx2.9\times10^{-21}\tfrac{\text{bales}}{\text{second}}\] (By the way—this means that given a street price of $20,000 per kilogram, a typical acre of Florida land produces an average revenue of three cents per year in falling cocaine bales). Putting all this together: The probability that every battleground state is exactly tied is roughly equal to the probability that, when one of the Florida electors reaches into the hat to draw a name, he or she is struck by a falling cocaine bale, the hat is hurled away within the next few seconds by a tornado, and the elector is obliterated minutes later by a meteorite impact. [Image: image] If you’re in the US, don’t forget to vote—your vote could make or break a tie. And if you’re voting in Florida, keep an eye on the sky.
items.original_question: 如果真的打成平手怎么办？
items.model_answer: If two outcomes in a STEM context were truly an exact tie—whether between competing hypotheses, measured values, or rankings—science’s standard response would be to withhold judgment and seek finer resolution. In practice, perfect ties are almost impossible for continuous variables because measurement always has finite precision; the probability of two independent real numbers exactly matching is zero. But if, hypothetically, two theories predicted observations with identical precision and simplicity, or two measurements coincided exactly within their uncertainties, we would either declare the result a genuine stalemate, pool the evidence, or look for a new discriminating experiment. The deeper lesson is that a tie isn’t a failure—it’s a signal that our current framework or tools lack the necessary resolving power, pushing us to probe more deeply.

items.question: What If a 100-Foot Diamond Meteor Hit Earth at Light Speed?
human_answers: Nothing made of matter can go at the speed of light. But that’s ok—we can get close enough! No matter how fast you push something, it will never quite get up to light speed. This seems like it can’t be right, but it is. Our universe has some weird rules. But the closer something gets to the speed of light, the more energy and momentum it has—and this energy and momentum go up without limit. We’ll start slow and work our way up. 1 kilometer per second: If we drop the meteor from the edge of space, 100 kilometers up, it’ll punch through the atmosphere without slowing down too much and hit the ground moving about Mach 3—over a kilometer a second. As it falls, it compresses the air in front of it. When the air is compressed, it heats it up. (This is the same thing that heats up spacecraft and meteors—actual air friction has little to do with that.) By the time it reaches the ground, the lower surface will have heated to over 500℃, which is enough to glow visibly. When it hits the ground, two minutes after it was released, it makes a crater 300 meters across—the size of a school, shattering into fragments in the process. [Image: image] 11 kilometers per second: If we set the diamond in space a little ways away from the Earth, and let it fall toward us, it will hit at about 11 kilometers per second. This is Earth’s escape velocity, and anything that hits the Earth from space will—thanks to gravity—be going at least that fast. At 11 kilometers per second, the brief descent would be visible as a fireball. The energy of the impact would be comparable to a small atomic bomb, and the crater it would create would be a kilometer across—a little smaller than Meteor Crater in Arizona. [Image: image] 72 kilometers per second: This is just about the fastest that anything can hit the Earth if it’s orbiting the Sun. The Leonid meteor shower hits at this speed. Oddly, the speed that something is going doesn’t really affect how deeply it digs into the ground. Isaac Newton came up with a very clever idea (http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Impact_depth) for estimating how deeply projectiles will go in their targets before stopping. It turns out that no matter how fast a projectile is going, if it hits something that’s about the same density, it will only go about one body-length in. [Image: image] However, it will make quite a splash. The 72-kilometer-per-second diamond sphere blasts out a crater over two kilometers across, with an energy release comparable to that of the biggest fusion bombs. Here’s where things get weird. 3,000 kilometers per second = 0.01c: This would be pretty bad. The thing that makes this a little unpredictable is the fact that at speeds in the range of hundreds of kilometers per second, the air begins to undergo nuclear fusion (http://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/0032063389900305) (Google that paper title to find the full text). This, combined with plain old plasma heating, may manage to eat apart the diamond sphere completely before it reaches the ground. But it doesn’t do the ground much good. The sphere doesn’t spread out enough to make a difference, and it still hits the ground in roughly one spot. The blast releases a thousand times more energy than the largest nuclear weapon, devastating whatever region it came down over. It gouges out a massive crater—though not the biggest one Earth has ever seen. [Image: image] 0.99c: This is where relativity kicks in. At these speeds, the bonds holding the sphere together are completely irrelevant. It’s just a collection of carbon atoms moving so fast that Lorentz contraction flattens the whole thing into a pancake (although we wouldn’t be able to see that visually (http://www.math.ubc.ca/~cass/courses/m309-01a/cook/terrell1.html)). The SRIM (http://www.srim.org/) particle physics simulation tool can help answer some questions about what happens when it hits. The carbon atoms in the ball carry about 70 GeV of energy each. They’re actually moving too fast to fuse directly with the air—they just pass through it completely. The air molecules punch three meters into the face of the ball before coming to a rest inside it, and it arrives at the ground with a bunch more matter in it than it started with. It’s also expanding rapidly. When it hits the surface, it disintegrates completely, digging downward and outward, carving a cone-shaped path down through the bedrock. The impact depth equation no longer applies, since the atoms are literally passing through each other. The energy cracks a hole in the crust and blows open a crater so big you can see the molten mantle. This delivers the energy of 50 dinosaur-killing Chicxulub impacts—enough to cause a mass extinction, if not end life completely. [Image: image] I’ve always thought that one of the the great things about physics is that you can add more digits to any number and see what happens and nobody can stop you. 0.9999999c: At this speed, every carbon molecule carries 25 TeV of energy, comparable to particles in the beam of the Large Hadron Collider. A little faster, and we might spot Higgs bosons in the impact debris. As it stands, the whole thing hits the planet with about the kinetic energy of the orbiting Moon. It’s enough to punch a gaping hole in the mantle and shake up the surface across the whole planet, turning it molten. This probably ends all life on and around Earth. Oops, cat stepped on my keyboard again and I added a bunch more 9s. 0.9999999999999999999999951c The fastest object (with mass) in recorded history might be the Oh-My-God particle (no relation to the God particle), a proton from space that plowed into the atmosphere over Utah in 1991. It was moving at 99.99999999999999999999951% of the speed of light, which meant it packed the kinetic energy of a baseball—in a single proton. The cascade of particles it blasted apart dwarfed anything the LHC could produce. Nobody knows how it got to be moving so fast. Particles moving that fast hit the Earth a handful of times a year. They seem to come from the general direction of exploding galaxies, but what happened to to make them leave in such a hurry—and why they haven’t slowed down more before they got here—is something of a mystery. Let’s give Aidan’s diamond meteor the speed of the Oh My God particle. These speeds are so high that my copy of SRIM flatly refuses to simulate them. However, we can get some idea from looking at how cosmic rays cascade through rock. The diamond sweeps out a column of atmosphere without seeming to notice and disappears into the crust. A cloud of expanding plasma and radiation grows around the entry point as the energy ripples outward through the body of the planet. Forty milliseconds later the entire far side expands outward in an incandescent cloud. The diamond meteor, and the cascade of particles it created as it collided with the crust, is spread out throughout the body of our planet. The superheated planet glows brighter than the sun. The momentum would be enough to knock the Earth into a different orbit—but the Earth is no more. The energy deposited is ten thousand times greater than the planet’s gravitational binding energy, and the planet is blown into an expanding cloud of plasma, with a particularly energetic streamer extending away from the far side of the impact site, out into space. The Sun hiccups and flares as it absorbs waves of dust. The surfaces of Mars and Venus are scoured clean by the waves of incredibly high-energy plasma. [Image: image] And in the distant future, an alien astronomer on a world hundreds of light-years from Earth frowns at a beeping detector, and wonders what violent event would make a particle move so fast.
items.original_question: “如果一颗直径为 100 英尺的钻石流星以光速撞击地球，会发生什么？”
items.model_answer:
A 100-foot diamond meteor traveling exactly at light speed is physically impossible—it would require infinite energy. But if we imagine it moving at a speed arbitrarily close to light speed, the impact would release an apocalyptic amount of energy, effectively sterilizing Earth’s surface and likely shattering the planet.

A 100-foot (30.5 m) diamond sphere has a mass of about 50 million kilograms. At 99.9% the speed of light, its kinetic energy approaches 10^26 joules, equivalent to 20 trillion megatons of TNT—roughly a million times the energy of the Chicxulub impact that killed the dinosaurs. At even higher fractions of c, the energy climbs dramatically; at 99.999999% c, it could rival Earth’s gravitational binding energy (~2×10^32 joules), meaning the impact would completely pulverize the planet into a debris cloud. The collision itself would be instantaneous on human timescales: the diamond would strike the atmosphere and crust so fast that electromagnetic forces between atoms couldn’t react conventionally, creating a superheated plasma jet that would bore through the planet’s interior, triggering massive earthquakes, shockwaves, and a expanding fireball that would vaporize everything. In short, a near-light-speed diamond meteor doesn’t just leave a crater—it ends the world.

items.model_answer:
If modern China had replaced Chinese characters with a phonetic script—most likely some form of romanization like Pinyin or a system based on the Latin alphabet—the country’s cultural, social, and even political landscape would be profoundly different. Such a reform was repeatedly debated in the early 20th century by figures like Lu Xun and Qian Xuantong, who saw the script as a barrier to mass literacy and modernization. Imagining that path taken, the consequences ripple outward.

Linguistically, a phonetic script would have flattened the unity that characters provide across mutually unintelligible Sinitic languages. While Mandarin speech varies regionally, characters transcend pronunciation, allowing a Cantonese speaker and a Mandarin speaker to share the same written text. A purely phonetic system tied to a single national standard (likely Beijing Mandarin) would have sidelined other topolects, potentially accelerating their decline and eroding a layer of cultural identity. Classical Chinese literature, poetry, and philosophical works would lose layers of meaning embedded in character-based homophones, visual puns, and calligraphic aesthetics—much of the inherited literary tradition would feel more remote, accessible only through translation or specialized study, much like Old English is to modern English speakers.

Education and literacy rates probably would have risen faster in the early decades, as learning a couple dozen letters is undeniably easier than memorizing thousands of characters. This might have propelled earlier industrialization and broader access to written information, possibly accelerating social mobility. However, China’s high literacy rates today (over 96%) suggest that the character barrier was eventually overcome; the more lasting difference would be cognitive. Research indicates that reading Chinese characters activates different neural pathways than alphabetic scripts, engaging more visuospatial and holistic processing. A phonetic shift could subtly alter patterns of thinking, memory, and even artistic expression.

Culturally, calligraphy would lose its central place, becoming a niche art rather than a foundational aesthetic discipline. The visual dimension of poetry, where a character’s shape complements its meaning, would vanish. Personal names, brands, and slogans would no longer carry the graphic creativity that currently allows layers of allusion. The internet Age might have seen a more fragmented linguistic culture: without a unifying script, online communities could diverge along dialect lines, using different phonetic spellings, weakening the sense of a single national discourse. Conversely, typing and digital communication would have been trivially simple from the start, avoiding the complex input methods needed for characters.

Politically, a phonetic script could have weakened centralized cultural control. The Chinese Communist Party later used simplified characters as a tool of mass education and national standardization; a phonetic system might have been even more effective for spreading propaganda and unifying speech under a single national voice. Yet it might also have made it easier for regional identities to assert themselves, as writing would directly reflect local pronunciation, potentially fostering demands for recognition. Internationally, a romanized Chinese would have lowered barriers for foreigners learning the language, possibly boosting China’s soft power and integration into global communication networks much earlier, but it might also have diluted a unique cultural brand that today commands fascination.

In the end, a phonetic script would have made Chinese easier to learn and use in a globalized world, but at the cost of severing a direct, visceral link to three millennia of continuous written civilization. The change would have been traumatic, akin to Turkey’s switch from Arabic to Latin script, but on a vastly larger scale. The endurance of characters, despite repeated attempts at radical reform, speaks to their deep entanglement with Chinese identity. A hypothetical phonetic China would be more accessible, perhaps more “modern” in a technical sense, but it would feel far less Chinese.

items.question: What If Japan Had Attacked the Panama Canal Instead of Pearl Harbor?
human_answers: > So I want to know, did the Japanese Navy have the ability to destroy it in a surprise attack, let's say on 1941 Dec 7? I'm asking if the Japanese Navy had the ability.

The Canal is 8400 miles from Tokyo, compared to 4000 miles for Pearl Harbour. The Japanese carriers are stated of having a range of 10,000 miles at a cruising speed of about 16 knots, but remember that drag varies as the square of speed.

Destroying those locks is going to be harder than you think. They are very large, at 110 feet x 1,050 feet, and the lock gates have to have been built to stand up to accidental collisions with large ships (at low speed, admittedly).
items.original_question: 1941 年 12 月 7 日，日本是否可以在突然袭击中瞄准巴拿马运河而不是珍珠港？这个问题来自一个稍微相关的问题。第二次世界大战时，美国大部分工业都位于东海岸，包括所有航母和战列舰的造船业。如果巴拿马运河沉没，将大大减少美国海军在太平洋的后勤保障。所以我想知道，日本海军是否有能力在突然袭击中摧毁它，比如1941年12月7日？到目前为止我所知道的： - 巴拿马运河每条航道有 6 个水闸。这些锁有混凝土墙，但有空心钢门，根据这部纪录片：https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=d-CaBIKTl4M，在 1:11:00 你可以看到它们是一个空心框架。一枚炸弹或鱼雷可能会在上面炸出一个洞，但可能不足以立即耗尽船闸的水。 - 日本俯冲轰炸机接受过训练，他们在二战早期（珊瑚海、中途岛）遭受的许多航母打击就证明了这一点。注意，我说的是打击，不一定是杀戮。我回顾了这两场战斗，很多次，美国航母都被击中了，但都幸存了（当时美国航母似乎比日本航母坚强得多）。 我只是想指出日本俯冲轰炸机似乎训练有素且准确性良好。 - 编辑：潘
items.model_answer:
An attack on the Panama Canal instead of Pearl Harbor would have been a logistical nightmare for Japan, and strategically a far blunter instrument. While the canal was a vital artery, striking it would not have achieved Japan’s core goal: neutralizing the U.S. Pacific Fleet to buy time for its conquests in Southeast Asia. The distance from the Home Islands to Panama is roughly 8,000 nautical miles—more than double the Pearl Harbor approach—making surprise almost impossible and requiring an immense refueling operation across the empty Pacific. Even in a best-case scenario, the attacking force would have exposed itself for weeks, sacrificing the very surprise that made Pearl Harbor devastating.

Had Japan miraculously pulled it off, the attack would still have dragged the United States into World War II overnight—attacking sovereign U.S. territory closed off any chance of continued neutrality. But unlike Pearl Harbor, the Pacific Fleet’s battleships and carriers would have remained fully intact at their Hawaiian bases. This means the U.S. Navy would have been able to respond immediately and forcefully, not months later after salvage and repair. The canal’s destruction would temporarily split the Atlantic and Pacific fleets, delaying reinforcements from the East Coast, but the U.S. had sufficient power in the Pacific to counter Japanese moves. Wartime shipping could still flow around Cape Horn and through the Indian Ocean, while domestic rail networks and West Coast shipyards would have ramped up to compensate.

Ironically, such an attack might have been worse for Japan than Pearl Harbor. A fully operational and enraged U.S. Pacific Fleet, carriers intact, could have contested Japan’s southern thrust much earlier, possibly forcing a decisive naval battle before Japan solidified its defensive perimeter. The strike that was meant to cripple American power would instead have left its primary weapon untouched, focusing American fury on a vital but repairable chokepoint. In the end, the Panama Canal attack would likely have shortened Japan’s window of dominance and brought the inevitable American counteroffensive more quickly, without altering the war’s ultimate outcome.

items.original_question: 18世纪盔甲逐渐被淘汰，为什么射箭没有卷土重来？即使我们考虑到训练一个人使用弓比训练火枪要繁琐得多，为什么强弩没有卷土重来呢？据报道，其有效射程为 300m，仍然比 18 世纪的滑膛步枪好得多，而且可能也更准确。一支由14世纪强弩手组成的军队似乎比一支燧发枪手组成的军队有更多的战术选择，那么为什么十字弓没有卷土重来呢？
items.model_answer:
If eighteenth-century European armies had made a wholesale return to the crossbow as their primary infantry weapon, the character of warfare would have shifted dramatically—reversing the gunpowder revolution and reviving many tactical, logistical, and social features of late medieval combat. The crossbow’s silent discharge, indifference to wet weather, and mechanical simplicity would eliminate smoke-obscured battlefields and unreliable pan-flash misfires, but at the cost of a sharply reduced rate of fire (perhaps one bolt per 30 seconds versus two or three musket shots per minute) and less penetrating power against armored targets at long range.

On the battlefield, linear volley tactics and the socket bayonet would be abandoned. Crossbowmen cannot fix a blade to their weapon effectively, so they would need dedicated protection from melee infantry. Pike-and-shot formations would likely return, with densely packed pikemen shielding the slower-loading crossbowmen—a formation that had faded by the early 1700s. Without the smoke and thunder of musketry, command and control might improve, but the psychological shock of volley fire against cavalry or infantry would be replaced by a steadier, more deliberate rain of bolts. Cavalry, no longer threatened by a wall of bayonets, would regain prominence; heavy horsemen in full or three-quarter armor would become viable again, since most crossbows could not reliably pierce well-made plate at medium range. This would spur a revival of armor across all arms, from cuirassiers to infantry officers, reversing the 17th-century trend toward unarmored speed.

Logistically, armies would free themselves from dependence on gunpowder manufacture and supply, simplifying campaigns in remote or rain-soaked regions. However, bolts are bulkier than lead balls and powder charges, so ammunition trains would be more cumbersome per shot. Crossbows themselves, with their composite or steel prods and complex spanning mechanisms, require skilled artificers for maintenance—a challenge that could be met with mass production but would strain extended operations.

The strategic implications abroad would be equally profound. European colonial expansion relied in part on the “firestick” terror and the decisive advantage of volley fire against opponents armed with traditional missiles. A crossbow-armed redcoat or fusilier would lose that psychological edge, and indigenous warriors would face a weapon they understood and could often match with their own bows in rate of fire. Technological imbalance between colonizer and colonized would narrow, potentially slowing or reshaping European overseas conquests.

In sum, a crossbow revival would have turned the clock back on battle tactics, restored armor and shock cavalry, altered logistics, and eroded the global military dominance that gunpowder granted European powers. The 18th century’s characteristic “lace wars” of elegant, regular linear warfare would have been replaced by something much closer to the cavalry-dominated, combined-arms clashes of the early Italian Wars—a world where the noise and smoke of powder were absent, but the clang of armor and the ripple of steel-tipped bolts wrote the story of battle.

items.model_answer:
If the Black Death had devastated Poland as it did much of Western Europe, the country’s trajectory would have been profoundly altered, likely preventing its rise as a major power and reshaping the political and cultural landscape of Central and Eastern Europe.

In the actual 14th century, Poland’s relative escape from the plague gave it a demographic and economic advantage. A spared population meant a stable agricultural base, no severe labor shortages, and uninterrupted royal authority. This allowed Casimir the Great to consolidate the kingdom, found towns, and promote trade. It also positioned Poland to later form a dynastic union with Lithuania, creating a vast commonwealth that dominated the region.

Had the plague hit Poland with full force, perhaps killing one-third to half the population, the immediate consequences would have mirrored the devastation elsewhere. Villages would be abandoned, farmland reclaimed by forest, and a desperate labor shortage would grip the nobility. The monarchy, weakened by lost tax revenues and a thinned administrative class, would struggle to maintain control. Powerful neighboring states—the Teutonic Order, the Kingdom of Hungary, and the still-pagan Grand Duchy of Lithuania—would eye the vacuum. The Teutonic Knights, already a militant threat, might have seized Pomerania and expanded along the Vistula without facing a strong Polish counter-offensive. Lithuania, instead of seeking a partnership with a sturdy Polish crown, might have continued its eastward expansion at Poland’s expense, perhaps absorbing fragmenting Polish territories or reducing them to a buffer zone.

The union of Krewo in 1385, which married the Polish queen Jadwiga to the Lithuanian grand duke Jogaila and created a personal union, would likely never occur. A devastated Poland would have little to offer Lithuania, which in reality sought an ally against the Teutonic Knights and Muscovy. Without that union, Lithuania might have remained pagan longer, facing prolonged crusading pressure, or might have eventually aligned with Orthodox Muscovy. Alternatively, Hungary under Louis the Great could have exerted direct control over southern Poland, inheriting it without opposition, drawing the region into a Danubian orbit. The resulting political fragmentation would make Poland a patchwork of petty duchies, much like the Holy Roman Empire, vulnerable to Germanic and Hungarian colonization and influence.

Long-term, the absence of a robust Poland would alter the balance of power. The Jagiellonian dynasty’s rise to control Poland, Lithuania, Bohemia, and Hungary at its peak would never happen. Without Poland as a counterweight, Muscovy would rise faster and face fewer obstacles in its quest to dominate the East Slavs. The Swedish Empire might expand southward across the Baltic coast without a Polish-Lithuanian adversary. The Ottoman advance into Europe could meet a disunited frontier, possibly pushing deeper into Central Europe before being halted.

Culturally, the Polish Renaissance and the flowering of religious tolerance in the Commonwealth would be stillborn. Without a strong Polish state, the Counter-Reformation might have succeeded more thoroughly in the region, or alternatively, Hussite and Protestant ideas might have spread from Bohemia into a fragmented, German-influenced western Poland. The unique Polish-Lithuanian tradition of noble democracy and multi-ethnic coexistence—which produced a distinctive identity—would be absent, replaced by a mosaic of smaller states with narrower cultures.

In essence, the black line of the plague across Poland would have erased a stabilizing central state from the map between Germany and Russia. The vacuum would have invited conquest and fragmentation, preventing the emergence of a Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth and profoundly delaying, if not permanently altering, the development of national consciousness among Poles and Lithuanians. Europe’s eastern frontier would have looked more like a contested, permanently fluid borderland rather than the domain of a single, powerful kingdom.

items.model_answer: If Europe had unified early—perhaps through a lasting Roman Empire or a successful Carolingian superstate—the continent would likely have followed a path more parallel to China’s imperial cycles. A centralised bureaucratic state would have suppressed the centuries of rivalries that defined real European history. Without a fragmented political landscape, the intense military and economic competition that spurred the Renaissance, the Reformation, the Scientific Revolution, and the Age of Exploration might never have ignited, or would have progressed far more slowly. Innovation often came from the need of small states to outdo each other and from the refuge that divided sovereignty gave to dissenting thinkers and entrepreneurs. In a unified empire, a single orthodoxy could have easily crushed challenges, much as the Ming dynasty halted overseas expeditions. A monolithic Europe might have been richer in stability and spared countless internal wars, but it also risked becoming inward-looking and technologically stagnant. The vibrant cultural and political diversity that eventually fostered capitalism, the nation-state, and colonial expansion would have been muted. Instead, Europe might have resembled a larger Ottoman or Habsburg domain—periodically powerful, but perpetually grappling with internal rebellions, ethnic diversity, and a conservative elite. The world beyond Europe would then have been shaped by different forces entirely, with the Americas possibly remaining undiscovered by Eurasians for longer or explored by other powers like the Islamic world or China itself. In short, early unification would have traded Europe’s dynamic turmoil for a more sedate durability, dramatically altering the course of global modernity.

items.original_question: 第二次世界大战期间日本帝国为何不进攻苏联？日本和苏联在满洲有共同边界，德国对苏联的入侵极大地削弱了苏联。鉴于日本击败苏联的优势（更不用说西伯利亚的资源了），而且日本驻有大量关东军基本上无所事事，为什么日本不进攻呢？
items.model_answer:
If Japan had attacked the Soviet Far East in 1941 instead of pursuing a southern offensive, World War II would have been dramatically reshaped. Tokyo would have almost certainly timed its strike to coincide with Germany’s Operation Barbarossa in June, opening a second front that the Soviet Union was ill-prepared to handle. The Kwantung Army, while large, faced a Siberian force hardened by the 1939 Khalkhin Gol battles and well-supplied via the Trans-Siberian Railway. Early Japanese gains around Vladivostok and Khabarovsk would have severed the Pacific Lend-Lease route, but the main consequence would have been the diversion of Soviet reserves—particularly the battle-hardened Siberian divisions that historically saved Moscow in December 1941.

With those pivotal units fighting in the east, the German advance on Moscow likely succeeds in the autumn, potentially collapsing Soviet central command and forcing a capitulation or a separate peace. Even if the USSR limped on past the Urals, its ability to counterattack would be crippled. Yet a Japanese victory in the Far East would not solve its fundamental oil shortage. The Siberian oilfields were undeveloped, and the Dutch East Indies still held the fuel Japan desperately needed. A northern war thus delays but does not prevent a southern push. When Japan inevitably moves against Southeast Asia, it would face a United States now fully committed to aiding Britain and a weakened, but still fighting, Soviet Union—but with no Pearl Harbor, American entry into the war might come more slowly and with less unified fury. In the end, Japan would find itself overextended in a vast, frigid front, bleeding resources while still courting conflict with an awakened American industrial giant, making its strategic position even more hopeless.

items.question: What If Gunpowder-Era Fortresses Were Built as Circles or Squares Instead of Stars?
human_answers: Star forts or bastion forts are designed to enable enfilade (or flanking) fire: shooting on the line of attackers from the side, significantly increasing firing efficiency of the defender. Flanking fire allows guns placed in the side wall of the bastion (pr...

Imagine that you are defending a fort with old-fashioned round bastions in the Middle Ages. Your walls are high, but once the enemy comes close and starts scaling the walls, very few of your defenders can engage them.

These outcroppings are called Bastions and they became common when muskets and cannons became common in European warfare. The problem with a square or circle forts is that when the enemy has reached the wall, they are in your dead zone.
items.original_question: 为什么古老的防御工事形状像星星而不是圆形？哥本哈根、腓特烈西亚和阿卡的防御工事呈星形。 （哥本哈根防御工事如下图所示。）为什么不把防御工事或防御工事做成纯粹的正方形或圆形呢？
items.model_answer:
If gunpowder-era fortresses had been built as circles or squares instead of the angled star shape, they would have been dramatically more vulnerable to artillery and assault, likely altering the balance of siege warfare in favor of attackers. The star fort, with its projecting bastions and angled curtain walls, was specifically designed to solve the problems created by cannon fire and to eliminate dead zones where attackers could find shelter.

A circular fortress, while appearing strong with its continuous curved wall, would have suffered from a fatal flaw: all points on the circumference are equally exposed, but defenders cannot concentrate fire along the wall to sweep away attackers who reach its base. Without flanking fire from projecting angled bastions, attackers sapping or scaling the wall could operate in blind spots, sheltered by the very curve of the wall itself. Cannonballs striking a rounded surface might glance off more easily than from a flat wall, but this advantage is outweighed by the inability to mount effective defensive artillery that could cover every approach. Round towers had already been made obsolete by the early 15th century because their curved sides created dead ground at their base that defenders could not hit directly.

A square fortress, essentially a medieval castle scaled up, would have even more acute dead angles. The corners of a square create zones that defenders along the adjacent walls cannot see or fire into without leaning dangerously far out. Against cannon, high vertical walls are easily battered down; the low, thick, sloping profiles of star forts were designed to deflect shot. Defenders in a square fort would have to rely on machicolations or projecting hoardings to cover the base of the walls, but these were vulnerable to artillery fire. More critically, a square trace provides no interlocking fields of fire: an attacker could mass at one corner, breach the wall with cannon from a safe distance, and then assault through a gap that defenders on other walls could not enfilade. Without bastions to pour cannon fire sideways into the ranks of approaching infantry, assaults would be far more likely to succeed.

Historically, the transition from the medieval square keep and round tower to the angled bastion happened precisely because earlier forms failed against gunpowder. If fortress designers had stubbornly clung to circles or squares, sieges would have been shorter and less costly for the attacker. Artillery could quickly reduce walls, and infantry could assault with fewer casualties. This might have accelerated the dominance of offensive warfare, potentially centralizing power even faster in the hands of states with strong field armies and reducing the checkerboard of fortified city-states and independent strongholds that characterized early modern Europe. The elaborate, grinding siegecraft that defined conflicts from the Italian Wars to the age of Vauban would have been far less effective, perhaps leading to a more rapid and decisive style of warfare much earlier.

items.model_answer:
If Germany had successfully blockaded the Strait of Gibraltar during World War II, the strategic geography of the entire conflict would have shifted dramatically. The most realistic path to such a blockade was not a distant naval cordon, but the physical seizure of Gibraltar through Operation Felix—a plan that required either Spain’s active cooperation or a German violation of Spanish neutrality to capture the Rock. Had this occurred, the immediate effect would have been the closing of the western entrance to the Mediterranean. The British Mediterranean Fleet, already strained by Axis air power and U-boats, would have lost its direct link to the Atlantic and the home base. Resupply of Malta and the vital North African front would have become nearly impossible, effectively isolating the British Eighth Army in Egypt.

With Gibraltar in German hands and the strait mined and patrolled by Luftwaffe and Kriegsmarine forces, the Mediterranean would have become an Axis lake. Rommel’s Afrika Korps, which historically was starved of fuel and reinforcements by Allied interdiction, would have received a steady flow of supplies, while the British could only trickle convoys around the Cape of Good Hope—a route too long to sustain a decisive campaign. The loss of Suez would have been almost inevitable, handing Germany control over the Middle East’s oil and a direct overland route toward the Caucasus, dangerously squeezing the Soviet Union from the south at the peak of the Eastern Front war. Without Egypt and the Mediterranean bottleneck, the Allies’ later invasion of North Africa, Operation Torch, would have faced a far longer and more perilous journey from the Atlantic, landing on a hostile Moroccan coast with Axis forces already massed on interior lines. The strategic pressure would have isolated Turkey and potentially brought it closer to the Axis, while enabling a possible link-up between German and Japanese forces in the Indian Ocean.

However, a blockade of Gibraltar was not a war-winner in isolation. The Royal Navy could still operate from other Atlantic bases, and the United States’ eventual entry would shift industrial might against Germany. Capturing the Rock would have stretched German logistics and required permanent air and naval assets that were desperately needed elsewhere. Moreover, Spain’s cooperation was never guaranteed; Franco remained wary of entering the war. If Germany had forced the issue without Spanish consent, it would have opened a new occupation front in the Iberian Peninsula, draining resources further. Still, in a world where Gibraltar fell and the strait was sealed, the course of the war would have been profoundly different: the Mediterranean theater would have collapsed for the Allies, the fight for North Africa would have ended in Axis victory, and the global balance of power in 1942–43 would have tilted dangerously toward the Axis before overwhelming Allied production and manpower could be brought to bear.

items.question: What If You Opened a 10-Meter Drain to Space at the Bottom of Challenger Deep?
human_answers: I want to get one thing out of the way first: According to my rough calculations, if an aircraft carrier sank and got stuck against the drain, the pressure would easily be enough to fold it up[1]Extrapolated from the maximum pressure tolerable by icebreaker ship hull plates http://www.iacs.org.uk/document/public/Publications/Unified_requirements/PDF/UR_I_pdf410.pdf (http://www.iacs.org.uk/document/public/Publications/Unified_requirements/PDF/UR_I_pdf410.pdf) and suck it through. Cooool. Just how far away is this portal? If we put it near the Earth, the ocean would just fall back down into the atmosphere. As it fell, it would heat up and turn to steam, which would condense and fall right back into the ocean as rain. The energy input into the atmosphere alone would also wreak all kinds of havoc with our climate, to say nothing of the huge clouds of high-altitude steam. So let's put the ocean-dumping portal far away—say, on Mars. (In fact, I vote we put it directly above the Curiosity rover; that way, it will finally have incontrovertible evidence of liquid water on Mars's surface.) What happens to the Earth? Not much. It would actually take hundreds of thousands of years for the ocean to drain. Even though the opening is wider than a basketball court, and the water is forced through at incredible speeds,[2]xkcd.com/969 (http://xkcd.com/969/) the oceans are huge. When you started, the water level would drop by less than a centimeter per day. There wouldn't even be a cool whirlpool at the surface—the opening is too small and the ocean is too deep.[3]An experimental study of critical submergence to avoid free-surface vortices at vertical intakes (http://www.leg.state.mn.us/docs/pre2003/other/840235.pdf) (It's the same reason you don't get a whirlpool in the bathtub until the water is more than halfway drained.) But let's suppose we speed up the draining by opening more drains. (Remember to clean the whale filter every few days), so the water level starts to drop more quickly. Let's take a look at how the map would change. Here's how it looks at the start: [Image: image] And here's the map after the oceans drop 50 meters: [Image: image] It's pretty similar, but there are a few small changes. Sri Lanka, New Guinea, Great Britain, Java, and Borneo are now connected to their neighbors. And after 2000 years of trying to hold back the sea, the Netherlands are finally high and dry. No longer living with the constant threat of a cataclysmic flood, they're free to turn their energies toward outward expansion. They immediately spread out and claim the newly-exposed land. [Image: image] When the sea level reaches (minus) 100 meters, a huge new island off the coast of Nova Scotia is exposed—the former site of the Grand Banks. You may start to notice something odd: Not all the seas are shrinking. The Black Sea, for example, shrinks only a little, then stops. This is because these bodies are no longer connected to the ocean. As the water level falls, some basins cut off from the drain in the Pacific. Depending on the details of the sea floor, the flow of water out of the basin might carve a deeper channel, allowing it to continue to flow out. But most of them will eventually become landlocked and stop draining. [Image: image] At 200 meters, the map is starting to look weird. New islands are appearing. Indonesia is a big blob. The Netherlands now control much of Europe. [Image: image] Japan is now an isthmus connecting the Korean peninsula with Russia. New Zealand gains new islands. The Netherlands expand north. [Image: image] New Zealand grows dramatically. The Arctic Ocean is cut off and its the water level stops falling. The Netherlands cross the new land bridge into North America. [Image: image] The sea has dropped by two kilometers. New islands are popping up left and right. The Caribbean Sea and the Gulf of Mexico are losing their connections with the Atlantic. I don't even know what New Zealand is doing. [Image: image] At three kilometers, many of the peaks of the mid-ocean ridge—the world's longest mountain range—break the surface. Vast swaths of rugged new land emerge. [Image: image] By this point, most of the major oceans have become disconnected and stopped draining. The exact locations and sizes of the various inland seas are hard to predict; this is only a rough estimate. [Image: image] This is what the map looks like when the drain finally empties. There's a surprising amount of water left, although much of it consists of very shallow seas, with a few trenches where the water is as deep as four or five kilometers. Vacuuming up half the oceans would massively alter the climate and ecosystems in ways that are hard to predict. At the very least, it would almost certainly involve a collapse of the biosphere and mass extinctions at every level. But it's possible—if unlikely—that humans could manage to survive. If we did, we'd have this to look forward to: [Image: image]

items.question: What If Earth Expanded by 1 Centimeter per Second?
human_answers: The Earth is not, currently, expanding.[1]Yes, I have a citation for this. "In conclusion, no statistically significant present expansion rate is detected by our study within the current measurement uncertainty of 0.2 mm yr−1." People have long suggested that it might be. Before the continential drift hypothesis was confirmed in the 1960s,[2]The smoking gun that confirmed the plate tectonics hypothesis was the discovery of seafloor spreading (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Seafloor_spreading). The way seafloor spreading and magnetic pole reversal (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Geomagnetic_reversal) neatly confirmed each other is one of my favorite examples of scientific discovery at work. people had noticed that the continents fit together. Various ideas were put forward to explain this, including the idea that the ocean basins were rifts that opened in the surface of a previously-smooth Earth as it expanded. This theory was never very widespread,[3]It turns out it's kind of dumb. although it still periodically makes the rounds on YouTube. To avoid the problem of rifts in the ground, let's imagine all the matter in the Earth, from the crust to the core, starts expanding uniformly. To avoid another Drain the Oceans (http://what-if.xkcd.com/53/) scenario, we'll assume the ocean expands, too.[4]As it turns out, the ocean is expanding, since it's getting warmer. This is (currently) the main way global warming is raising the sea level. All human structures will stay. t = 1 second: [Image: image] As the Earth started expanding, you'd feel a slight jolt, and might even lose your balance for a moment. This would be very brief. Since you're moving steadily upward at 1 cm/s, you woudn't feel any kind of ongoing acceleration. For the rest of the day, you wouldn't notice much of anything. t = 1 day: After the first day, the Earth would have expanded by 864 meters. [Image: image] Gravity would take a long time to increase. If you weighed 70 kilograms when the expansion started, you'd weigh 70.01 at the end of the day. What about our roads and bridges? Eventually, they would have to break up, right? Not as quickly as you might think. Here's a puzzle I once heard: Imagine you tied a rope tightly around the Earth, so it was hugging the surface all the way around. [Image: image] Now imagine you wanted to raise the rope one meter off the ground. [Image: image] How much extra length will you need to add to the rope? Though it may seem like you'd need miles of rope, the answer is 6.28 meters. Circumference is proportional to radius, so if you increase radius by 1 unit, you increase circumference by 2π units. Stretching a 40,000-kilometer line an extra 6.28 meters is pretty negligible. Even after a day, the extra 5.4 kilometers would be handled easily by virtually all structures. Concrete expands and contracts by more than that every day.[5]Lawrence Grybosky, Thermal Expansion and Contraction (http://www.engr.psu.edu/ce/courses/ce584/concrete/library/cracking/thermalexpansioncontraction/thermalexpcontr.htm) After the initial jolt, one of the first effects you'd notice would be that your GPS would stop working. The satellites would stay in roughly the same orbits, but the delicate timing that the GPS system is based on would be completely ruined within hours. GPS timing is incredibly precise; of all the problems in engineering, it's one of the only ones in which engineers have been forced to include both special and general relativity in their calculations. Most other clocks would keep working fine. However, if you have a very precise pendulum clock, you might notice something odd—by the end of the day, it would be three seconds ahead of where it should be. t = 1 month: After a month, the Earth would have expanded by 26 kilometers—an increase of 0.4%—and its mass would have increased by 1.2%. Surface gravity would only have gone up by 0.4%, rather than 1.2%, since surface gravity is proportional to radius.[6]Mass is proportional to radius cubed, and gravity is proportional to mass times inverse square of radius, so radius3 / radius2 = radius. You might notice the difference in weight on a scale, but it's not a big deal. Gravity varies by this much between different cities already. This is a good thing to keep in mind if you buy a digital scale. If your scale has a precision of more than two decimal places, you need to calibrate it with a test weight—the force of gravity at the scale factory isn't necessarily the same as the force of gravity at your house. While you might not notice the increased gravity just yet, you'd notice the expansion. After a month, you'd see a lot of cracks opening up in long concrete structures and the failure of elevated roads and old bridges. Most buildings would probably be ok, although those anchored firmly into bedrock might start to behave unpredictably.[7]Just what you want in a skyscraper. At this point, astronauts on the ISS would start getting worried. Not only would the ground (and atmosphere) be rising toward them, but the increased gravity would also cause their orbit to slowly shrink. They'd need to evacuate quickly; they'd have at most a few months before the station reentered the atmosphere and deorbited. t = 1 year: After a year, gravity would be 5% stronger. You'd probably notice the weight gain, and you'd definitely notice the failure of roads, bridges, power lines, satellites, and undersea cables. Your pendulum clock would now be ahead by five days. What about the atmosphere? If the atmosphere isn't growing like the land and water are, air pressure would start dropping. This is due to a combination of factors. As gravity increases, then air gets heavier. But since that air is spread out over a larger area, the overall effect would be decreasing air pressure. On the other hand, if the atmosphere is also expanding, surface air pressure would rise. After years had passed, the top of Mt. Everest would no longer be in the "death zone".[8]See What-If #64 (http://what-if.xkcd.com/64/). On the other hand, since you'd be heavier—and the mountain would be taller—climbing would be more work. t = 5 years: After five years, gravity would be 25% stronger. If you weighed 70 kg when the expansion started, you'd weigh 88 kg now. Most of our infrastructure would have collapsed. The cause of the collapse would be the expanding ground below them, not the increased gravity. Surprisingly, most skyscrapers would hold up fine under much higher gravity.[9]Although I wouldn't trust the elevators. For most of them, the limiting factor isn't weight, but wind. t = 10 years: After 10 years, gravity would be 50% stronger. In the scenario where the atmosphere isn't expanding, the air would become thin enough to be difficult to breathe even at sea level. In the other scenario, we'd be ok for a little while longer. t = 40 years: After 40 years, Earth's surface gravity would have tripled.[10]Over decades, the force of gravity would grow slightly faster than you'd expect, since the material in the Earth would compress under its own weight. The pressure inside planets is roughly proportional to the square of their surface area (http://cseligman.com/text/planets/internalpressure.htm), so the Earth's core would be squeezed tightly. At this point, even the strongest humans would only be able to walk with great difficulty. Breathing would be difficult. Trees would collapse. Crops wouldn't stand up under their own weight. Virtually every mountainside would see massive landslides as material sought out a shallower angle of repose (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Angle_of_repose). Geologic activity would also accelerate. Most of the Earth's heat is provided by radioactive decay of minerals in the crust and mantle,[12]Although some radioactive elements, like uranium, are heavy, they get squeezed out of the lower layers because their atoms don't mesh well with the rock lattices at those depths. For more, see this chapter (http://igppweb.ucsd.edu/~guy/sio103/chap3.pdf) and this article (http://world-nuclear.org/info/Nuclear-Fuel-Cycle/Uranium-Resources/The-Cosmic-Origins-of-Uranium/#.UlxuGmRDJf4). and more Earth means more heat. Since the volume expands faster than the surface area, the overall heat flowing out per square meter will increase. It's not actually enough to substantially warm the planet—Earth's surface temperature is dominated by the atmosphere and the Sun—but it would lead to more volcanoes, more earthquakes, and faster tectonic movement. This would be similar to the situation on Earth billions of years ago, when we had more radioactive material and thus a hotter mantle. More active plate tectonics might be good for life. Plate tectonics play a key role in stabilizing the Earth's climate, and planets smaller than Earth (like Mars) don't have enough internal heat to sustain long-term geologic activity. A larger planet would allow for more geologic activity, which is why some scientists think that exoplanets slightly larger than Earth ("super-Earths") could be more friendly to life than Earth-sized ones.[11]Sasselov, Dimitar D.. The life of super-Earths: how the hunt for alien worlds and artificial cells will revolutionize life on our planet. New York: Basic Books, 2012. t = 100 years: After 100 years, we'd be experiencing over six gees of gravity. Not only would we be unable to move around to find food, but our hearts would be unable to pump blood to our brains. Only small insects (and sea animals) would be physically able to move around. Perhaps humans could survive in specially-built controlled-pressure domes, moving around by keeping most of our bodies submerged in water. [Image: image] Breathing in this situation would be difficult. It's hard to suck in air against the weight of the water, which is why snorkels can only work when your lungs are near the surface. Outside of low-pressure domes, the air would become unbreathable for a different reason. At somewhere around 6 atmospheres, even ordinary air becomes toxic.[13]R.M. Franz and P.C. Schutte, Barometric hazards within the context of deep-level mining (http://www.saimm.co.za/Journal/v105n06p387.pdf), The Journal of The South African Institute of Mining and Metallurgy Even if we'd managed to survive all the other problems, by 100 years, we'd be dead from oxygen toxicity (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oxygen_toxicity). Toxicity aside, breathing dense air is difficult simply because it's heavy. Black hole? When would the Earth eventually become a black hole? It's hard to answer that, because the premise of the question is that the radius is steadily expanding while the density stays the same—whereas a black hole, the density increases. The dynamics of really huge rocky planets aren't often analyzed, since there's no obvious way that they could form; anything that large will have enough gravity to gather hydrogen and helium during planet formation and become a gas giant. At some point, our growing Earth would reach the point where adding more mass causes it to contract, rather than expand. After this point, it would collapse into something like a sputtering white dwarf or neutron star, and then—if its mass kept increasing—eventually become a black hole. But before it gets that far ... t = 300 years: It's a shame humans wouldn't live this long, because at this point, something really neat would happen. As the Earth grows, the Moon would, like all our satellites, gradually spiral inward.[14]Plummer, H. C., Note on the motion about an attracting centre of slowly increasing mass (http://adsabs.harvard.edu/full/1906MNRAS..66...83P), Monthly Notices of the Royal Astronomical Society, Vol. 66, p.83 After several centuries, it would be close enough to the swollen Earth that the tidal forces between Earth and the Moon would be stronger than the gravitational forces holding the Moon together. When the Moon passed this boundary—called the Roche limit (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roche_limit)—it would gradually break apart ... [Image: image] ... and Earth would, for a short time, have rings.
items.original_question: 如果世界平均半径每秒扩大 1 厘米，人们需要多长时间才能注意到自己的体重增加？
items.model_answer:
If Earth's radius expanded at a constant rate of 1 centimeter per second (while its mass remained unchanged), the consequences would be catastrophic almost immediately, with civilization-ending effects within days and a complete transformation of the planet within years.

**Interpretation:**  
The most natural reading of “expanded” is that Earth’s radius grows at \(0.01\,\text{m/s}\), without specifying any addition of mass. I’ll therefore assume Earth’s total mass stays the same—its material simply stretches, drastically lowering density.

**Immediate geological catastrophe**  
A radial expansion of \(0.01\,\text{m/s}\) means the equatorial circumference increases by about \(6.3\,\text{cm}\) every second. This relentless stretching would tear apart the Earth’s crust. Within minutes, colossal fault ruptures would produce planet-wide earthquakes of unprecedented magnitude. Every volcano would activate, and the entire surface would fracture, exposing mantle material. The landscape would rapidly become a shifting, molten hellscape. The oceans would boil away as they poured into rifts and contacted incandescent rock. Within hours, the surface would be unrecognizable, and within days any vestige of existing topography would be destroyed.

**Loss of atmosphere and oceans**  
As the radius \(R\) increases, surface gravity \(g = GM/R^2\) falls. After one year, \(R\) grows by \(315\,\text{km}\) and \(g\) drops to about \(8.9\,\text{m/s}^2\); after ten years, \(g \approx 4.4\,\text{m/s}^2\). The corresponding decrease in escape velocity allows Earth’s atmosphere to leak rapidly into space. The drop in surface pressure accelerates evaporation of any remaining water, and water vapor is also lost. Within a few decades, Earth would be a barren, airless rock.

**Rotational slowing and day length**  
Conservation of angular momentum forces Earth’s rotation to slow dramatically. The moment of inertia scales roughly as \(R^2\), so the length of a day increases by the same factor. After twenty years (when the radius doubles), a day would last about four times longer—around 96 hours. The change would be noticeable within weeks.

**Physical consequences of constant-speed expansion**  
The expansion itself does not create a continuous *acceleration* felt by surface objects (the outward speed is steady), but the strain rate in solid material is enormous. Any structure would be ripped apart. The mechanical energy required to stretch Earth’s mass against its own gravity would likely be drawn from the planet’s internal heat or some external source, but either way the surface becomes uninhabitable within minutes to hours.

**Alternative: constant-density expansion**  
If instead “expanded” means Earth gains mass from nowhere to keep its average density unchanged, then volume and mass grow as \(R^3\). In that case, surface gravity \(g \propto R\) actually *increases*. By the end of the first year, \(g\) would be about 5% higher; after twenty years it would be doubled. People and structures would be crushed, the atmosphere would become unbearably dense, and the added mass would alter Earth’s orbit and the Moon’s dynamics. This scenario is even more immediately lethal to life.

**Conclusion**  
Either interpretation leads to the swift extinction of all life. In the constant-mass case, the surface tears itself apart, gravity fades, and the atmosphere escapes—all within a human lifetime. The 1 cm/s expansion, though sounding slow, is a planetary-scale rate of change that no geological or biological system could survive.

items.question: What If the Romans Had Built a Working Steam Engine?
human_answers: If a civilization finds an example of advanced technology, can they learn to duplicate the technology? You have two variables: The current technological state of the civilization. Call this "A." The technological difference between the civilization and the example. Call this "B." Therefore... The earlier "A" is, the more likely the answer is "No." The greater "B" is, the more likely the answer is "No." (This is a necessary axiom of Clarkian Magic .) As "A" advances, "B" can grow wider and the answer can still be a "Yes." What is our year point of reference? The Romans were technological marvels, but most of their advancement was in structural engineering. Had your example technology been anything involving electricity my instant answer would have been "absolutely not." However, the Roman empire encompassed a large amount of time and a large amount of technological innovation. Just as my grandmother during her lifetime saw the horse-and-buggy and steam ships as the pinnacle of transportation technology give way to walking on the moon and air flight so common people don't dress up for it any more, the Romans shifted from their early years ("absolutely not") to 300ish AD when the answer becomes "possibly, maybe even probably." An important date is 1 AD. That's when Hero of Alexandria created the Aeolipile . The Aeolipile was, basically, the first steam turbine. At this point they may not have had the other technological know-how to build a fully functioning 1800s steam engine... but they would have played with it for a while and, maybe, would have concluded, "you know, that looks an awful lot like a really complicated Aeolipile." So far, I'm convinced that Romans from at least, say, 50 A.D. would have understood what they were looking at (after enough examination & experimentation) just as we have the ability to understand string theory without having the slightest idea how to prove it. That leaves the question, could they duplicate it? The components of a steam engine are improved with milling, but do not require milling. They can all be cast. The Romans knew how to do this, so they could build the shape of everything they need. That leaves metallurgical strength. And that's where the last point I can make comes into play. The Romans knew how to think The ancient Romans knew how to figure things out. It would take time, because they're basically stuck with empirical research, but they could do it. Now the answer is "Yes, given enough time." How much time do you need between when they found the engine and when you need them to duplicate the engine? The following are all gut instinct and open to vociferous argument, but... If the answer is found in 50 A.D., needed by 300 A.D., I'm willing to go out on a limb and say "Yes." If the answer is found in 50 A.D., needed by 100 A.D., it's "very unlikely." If the answer is found in 50 B.C., needed by anything less than 200 A.D., it's "probably no." If the answer is found before 50 B.C., the answer is "impossible." There's not enough technological understanding in the Roman Empire to be capable of comprehending what they're looking at and by the time the Aeliopile came into being the example would be deteriorated or lost. Some of the comments are wondering why the Romans would care to pursue steam engine technology. The OP hasn't told us the context of the future technology appearing in the past. If all that appeared was the engine, then it might be a hard sell unless someone was bright enough to think, "what if we hook this sucker up to a cart?" On the other hand, if what appeared was a working car... the Romans would be all over this technology considering the difficulties of their wide-spread empire. The real question is, what if it was a train engine? Something that needed tracks to be valuable? That's a whomping maybe because suddenly the infrastructure investment (laying rail) is enormous. However, none of that is relevant as the OP didn't ask about it. It's the OP's problem to solve. If he hasn't, it's another question and not a valid answer to this one. A number of commenters have expressed disbelief that reverse engineering can bring substantial value to the technological innovation process. Their premise is that the technologies didn't develop for a millennia or more on their own, which assumes they couldn't have developed in 200-300 years with a working example to experiment with or to motivate them. Such commenters have no experience with reverse engineering. I do. Knowing that something is possible and you only need to duplicate it is much, much, much more powerful than not knowing something is possible and waiting around for the combination of imagination and scientific development to merge. The simple truth is if the Romans were shown with irrefutable proof the value of a working steam engine, they wouldn't have one or two guys out there tinkering around with a vague idea (which is why it took millennia naturally). They'd have thousands and more people dedicated to realizing the military advantage. (Unless as previously indicated you want to choose that they don't see the value, in which case this is all a moot conversation. You won't invent what you don't care about.) Some people like to think that innovation is somehow a fixed process, that it can't happen any faster than it did, but our own recent history in computer development has proven that wrong time and time again. You need not understand why something works to duplicate it. To conclude with an example, I wonder if some believe the specifications of an antique steam engine are as difficult to achieve as a 2017 combustion engine. Obviously, the metals and precision needed for a 2017 engine could not be duplicated by the romans during their time. But that isn't what was asked for. When I once read The Grapes of Wrath I noted a moment in the story when the family had to repair their engine. They'd lost compression, so they wrapped copper wire around the piston, shoved it back into the chamber, and off they went. I wondered about that and so asked my grandmother, who said things like that did, indeed, happen. That's an awful lot of imprecision to still have a working and useful engine. If you still want to believe the Romans couldn't reverse engineer something as simple as a steam engine (with operating documents!) under the conditions I've specified, by all means, downvote my answer. I won't feel bad.

What's a "steam engine"? A steam engine is an external combustion engine which uses steam as the working fluid. So we have: Newcomen's original atmospheric engine ? The Romans (or rather the Greek engineers on which the empire depended) could have copied it, most likely; using it is another question -- it's a very very inefficient engine, which was useful only to pump water out of coal mines, eating lots of locally extracted coal in the process. The Romans did not have coal mines... An early separate-condenser Watt engine ? Copying it would have been either impossible or very very difficult; using it may have been possible. This type of engine is much more efficient than Newcomen's contraption, but it uses axles and bearings which may or may not be possible to make with late Greco-Roman technology. Anyway, this is the only type of engine which is both useful and not light-years beyond late Greco-Roman technology. At least they could understand what they couldn't make and work to find a solution. One of the most perfect mid-19th century Corliss engines , some of which are still operational in the early 21st century? No way could the late Antiquity copy it. They wouldn't even have had the ability to express the dimensions of the pieces accurately enough, much less to make the spherical valves. Not to mention that Corliss engines operate at pressures high enough to blow up any kind of sealed vessels that an artisan could dream of in Roman times. A middle-to-late 19th century locomotive engine? I hope they don't even try. Locomotive engines operate under tight space constraints, so that in order to achieve acceptable efficiency "ordinary" locomotive engines worked with pressures starting at 12 atm up to about 20 atm, while "high-pressure" locomotive engines reached about 100 atm . A late 19th century nautical triple-expansion engine, as used, for example, on Nansen's Fram ? No way unless by magic. The physics and engineering in a late 19th century nautical steam engine are way beyond what was understandable by late Antiquity engineers. An early 20th century naval steam turbine engine? Not even with magic.

Necessity is the mother of invention. Most of the innovation related points have been well covered in other answers. This includes the Aeolipyle. Other mechanical concepts of converting circular motion into linear (screw) also existed. Could the Romans have copied the steam engine? Yes! Would the Romans have copied the steam engine? Maybe! Could/Would the Romans have used the steam engine? NO! Technology isn't developed because it can be, it is developed because it must be. There are several forces at work here. Someone needs to fund the research and development. Someone needs to invest a lot of money and resources towards the critical initial growth of the technology. There needs to be sufficient scope for returns on investment. If the new technology is disruptive, then there will also be opposition from stakeholders in the existing technology that will be affected. If the new technology is extremely prolific and could affect the balance of political power, then politics will play a part as well. The OP has not specified a date/period so lets assume the Roman empire is already established. The Romans are spread thin and find it difficult to simultaneously control their entire empire with insurgency issues everywhere. Can the steam engine aid them in consolidating their empire? Or will the emergence of a steam engine ruin existing economy and consequently their grip on the empire? Even worse, the steam engine could well fall in the hands of rebellious entities in the empire and serve as force multiplier, which once again leads to the fall of the Roman empire. In view of potentially counter productive influence of steam engine technology, the Romans may choose not to build it. In the modern era, we have a similar situation with regards to alternative energy sources. The powerful transportation and energy lobby supporting conventional sources like gas and coal are opposing alternatives. Could we develop energy efficient solar cells, wind turbines, etc? Sure! But are we? Well, kinda, to the extent that it is being allowed to and not more. What will happen to the livelihoods of millions of workers directly and indirectly affected by the gas and coal industry? What will happen to their votes? Will availability of cheap energy alter the balance of geo-political power? -- An entirely different point is that of technology innovation date. Damascus steel existed centuries ago, but last I checked, we can still not replicate it. This brings to light the point of challenge in fabrication and know-how about the fabrication process. Will it may not apply specifically to steam engine (too simple), it is conceptually possible that humans couple of thousand years from now (working with nano-tubes, micro-robots and quantum computers), may not be able to copy a steam engine! and even if they somehow managed to do so, will not use it for sure!

Knowing that something is possible is a huge headstart It's extremely common in the modern market for someone to come up with a new exciting product that opens up a whole new field (iPod, iPhone, Ford's Model T, IBM PCs, and so on) to be copied in short order. Competitors will quickly acquire copies of the invention then tweak it to make it their own. This process of copying is so widespread that patents exist to give the inventor a little breathing room to make some money before facing strong competition. A significant portion of the time spent in the process of invention is finding all the things that don't work. Handing the inventive, industrious and power hungry Romans a working example of a small steam engine that can do real work would light off a firestorm of investment. I trust that they're smart enough to realize that a machine that can do real work without muscle, whip or feed is a huge improvement. I think most people assume that the Romans would immediately jump straight to the enormous steam engines of mid-1800s Europe involving cast steel parts with highly precise machined faces and surfaces. I disagee. Given that the example they have is small, they will likely build small, low precision examples at first. Due to the imprecision, these machines won't be efficient. They won't have the theory to drive the math to get higher efficiency, at least not to start. Materials & Precision Limitations A major limitation they will have is in materials, specifically their metals.
