Perhaps fairies don't age or experience natural deaths, but can still die from other causes. What would kill the fairies? Who knows.[6]J. M. Barrie introduces a fairy-killing mechanism in Peter Pan; any time anyone says "I don't believe in fairies", a random fairy dies. In a world of immortal fairies, this could serve as an effective feedback. If no one has heard of fairies, no one will say they don't believe in them, and their population will grow. As fairies start to be common enough to be noticed, people will have a reason to say they don't believe in them, and their population will drop. Eventually, civilization would start documenting (http://xkcd.com/1235/) the existence of fairies, and then no one would have any reason to disbelieve their existence, and the feedback loop would break down. But ecosystems aren't static. If you mess with one part, the other parts change in response. Fairies could become the dominant species, but the system they learned to dominate wouldn't be there forever. If fairies represent most of the biomass in the ecosystem, eventually, given enough time ... [Image: image] ... something will learn to eat them.
items.original_question: 如果每个仙女都是从孩子的第一声笑声中诞生并且仙女是不朽的，那么会有多少仙女飞来飞去？
items.model_answer:
If every child’s first laugh spontaneously created an immortal fairy, the world would be radically reshaped—not by magic alone, but by the sheer mathematics of exponential fairy accumulation. Assuming current global birth rates, over 130 million fairies would appear each year. Since they are immortal, none would ever die, leading to an ever-growing fairy population that would eventually dwarf humanity. Within a century, fairies would outnumber humans by orders of magnitude, competing for space and resources unless they were ethereal and needed no sustenance.

Physically, if these fairies were material, the mass-energy required for their sudden, repeated creation would violate conservation laws on a planetary scale. Earth would either hemorrhage energy or draw it from some unseen source, potentially cooling the planet or destabilizing matter. If fairies were instead incorporeal, their presence might still interact with light, sound, or gravity, gradually turning the atmosphere into a shimmering, noisy haze. Immortal beings, even tiny ones, would accumulate environmental impacts—fairy dust, discarded laughter-trance residues, or accidental magical interference—leading to a new kind of magical pollution.

Socially, the laughing-child-fairy bond would become a universal constant. Every person would have a personal, deathless companion from infancy. This could fundamentally alter concepts of family, loneliness, and mortality. A society where everyone has a lifelong, ageless witness might become either deeply empathetic or profoundly stagnant, as personal growth could be inhibited by an ever-present nurturing figure. Human death would become even more poignant: the fairy would outlive its human, creating legions of grieving, companionless fairies. Would they bond with new children? Would they grow misanthropic or feral? The psychological fallout could reshape cultures, perhaps leading to fairy-management industries or rites to release them.

Economically, immortal fairies might offer a perfect labor force, but their nature—tied to joy and infancy—might make them unsuitable for drudgery. Instead, they could become the ultimate historians, artists, or custodians of memory, since they never forget. Power structures would shift: rulers could amass fairy armies, but fairy loyalty likely lies with their original child, not institutions. Conflict might arise between fairy allegiances and state demands.

Evolutionarily, the relationship could become symbiotic. Natural selection might favor children whose laughs produced more effective fairies—perhaps calmer, more industrious, or protective ones—gradually domesticating humans to a magical entity. Over millennia, humans might evolve to laugh earlier or more loudly, altering infant development.

In the deepest sense, the very concept of immortality would cheapen. When every giggle births the undying, eternity becomes mundane. Art, love, and ambition might wither or transform entirely, as the shadow of infinite time looms from every human’s first mirthful moment. The world would not end with a bang, but with a giggle—multiplied until the very air is thick with deathless, tinkling witnesses.

items.question: What If There Were a Lake on the Moon?
human_answers: This would be so cool. In fact, I honestly think it's cool enough that it gives us a pretty good reason to go to the Moon in the first place. At the very least, it's better than the one Kennedy gave. [Image: image] Floating would feel about the same on the Moon as on Earth, since how high in the water you float depends only on your body's density compared to the water's, not the strength of gravity. Swimming underwater would also feel pretty similar. The inertia of the water is the main source of drag when swimming, and inertia is a property of matter[1]♬ BILL NYE THE SCIENCE GUY ♬ independent of gravity. The top speed of a submerged swimmer would be about the same on the Moon as here—about 2 meters/second. Everything else would be different and way cooler. The waves would be bigger, the splash fights more intense, and swimmers would be able to jump out of the water like dolphins. This[2]Not this one. The other one.​[3]The simplest approach, which gives us an approximate answer, is to treat the swimmer as a simple projectile. The formula for the height of a projectile is: \( \frac{\text{speed}^2}{2\times\text{gravity}} \) ... which tells us that a champion swimmer moving at 2 meters per second (4.5 mph) would only have enough kinetic energy to lift their body about 20 centimeters (http://www.wolframalpha.com/input/?i=%282+m%2Fs%29%5E2+%2F+%282+*+earth+gravity%29) against gravity. That's not totally accurate, although it's enough to tell us that dolphin jumps on Earth probably aren't in the cards for us. But to get a more accurate answer (and an equation we can apply to the Moon), we need to account for a few other things. When a swimmer first breaks the surface, they don't have to lift their full weight; they're partially supported by buoyancy. As more of their body leaves the water, the force of buoyancy decreases, since their body is displacing less water. Since the force of gravity isn't changing, their net weight increases. You can calculate how much potential energy is required to lift a body vertically through the surface to a certain height, but it's a complicated integral (you integrate the displacement of the submerged portion of their body over the vertical distance they travel) and depends on their body shape. For a human body moving fast enough to jump most of the way out of the water, this effect probably adds about half a torso-length to their final height—and less if they're not able to make it all the way out. The other effect we have to account for is the fact that a swimmer can continue kicking as they start to leave the water. When a swimmer is submerged and moving at top speed, the drag from the water is equal to the thrust they generate by kicking and ... whatever the gerund form of the verb is for the things your arms do while swimming. My first thought was "stroking," but it's definitely not that. Anyway, once the jumping swimmer breaks the surface, the drag almost vanishes, but they can keep kicking for a few moments. To figure out how much energy this adds, you can multiply the thrust from kicking by the distance over which they're kicking after breaking the surface, since energy equals force times distance. The distance is most of a body length, or 1 to 1.5 meters. As for the force from kicking, random Google results for a search for lifeguard qualifications suggest that good swimmers might be able to carry 10 lbs over their heads for a short distance, which means they're generating a little more than 10 pounds-force (50+ N) of kicking thrust. We can combine all these together into a big ol' equation: \[ \text{Jump height}=\left(\frac{\tfrac{1}{2}\times\text{body mass}\times\left(\text{top speed}\right)^2+\text{kick force}\times\text{torso length}}{\text{Earth gravity}\times\text{body mass}}\right)+\left(\text{buoyancy correction} \right) \] footnote contains some detail on the math behind a dolphin jump. Calculating the height a swimmer can jump out of the water requires taking several different things into account, but the bottom line is that a normal swimmer on the Moon could probably launch themselves a full meter out of the water, and Michael Phelps may well be able to manage 2 or 3. [Image: image] The numbers get even more exciting when we introduce fins. Swimmers wearing fins (http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Finswimming) can go substantially faster than regular swimmers (http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_Schwimmer) without them (although the fastest swimmer wearing flippers will still lose to a runner, even if the runner is also wearing flippers and jumping over hurdles (https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=sRDnajV1A3w)). Champion finswimmers can go almost 3.2 m/s wearing a monofin, which is fast enough for some pretty impressive jumps—even on Earth (https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=z09RmuaPyVU). Data on swimfin top speeds (http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_world_records_in_finswimming) and thrusts[4]This paper (http://archive.rubicon-foundation.org/xmlui/bitstream/handle/123456789/3936/12841609.pdf) provides some sample data. suggest that on the Moon, a champion finswimmer (http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hanna-Maria_Sepp%C3%A4l%C3%A4) could probably launch themselves as high as 4 or 5 meters into the air. In other words, on the Moon, you could conceivably do a high dive in reverse. [Image: image] But it gets even better. A 2012 paper (http://www.plosone.org/article/fetchObject.action?uri=info%3Adoi%2F10.1371%2Fjournal.pone.0037300&representation=PDF) in PLoS ONE, titled Humans Running in Place on Water at Simulated Reduced Gravity, concluded that while humans can't run on the surface of water on Earth,[5]They actually provide a citation for this statement, which is delightful. they might just barely be able to do so on the Moon. (I highly recommend reading their paper, if only for the hilarious experimental setup illustration on page 2.) Because of the reduced gravity on the Moon, the water would be launched upward more easily, just like the swimmers. The result would be larger waves and more flying droplets. In technical terms, a pool on the Moon would be more "splashy".[6]The SI unit of splashiness is the splashypant. To avoid splashing all the water out, you'd want to design the deck so water drains quickly back into the pool. You could just make the rim higher, but then you'd spoil one of the key joys of a pool on the Moon—exiting via Slip 'N Slide: [Image: image] I 100% support this idea. If we ever build a Moon base, I think we should absolutely build a big swimming pool there. Sure, sending a swimming pool's worth of water (135 horses (http://xkcd.com/1461/)) to the Moon's surface would be expensive.[7]If you decided to bundle a backyard pool into individual two-liter bottles, and sent them in 3,000 batches of 10 each via the startup Astrobotic (https://www.astrobotic.com/), it would cost you $72 billion (according to their website's calculator (https://www.astrobotic.com/configure-mission)). But on the other hand, this lunar base is going to have people on it, so you need to send some water anyway.[8]Sending a supply of water and a filter system is probably cheaper than sending a replacement astronaut every 3 or 4 days, although I encourage NASA to run the numbers on that to be sure. And it's really not impossible. A large backyard swimming pool weighs about as much as four Apollo lunar landers. A next-generation[9](or, heck, previous-generation (http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saturn_V)) heavy-lift rocket, like Boeing's NASA SLS or Elon Musk's SpaceX Falcon Heavy, would be able to deliver a good-sized pool to the Moon in not too many trips. So maybe the next step, if you really want a swimming pool on the Moon, is to call Elon Musk and ask for a quote. [Image: image]
items.original_question: 如果月球上有一个湖会怎样？在里面游泳会是什么感觉？假设它被隐藏在一个规则的大气层中，比如某个巨大的圆顶或其他什么地方。
items.model_answer:
If a lake suddenly appeared on the Moon’s surface, it would be a fleeting, violent spectacle, and within hours—or at most days—it would be gone. The lunar environment is utterly hostile to liquid water: the pressure is a near-perfect vacuum (about 10⁻¹² bar), gravity is only 1/6 of Earth’s, and temperatures swing from +127°C in sunlight to -173°C at night.

The moment the lake materializes, the water would boil furiously, even if its temperature is near freezing. In a vacuum, the boiling point of water drops well below 0°C, so the entire surface of the lake would turn into a churning froth. This rapid evaporation pulls heat from the remaining liquid, so simultaneously the lake begins to freeze from the top down, forming a thin crust of ice. On the sunlit side, the intense heat would sublimate that ice directly into vapor, while on the night side, the freezing would progress deeper. Because of the low gravity, water vapor molecules escape more easily, and a large fraction would reach escape velocity or be stripped away by the solar wind, leaving the Moon forever.

The lake would create a temporary, localized atmosphere of water vapor, but without any magnetic field or substantial gravity to hold it, this vapor would quickly dissipate into space. The boiling would also fling droplets of water and ice, some of which could land meters or even kilometers away, forming tiny, short-lived streaks of frost. Lunar dust disturbed by the outgassing might settle back in a slightly rearranged pattern, but there would be no lasting erosion—just a dried, salt-flat-like scar of any dissolved minerals that were left behind as ice.

In the end, the Moon would return to its dry, airless state, with perhaps a faint, fleeting puff of OH molecules detectable from Earth. The lake, dramatic as it would be, could never persist without a sealed, pressurized environment to protect it.

items.question: What If You Dropped a 7-Kilogram Bowling Ball into the Mariana Trench?
human_answers: It is a good thing you mentioned the weight, because of a very surprising fact: Most bowling balls float. It's true. Bowling balls all have about the same volume, so they all displace the same weight in seawater—12.13 lbs, or about 5.5 kg. But their weights vary substantially, from as little as 6 lbs to a max of 16. Only the balls that weigh more than 12.13 lbs will sink. [Image: image] "Hang on a moment," the serious bowlers reading this are saying, "most bowling balls are at the heavy end of that range. The usual range is more like 14-16 lbs for men and 10-14 lbs for women. Maybe the average women's ball floats, but the overall average ball surely sinks." This is definitely true for serious bowlers, but for casual bowlers, it might be better to define the "average" ball using the distribution on the rack of balls at the local bowling alley. These house balls often list the weight on them, so rather than go to a bowling alley, I just sifted through all the Flickr photos of bowling balls and tallied up all the visible weights. The average was 10½ lbs. [Image: image] So at the very least, for most people, the average bowling ball they've picked up in their lives probably floats. If nothing else, this makes the popular simile "sank like a bowling ball"—which appears in a number of books (https://www.google.com/search?q=%22sank+like+a+bowling+ball%22&btnG=Search+Books&tbm=bks&tbo=1)—seem a little poorly chosen.[1]In defense of the authors of Volume 53 of North Dakota Quarterly, the simile they used is, "sank like a bowling ball in whipped cream," which is perfectly reasonable. On the other hand, How To Hook a Man (And a Baby) and The Year's Work in Lebowski Studies are on their own. But Doug's bowling ball is 7 kg (15.5 lbs), making it plenty heavy enough to sink in the ocean. How fast will it fall? Small falling spheres in viscous (goopy) liquids (like hair gel (http://arxiv.org/pdf/1108.3427.pdf)) exhibit weird behaviors and sometimes complex oscillation, but bowling balls falling through water are pretty straightforward. Their falling speed is determined by the drag equation (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Drag_equation) and their weight (accounting for buoyancy). For Doug's bowling ball, that terminal velocity will be roughly 1.3 meters per second, which means it will take two hours and 20 minutes to reach the bottom. That's plenty of time to enjoy a two-hour movie (http://www.imdb.com/title/tt0118715/). A 13-pound bowling ball, which is much closer to neutrally buoyant in seawater, would take four and a half hours to reach the bottom. On the other hand, a bowling ball made of solid iron would reach the bottom in half an hour. A bowling ball made of lead would reach the bottom in 23 minutes, and a bowling ball made of solid gold would make it in 17. However, a bowling ball made of solid gold would also weigh more than the average bowler.[2]At least, I think it would, but I can't think of a way to sample the weight of the average bowler without getting punched. A bowling ball made of solid osmium, the heaviest naturally-occurring element, would weigh 120 kilograms, and could sink to the bottom of the Mariana Trench in just 16 minutes. But what if you got the weight wrong? What if the bowling ball you were using turned out to be 7 pounds, not 7 kilograms? Or maybe it's 10.5 pounds—the "average" bowling ball, at least according to a dubious Flickr sample. In that case, the ball would never reach the bottom. Instead, it would drift sideways with the currents. We can track what course it would take using the Adrift.org.au ocean plastic tracking tool (http://www.adrift.org.au/map?lat=11.3&lng=142.6&center=-180&startmon=Jan). The bowling ball would first drift west, past Luzon in the Philippines, then probably north along the coast of China, turning right at Japan and heading out over the Pacific. Sometime in the summer of 2018, it would approach the coast of California. Most likely, it would follow the coast for a little while, then become swept up in the great Pacific garbage patch (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Pacific_garbage_patch). However, it's possible that it would be swept up on shore instead. If, during those three years, Doug took his boat from the Mariana islands to Los Angeles, found a nice, sheltered cove, and set up ten carefully weighted bowling pins just below the surface, then there is a tiny, tiny chance ... [Image: image] ... that he could succeed in bowling the single most improbable strike of all time.
items.original_question: 您正坐在马里亚纳海沟上方的船上。如果将一个 7 公斤重的保龄球从侧面掉下来，需要多长时间才能落到底部？
items.model_answer:
If you dropped a 7‑kilogram (15.4‑pound) bowling ball into the Mariana Trench, it would sink with surprising slowness, endure the deepest ocean in the world without imploding, and eventually come to rest on the seafloor roughly 2.5 hours later.

**Buoyancy and sink rate**  
A typical 7‑kg bowling ball has a diameter of about 21.8 cm (8.6 in) and an overall density around 1.3 g/cm³. Seawater at the surface is about 1.025 g/cm³, so the ball is only slightly negatively buoyant. Its net downward force is small, and its bulk creates substantial drag. Terminal velocity works out to roughly 1.2 m/s (4 ft/s). That means covering the 11 km (6.8 miles) depth of the Mariana Trench would take about 2.5 hours—a leisurely descent compared to far denser objects like rocks or metal spheres.

**Pressure and structural integrity**  
At the bottom of the trench, the pressure reaches ~1,100 atmospheres (110 MPa). Because a modern bowling ball is a solid composite—a dense inner core surrounded by a thick coverstock—it contains no large air pockets or compressible voids. There is nothing inside to violently collapse. The immense pressure would compress the material slightly, maybe shrinking its volume by a few percent, but the ball would remain intact. It wouldn’t crack, shatter, or implode; it would just get a bit denser and sink marginally faster as it goes deeper.

**The bottom landing**  
Once the ball reaches the muddy abyssal plain, it would strike the soft, silty sediment at a couple of metres per second, making a shallow indentation. It would then sit there, perfectly unharmed, slowly being draped by the perpetual rain of marine particles. Over centuries, it would become buried and might eventually be joined by the occasional whale bone or manganese nodule.

In short, the bowling ball handles the journey comfortably—a remarkably mundane outcome for an otherwise extraordinary trip.

items.question: What If There Were Both a Space Elevator and a Stairway to Space?
human_answers: A week or two, if you're a champion stair-climber. Or 12 hours if you're on a motorcycle. A tower to space would be very different from a space elevator. A space elevator (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_elevator) would be about 100,000 kilometers tall, while a tower "to space" would only need to be 100 kilometers. As Ethan mentions, it would need to be pressurized, with an airlock every few miles. [Image: image] A stairway to space[1]If there's a bustle in your hedgerow, well, uh, boy, I don't know what to tell you. I guess ask it to leave? would have about half a million steps. World-champion stair-climbers[2]or "towerrunners" like Christian Riedl (http://stairsport.com/12h-stair-climbing-world-record-attempt-by-christian-riedl/) or Kristin Frey (http://www.kristinfrey.com/) can travel roughly a Mount Everest's height in a day; Riedl set the half-day record last October by climbing 13,145.65 meters (http://www.guinnessworldrecords.com/world-records/stair-climbing-vertical-height-%2812-hours%29) in 12 hours. At that pace—taking the other twelve hours to rest, eat, and sleep each day—it would take him a little over a week to reach the top. Climbing all those stairs would burn calories, which would mean you'd need to carry food. It turns out that the most efficient food you can carry, in terms of calories per pound, is butter—which is why Arctic explorers carry so much of it (http://abcnews.go.com/Technology/GlobalWarming/story?id=4853093). Suppose your backpack (http://www.amazon.co.uk/Disney-Frozen-Childrens-Multicoloured-FROZEN001018/dp/B00O2EO8XU) holds 9 liters. Climbing 10 stairs (http://journals.lww.com/acsm-msse/pages/articleviewer.aspx?year=2002&issue=04000&article=00021&type=abstract) burns about a calorie, which means climbing all the way up to space will burn about 72,000 calories. If you fill your backpack with butter, it would hold almost enough calories (http://www.wolframalpha.com/input/?i=9+liters+of+butter) to get you to the top. However, since it would take you weeks to climb all those stairs, you'd also need your normal dietary allowance of 2,000 calories (three sticks of butter) per day. Combining that with the 72,000 calories just from climbing the stairs, and you'd probably need to upgrade to a more serious 16-liter backpack (http://www.disneystore.com/anna-and-elsa-backpack-for-girls-personalizable/mp/1367267/1000290/). If you fill that backpack with butter, it will let you carry around 110,000 calories,[3]Coincidentally, about the amount you get (http://www.topatoco.com/merchant.mvc?Screen=PROD&Product_Code=QW-PERSON) from eating a human body. which should be enough to get you to the top if you're really dedicated. If you didn't want to eat 35 pounds of butter,[4]For whatever weird reason. you could try getting to the top by motorcycle. Based on how quickly this rider (https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=k8CZiqEjQDk) ascends 45 stairs, a motorcycle could conceivably make it to the top in a day. [Image: image] Ok, so you got to the top. Now what? Getting up to space isn't that hard, after all—the hard part is getting into orbit (http://what-if.xkcd.com/58/), and the tower doesn't help you very much with that. So what else could you do? Michael Longuet-Higgins (http://noc.ac.uk/about-us/history/national-oceanography-centre-southampton/influential-scientists/professor-michael-s) was a research professor at the University of Cambridge and an expert in fluid dynamics, bubbles, and unusual types of waves.[5]Given his apparent research interests, this video (https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=p70s1BNvBXI) would blow his mind.​[6]Or this one (https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=711bZ_pLusQ), or this gadget (https://www.kickstarter.com/projects/creatableslabs/project-nesm-never-ending-slinky-machine), or this (https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=JwohMl9Toww). In 1953, Dr. Longuet-Higgins was shown, by a colleague, an "interesting toy" which had recently appeared on the market. This toy, "Slinky," had some unusual properties. The professor immediately set to work analyzing it, and wrote up his results in a paper (http://www2.eng.cam.ac.uk/~hemh/TV/On_Slinky_the_dynamics_of_a_loose_heavy_spring.pdf). Dr. Longuet-Higgins first determined through mathematical modeling that the rate at which the Slinky descends steps should depend only on the properties of the spring itself, and not the size or shape of the stairs. He and his colleague conducted a series of experiments "on five different flights of stairs, of various dimensions, in Trinity College, Cambridge." Their conclusion: The Slinky descended a constant rate of about 0.8 seconds per step.[7]Except on some wide, flat stairs, where the Slinky "came to rest after three or four steps at most," which gives me a wonderful mental image of two disappointed British professors at the bottom of a staircase.​[8]Sadly, this was before the invention of the StairMaster. Fun fact: After a surprise StairMaster management shakeup in 2011, for some reason not a single newspaper ran the headline "StairMaster CEO steps down". Dr. Longuet-Higgins determined that the Slinky quickly reached a constant descent rate after first few steps. This tells us that if you placed a Slinky (similar to his) at top of the stairway to space, and gave it just the right nudge ... [Image: image] ... it would make it back to the bottom in just over five days. Or, to put that in more appetizing units: [Image: image]
items.original_question: 如果你制造了一部可以进入太空的电梯（就像你提到的十亿层建筑中的电梯）并建造了一个向上的楼梯（假设气压受到调节），那么爬到顶部需要多长时间？
items.model_answer:
If both a space elevator and a stairway to space existed, they would offer two radically different—and in some ways complementary—pathways to orbit, each reshaping civilization’s relationship with the cosmos.

A space elevator is an orbital tether: a ribbon of carbon-nanotube-like material stretched from an anchor on the equator to a counterweight beyond geostationary orbit, kept taut by Earth’s rotation and gravity. Climbers ascend the ribbon electrically, carrying cargo and passengers to orbit in a matter of days. A stairway to space, by contrast, would be a compressive megastructure—a literal tower with steps—rising from the ground into the vacuum above. By its nature, it is far more architecturally audacious. Every stair must support all the weight above it, a problem that forces the lower portion to be unimaginably massive and wide, tapering as it rises. With known materials, such a tower cannot exceed a few tens of kilometres before crushing itself; to reach geostationary altitude (35,786 km) would require magic or physics-defying materials like perfect dynamic compression members or active support. But in this thought experiment, both structures exist.

The most immediate difference is how you travel on them. On the stairway, travel is self-powered and incremental. You could theoretically walk to space, one step at a time, breathing thinning air and eventually relying on built-in life‑support shelters. The journey would take months at an unhurried pace, but it would involve no launch g-forces, no rockets, no climber motors. It turns space access into a terrestrial hiking trail—slow, intensely human, and open to anyone with enough food and determination. The space elevator, while gentle compared to a rocket, still relies on mechanical climbers that lock onto the ribbon and crawl upward at hundreds of kilometres per hour; the trip takes days, within a controlled cabin, not a stroll.

With both, you get a dual‑track space transport system. The elevator excels at high‑volume, high‑mass cargo. It can lift entire habitats, bulk water, and raw materials for orbital industry at costs far below rockets. The stairway, despite being slower, offers unique advantages. It can be accessed continuously without scheduling; there is no need for a powered vehicle, so it never breaks down the way a climber might. In an emergency, people could evacuate en masse by simply walking down the stairs, whereas an elevator’s climbers are limited in number and speed. You might imagine the stairway serving as the ultimate emergency escape and a pilgrimage‑like ascent experience, while the elevator handles commerce and construction.

Energy economics also diverge. A space elevator’s climbers use electricity beamed or conducted up the ribbon, ideally drawing power from solar or beamed sources; the energy per kilogram lifted is predictable and relatively low. A stairway, if you walk up, harnesses human metabolism—extremely inefficient per joule but requiring no external infrastructure. In an advanced version, automated electric stairlifts or cable‑car‑like steps could move cargo more efficiently. Either way, the stairway’s simple, non‑synchronised motion removes complex control systems and failure modes. Conversely, the space elevator’s ribbon faces micrometeoroid and debris hazards, demanding constant monitoring and repair; a stairway might be even more vulnerable—a broken stair in the upper reaches could cascade into a catastrophic collapse if not designed with immense redundancy. The engineering resilience needed for a stairway that extends through the thermosphere and beyond is almost unfathomable: temperature swings, atomic oxygen corrosion, and the sheer weight would push it towards actively supported structures like the space fountain concept, where momentum of pellets or magnetic rings holds it up. But again, we are granting existence.

Socially, having both would democratise spaceflight in two distinct flavours. The elevator, once built, drops the price to GEO to roughly hundreds of dollars per kilogram, making space cities and solar power stations not just imaginable but economically inevitable. The stairway adds a layer of psychological accessibility: the knowledge that you could simply start climbing, in principle, changes the mental barrier. Even if few make the full ascent, the stairway becomes an icon of human ambition, a monument that belongs to everyone. Its lower reaches might be the greatest tourist attraction in history, with people ascending to ever‑thinner air, staying overnight at way‑station platforms with views of the curvature of Earth. The elevator, meanwhile, would be a more utilitarian bridge—though no less breathtaking.

From a safety and redundancy perspective, a space‑faring civilisation would treasure having two independent infrastructure methods. If a piece of space debris severs the elevator ribbon (a catastrophic but unlikely scenario), the stairway could still provide an escape route for orbital inhabitants, albeit a slow one, and vice versa. They could even intersect or connect at certain points—perhaps a transfer node at low‑Earth‑orbit altitude where stair‑based shelters and elevator climbers dock, creating a hub‑and‑spoke network. This turns a single‑point‑of‑failure system into a resilient web.

In the end, the coexistence of a space elevator and a stairway to space would change not just how we go to orbit, but why we go. The elevator makes space an industrial zone, a second home for humanity. The stairway makes the journey itself a frontier experience, a living metaphor for progress one step at a time. Together they would turn the sky into a landscape we walk into, not just a boundary we breach.

items.question: What If Tug-of-War Teams Pulled on an Iron Rod Instead of a Rope?
human_answers: A couple dozen people could pull a half-inch iron rod apart. Tug-of-war, a simple game in which two teams try to pull a rope in opposite directions, has a surprisingly bloody history. I don't mean that there's some kind of gruesome historical forerunner of modern tug-of-war.[1]Although it's definitely an ancient sport (http://www.usatowa.com/history.html), so I'm sure people have come up with all kinds of horrific variations over the centuries that I don't really want to spend hours reading about. Humans seem to be creative when it comes to that kind of thing. I mean that modern tug-of-war involves a lot more death and mutilation than you might expect—precisely because people underestimate how few people it takes to break "strong" things like heavy rope. As detailed in a riveting article (http://priceonomics.com/a-history-of-tug-of-war-fatalities/) in Priceonomics, recent games of tug-of-war have resulted in hundreds of serious injuries and numerous deaths—all caused, one way or another, by ropes snapping. In particular, this seems to happen when large groups of students try to set a world record for largest tug-of-war game. When a rope under many tons of tension suddenly snaps, the recoiling ends can—and do—cause a terrifying variety of injuries. [Image: image] Before we answer Markus's question, it's worth noting that the physics of tug-of-war can be a little tricky (https://www.lhup.edu/~dsimanek/scenario/insight.htm#mechanics). It seems like common sense that the "stronger" team has an advantage, but that's not quite right. To win, you need to resist sliding forward better than the other team. If you can't resist sliding, then increasing your arm strength means you'll just pull yourself forward. Since sliding friction is often proportional to weight, tug-of-war on many surfaces is simply a contest over who's heavier.[2]Champion tug-of-war teams focus on body angle, footwork, digging into the ground, and timing pulls to throw off the other team. The strongest team in the world would lose a tug-of-war with a six-year-old and a sack of bricks, as long as the sack had a firm grip. [Image: image] So, how much force can tug-of-war players exert? A 2011 paper (http://web.nchu.edu.tw/~biosimulation/journal/pdf/vol-3-no01/vol-3-no-1-b-0003.pdf) analyzing the immune systems of several "elite tug-of-war players"[3]The paper notes that "Few studies have been done to examine the effects of [the] tug-of-war sport on physiological responses," which seems likely enough to me. measured their average pull force (on a school gym floor) to be about 102.5 kilograms-force, or about 1.5x their body weight. The ultimate tensile strength (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ultimate_tensile_strength) of cast iron is about 200 megapascals (MPa), so we can use a simple formula to figure out how many players would be needed to break one. \[ \text{People required}=\frac{\pi\times\left(\tfrac{1}{4}\text{ inch} \right )^2\times200\text{ MPa}}{102.5\text{ kg}/\text{person}}\approx25\text{ people} \] Two teams of 25 people[4]I originally wrote 25 people total, forgetting that two people pulling with 100 units of force each will produce 100 units of tension on the rope, not 200! Thank you for Gordon McDonough for pointing this out. could probably pull a half-inch iron bar apart. An inch-thick iron bar could be torn in half by teams of 101 people,[5]People often play tug-of-war with their dogs. Going by weight alone, 30 humans would probably be about evenly matched against 101 dalmatians. and a 2-inch-diameter bar would need over 400. It's hard to have a tug-of-war with something thicker than about 2 inches. Since you're not allowed to install handles on the rope,[6]Or wrap it around your hand, for reasons which will become clear if you read some of the articles on tug-of-war injuries. it has to be narrow enough to grip easily. While "400 people" may be the limit for plain iron bars, there are much stronger substances out there. Common types of steel, for example, have a tensile strength about 10 times that of cast iron. Common half-inch rebar (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rebar), for example, would in theory take teams of over 200 people to pull apart, compared to 25 for cast iron. Other substances are even stronger; a half-inch shaft made from high-grade steel or a polymer like Kevlar (or, theoretically, a solid silicon crystal) could handle the pulling force from teams of anywhere between 500 and 800 competitive tug-of-war players. If we limit ourselves to a two-inch diameter rope, which seems to be about the maximum size for tug-of-wars,[7](William Safire (http://www.theonion.com/articles/william-safire-orders-two-whoppers-junior,3351/) returns from the grave to point out that it should really be tugs-of-war.) then the maximum number of tug-of-war players given a super-strong rope like Kevlar is in the neighborhood of 10,000.[8]Or several times that many, if they're not very athletic. If we figured out how to manufacture large ropes out of graphene ribbons, which have tensile strengths over 10 times higher (http://arxiv.org/pdf/0709.0992.pdf) than existing materials, we could theoretically support a tug-of-war between teams of up to 100,000 players each. Such a rope would be over 200 miles long, and could stretch from New York to Washington. [Image: image] If our experience with nylon ropes failing is any indication, when the graphene finally snapped, the death toll could be enormous among both players and bystanders. Lengths of graphene would crack across the landscape like bullwhips, slicing down forests and demolishing buildings. In the end, trying to develop stronger ropes leads only to greater danger to everyone, both participants and bystanders. In the ultimate game of tug-of-war ... [Image: image] ... the only winning move is not to pull.
items.original_question: 拔河比赛中的两队是否有可能克服铁棒的极限抗拉强度并将其拉开？团队必须有多大？
items.model_answer:
If tug-of-war teams pulled on an iron rod instead of a rope, the game would become radically different—and far more dangerous—because the rod’s rigidity and material properties fundamentally change how forces are transmitted and controlled.

The most immediate difference is that a rope only transmits tension and is flexible; it naturally curves under its own weight but straightens when pulled taut. An iron rod is rigid, so it resists any bending caused by its own weight or by uneven forces. If both teams pull straight out along the bar’s axis, the rod experiences pure tension, just like the rope. However, a long iron bar is heavy, and its own weight creates a bending moment that makes it sag in the middle unless the teams can hold it perfectly level. Even a small amount of sag introduces bending stress in addition to the tensile load, and the rod might permanently bend or snap if the combined stress exceeds its yield strength—especially if it’s brittle cast iron rather than ductile steel.

Gripping a smooth, rigid metal bar is vastly harder than gripping a textured rope. To prevent slipping, participants would need gloves with extreme friction or mechanical clamps. Without that, they’d quickly lose their hold, and the rod could slip out violently. The lack of stretch is another critical factor: a rope has some elasticity, so it absorbs sudden surges of force, making the pull feel more gradual. An iron rod transmits force almost instantaneously, so any jerk or shock from one side is felt immediately by the other. This would increase the risk of muscle strains, joint injuries, and even sheer bone fractures if teams apply rapid, high-magnitude pulls.

The most dangerous twist occurs if one team suddenly releases. With a rope, the slack simply falls to the ground. A rigid iron rod under tension stores negligible elastic energy in tension but may store significant bending energy if it’s already sagging. When one side lets go, the bar becomes a spear: it will accelerate toward the still-pulling team due to the unbalanced force, potentially causing impalement or severe impact injuries. Even if both sides release simultaneously, a bent rod could spring back violently.

In short, the physical mismatch between human hands and a rigid, heavy, unforgiving metal bar would turn the cooperative contest of tug-of-war into a hazardous exercise in grip strength and injury avoidance.

items.question: What If the Moon Were Replaced by a Black Hole of the Same Mass?
human_answers: "Not much" and "not much." [Image: image] A black hole the mass of the Moon would have an event horizon about the size of a sand grain. Specifically, according to one of my favorite charts (http://pubs.usgs.gov/of/2003/of03-001/htmldocs/images/chart.pdf), a black hole moon would be a grain of fine to medium-fine sand, and could pass through a sieve of size ASTM No. 70 or larger. I mean, I guess a black hole with the mass of the Moon would pass right through any sieve, destroying it in the process, but that's neither here nor there.[1]The expression "that's neither here nor there" can be kind of confusing and ambiguous, but I guess that's neither here nor there. Since the Moon's mass and position wouldn't change, the tides on Earth wouldn't change, either. When you're floating outside a spherical mass, its pull on you is the same regardless of whether the mass is concentrated at the center of the sphere or spread out throughout it. If the Sun were replaced by a black hole of the same mass, the Earth's orbit wouldn't change, although life on Earth might (http://what-if.xkcd.com/49/). With the Moon gathered into a point, there'd be no moonlight, which would affect the life cycles of all kinds of nocturnal animals. But compared to a lot of the other (http://xkcd.com/1338/) things we've done, that would be fairly minor. The Earth's orbit is stabilized by the Moon (http://www.nature.com/nature/journal/v361/n6413/abs/361615a0.html), but the lunar-mass black hole would probably serve the same role. This black hole Moon (https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=3mbBbFH9fAg) would be pretty low-profile. If it were much smaller, it would evaporate through Hawking radiation (http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hawking_radiation), but a black hole the size of the Moon actually absorbs more energy from the cosmic background radiation than it emits through the Hawking mechanism. Our black hole would really be black. [Image: image] At least, if it didn't eat anything. If the black hole devoured any objects, it would let off a tremendous blast of radiation. Black holes burn brightly as they devour things; the whirlpool of matter heats up as it falls inward (http://www.gothosenterprises.com/black_holes/outside_black_holes.html), causing it to glow brightly.[2]A black hole can't devour matter too fast, though, because at some point it would be producing so much radiation that it would blast its own "food" away. This is called the Eddington limit (http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eddington_luminosity). If our black hole were devouring matter at the Eddington limit, it would be hot enough to sterilize the Earth. Fortunately, there's not a lot out there for it to eat, so it wouldn't glow very brightly for now. It would spend most of its time drastically altering the orbits of nearby dust particles—one sand grain pushing other sand grains around.[3]Even if it sucked in matter at the rate the Earth—with its much larger "collecting area"—sucks in interplanetary dust, it wouldn't necessarily be a problem for us. But there would be one interesting effect: In addition to getting darker, Earth would get colder, because moonlight warms the Earth. It's a very tiny contributor to our global energy balance; the Moon is five or six orders of magnitude dimmer than the Sun. But it's there. Measurements show that global temperature varies with a 28-day cycle (http://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1029/2000GL011651/abstract); all else being equal, the Earth is hottest during the full moon. It's a tiny difference—small fractions of a degree—but it's there. But it turns out most of this effect is not due to moonlight. The largest contributor is the fact that the Earth is slightly closer to the Sun during a full Moon: [Image: image] Calculating the amount of energy radiated back to Earth by the Moon is deceptively tricky. The Moon reflects sunlight, but with some surprising twists. When the Moon is half-illuminated, you might think it would be half as bright as when full—but it's much less bright than that (http://home.earthlink.net/~kitathome/LunarLight/moonlight_gallery/technique/moonbright.htm). And once you account for that, there are even trickier effects to deal with, because science is the worst.[4]Like the fact that the waxing Moon is 20% brighter (http://www.jstor.org/discover/10.2307/2402251?sid=21105340972791&uid=2&uid=4&uid=3739808&uid=3739256) than the waning Moon, or that the Moon is a mild retroreflector (http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Opposition_surge). Then, on top of all the weird visible-light effects, the Moon also heats up under the Sun, then radiates that heat as infrared light. There's a great discussion of the Moon's effect on the Earth's energy budget in this article (http://scitation.aip.org/content/aapt/journal/ajp/67/12/10.1119/1.19109?ver=pdfcov) by Robert Knox. The upshot is that the Moon's infrared heat radiation turns out to affect Earth's temperature about 10 times more than the visible moonlight, but still about 10 times less than the effect from gravity moving Earth closer and farther from the Sun. Knox even quantifies the effect this has on Earth's radiation balance—the presence of infrared moonlight warms the planet by 1.2 milli-degrees Fahrenheit (m°F). [Image: image] Without moonlight, the planet would cool down slightly. But given the accelerating rate at which we're adding (http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Keeling_Curve) CO2 to the atmosphere—which changes the Earth's energy balance—we'd make up the difference in a couple of weeks. So all in all, the conversion of the Moon to a black hole might not even be that big of a deal. Unless, of course, it happened on certain days between 1969 and 1972, in which case Nixon (http://www.archives.gov/presidential-libraries/events/centennials/nixon/images/exhibit/rn100-6-1-2.pdf) would've needed yet another one of those speeches (http://xkcd.com/1484/). [Image: image]
items.original_question: 如果月球被同等质量的黑洞取代会发生什么？如果可能的话，月食会是什么样子？
items.model_answer: If the Moon were instantly replaced by a black hole of exactly the same mass, the Earth and everything on it would notice almost no gravitational difference. The black hole’s mass and position would be unchanged, so the Earth–Moon system’s orbit, tides, and the barycenter shift would remain identical. The black hole itself would be utterly dark and incredibly tiny—a Schwarzschild radius of about 0.1 millimeters—so it would emit no visible light (Hawking radiation is completely negligible for an object of lunar mass, corresponding to a temperature far colder than the cosmic microwave background). The most immediate and dramatic change would be the permanent loss of moonlight, plunging nights into much deeper darkness and likely disrupting the biological rhythms of many nocturnal species. Over astronomical timescales, there would be no danger of the black hole “sucking in” the Earth; its gravitational influence at our distance is exactly the same as the Moon’s was.

items.question: What If You Mounted a High-Power Microwave on a Car to Melt Ice?
human_answers: Believe it or not, your flamethrower idea is actually the more practical of the two. The flamethrower also has the advantage that, unlike the microwave, it won't interfere with wifi (unless you aim it directly at the router). [Image: image] I'm writing this article from Boston, which is currently buried under a truly ridiculous amount of snow (http://www.buzzfeed.com/mjs538/please-stop-snowing). We've had more snow in the past 30 days (http://weather.ou.edu/~splillo/misc.html) than Anchorage, Alaska usually gets in an entire winter.[1]Meanwhile, Anchorage is on Twitter wondering (https://twitter.com/NWSBoston/status/567172928593485824) where their snow went and threatening revenge (https://twitter.com/NWSAnchorage/status/567566488517619712). Here's (https://twitter.com/EricHolthaus/status/567350490912931840) a neat visualization of the atmospheric pattern during these polar vortexes. Vortices. Whatever. Our transit system has broken down (http://www.bostonglobe.com/metro/2015/02/14/transportation/U7vNqP861gKQFRly2jmjdL/story.html) and our roofs[2]Tolkien prefers rooves. are collapsing (http://www.whdh.com/story/28133433/dozens-of-roof-collapses-reported-across-new-england). The mayor gave a press conference (http://www.boston.com/news/local/massachusetts/2015/02/15/boston-mayor-seems-pretty-tired-all-this-dang-snow/OYtAnLLNQ2iMBMRaxTJYzJ/story.html?s_campaign=bcom%3Asocialflow%3Atwitter) in which he announced, "I don't know what to say to anybody anymore. Hopefully it will stop eventually." So snow removal is on all our minds. But snow is hard to melt. (And we've been trying (https://twitter.com/NotifyBoston/status/564524089017401347)[3]I love that tweet because it sort of sounds like it comes from an alternate fairy-tale universe where cities farm snow and snow-melters form the base of the economy.) Your microwave idea certainly sounds like it should be more practical than a flamethrower. Microwaves seem clean and efficient; after all, we don't use flamethrowers in our kitchens. [Image: image] But there's a big problem: Microwaves heat water very well, but they don't really work on ice (http://www.thenakedscientists.com/HTML/content/kitchenscience/exp/-324719c1f8/). Fortunately, there are other ways to get energy into the ice. In addition to your flamethrower suggestion, you could, for example, use infrared heat lamps or lasers.[4]Pick a frequency where snow has a low albedo; otherwise, the FBI may hunt you down for lasering aircraft (http://www.nbcnews.com/tech/tech-news/why-its-terrible-idea-point-lasers-airplanes-n28841). But whatever you use, you'll run into another problem: It takes an awful lot of energy to melt snow. Melting a gram of snow takes about 335 joules of energy. To put that another way, a 60-watt lightbulb is capable of melting about a pound of snow an hour. A foot of snow contains roughly the same amount of water as an inch of rain, give or take (http://www.theweatherprediction.com/habyhints/346/). Let's assume you've had a decent snowstorm of about a foot[5]For the record, by this standard, Boston has had a "decent snowstorm" every few days for the past month.—meaning an inch worth of water—and that you want to melt a 9-foot-wide swath while driving along at 55 mph. Luckily, this happens to be one of those happy physics situations where we can just multiply together every number we're looking at, and the answer (http://www.wolframalpha.com/input/?i=55+mph+*+water+density+*+1+inch+*+9+feet+*+335+J%2Fgram) turns out to be the measurement we want: \[55\text{ mph}\times1\text{ inch}\times9\text{ feet}\times\text{water density}\times335\tfrac{\text{J}}{\text{gram}}=574\text{ megawatts}\] Unfortunately, it's not the answer we'd like. The nuclear reactor on an aircraft carrier, for example, produces less than 200 megawatts. To melt snow in front of your car, you'd need three of those. [Image: image] What about your your original flamethrower idea? Gasoline may have a phenomenally high energy density (http://what-if.xkcd.com/128/), but it's not high enough. No matter how big the tank on your flamethrower was, you'd run out of fuel constantly. Gas mileage in the US is often measured in "miles per gallon" of gasoline. With your flamethrower guzzling fuel, your mileage would be about 17 feet per gallon. You might be better off dropping the flamethrower entirely. Instead, take a cue from the rail agencies, who use jet-engine-powered snowblowers (http://www.boston.com/news/local/massachusetts/articles/2011/01/23/mbtas_mattapan_line_relies_on_snowzilla_in_worst_weather/) to clear train tracks. In the end, it's easier to just move the snow out of your way. [Image: image]
items.original_question: 我长期以来一直在考虑在汽车前部安装一个火焰喷射器，以便在开车穿过汽车之前融化冰雪。现在我意识到火焰喷射器不切实际，但是高功率微波发射器呢？
items.model_answer:
Mounting a high‑power microwave (HPM) source on a car to melt ice sounds like a futuristic de‑icing solution, but the physics and engineering hurdles make it highly impractical—and dangerous—for real‑world use.

Microwaves heat ice (and water) by causing polar molecules to rotate rapidly, generating thermal energy. In theory, a sufficiently intense beam aimed at an icy road or windshield could melt the ice directly, especially if it penetrates the ice and heats the underlying surface as well. However, the power levels needed are enormous. A typical home microwave oven uses about 1 kW to heat a small enclosed volume. To melt ice on an open road while the car is moving, you would need to deliver tens to hundreds of kilowatts of microwave energy per square meter over a broad area, accounting for heat loss to the cold ground and air. A car’s electrical system supplies only a few kilowatts, not the megawatts an HPM would require, so you’d need a dedicated generator or massive battery bank, which is prohibitive.

Beyond power, there are severe safety and regulatory issues. Unconfined high‑intensity microwaves would expose passengers, bystanders, and electronics to dangerous non‑ionizing radiation, risking burns, eye damage, and interference with vehicle control systems. Microwave leakage is strictly regulated (e.g., by the FDA and FCC), and a car‑mounted HPM would easily exceed safe limits. Additionally, the beam would reflect off metal surfaces (cars, signs) and could superheat water pockets in ice, causing violent steam explosions that scatter ice and hot water unpredictably.

Even if you solved the power and safety problems, the physics isn’t favorable. Ice absorbs microwaves much less efficiently than liquid water, so much of the energy might reflect away or pass through without melting. To be effective, you would need a precise frequency and beam shape, and the moving car would complicate aiming. Alternative de‑icing methods—like resistive heating elements, infrared lamps, or chemical sprays—are far simpler, safer, and more energy‑efficient. So while a microwave ice‑melter is a thought‑provoking concept, it’s not a viable technology for everyday driving.

items.question: What If a Falling Person Grabbed a Flagpole and Swung Back to the Roof?
human_answers: If you're like me, your first thought on hearing this question was, "That's ridiculous; there's no way that could work." Your first thought is right. But just to be sure, let's take a closer look. Grip strength depends on a lot of factors, like hand slickness and surface material. But for the moment, let's assume Rex's hands are able to grab the pole tightly. What happens to the rest of his body? [Image: image] It's hard to find good numbers on how much force it takes to tear off a person's arm.[1]Which is probably a good thing, to be honest. There are threads on the question on MetaFilter (http://ask.metafilter.com/133821/How-much-force-to-tear-off-a-limb) and the Straight Dope message boards (http://boards.straightdope.com/sdmb/showthread.php?t=515612), and frequent discussion of the death of Robert-François Damiens (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert-Fran%C3%A7ois_Damiens),[2]Damiens was tortured to death for attempting to assassinate Louis XV, but a team of horses had trouble tearing him limb from limb. but not too much hard data. For the record, there are lots (https://journals.biologists.com/jeb/article/215/20/3552/11014/Tendon-material-properties-vary-and-are) of studies (http://www.udel.edu/PT/PT%20Clinical%20Services/journalclub/sojc/95_96/apr96/itoi.pdf) and lectures (http://wings.buffalo.edu/eng/mae/courses/417-517/Orthopaedic%20Biomechanics/Lecture%203u.pdf) on the breaking strength of tendons, which tend to give values of around 50-150 MPa. That's stronger than skin (27 MPa (http://www.ircobi.org/downloads/irc12/pdf_files/59.pdf)) but weaker than bone (120 MPa (http://www.robmech.co.za/proceed/ROBMECH2011_Unene%20N.%20MAnganyi_Biological%20considerations%20in%20the%20structural%20design%20of%20smart%20prosthetics.pdf)). However, to figure out the overall strength of the arm, we need to tally up all the tendons, muscles, and tissues in the wrist, arm, and shoulder, their cross-sectional area, and figure out which parts would be put under strain in what order. Instead, it might be easier to consider people who try to pull off this maneuver in real life: Gymnasts. A gymnast on the uneven parallel bars pushes the human body to its limits while performing maneuvers very similar to Rex's flagpole stunt.[3]In some ways, at least. A 2009 study (http://www.jbiomech.com/article/S0021-9290(09)00609-5/fulltext) used 3D motion capture to measure the forces involved in an elite gymnast's routine. They found that the athlete's hands exerted a force of over 3 kN on the bar at the bottom of a swing. In other words, the gymnast was briefly supporting almost 700 lbs of weight. Let's be generous and assume that Rex is even better than the elite gymnast in the study. (After all, the gymnast has to worry about long-term injury, while Rex's concerns are a lot more short-term). Suppose Rex's arms can handle a swing force of over 10 kN, three times more than the gymnast (and twice as much as these (https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=V1JBx2Mm9e8) guys (https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=iJYOs5VFjwk)!). How will he do? Let's see how much force Rex needs to withstand. The "tallest building in town" here in Boston is the 240-meter-tall Hancock Tower (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Hancock_Tower); if he jumped off the top, he'd be going nearly 100 mph by the time he was halfway down. At that speed, the force on his arms (speed squared over the radius of his turn[4]Which is effectively somewhere between 1 and 2 meters here.) would be around ... 100 kN (http://www.wolframalpha.com/input/?i=100+lbs+*+(100+mph)%5E2+%2F+(1.5+meters)). [Image: image] Really, the numbers are just telling us what common sense told us from the start: You can't grab hold of something while going 100 mph, much less swing around it. If you want get a more vivid intuitive sense of the forces involved, consider this: In 2006, GQ put baseball star Albert Pujols in a lab and measured his swing. They clocked the speed of his bat at 87 mph, similar to the speed of the flagpole relative to our falling person. So if you want to pull off Rex's stunt, first go find Albert Pujols, have him swing his bat as hard as you can ... and try to grab it. [Image: image] And remember: You're just trying to stop the momentum of a 31-ounce piece of wood. When you're falling past the flagpole, you're going to be catching your whole body, so it's going to be up to 100 times worse. Good luck! [Image: image]
items.original_question: 因此，您从镇上最高的建筑物上方的高处坠落，并且您没有降落伞。但是等等！在那座摩天大楼一侧的中间有一根旗杆伸出来，没有旗帜！你倾斜下降角度并抓住杆子足够长的时间来旋转，这样当你松开杆子时，你现在就会回到天空。当重力减慢你的速度并使你停下来时，你到达摩天大楼的顶部，在那里你伸出手将自己拉到安全的地方。这种情况发生的可能性有多大？
items.model_answer:
If a falling person grabbed a flagpole in an attempt to swing back onto the roof, they would almost certainly fail—and the outcome would be disastrous. The physics of the situation makes it essentially impossible for a human to execute successfully outside of a choreographed movie stunt.

First, consider the forces involved. A typical flagpole projecting horizontally from a building wall is designed to hold a static weight—usually a flag and perhaps some wind load—not the dynamic load of a 70 kg (150 lb) person suddenly grabbing it at speed. The person would have already fallen some distance, gaining kinetic energy. When they catch the pole, their downward momentum must be redirected into a circular arc. The required centripetal force would cause a tension in the pole and a grip force on the hands far exceeding body weight. For a fall of just 1 meter before grabbing, the instantaneous force on the hands could be several hundred pounds. Human grip strength, even in an adrenaline-fueled scenario, cannot reliably sustain such a load on a smooth metal cylinder. The hands would simply tear off.

Even if by some miracle the grip held, the flagpole itself would likely fail. Most flagpoles are thin-walled aluminum or steel tubes anchored to the wall with relatively small brackets. The bending stress from a person swinging at the end would exceed the material’s yield strength, causing the pole to bend, snap, or pull out of its mounts. The attachment points are not engineered for a sudden lateral load of that magnitude.

Then there is the geometry of the swing. To “swing back to the roof,” the person would need to convert their downward motion into an upward arc that deposits them on the same roof edge. This requires the pole to be positioned exactly so that the swing’s apex coincides with the roof’s edge—a condition practically impossible to meet by chance. If the pole is too short, the person hits the wall below the roof; too long, they crash into the wall or swing past but without the necessary upward trajectory. Moreover, because the pivot is at the wall, the natural path of a pendulum swing takes the person away from the wall at the bottom and then back toward the wall as they rise—meaning they would likely smash into the building rather than land cleanly on the roof. The only way to land on top of the roof would be if the pole itself were angled outward or if the person released at precisely the right instant, which requires extraordinary timing and control that no untrained person would possess under stress.

In short, the combination of insufficient grip, structural failure, and unfavorable swing geometry makes this a physical impossibility. It’s a compelling visual for fiction, but in reality, the falling person would simply continue downward, possibly with a dislodged flagpole in their hands.

items.question: What Would Happen to a Human Body Left in Orbit?
human_answers: This isn't really relevant, but I have to ask: Is there a reason you specifically wanted your corpse to be naked? Just making things extra weird for the technicians loading up the capsule and/or throwing you out of the airlock? [Image: image] If you tried this, the first thing that would happen to your corpse would be that it would dry out. This would probably start before you made it to space; the dry, climate-controlled air in the pre-launch waiting area would help draw moisture from your body. In the Manual of Forensic Taphonomy, Franklin Damann and David Carter outline the process of human decomposition. According to them, it takes a lot of effort to keep corpses from drying out during the embalming process.[1]The citation they give for that fact is "(C. A. Wacker, pers. comm.)," which I like to think means it was shared in a conversation that totally broke up the dinner party they were both at. In extremely dry environments like the Atacama Desert in Chile, "spontaneous mummification" can occur—and space is even drier than Chile.[2]The space tourism industry has not adopted this as a slogan. Also, "Chile: Not as Dry as Space!" was probably nixed by the Chilean tourism board. Once your body made it to space, this process would ramp up quickly. Most of the "ecology" responsible for decomposing your corpse would be killed off quickly by the drying process (along with the lack of oxygen, temperature swings, and solar radiation levels), so your body wouldn't decay very much. Instead, you'd become a freeze-dried mummy, after losing about 80% of your body weight in water.[3]This is how much liquid you can remove from fresh animal tissue, according to lab experiments reported in Arthur C. Aufderheide's book The Scientific Study of Mummies. That makes sense; after all, according to that commonly-repeated piece of trivia, human bodies are around 70% water. Or is it 65%? Or 80%? The exact number is a little vague, and seems to depend on who you ask. In a footnote in her wonderful book, Stiff: The Curious Lives of Human Cadavers, writer Mary Roach mentioned that she had methodically Googled the phrase "human body is <X> percent water", for X from 0 to 100. She reported a wide range of claims, including several pages asserting that we're 98% water. It's really gratifying to know I'm not the only person who spends a lot of time carefully cataloging weird stuff like that. What happens next depends on exactly where in space you are. If you're in an orbit that passes near the Earth, your orbit will quickly decay, and before long you'll re-enter the atmosphere and burn up. If you're in a slightly higher orbit, you'll last longer, but you'd also be in the zone where space debris (http://commons.erau.edu/cgi/viewcontent.cgi?article=1000&context=stm) was thickest. Impacts with small bits of debris would start to leave pits and scars on your surface; they would often find these on Space Shuttle windows after a flight. Eventually, probably after a few decades, you'd probably have a violent collision with something. Higher orbits are safer. If you were some distance away from the Earth, near where geosynchronous satellites orbit, there would be less debris to run into. Furthermore, for large, dense objects, orbits out there are stable (http://www.readcube.com/articles/10.1029%2F92JE00032?show_checkout=1) for a very long time. You could spend centuries drifting among TV broadcast satellites. [Image: image] If you wanted to last even longer, you could launch yourself away from Earth completely, finding a quiet and stable orbit somewhere in interplanetary space. There, over the course of millennia, you'd be slowly baked by the Sun's radiation and pitted and powdered by micrometeorites. But if your goal is to weird out future space travelers, that might not be the best plan. Space is big; if someone randomly stumbles on your corpse, it suggests that there must be a lot of people zipping around the solar system. And if space travel has become that common, there will be lots of corpses floating around;[4]Weird that "lots of corpses floating around" is somehow an optimistic prediction about the future of space travel. discovering yours will be more archaeologically exciting than anything. You'll be stuck in a lab or museum somewhere and contribute to someone's research paper—a bland end to your exciting prank. Unless, of course, you happen to be found by the only people in space even weirder than you. [Image: image]
items.original_question: 我经常开玩笑说我希望将我的遗体送入轨道。不是“撒我的骨灰”的意思，而是“把我赤裸的尸体扔出气闸”的意思。老实说，我的主要动机是让遥远的未来的某人感到困惑，但这是一个有趣的科学问题：在几年、几十年或几个世纪的过程中，我在轨道上的身体会发生什么？
items.model_answer:
If a human body were left in orbit without a spacesuit, the individual would lose consciousness within about 10–15 seconds due to oxygen deprivation and would die within a minute or two. The immediate hazards are the vacuum and lack of breathable atmosphere, not explosive decompression as often depicted. Gases trapped in the lungs would expand rapidly, so holding one’s breath would cause fatal lung rupture; any air remaining in the digestive tract would force its way out. Bodily fluids exposed to vacuum—saliva, tears, moisture on the skin—would boil off in a process called ebullism, causing localized swelling and evaporative cooling, but the skin and circulatory system would largely contain internal pressure, preventing the body from bursting.

After death, the body would undergo a complex, long-term transformation driven by the extreme thermal, radiative, and vacuum environment. In direct sunlight, the side facing the Sun would heat to over 120°C (250°F), while the shaded side would plunge to around -150°C (-238°F). This temperature gradient would freeze-dry the body: water would sublimate from tissues, gradually desiccating and mummifying the remains. Ultraviolet and ionizing radiation would break down skin and soft tissues, darkening and eroding them over months to years. Micrometeoroids and orbital debris would pummel the body, causing pitting and fragmentation. Unless actively preserved, the body would not decompose microbially in the normal sense, as most internal bacteria would be killed by radiation and extreme conditions, though some spores might survive.

Orbital decay determines the ultimate fate. In low Earth orbit (e.g., ISS altitude ~400 km), the tenuous atmosphere would gradually slow the body down. Over months to a few years, drag would lower its orbit until it entered the denser atmosphere, where frictional heating would incinerate it, leaving only charred fragments if any reached the surface. In a higher, more stable orbit, the desiccated, radiation-blasted corpse could remain circling Earth for centuries or millennia, becoming a slowly eroding piece of human-made space debris.

items.question: What If You Dug Straight Down at One Foot per Second?
human_answers: This question is the reverse of question #64 (http://what-if.xkcd.com/64/), which asked how you'd die if you rose steadily at a foot per second. Digging at the same rate would kill you more quickly. [Image: image] After you get through the surface layers,[1]See question #132 (http://what-if.xkcd.com/132/) for more on that. temperatures rise pretty steadily as you go deeper, a trend that continues all the way to the core. In some areas, where the hot magma[2](Lava (http://xkcd.com/1405/).) is closer to the surface, the ground gets hotter more quickly. The Southern Methodist University Geothermal Lab has produced some superb maps (http://www.smu.edu/Dedman/Academics/Programs/GeothermalLab/DataMaps/TemperatureMaps) showing the temperature of deep rocks in different parts of the United States. If you look at the map of the 3.5 km layer (http://www.smu.edu/~/media/Site/Dedman/Academics/Programs/Geothermal%20Lab/Graphics/TemperatureMaps/SMU_2011_35kmTemperature.ashx?la=en), you see that at that depth, most of the US is colored greenish-yellow, representing temperatures somewhere around 100°C—with one glaring exception. In northwest Wyoming, there's a circle of ground colored bright red, where the rock is much hotter than normal. That circle is the Yellowstone supervolcano (http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yellowstone_Caldera). [Image: image] The SMU maps show that even if you avoided digging in Yellowstone, you'd quickly encounter temperatures too hot for an unprotected human. The ground typically gets hotter at an average of about 35°C per kilometer, so at a rate of a foot per second, you'd encounter lethal heat within an hour or two. But wait a moment. Let's say your hole is about a meter wide. At the rate you're digging, you have to remove roughly half a ton of material every second. No human would be capable of lifting that first foot of material out of the hole so quickly, and it only gets worse after that. After a minute of digging, you'd be 60 feet down, and would have to lift all that rock and dirt a huge distance vertically to get it out of the hole. The power required to do that lifting—just after the first minute—would be roughly 150 horsepower. [Image: image] Even if you're not doing the lifting yourself, the way your question is worded makes it pretty clear that you are in this hole. Whatever process you're using is going to require huge amounts of energy to lift all that rock, and that energy is inevitably going to result in the hole being heated somehow. Even if the layer you're digging through wasn't hot when you started, it will be. What if we assume you're protected against the heat from the ground (and the digging mechanism)? Well, in that case, the pressure would become a problem. As you go deeper, air pressure increases. Below about 5 km, the pressure is high enough that oxygen (http://www.scuba-doc.com/oxygentox.html) becomes toxic (https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=LOZuxwVk7TU). So what if you're protected against the heat, pressure, and the digging process? Well, at that point, we've redefined the rules so much that I'm not sure it makes sense to try to calculate an answer. The question—"what would kill you if you kept digging downward"—has left the realm of physics and become fantasy. Which, come to think of it, makes the answer perfectly clear. [Image: image]
items.original_question: 如果我以每秒 1 英尺的速度直接向下挖掘会发生什么？什么会先杀死我？
items.model_answer:
If you could somehow dig straight down through the entire Earth at a constant speed of one foot per second, the journey from one side of the planet to the other would take about **1.33 years** (roughly 485 days). In reality, you’d be dead from unimaginable heat and pressure long before you got more than a few miles deep — but let’s explore the hypothetical physics.

**Time and distance**  
Earth’s diameter is about 7,918 miles, or 41.8 million feet. Moving at 1 ft/s, you cover 86,400 feet per day, so:  
41,800,000 feet ÷ 1 ft/s = 41,800,000 seconds ≈ 484 days (1.33 years).  
If you started on the surface, passed through the center, and stopped when you reached the antipodal point, you’d need a little over a year and four months, assuming you never pause.

**What you’d feel: gravity**  
At 1 ft/s, gravity doesn’t act like the famous “free-fall through the Earth” scenario. You’re not in free fall; you’re boring your way down, so your weight changes gradually.

- At shallow depths, gravitational pull is almost unchanged. In the real Earth, gravity actually increases slightly in the upper mantle (due to the dense core) before it begins to drop.
- Once inside the mantle, gravity roughly declines linearly toward zero at the center, if we imagine uniform density. The real profile is more complex, but you would feel lighter and lighter, reaching weightlessness at the very center.
- As you ascend the other side, gravity builds back up, pulling you downward toward the center (which now feels like “up” relative to your direction of motion). You’d need to actively pull yourself along or dig against that growing force to maintain 1 ft/s.

**Rotation and the Coriolis effect**  
Earth rotates. If the shaft were truly straight (along a diameter), the Coriolis force would push you into the side of the hole because your angular velocity must increase to match the rotation of the material around you as you go deeper. At constant speed, you’d be scraped against the wall unless you continuously steered or braced. In a free-fall gravity train, you’d build up huge sideways speed; here, your slow pace would make the effect mild but persistent, causing a constant sideways drift you’d have to fight.

**The fatal environment**  
Long before the weird gravity, you’d be killed by the Earth’s interior:

- **Temperature**: Just 10 miles down, the ambient rock is well over boiling point. The geothermal gradient (~25°C per km) means that at 100 km depth, temperatures exceed 2,500°C. You’d be incinerated within hours of digging, even if your suit could withstand the pressure.
- **Pressure**: At the center, pressure is roughly 360 gigapascals (3.6 million atmospheres). At 1 ft/s, you’re crawling through solid rock, then liquid outer core (you’d be swimming/molten), then solid inner core. The hole would collapse instantly behind and ahead of you, and your body would be crushed to a smear long before you left the lithosphere.

**Why it’s impossible even hypothetically**  
No material can remain open against the immense lithostatic pressure at mantle depths. The tunnel would self-seal in an instant, and the heat would melt any drilling apparatus. The constant 1 ft/s isn’t a physical limit — it’s just a narrative rate that highlights how enormous Earth is. At walking speed, it would take you well over a year of nonstop digging to reach the other side, but you’d never survive the first few dozen miles.

So, the short answer: it would take 1.33 years to travel through the Earth at 1 ft/s, but the planet’s internal heat and pressure make any such journey instantly lethal and the shaft physically unsustainable.

items.question: What If You Dropped a Submarine into Jupiter?
human_answers: Nope! Jupiter's pressure, density, and temperature curves are different from ours. At the point in Jupiter's atmosphere where the density is high enough for a submarine to float, the pressure is high enough to crush the submarine,[1]Which makes it more dense. and the temperature is high enough to melt it.[2]Which makes it harder to drive. [Image: image] But there's another problem: Jupiter is a gas giant, but submarines—as you can figure out from etymology—go under water. [Image: image] Air and water are different. This seems straightforward enough, but they're also the same in a lot of ways. They're both "fluids," and some of the same rules apply to each. In some sense, when you look up at the sky (http://xkcd.com/1556/), you're looking up from the bottom of a deep sea of air. Things float when they're less dense than the fluid around them. This works the same for balloons in air and boats in water. The late Terry Pratchett wrote a truly beautiful passage about this, in the prologue to his book Going Postal. He says that since water is in many respects a wetter form of air,[3]Sounds reasonable enough to me. as ships sink, eventually they reach a point where the water was too dense to sink any further. This layer forms an underwater surface on which shipwrecks collect, drifting around beneath the waves but far above the sea floor:It’s calm there. Dead calm.Some stricken ships have rigging; some even have sails. Many still have crew, tangled in the rigging or lashed to the wheel.But the voyages still continue, aimlessly, with no harbour in sight, because there are currents under the ocean and so the dead ships with their skeleton crews sail on around the world, over sunken cities and between drowned mountains, until rot and shipworms eat them away and they disintegrate.Sometimes an anchor drops, all the way to the dark, cold calmness of the abyssal plain, and disturbs the stillness of centuries by throwing up a cloud of silt. I love that passage. It's also completely wrong. Ships sink all the way to the bottom. (Sir Terry knew this, as the rest of the passage makes clear, but he's describing how ships work on Discworld, not Earth.) Air follows the ideal gas law (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ideal_gas_law). The more pressure you put on it, the smaller (and denser) it gets. Water, on the other hand, is pretty much incompressible. When you dive into the ocean, the pressure increases as you go deeper (rising by one atmosphere every 10 meters or so) but the water's density barely changes all the way down to the sea floor. Buoyancy depends on density, not pressure. There's a point in Jupiter's atmosphere where the pressure is equal to a little more than an Earth atmosphere—which is the pressure a submarine is used to—but the air there is barely a tenth as dense as ours. A submarine in that layer would fall even faster than it would in the air on Earth. [Image: image] To reach a depth where it could "float" in Jupiter, the submarine would have to go halfway to the center of the planet, where the intense pressure turns the air into a metallic soup (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Metallic_hydrogen) that's hotter than the surface of the Sun. The pressure there would be so high that not only would the submarine be crushed, the substances that make it up would probably be converted into new and exciting forms. It's hard to create those kinds of conditions in a lab, so we don't know a lot about how materials behave with that much pressure pushing down on them.
